items.title: Operating Room Air Filtration-Sterilization and Surgical Infections: The ORACLE Randomized Trial in 110,538 Surgeries
items.abstract: Background: Surgical infections are the most common nosocomial infections and cause substantial morbidity and mortality. Operating rooms are relatively clean, but far from sterile. An unknown fraction of infections result from wound contamination by air-borne bacteria. We therefore tested the hypothesis that supplemental air purification reduces wound infections and related complications. Methods: Operating rooms, our clusters, were each randomized in each 4-week blocks to either active or identical-looking sham supplemental air sterilization. All investigators, clinicians, and patients were fully blinded to treatment. No other aspect of anesthetic or surgical management was proscribed. Intent-to-treat analysis was restricted to adults who had surgery lasting at least an hour without evidence of pre-existing wound infections. We tested the primary hypothesis that supplemental active purification reduces a collapsed (one or more) composite of surgical wound infections, infection-related complications, or death within 30 days after inpatient surgery. Secondarily, we tested the hypothesis that supplemental air purification reduces the same composite after combined inpatient and outpatient surgeries. Results: A total of 110,538 combined inpatients and outpatients were enrolled across 68 operating rooms, with 107,334 qualifying for analysis. At the third interim analysis, the futility boundary on the composite outcome was crossed for inpatients and for all patients. Enrollment thus stopped with 58,938 randomized inpatients. The primary composite outcome occurred in 8.1% (n=2,389) of inpatients randomized to active purification versus 8.2% (n=2,405) with sham purification: odds ratio 0.98 (95%CI: 0.92 to 1.05), P=0.609. Across all patients, the secondary composite outcome occurred in 5.5% (n=2,959 / 53,730) of active purification cases versus 5.6% (n=2,981 / 53,604) sham cases: odds ratio 0.98 (95% CI: 0.93 to 1.05), P=0.669). Treatment effect did not vary over the weeks in the randomized periods. Conclusion: Supplemental active purification did not reduce surgical wound infections or mortality in surgical patients. Infection-control efforts might better focus on limiting direct wound contamination. Trial registration: A priori registration at ClinicTrials.gov: NCT04610294. Funding: Supported by a grant from ActivePure (Bristol, VA) to the Cleveland Clinic. The funder approved the original protocol which was written by the lead author. The funder was not involved in data acquisition, analysis, or manuscript preparation. A draft of the manuscript was provided to the funder as a courtesy.

items.title: Childhood Exposure to General Anesthesia For Surgery: Identification of a Subtle Post-Operative Cognitive Phenotype.
items.abstract: Background: Early-life exposure to general anesthesia has not been consistently associated with overall cognitive deficits, yet its impact on executive functions and visuo-spatial processing remains unclear. The primary objective was to assess executive function performance, according to general anesthesia exposure for surgery. The secondary objectives were to explore distinct cognitive profiles and their associated factors, as well as to examine visuo-spatial attention as a complementary domain. Methods: In this ambidirectional cohort study, 77 children aged 9-11 years, with or without prior general anesthesia exposure for surgery, completed a cognitive battery yielding eight cognitive measures assessing inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, working memory, and visuo-spatial attention. Measures were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model. Exploratory latent profile analysis was used to identify cognitive performance profiles. Results: No significant main effect of general anesthesia exposure for surgery was observed (χ²(1) =.01, p =.92), indicating comparable overall executive function performance between exposed (mean age at exposure: 4.47 ± 3.00 years) and non-exposed. Latent profile analysis identified two executive function profiles: Efficient and Vulnerable Executive Control. General anesthesia exposure was associated with lower odds of belonging to the Efficient profile group (OR = 0.71, 95% CI [0.705, 0.710], p <.001). Regarding visuo-spatial attention, GA-exposed participants showed higher Global-Local precedence measures (estimate = 0.53, 95% CI [0.04, 1.01], p =.036). Conclusions: Early childhood exposure to general anesthesia was not associated with reduced overall executive function. However, a potential post-operative cognitive phenotype is suggested by a reduced likelihood to belong to an efficient executive control profile with greater visuo-spatial global-local precedence.

Project SPRUCE: Formation of an International Consortium of Pediatric Anesthesia Groups to Reduce Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Inhaled Anesthetics
items.abstract: Background: Inhaled anesthetic use contributes to environmental harm through release of potent greenhouse gases (GHG). Emissions can be reduced with the use of safe practice changes, including avoidance of high impact agents like desflurane and nitrous oxide, use of low fresh gas flows, and adoption of total intravenous and regional anesthesia when clinically appropriate. These evidence-based practices have been recommended for years, but actual practice changes have not been widely adopted. Methods: The Project SPRUCE (Saving our Planet by Reducing Carbon Emissions) consortium brought together twelve pediatric anesthesia groups into a partnership working to reduce GHG emissions from pediatric anesthesia care. The consortium implemented quality improvement strategies, including change management methods, to reduce GHG emissions from inhaled anesthetics by at least 50%. Change management and quality improvement strategies were utilized to disseminate strategies, implement emissions reduction techniques, and track emissions in pediatric anesthesia care. Specific interventions included education and socialization, practice constraints, and direct data feedback to clinical teams. Results: The consortium facilitated adoption of practice changes among anesthesia groups, and sustained emissions reductions though shifts in culture. Greenhouse gas emissions from inhaled anesthesia decreased by 63% (range 43-91%) During the study period, the incidence of nitrous oxide use was reduced by 62.4%, and the average volume of nitrous oxide used per case decreased by 83.5%. Project SPRUCE prevented a total of 14,381 metric tons of excess carbon dioxide equivalent (CO 2 e) emissions from inhaled anesthetics. Conclusions: Collaborative action within our consortium supported widespread and significant reductions in harmful greenhouse gas emissions from pediatric anesthesia care through education and socialization, practice constraints, and direct data feedback to clinical teams.

items.title: Intraoperative Noise Isolation and Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting after Gynecological Laparoscopic Surgery: A Randomized Controlled Trial
items.abstract: Background: Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) remain common after gynecological laparoscopic surgery despite guideline-based prophylaxis. Auditory information is still processed during clinically adequate general anesthesia, and operating rooms are persistently noisy, but whether attenuating intraoperative sound exposure alters PONV is unknown. Methods: In this single-center, patient- and assessor-blinded randomized trial, women aged 18 to 65 yr undergoing elective gynecological laparoscopic surgery were randomized 1:1 to wear passive noise-attenuating earmuffs from induction until the end of surgery or to usual care. All patients received dexamethasone and palonosetron. The primary outcome was PONV incidence within 48 h, defined as any episode of nausea, retching, or vomiting, assessed across three prespecified windows (post-anesthesia care unit, to 24 h, and 24 to 48 h). Secondary outcomes included PONV severity, its components, rescue antiemetic use, pain, and quality of recovery. Results: Of 364 patients assessed, 192 were randomized. PONV within 48 h occurred in 34 of 96 patients (35.4%) with noise isolation and 50 of 96 (52.1%) with control (adjusted risk difference, −0.179 [95% CI, −0.318 to −0.040]; P = 0.012). Across the three windows the overall adjusted risk difference was −0.134 (95% CI, −0.215 to −0.053; P = 0.001), with no treatment-by-window interaction ( P = 0.332); window-specific values were −0.162, −0.172, and −0.068. PONV severity, retching, and three post hoc endpoints (the vomiting-or-retching composite, complete response 72.9% versus 56.2%, and total response 64.6% versus 47.9%) favored noise isolation after false discovery rate correction. Adverse events, quality of recovery, and opioid exposure (post hoc) showed no evidence of a difference. Conclusions: Among women receiving dual antiemetic prophylaxis for gynecological laparoscopic surgery, intraoperative noise isolation was associated with a lower incidence and severity of PONV.

items.title: Intravenous Lidocaine in Liver Surgery ‒ A Randomized Double-Blind Trial
items.abstract: Background: Managing postoperative pain is a complex challenge in liver surgery. Perioperative intravenous (IV) lidocaine can reduce postoperative pain, opioid use, bowel recovery time and the length of stay, in various types of surgery. Lidocaine is eliminated via hepatic metabolism, and IV lidocaine is rarely evaluated in liver surgery. This study aimed to evaluate the postoperative analgesic efficacy and safety of IV lidocaine administration in patients undergoing minor liver surgery. Methods: Patients planned for minor liver surgery were randomized 1:1 to receive either perioperative IV lidocaine, administered as a 1.5 mg/kg bolus followed by a continuous infusion of 1.5 mg/kg/h until 1 hour after surgery, or placebo. All patients received postoperative opioid analgesia via a patient-controlled analgesia device. The primary outcome was postoperative opioid consumption during the first 24 hours after surgery. Secondary outcomes included postoperative pain scores, quality of recovery, adverse events, length of stay, and plasma lidocaine concentrations. Results: In total, 124 subjects were included. Postoperative opioid consumption during the first 24 hours after surgery was 83 (50 – 129) mg oral morphine equivalents (OME) in the lidocaine group, and 97 (60 – 135) mg OME in the placebo group, p=0.429. Patients in the lidocaine group experienced lower pain scores at early postoperative time points, but not from postoperative day 1 onward. The Quality of recovery-40 score did not differ, and adverse events were similar between groups. In two cases, plasma concentrations of lidocaine were transiently above 5 µg/ml after bolus administration, without clinical signs of toxicity. All plasma concentrations after resection and at end of infusion were safely below toxic levels. Conclusions: Perioperative intravenous lidocaine did not reduce postoperative opioid consumption after minor liver surgery but conferred transient early analgesic benefits and was found to be safe.

items.title: Individualized mean arterial pressure during cardiac surgery The OPTIPAM Randomized Clinical Trial
items.abstract: Background: Whether targeting an individualized mean arterial pressure (MAP) during cardiac surgery improves outcomes remains uncertain. The balance between improved perfusion and vasopressor-driven blood pressure augmentation is unclear. Methods: In this single-blind, multicenter randomized clinical trial conducted in 10 tertiary centers in France, adult patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass were assigned to either individualized MAP management (target within ±10% of preoperative baseline during surgery and for 24 h postoperatively) or standard management (target MAP ≥65 mm Hg). The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause death, acute kidney injury, or prespecified neurologic complications within 7 days. Safety outcomes included hemorrhagic complications and transfusion requirements. Results: A total of 172 patients were enrolled before the trial was stopped early by the data and safety monitoring board because of increased bleeding in the individualized group. Mean intraoperative MAP was higher with individualized management (80.6 vs 75.6 mm Hg; P<0.001), despite limited target adherence (33% of intraoperative time) and greater vasopressor use. The primary outcome occurred in 27 of 85 patients (32%) in the individualized group and 25 of 87 (29%) in the standard group (relative risk, 1.1; 95% CI, 0.7 to 1.8; P=0.76). Hemorrhagic complications occurred more frequently in the individualized group (18% vs 3%; P=0.003). Conclusions: In patients undergoing cardiac surgery, it was not possible to determine whether an individualized MAP strategy reduced major postoperative complications. More bleeding complications were observed in the individualized group. Future studies should further investigate this safety signal when evaluating individualized blood pressure targets.

Association of Altered Anteriorization of Electroencephalographic Alpha Oscillation During Transition to Unconsciousness With Postoperative Delirium: A Prospective Observational Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: During sevoflurane-induced anesthesia, electroencephalography analysis demonstrates alpha oscillations shifting from the occipital to the frontal regions, with further characteristic changes during maintenance and emergence. We aimed to exploratorily investigate whether alterations in alpha anteriorization and functional network efficiency are associated with postoperative delirium. METHODS: This prospective, exploratory observational study enrolled 100 patients from a single tertiary university hospital. Patients were classified into nondelirium (n = 81) and delirium (n = 19) groups based on delirium assessments. After excluding 17 patients due to artifacts on electroencephalography, 19-channel electroencephalography data were collected from 83 elderly patients under sevoflurane-induced anesthesia. Artifact-free epochs were extracted during the induction, maintenance, emergence, and postanesthesia care unit phases. Spectral, topographical, and network analyses were conducted. Postoperative delirium was assessed using confusion assessment method for intensive care unit and a chart review. RESULTS: Significant group differences emerged just before the loss of responsiveness, with the nondelirium group exhibiting robust alpha power amplification across all brain regions (median [interquartile range {IQR}] in dB; frontal: 4.24 [1.86–6.57] vs −0.88 [−1.59–3.38], P = .007; parietal: 3.71 [0.51–5.55] vs −0.95 [−2.33–1.11], P = .046; occipital: 2.81 [0.49–5.71] vs −0.04 [−2.06–1.27], P = .048), whereas the delirium group showed minimal changes. During the maintenance phase, spectral analysis revealed higher alpha power in the nondelirium group across all 19 channels (frontal: 5.42 [2.90–8.16] vs 2.89 [−0.03–5.09], P = .007; 18 of 19 channels significant by false-discovery-rate (FDR)-corrected permutation test). Network analysis demonstrated longer averaged characteristic path lengths in the delirium group (mean ± standard deviation [SD], 4.49 ± 0.62 vs 3.57 ± 0.16, P = .026, FDR-corrected), consistently in the frontal, parietal, and occipital regions, suggesting reduced network efficiency. CONCLUSIONS: Delirium was associated with early disruption of alpha anteriorization during induction and globally reduced functional network efficiency during maintenance. Perioperative electroencephalogram (EEG) transition features may serve as early markers of delirium susceptibility.

items.title: Influence of Preoperative Virtual Reality on Preoperative State Anxiety in the Ambulatory Setting: The AMBLUMEEN Randomized Controlled Trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Preoperative anxiety affects 30% to 80 % of ambulatory surgery patients and is associated with increased anesthetic requirements, postoperative pain, and delayed recovery. Virtual reality (VR) is a promising nonpharmacological anxiolytic, but evidence remains limited in the ambulatory setting. METHODS: The AMBLUMEEN (AMBulatory LUMEEN) trial is a single-center, randomized, open-label, superiority trial conducted in an adult ambulatory surgery unit. Patients with moderate-to-severe preoperative anxiety (State-Trait Anxiety Inventory Form Y-A [STAI-YA] > 45) were randomized 1:1 to standard care alone (control) or standard care and a single 20-minute preoperative VR session (immersive 360° natural contemplative scenes). The primary end point was the change in STAI-YA score from arrival in the ambulatory unit (baseline) to immediately before operating room transfer (presurgery), analyzed under the intention-to-treat principle with a linear mixed model. Secondary end points included preoperative benzodiazepine use, postoperative morphine requirement, unplanned overnight admission, patient satisfaction, and device acceptability. RESULTS: Of 106 randomized patients (53 per group) with a median [interquartile range] baseline STAI-YA of 49 [46–55] and 49 [46–58] respectively in the control and VR group, the VR group experienced a markedly greater reduction in state anxiety than controls. Adjusted mean between-group difference in STAI-YA change from baseline to presurgery was −18.7 95% confidence interval (CI) [−21.4 to −16.1] points in favor of VR. Although benzodiazepine requirement, postoperative pain, and unplanned overnight admission were comparable between groups, the morphine requirement in postanesthesia care unit was lower in the VR group (6/53 [11.3% 95% CI, 11.3 {4.3–23.0}] vs 0/53 [0.0%, 95% CI, {0.0–6.7}]; P = .027). Global perioperative satisfaction was high in both groups (median 8 [8–9] on 10). CONCLUSIONS: A single 20-minute session of medical-grade VR significantly reduced preoperative anxiety in ambulatory surgery patients, with high acceptability and an excellent safety profile.

items.title: The Association Between Perioperative Enhanced Care Unit Characteristics and Surgical Cancelation: A Nationwide Observational Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Patients referred for postoperative care within enhanced care units in the United Kingdom are less likely to have their surgery canceled than those referred to critical care. Presently, it is unclear whether this association remains when examined at an individual hospital level, and whether specific structure and process features of enhanced care services influence cancelation rates within a facility. METHODS: We conducted a nationwide, retrospective, observational study documenting clinical and organizational features of enhanced and critical care facilities in the United Kingdom. Features of interest included resource protections, staffing, and clinical scope. Sites with availability of both enhanced and critical care facilities, with >10 referrals to enhanced care during the study period, were selected for analysis. Cancelation rates of elective surgery within these facilities were quantified over a 3-month period between September 1, 2023, and November 30, 2023. Rates were defined as the number of elective cases canceled divided by the number of elective referrals to each facility. Multilevel regression was used to explore relationships between structure and process features of enhanced care units and surgical cancelation, using a two-level model with cases nested within hospitals to account for institutional confounding. RESULTS: Complete data were available for 65 sites, of which 28 had an enhanced care facility with sufficient activity for analysis, representing 4112 patients referred to enhanced or critical care. In most institutions, surgical cancelation rates were lower within their enhanced care facility than in critical care. Enhanced care units with beds reserved exclusively for elective cases (odds ratio [OR], 0.54 [0.39–0.76]; P < .001) and clinical care involving multiple specialities (OR, 0.48 [0.33–0.69]; P < .001) were associated with reduced odds of cancelation. On the other hand, enhanced care units that permitted admission of emergency cases (OR, 1.61 [1.06–2.43]; P = .024) were associated with a greater odds of cancelation. CONCLUSIONS: Structure and process features of enhanced care pathways are associated with cancelation rates among high-risk surgical patients in the United Kingdom. These findings may explain why cancelation rates in enhanced care are typically lower than within critical care and may have important policy implications.

The Influence of Anesthetic and Surgical Factors on Spinal Late Motor Responses: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Late motor responses, including F-waves and H-reflexes, are commonly recorded during electrophysiological diagnostic evaluation in awake patients. Although these responses could offer added value during intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring, their use has not yet been widely adopted. This systematic review aims to assess current knowledge on how anesthetic and surgical factors influence the recording and monitoring of spinal late responses during surgery. The authors searched PubMed and EMBASE for relevant articles on studies of late response recording. Studies were considered eligible if the influence of one or more of the following parameters on late responses were assessed: (1) ventilation and metabolic parameters, (2) volatile agents, (3) intravenous agents, (4) neuromuscular blocking agents, (5) epidural or intrathecal agents, or (6) surgical factors. The QUADAS-2 tool was used to assess the risk of bias and concerns regarding applicability. Sixty-two studies were included. Respiratory conditions like hypercapnia reduced H-reflex amplitude, whereas hyperoxia and intermittent hypoxia had limited impact. Volatile agents, including isoflurane, sevoflurane, and nitrous oxide decreased late response amplitudes, with dose-dependent effects. Most intravenous anesthetics, particularly propofol, reduced H-reflex amplitude and F-wave persistence in a dose-dependent manner. Conversely, ketamine was found to increase H-reflex amplitude. During spinal and vascular surgeries, H-reflex monitoring proved feasible and provided valuable supplementary data to the conventional motor evoked potential (MEP) and somatosensory evoked potential (SSEP) modalities. This systematic review demonstrates that H-reflexes and F-waves are significantly influenced by anesthetic factors. The reviewed studies indicate that intravenous and volatile anesthetics significantly affect late responses, by reducing H-reflex and F-wave amplitudes, whereas latencies appear unaffected. The methodological quality varied significantly across the included studies and affects the interpretation of their conclusions. These findings support the potential integration of late response monitoring into intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring (IONM) protocols, provided that anesthetic management and surgical context are carefully considered.

Socioeconomic position and preoperative characteristics in Perioperative Quality Improvement Programme participants: a UK national observational study
items.abstract: Background Patients from more deprived backgrounds experience poorer postoperative outcomes. We analysed preoperative characteristics in UK Perioperative Quality Improvement Programme participants according to socioeconomic position to explore opportunities for targeted interventions. Methods Participants were adults aged ≥18 yr undergoing major elective surgery at UK Perioperative Quality Improvement Programme sites. Socioeconomic position was determined using postcode data and the Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) standardised aggregate scale of area-level deprivation. Associations between IMD position and patient characteristics, health behaviours, and comorbidities were analysed using descriptive statistics with appropriate parametric and nonparametric testing. Results Of 55 938 participants included, quintile 1 (most deprived) represented the smallest subgroup (14.2%), with recruitment varying by region and site. Median age was 66 yr with IMD 1 participants 5 yr younger (62 yr) than IMD 5 (67 yr). Deprivation gradients (IMD 5 to 1) were seen for home ownership, occupation, and educational attainment. Prevalences of smoking, inactivity, and obesity increased from IMD 5 to 1. Higher prevalences of major long-term conditions including diabetes mellitus, heart failure, stroke, and ASA physical status 3-4 were observed in more deprived quintiles. Prevalence rates of dementia and renal impairment were similar across quintiles despite the age gradient. Notably, the proportions of patients living with frailty and disability increased with deprivation. Conclusions Patients presenting for major surgery from more deprived backgrounds do so in poorer overall health. They can encounter barriers to both research participation and available preoperative support. Addressing this unmet need to prevent widening perioperative health inequalities requires interventions tailored to the patient's socioeconomic context.

items.title: The association between pain intensity during epidural labour analgesia and intrapartum hyperthermia: a multicentre prospective observational study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Some women receiving epidural labour analgesia become hyperthermic. Assuming a causal mechanism, denser and more extensive sympathetic blocks might promote hyperthermia by inhibiting sweating. We therefore tested the hypothesis that hyperthermia is most common when epidural blocks are particularly effective, as indicated by excellent analgesia. METHODS: In this multicentre prospective observational study, we enrolled nulliparous women with term cephalic singleton pregnancies who planned vaginal delivery with epidural analgesia. Pain intensity was assessed using an 11-point numerical rating scale (0-10) during uterine contractions before analgesia, at 10, 30, and 60 min after initiating analgesia, and then hourly until the end of the third stage, and calculated as time-weighted average, average, area under the curve, and peak scores. Our primary endpoint was intrapartum hyperthermia (≥38°C). RESULTS: Intrapartum hyperthermia occurred in 13% (124/952) of participants (median age 29 yr). After adjustment for confounding factors, lower pain intensity was associated with higher odds of intrapartum hyperthermia across all four measures: time-weighted average (odds ratio 1.64; 95% CI 1.40-1.91; P<0.001), average (1.56; 1.35-1.81; P<0.001), area under the curve (1.05; 1.03-1.07; P<0.001), and peak scores (1.19; 1.09-1.30; P<0.001). The identified inflection points were a time-weighted average score ≤3 points (odds ratio 8.67; 95% CI 4.19-17.9; P<0.001), average score ≤3 points (6.63; 3.56-12.3; P<0.001), area under the curve ≤30 point⋅h (13.0; 3.75-45.0; P<0.001), and peak score ≤4 points (2.53; 1.65-3.89; P<0.001), all of which were associated with increased intrapartum hyperthermia. CONCLUSIONS: Among nulliparous women receiving epidural analgesia for labour, lower pain scores were associated with higher odds of hyperthermia. Extensive sympathetic blockade may promote maternal hyperthermia. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT04940091.

Electrolyte redistribution during acute respiratory acid–base changes: an in vivo study using apnoea testing
items.abstract: Background: Acute respiratory acid–base changes induce pH-dependent electrolyte redistribution. Although this response has been characterised in vitro , the in vivo changes depend on multicompartment buffering and remain poorly defined. Methods: We conducted a multicentre retrospective study of patients undergoing apnoea testing for organ donation after determination of brain death, a clinical model allowing in vivo study of acute ventilatory changes. The primary outcome was the pH-dependent change in strong ion difference (SID). Secondary analyses examined individual electrolytes, pH–SID effect modification by physiological variables, and how well the derived model agreed with observed SID changes compared with a simple bedside pH-correction method (ΔSID=−15×ΔpH). Results: In 263 participants, pH decreased from 7.40 (0.07) to 7.23 (0.07) and returned to 7.40 (0.08). Per pH unit increase, SID changed by −11.7 meq L −1 (95% CI −13.1 to −10.3; P <0.001), driven primarily by sodium ion (Na) (52% of change −7.2 mM; P <0.001) and chloride ion (Cl) (36% of change +3.7 mM; P <0.001). Higher haemoglobin concentration was associated with a higher pH-dependent SID change, together explaining 53% of within-patient variability. Agreement between predicted and observed SID changes was only modestly improved by using the derived model vs a simplified pH-correction model (sd of differences 1.74 vs 1.92 meq L −1 ). Conclusions: Acute respiratory acid–base disturbances produce in vivo Na and Cl redistribution associated with pH change that are modulated by haemoglobin concentration. The observed pH-dependent electrolyte redistribution is consistent with physiological buffering and can be reasonably approximated using a simple bedside pH-correction model.

Brain-derived tau in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid after surgery: a prospective cohort substudy
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Postoperative increases in plasma total tau (t-tau) protein have raised concerns that surgery can cause CNS injury. Brain-derived tau (BD-tau) is a novel biomarker that quantifies CNS-derived tau. We assessed BD-tau concentrations in plasma and CSF after surgery to investigate neuronal injury and mechanisms driving increases in plasma t-tau. METHODS: This was a substudy of a previous prospective cohort study enrolling adult patients undergoing hip and knee arthroplasty. We measured plasma and CSF BD-tau and t-tau before neuraxial anaesthesia (baseline) and at 4, 8, 24, 32, and 48 h after surgery and assessed cognitive performance at baseline and 3 months. Biomarker concentrations are reported as median (IQR) percentage change from baseline. RESULTS: Plasma BD-tau peaked at 4 h with a 254% increase (137-382%, P<0.001) and remained elevated by 31% (6-75%, P<0.001) at 48 h. CSF BD-tau was unchanged at 4 h but increased by 51% (21-82%, P=0.004) at 48 h. Plasma BD-tau was associated with plasma t-tau (β=1.09, 95% CI 0.95-1.23, P<0.001), whereas plasma BD-tau and CSF BD-tau were inversely associated (β=-0.71, -0.97 to -0.45, P<0.001). Higher postoperative plasma BD-tau was associated with both higher CSF albumin and worse cognitive performance at 3 months. CONCLUSIONS: Early postoperative increases in plasma t-tau are consistent with a CNS origin but not concomitant neuronal injury. Instead, the early plasma BD-tau increase and the inverse association between CSF and plasma BD-tau could indicate a redistribution of tau from the CNS to plasma.

Effect of electrical impedance tomography-guided positive end-expiratory pressure optimisation on postoperative pulmonary complications in laparoscopic colorectal surgery: a randomised controlled trial
items.abstract: Background Pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg positioning during laparoscopic colorectal surgery promote atelectasis and increase the risk of postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs). Electrical impedance tomography (EIT) enables individualised PEEP titration by visualising regional lung collapse, facilitating lung-protective ventilation. However, evidence of its effect on clinical PPCs remains limited. Methods In this single-centre, parallel-group RCT, adults with intermediate to high risk for PPCs (ARISCAT score ≥26) who underwent laparoscopic colorectal surgery were randomly assigned to receive intraoperative PEEP titration guided by EIT or a conventional fixed PEEP of 5 cm H 2 O. The primary outcome was PPCs incidence within 30 days, as determined by a multidisciplinary adjudication team using standardised criteria. Results Among the 117 randomised participants (mean [range] age: 62 [37-80] yr; 37% female), EIT-guided PEEP (n=59) resulted in lower driving pressure (16 [15-18] cm H 2 O) compared with fixed PEEP (n=58; 19 [17-22] cm H 2 O; P Conclusions Compared with conventional fixed PEEP of 5 cm H 2 O, EIT-guided PEEP was associated with a lower incidence of PPCs among patients at intermediate to high PPCs risk undergoing laparoscopic colorectal surgery, suggesting a role for EIT in intraoperative lung protection. Clinical trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2300076677.

State-dependent roles of inflammation across pain conditions: insights from human transcriptomics
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Inflammation is widely viewed as a driver of pain, yet clinical and transcriptomic studies report conflicting associations. A clearer understanding of how inflammatory processes relate to pain across clinical contexts is essential for improving diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of chronic pain. METHODS: We analysed whole-blood RNA sequencing from seven human cohorts spanning four pain conditions, including acute, postoperative, chronic localised, and chronic widespread pain in almost 500 blood samples with corresponding pain intensity scores. Using gene-level meta-analyses, pathway enrichment, and immune cell-specific gene ontologies, we tested how inflammatory responses relate to current pain, future pain trajectories, and within-person changes over time. RESULTS: Inflammation emerged as one of the strongest biological correlates of pain across all cohorts, yet its association direction depended on the pain state. In acute musculoskeletal and postoperative pain, higher inflammatory activation, which correlated with enhanced neutrophil and macrophage function, was associated with greater pain intensity but also correlated with better subsequent recovery, consistent with an adaptive inflammatory response. In chronic localised pain, this relationship was disrupted and inverted: higher inflammatory activity was linked to lower pain intensity and associated with worse long-term outcomes. In chronic widespread pain, macrophage-related inflammatory activity remained positively associated with both pain severity and persistence, suggesting progression toward a maladaptive immune state. CONCLUSIONS: These findings indicate that inflammation is not uniformly detrimental in pain but plays distinct roles depending on disease stage and context. Inflammation might support resolution during acute injury yet become dysregulated in chronic and nociplastic pain. Recognising these context-dependent roles could help explain conflicting findings in the literature and guide more precise use of anti-inflammatory therapies.

items.title: Regional analgesic techniques for postoperative pain after kidney transplantation: a systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis
items.abstract: Background Pain after kidney transplantation is often severe, and graft function constrains the use of systemic analgesia. Previous syntheses of regional techniques pooled them as a class, combined donors with recipients, and did not use a minimal clinically important difference (MCID). Methods We searched PubMed, Embase, and CENTRAL through 5 September 2026 for randomised trials of regional analgesia in adult kidney transplant recipients (PROSPERO CRD420261478933); a trial-registry search and network meta-analysis were added post hoc. Bayesian random-effects models with MCID-scaled priors yielded posterior probabilities of benefit and of exceeding the MCID, and certainty of evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework. Results Fourteen trials (903 participants) were included. Only quadratus lumborum (QL) and transversus abdominis plane (TAP) blocks could be pooled against control. Both yielded lower pain at every pooled time point, but no pairwise pain comparison reached 80% probability of exceeding the 1.0 point MCID. Opioid consumption at 24 h was lower with the QL block (-15.5 morphine milligram equivalents; 95% credible interval -23.6 to -6.7) and the TAP block (-10.5; -14.4 to -5.5), with each reduction exceeding the 5 mg MCID with a probability >97%. In the network meta-analysis, no difference between QL and TAP blocks in pain or opioid consumption reached 80% probability of exceeding the MCID. Graft function and safety data were too sparse to pool. Twelve eligible registered trials were unpublished; certainty of evidence was very low. Conclusions Quadrtus lumborum and transversus abdominus plane blocks reduce pain and opioid consumption at 24 h, but only the reduction in opioid consumption has a high probability of being clinically important. Certainty of evidence is very low; no technique is preferred, and effects on graft function are unknown.

Effects of perioperative esketamine infusion on chronic pain after video-assisted thoracoscopic lung resection: a multicentre, randomised, double-blind clinical trial
items.abstract: Background Chronic postsurgical pain after thoracoscopic surgery remains common. We investigated whether perioperative low-dose esketamine infusion would reduce chronic pain after video-assisted thoracoscopic lung resection. Methods In this multicentre, randomised controlled trial, 914 adults were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either esketamine or normal saline. Esketamine was administered as a 0.1 mg kg -1 bolus at induction, followed by continuous intraoperative infusion (0.1 mg kg -1 h -1 ) and postoperative infusion (0.015 mg kg -1 h -1 ) for 48 h. The primary outcome was chronic pain at 3 months, defined as persistent pain with a numeric rating scale score ≥1 during coughing in the surgical region. Secondary outcomes included postoperative pain, supplemental analgesics use, recovery of bowel function, in-hospital adverse events, and esketamine-related side-effects. Results We analysed 873 patients (median age, 55 yr; 63% female). The incidence of 3 month chronic pain was lower in the esketamine group than in the control group (14.7% vs 21.2%; adjusted odds ratio, 0.62; 95% confidence interval, 0.43-0.90; P=0.013). A reduction was also observed when using a post hoc outcome definition of a numeric rating scale pain score ≥3 during coughing at 3 months (adjusted odds ratio, 0.39; 95% confidence interval, 0.19-0.84; P=0.015). Esketamine also reduced overall pain scores at rest and during coughing within the first 48 h, and decreased supplemental analgesic requirements within 48 h and 3 months. Conclusions Perioperative low-dose esketamine infusion significantly reduced 3 month chronic pain after thoracoscopic lung resection without increasing adverse effects. Clinical trial registration ChiCTR2000040012. Trial registration This trial was registered on the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (Identifier: ChiCTR2000040012; principal investigator: Fu-hai Ji; dated November 18, 2020; https://www.chictr.org.cn/showprojEN.html?proj=62319).

Effect of remimazolam versus propofol anaesthesia on postoperative delirium in neurovascular surgery: a randomised noninferiority trial
items.abstract: Background Propofol-based total intravenous anaesthesia (TIVA) is commonly used in neurovascular surgery, in which intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring limits inhalation anaesthetic use. However, propofol causes hypotension, and prolonged infusions can delay emergence. Remimazolam, a benzodiazepine whose effects are reversible with flumazenil, has been associated with less intraoperative hypotension than propofol, but its use raises concerns about postoperative delirium (POD). We tested whether remimazolam-based TIVA is noninferior to propofol-based TIVA for POD. Methods In this single-centre, double-blind, randomised noninferiority trial, adults undergoing elective intracranial aneurysm clipping, arteriovenous malformation resection, microvascular decompression, or superficial temporal artery-middle cerebral artery bypass received remimazolam-based TIVA with flumazenil reversal at emergence, or propofol-based TIVA, both with remifentanil. The primary outcome was the cumulative incidence of POD within 5 days, assessed twice daily with the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) or the 3-Minute Diagnostic Interview for CAM-defined delirium (3D-CAM). The prespecified noninferiority margin was 10 percentage points. Results Among 686 patients in the modified intention-to-treat analysis, POD occurred in 44 of 344 (12.8%) with remimazolam and 37 of 342 (10.8%) with propofol (risk difference, 1.97 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.85 to 6.80; one-sided P Conclusions Remimazolam-based TIVA met the prespecified criterion for noninferiority to propofol-based TIVA with respect to postoperative delirium after elective neurovascular surgery. Interpretation should take into account that the observed incidence of postoperative delirium was lower than anticipated when the noninferiority margin was defined. Clinical trial registration NCT06115031 (ClinicalTrials.gov).

items.title: Ultrasound assessment of fluid tolerance in patients undergoing major gastrointestinal surgery: epidemiology of pulmonary and systemic congestion
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Fluid accumulation in surgical patients is associated with worse outcomes. Lung ultrasound (LUS) and venous excess ultrasound (VExUS) grading can assess congestion and thereby fluid tolerance. However, evidence regarding epidemiology, feasibility, and associations of reduced fluid tolerance with outcomes in surgical patients is lacking. METHODS: This was a prospective single-centre observational cohort study in patients undergoing major gastrointestinal surgery. LUS and VExUS were performed before surgery and daily for up to 5 days after surgery. Reduced fluid tolerance was defined as pulmonary congestion (B profile on LUS), systemic congestion (VExUS ≥2), or both. The primary outcome was the prevalence of reduced fluid tolerance. Secondary outcomes were feasibility of ultrasound assessments, Clavien-Dindo grade ≥3 complications, and length of stay (LOS). RESULTS: Of the 200 participants included, 73 (37%) exhibited signs of reduced fluid tolerance, most commonly on postoperative day 4 (n=28; 14%). Reduced fluid tolerance was primarily driven by pulmonary congestion (n=69; 95%), whereas systemic congestion was rare. In most affected patients (47 of 73; 64%), reduced fluid tolerance was limited to 1 day. Of 1200 planned assessments, 146 (12%) were missing: 123 because participants declined, mostly owing to the burden of repeated assessments, and 23 (2%) because of incomplete views. Reduced fluid tolerance was associated with LOS of >7 days (odds ratio 3.29; 95% CI 1.03-10.70), but not with major postoperative complications (hazard ratio 1.18; 95% CI 0.49-2.86). CONCLUSIONS: Reduced fluid tolerance detected by ultrasound is common after major gastrointestinal surgery and associated with increased LOS. Ultrasound assessments were technically feasible, but repeated assessments were perceived as a burden by a substantial proportion of patients. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT06166719 (principal investigator: A.P.J. Vlaar; first registered: 04-12-2023).

Conceptual model of multidisciplinary shared decision-making for high-risk surgical patients: a Delphi study
items.abstract: High-risk patients need to carefully consider the risks and benefits of surgery. Shared decision-making is a collaborative process that enables patients and clinicians to share information and weigh up options and preferences. There is limited evidence about how best to organise the participation of the full range of healthcare professionals who can contribute to such decision-making processes. We conducted a Delphi study with a panel of experts to clarify how, and for what purposes, different healthcare professionals can contribute to shared decision-making with high-risk surgical patients. Consensus was reached on a conceptual model of multidisciplinary shared decision-making. The model recommends that interactions between patients, supported by family members and informal carers, and healthcare professionals are organised around five areas: options for management and treatment; patient values, goals, and preferences; comprehensive needs assessment; social context and home environment; and perioperative preparations. Experts agreed that achieving multidisciplinary shared decision-making in practice requires four key facilitators: early identification of patients with complex decision-making needs, availability of specialist expertise and support, sufficient time for discussion and decision-making, and coordination and information sharing between interactions. This model organises multidisciplinary involvement in high-risk surgical shared decision-making into five conceptually distinct and operationally interdependent areas. The model has the potential to inform practice and enhance opportunities for shared decision-making for high-risk surgical patients and their multidisciplinary teams.

Counting reactions, not just variants: what malignant hyperthermia can teach precision medicine
items.abstract: Susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia is generally considered to follow an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with incomplete penetrance. In a recent study in the British Journal of Anaesthesia, Aboelsaod and colleagues integrate national epidemiological data, anaesthetic exposure histories, population genomics, contracture test phenotyping, and Bayesian modelling to estimate the prevalence of individuals capable of developing clinical malignant hyperthermia. Their findings support a threshold model in which variants contribute different degrees of biological liability, potentially modified by other genetic and environmental factors, whereas the probability of reacting during a triggering exposure seems relatively similar once an individual has crossed this threshold. The study also illustrates how combining complementary sources of imperfect evidence can improve risk estimation for rare, exposure-dependent disorders. Ultimately, malignant hyperthermia genetics needs to move beyond categorical variant classification towards variant-specific penetrance estimates that incorporate genetic background, ancestry, exposure history, and other determinants of clinical expression.

Cardiac output monitoring using an automatic arm cuff device in surgical patients
items.abstract: Abstract Pulse contour devices estimate cardiac output (CO) by analysis of an invasive blood pressure (BP) waveform. However, arterial catheters are only employed in the highest risk patients. By contrast, automatic arm cuff devices are used for non-invasive BP monitoring in numerous hospital patients. Furthermore, these devices directly measure cuff pressure oscillations, which are directly related to pulsatile blood volume rather than BP. The hypothesis of this study was that automatic arm cuff devices can offer an effective means to monitor CO. A custom-built cuff device was employed to measure cuff pressure and make a unique measurement of the volume of air pumped into and out of the cuff during linear deflation. Cuff device measurements, an invasive BP waveform via a radial artery catheter, and reference CO via pulmonary artery catheter-bolus thermodilution were obtained during major interventions from 24 liver transplant and 10 cardiac surgery patients. A basic analysis was applied to estimate CO in L/min as the product of heart rate, the maximum cuff pressure oscillation amplitude, the compliance of the cuff-arm system derived from the measured cuff volume-pressure relationship, and the body to arm surface area ratio derived using anthropometric information. This arm cuff-based method yielded a correlation of 0.60 and concordance rate of 83% against the reference CO. For comparison, classic pulse contour analysis of the invasive BP waveform produced a correlation of 0.62 and concordance rate of 81%. These initial findings indicate the potential for CO monitoring via a non-invasive automatic arm cuff device in surgical patients.

Infiltration between the popliteal artery and the capsule of the knee ( IPACK ) vs. selective tibial nerve block for analgesia after total knee arthroplasty: a triple‐blinded randomised controlled trial
items.abstract: Introduction Infiltration between the popliteal artery and the capsule of the knee (IPACK) and the selective tibial nerve block provide analgesia for the posterior aspect of the knee after total knee arthroplasty. This randomised controlled triple‐blinded trial tested the hypothesis that IPACK provides superior analgesia to selective tibial nerve block after total knee arthroplasty. Methods Patients having total knee arthroplasty under spinal anaesthesia with a femoral triangle block were allocated randomly to receive either IPACK with 19 ml ropivacaine 0.2% or a selective tibial nerve block with 5 ml ropivacaine 0.75%. The postoperative analgesic strategy included paracetamol; ibuprofen; and intravenous morphine patient‐controlled analgesia. Primary outcome was cumulative intravenous morphine consumption on postoperative day 1. Secondary analgesic outcomes included pain scores at rest and during movement measured on postoperative days 1, 2 and 3. Functional outcomes were quadriceps strength; walking distance; and range of motion. Results In total, data from 90 patients were analysed (45 allocated to each group). Cumulative intravenous morphine consumption on postoperative day 1 was similar between the patients allocated to the IPACK and selective tibial nerve block groups (mean (SD) 6 (7) mg vs. 5 (6) mg, respectively; p = 0.36). Four patients (9%) who received selective tibial nerve block had motor block of the common peroneal nerve. No other differences were seen between groups in secondary outcomes. Discussion The IPACK and selective tibial nerve block provide similar analgesia after total knee arthroplasty under spinal anaesthesia with a femoral triangle block.

items.title: Canadian evidence‐based guidelines on spinal procedures for chronic pain
items.abstract: Introduction Interventional procedures are commonly used to diagnose and treat chronic pain of spinal origin but guidance on: their indications; frequency; technical conduct; requirements for image guidance; outcome measurement; and management of complications is lacking. These guidelines were developed by a Canadian group of clinicians, researchers, patient partners and representatives from provincial healthcare regulatory and funding bodies. Methods Reviews of published literature were undertaken for commonly performed spinal procedures for pain, and the evidence was synthesised qualitatively. Evidence‐based recommendations for each procedure were graded on a scale from A (strongest level) to D (not recommended), or as insufficient (I), using US Preventive Services Task Force criteria with the level of certainty rated as high, medium or low. All consensus recommendations required at least 75% agreement among the guideline panel. Good clinical practice statements were also developed. Results We provide 15 key recommendations. The guidelines provide clinical practice recommendations and good clinical practice statements for procedures targeting chronic pain originating from the cervical, lumbar spine and sacroiliac joints. Clinical indications, evidence for efficacy and suggested frequency for repeated procedures have also been proposed. Discussion These guidelines provide evidence‐based recommendations and good clinical practice statements for performing diagnostic and therapeutic spinal interventions for chronic pain.

Delivery and adherence of biomarker‐guided antibiotic treatment protocols in the ADAPT ‐Sepsis clinical trial: an in‐trial descriptive process evaluation of daily procalcitonin‐ and C‐reactive protein‐guided protocols
items.abstract: Introduction Biomarker‐guided antibiotic protocols using daily procalcitonin or C‐reactive protein have been proposed to optimise antibiotic duration in sepsis. This pre‐planned process evaluation of the ADAPT‐Sepsis trial examined delivery and clinician adherence to procalcitonin‐ and C‐reactive protein‐guided protocols. Methods An embedded descriptive process evaluation was conducted within the multicentre ADAPT‐Sepsis trial including 2760 adults across 41 UK critical care units. Patients were assigned to procalcitonin‐guided, C‐reactive protein‐guided or standard care. Algorithm‐generated recommendations (strong stop, suggest stop or standard care) were relayed to research staff and clinicians who remained blinded to group allocation. Adherence was defined as stopping biomarker sampling after advice. Advice timings, frequencies, adherence rates and reasons for non‐adherence were recorded and analysed. Results Among 2760 patients, strong stop advice occurred earlier in those allocated to the procalcitonin‐guided group compared with the C‐reactive protein‐guided group (mean difference ‐1.7 days, 95%CI ‐2.5 to ‐0.9, p < 0.001). C‐reactive protein guidance generated a higher proportion of standard care advice (mean difference ‐9.1%, 95%CI ‐10.9% to ‐7.3%, p < 0.001). Overall advice adherence was greater in patients allocated to the C‐reactive protein group than those allocated to the procalcitonin group (mean difference ‐6.8%, 95%CI ‐9.0 to ‐4.5, p < 0.001), driven by the higher proportion of standard care advice and later stronger stop advice with higher adherence (mean difference ‐14.3%, 95%CI ‐21.8 to ‐6.8, p < 0.001). Reasons for advice non‐adherence included fixed‐duration microbiology guidance, illness severity, continuing fever and elevation of routine inflammatory markers, which did not differ between groups. Discussion A C‐reactive protein‐guided discontinuation protocol achieved higher clinician adherence, probably because its recommendations aligned more closely with established prescribing norms. In contrast, procalcitonin guidance produced earlier and more frequent stop signals, offering greater potential to reduce antibiotic exposure but requiring clinicians to accept earlier discontinuation than usual practice.

items.title: Optimum timing of cerebral computed tomography angiography for determination of death using neurological criteria: a retrospective sensitivity cohort study
items.abstract: Introduction Cerebral computed tomography angiography (CTA) is increasingly incorporated into national guidelines to confirm cerebral circulatory arrest during the determination of death using neurological criteria. However, implementation remains limited due to studies showing variable sensitivity. Clinical observations suggest the time elapsed from the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia, defined as the appearance of fixed and dilated pupils and loss of cough and gag reflexes, significantly influences CTA sensitivity. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of this time interval on test sensitivity. Methods We retrospectively assessed 118 intensive care unit patients undergoing determination of death using neurological criteria. Cerebral CTA was used to confirm cerebral circulatory arrest based on a four‐point scoring system. Patients were categorised according to the time elapsed from the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia to the investigation. Results Cerebral CTA did not confirm cerebral circulatory arrest in 15/118 (13%) patients, yielding an overall sensitivity of 87.3% (95%CI 79.6–92.5%). Notably, 93.3% (95%CI 66.0–99.7%) of false‐negative results occurred within 12 h of the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia. Patients were secondarily stratified into early (≤ 12 h) and late (> 12 h) groups, revealing a significantly higher sensitivity in the late group (67.4%, 95%CI 51.3–80.5% vs. 98.7%, 95%CI 91.8–100%, p < 0.001). Discussion The sensitivity of cerebral CTA increases with the time elapsed after the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia. We recommend delaying cerebral CTA until at least 12 h after the onset of initial signs of brainstem areflexia, and, in case of inconclusive results, test repetition at least 12 h later. Further work is required to confirm our findings and increase diagnostic confidence.

items.title: Pain management after total shoulder arthroplasty: a systematic review and procedure‐specific postoperative pain management ( PROSPECT ) recommendations
items.abstract: Introduction Total shoulder arthroplasty is associated with moderate‐to‐severe postoperative pain. The aim of this systematic review was to assess the available literature and provide PROSPECT (PROcedure SPECific Postoperative Pain ManagemenT) recommendations for optimal pain management after total shoulder arthroplasty. Methods A systematic review utilising PROSPECT methodology was performed. Randomised controlled trials and systematic reviews published in the English language that assessed postoperative pain using analgesic, anaesthetic and surgical interventions were identified from databases. Results Of the 1809 articles identified, 30 randomised controlled trials and seven systematic reviews/meta‐analyses met our inclusion criteria. Interventions that improved postoperative pain relief included: paracetamol and non‐steroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs; dexamethasone; interscalene brachial plexus block and, as an alternative, local infiltration analgesia. Conflicting evidence was found for continuous interscalene brachial plexus block (catheter) or liposomal bupivacaine for interscalene block or local infiltration analgesia. No evidence was found for a specific surgical technique. Discussion In the absence of contraindication, the analgesic regimen should include: paracetamol; a non‐steroidal anti‐inflammatory drug administered peri‐operatively and continued postoperatively; intravenous dexamethasone (8–10 mg); and postoperative opioids for rescue analgesia. As a regional technique, an interscalene brachial plexus block with a single‐bolus injection of long‐acting local anaesthetic (bupivacaine or ropivacaine), but not liposomal bupivacaine, should be provided. In case of contraindications or absence of expertise, local infiltration analgesia is a reasonable alternative. Further studies are required to investigate the analgesic benefit of a continuous infusion for the interscalene brachial plexus block.

items.title: Salmon calcitonin prescribing for acute phantom limb pain after amputation
items.abstract: Salmon calcitonin prescribing for acute phantom limb pain after amputation Phantom limb pain is common after amputation and remains difficult to treat.Salmon calcitonin has been used for acute phantom limb pain for several decades and has several plausible analgesic mechanisms, including modulation of serotonergic and endogenous opioid signalling [1], but its clinical role remains uncertain.Existing evidence is limited to small, heterogeneous studies using different doses, routes and treatment schedules, and there is no established prescribing standard [2-4].Contemporary practice is therefore described poorly, and it is unclear which regimen should be taken forward for definitive evaluation.We sought primarily to characterise real-world prescribing of salmon calcitonin for acute postoperative phantom limb pain at a tertiary Australian hospital and to describe changes in pain scores, opioid requirements and patient-reported symptoms during treatment.The study was not designed to determine efficacy.We conducted a single-centre retrospective observational cohort study using an acute pain service database.The study was approved by the local Human Research Ethics Committee with waiver of written informed consent.Between January 2020 and December 2023, adults who received salmon calcitonin for phantom limb pain within 7 days of elective or emergency surgical amputation were eligible.Patients undergoing repeat treatment episodes within 3 months of a previous calcitonin course and those with calcitonin prescribed for indications other than acute phantom limb pain were not eligible.We recorded: concurrent analgesic therapies; calcitonin timing, dose, route and duration; adverse effects; and documented patient-reported symptom resolution.Visual analogue pain scores and oral morphine equivalent daily dose were recorded before calcitonin and after treatment completion.Continuous outcomes were assessed over time using linear mixed-effects models with patient-level random intercepts and time as a fixed effect.

items.title: Interpreting bispectral index monitoring during remimazolam and propofol anaesthesia: a reply
items.abstract: We thank Wang et al. [1] for their thoughtful comments on our study [2]. We agree that the bispectral index (BIS) may not be an ideal or fully validated measure of anaesthetic depth during remimazolam-based anaesthesia. Clinically, adequate remimazolam anaesthesia may occur at BIS values higher than those typically seen with propofol, which is consistent with published evidence [3] and our clinical experience. We used BIS as one reference for anaesthetic depth, not as the sole basis for drug administration. Anaesthetic titration also considered haemodynamic responses; clinical signs; surgical stimulation; and the judgement of the attending anaesthetist. Because there is currently no validated monitoring index designed specifically for remimazolam-based sedation or anaesthesia, a BIS of 40–60 was used only as a reference range, not as proof of equivalent hypnotic depth between remimazolam and propofol. The remimazolam infusion was adjusted within the protocol-specified range according to the overall clinical condition of patients, rather than simply to target BIS below a fixed threshold. We also agree that anaesthetic dose and exposure may influence emergence quality and delirium-related outcomes. This issue is acknowledged in the limitations section of the discussion. The relationships among remimazolam dose, drug exposure, BIS values and recovery profile require further study. Importantly, this limitation does not change the main clinical conclusion of our trial. Our study was designed to compare two clinically used anaesthetic regimens in older patients undergoing lung resection, not to perform a pharmacological experiment under strictly matched electroencephalographic or exposure conditions. Under the regimen studied, remimazolam anaesthesia without routine flumazenil reversal, guided by BIS, haemodynamics and clinical assessment, did not meet the prespecified non-inferiority criterion compared with propofol for postoperative delirium, with excess events mainly occurring during emergence. Thus, our findings should be interpreted as showing that the remimazolam-based regimen used in our trial was associated with less favourable emergence period neurocognitive outcomes than the propofol-based regimen. The findings also suggest that anaesthetists should pay close attention to emergence quality, recovery trajectory and early neurocognitive status when using remimazolam in older patients having thoracic surgery.

items.title: Liberal vs. conventional pre‐operative clear fluid fasting policies in children: a systematic review and meta‐analysis of randomised and non‐randomised studies
items.abstract: Introduction Pre‐operative clear fluid fasting in children aims to reduce the risk of pulmonary aspiration. Recent studies have shown the safety of shorter clear fluid fasting durations. However, because pulmonary aspiration is rare, it remains uncertain whether the incidence differs between the liberal (< 2 h) and conventional (≥ 2 h) clear fluid fasting policies. Methods We conducted a systematic review and meta‐analysis, performing comprehensive searches across five databases. We included studies with patients aged < 18 y who underwent general anaesthesia or sedation for surgery or procedures. Primary outcome was pulmonary aspiration and secondary outcome was vomiting without pulmonary aspiration. We performed meta‐analyses to estimate pooled incidences according to fasting policy (< 2 h vs. ≥ 2 h). Results We included 33 studies involving 580,197 patients. Twenty‐nine studies (579,737 patients) reported pulmonary aspiration. The pooled incidence of pulmonary aspiration was 0.03% (95%CI 0.01–0.09%) with conventional fasting policies and 0.03% (95%CI 0.01–0.09%) with liberal policies. Risk ratios were available from 14 studies (475,399 patients) and showed no difference in pulmonary aspiration between policies (risk ratio 0.77, 95%CI 0.40–1.47). Seventeen studies (344,653 patients) reported vomiting; the pooled incidence was 0.99% (95%CI 0.27–3.51%) with conventional policies and 0.76% (95%CI 0.18–3.14%) with liberal policies. The certainty of evidence was very low for both outcomes. Discussion Pulmonary aspiration is rare in children, and similar incidences of aspiration and vomiting were observed under liberal and conventional clear fluid fasting policies. The results should be interpreted cautiously due to the very low certainty of evidence.

Rapid sequence induction: a narrative review
items.abstract: Introduction Pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents remains an important cause of anaesthetic morbidity and mortality, and is important medicolegally. Rapid sequence induction is a multi‐element technique designed to mitigate risk in those patients at increased risk of pulmonary aspiration during induction of general anaesthesia. Methods We undertook a narrative review to summarise evidence and evidence gaps focusing on controversial aspects of rapid sequence induction. Results Despite widespread use of rapid sequence induction, many elements of the technique lack robust evidence and consensus. Nasogastric tubes can be used to reduce gastric content, but do not empty the stomach reliably. Correctly applied cricoid force obstructs the hypopharynx and has a limited impact on airway management, but incorrect application can cause clinically significant difficulties. Correct location of cricoid force may require ultrasound localisation of the cricoid cartilage. Applying the correct force, which varies with age and sex, is improved by education, practice and feedback. The use of videolaryngoscopy during rapid sequence induction is supported by evidence. The role of gastric ultrasound in determining anaesthetic technique is uncertain. Cardiovascular complications of rapid sequence induction are common, particularly in the patients who are critically ill, and modifications to the technique may reduce their frequency and severity. Effective use of airway rescue techniques may require removal of cricoid force. Discussion There is insufficient evidence for many of the elements of rapid sequence induction to determine whether they reduce patient harm or to state confidently that they do not. Controversies and evidence gaps should be acknowledged. Despite this, optimal use of rapid sequence induction requires a thorough knowledge of the subject, including areas of uncertainty to guide individualised risk assessment; clinical decision‐making; and practical conduct of the technique.

items.title: Causes of bias in Delphi studies and consensus statements: a methodological review
items.abstract: Introduction The Delphi methodology is a widely‐used tool for achieving expert consensus in healthcare, particularly in areas where empirical evidence is limited or uncertain. Despite its structured design, the Delphi process remains vulnerable to implicit cognitive biases that may influence judgement and group decision‐making. Such biases may inadvertently affect the quality of the consensus process, allow louder voices to influence outcomes, restrict inclusivity and undermine the validity, transparency and evidence‐based nature of recommendations. Methods We conducted a methodological review synthesising literature from cognitive psychology, behavioural science and methodological research on consensus development and Delphi processes. Using a concept‐mapping approach, established cognitive biases were mapped to different stages of the Delphi process, including study design; panel selection; survey development; iterative scoring; and consensus interpretation. Results Ten cognitive biases were organised into four domains reflecting different levels of influence within consensus development: steering‐group and design‐level biases, panel composition and contextual biases, social influence and conformity biases; and individual cognitive heuristic biases. A conceptual framework was developed to systematically identify these biases within Delphi‐based consensus studies. Examples illustrating how these biases may arise in healthcare Delphi processes are presented, alongside potential mitigation strategies. Discussion Recognition and mitigation of cognitive biases are essential for strengthening the methodological rigour and credibility of Delphi studies. Strategies to reduce bias include diversifying expert panels; using neutral language in survey statements; maintaining anonymity during voting; involving methodological expertise in Delphi design; and ensuring transparent iterative feedback. The framework needs prospective validation before its widespread use and may assist journal editors and peer reviewers in critically appraising Delphi studies and improving reporting standards in consensus research.

Development and temporal validation of a simple CT-based body surface landmark approach for optimising central venous catheter tip position in the superior vena cava
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Accurate positioning of central venous catheter (CVC) tips is essential to avoid complications, yet consistent appropriate placement within the superior vena cava remains challenging without a simple method for depth adjustment. OBJECTIVES To develop and temporally validate a simple computed tomography-based (CT-based) body surface landmark approach for estimating optimal insertion depth (OID) and to assess its impact on appropriate catheter tip positioning. DESIGN Single-centre prospective observational cohort study. SETTING Tertiary care hospital in Japan; February 2017 to June 2019. PATIENTS Adult patients undergoing surgery requiring CVC placement via the right internal jugular vein with preoperative chest CT. After exclusions, 86 patients were included in the derivation cohort and 100 in the validation cohort. INTERVENTION In the derivation cohort, insertion depth was determined by the attending anaesthesiologist; in the validation cohort, it was determined using a model derived from the derivation cohort. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURE The primary outcome was the proportion of appropriately placed catheter tips. RESULTS The final model retained the insertion point-to-body surface landmark distance (ILD), defined using a body surface landmark corresponding to the CT-identified midpoint of Zone B, as the sole predictor: OID (cm) = 0.64 × ILD + 3.64. The proportion of appropriately placed catheter tips was higher in the validation cohort than in the derivation cohort (92.0% (95% CI, 85.0 to 95.9%) vs. 73.3% (95% CI, 63.1 to 81.5%); P < 0.001). Model-guided placement was associated with increased likelihood of appropriate positioning (adjusted odds ratio 4.68 (95% CI, 1.97 to 12.27)). Model performance showed good calibration and moderate explanatory ability ( R 2 approximately 50%) in both cohorts. CONSLUSIONS A CT-based body surface landmark approach was associated with improved consistency of appropriate CVC tip placement and enables patient-specific estimation of insertion depth. TRIAL REGISTRY UMIN Clinical Trials Registry (UMIN000026252).

items.title: Postoperative delirium and 1-year functional decline, institutionalization and mortality
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Postoperative delirium is a common and serious complication in older surgical patients and has been associated with increased morbidity, healthcare costs, long-term functional decline and mortality. OBJECTIVE To determine whether postoperative delirium is associated with functional status, quality of life, institutionalisation and mortality at 1 year after surgery in a large multicentre surgical cohort. DESIGN Prospective multicentre observational study. SETTING Forty-three hospitals in Spain. Surgical patients were recruited in November 2023 and assessed for delirium 48 h after surgery, with follow-up at 1 year. PATIENTS, OTHER PARTICIPANTS A total of 2442 adult surgical patients undergoing elective or urgent procedures requiring hospital admission. Postoperative delirium was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM), CAM for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) or the telephone-administered 4AT according to clinical setting. INTERVENTIONS None. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES Functional status and quality of life at 1 year assessed using the 12-item World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS 2.0). Secondary outcomes included institutionalisation and mortality. RESULTS After excluding 81 deaths and 462 nonresponders, the 1-year telephone follow-up was completed for 1899 patients. Postoperative delirium within the first 48 h was independently associated with a 4.6-point higher WHODAS score at 1 year: adjusted mean difference = 4.60 [95% confidence interval (CI), 1.57 to 7.64, P = 0.003]. Delirium was also associated with increased institutionalisation and higher mortality: odds ratio (OR) 2.5 (95% CI, 1.07 to 5.84, P = 0.03), and (16.7 vs. 3.1%; P < 0.001), including 30-day, 60-day, and 365-day mortality (all P < 0.001), respectively. CONCLUSIONS Postoperative delirium is independently associated with long-term functional decline, loss of independence, institutionalisation and increased 1-year mortality. These findings highlight delirium as a key perioperative complication and support prevention strategies and structured long-term follow-up after surgery. TRIAL REGISTRATION ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NC-T06127901).

items.title: Antibiotic prophylaxis with vancomycin and gentamicin and the occurrence of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Vancomycin combined with gentamicin (VGA) is used as an alternative antibiotic prophylaxis in cardiac surgery when cephalosporins are contraindicated. However, the nephrotoxic potential of this combination raises concerns regarding postoperative acute kidney injury (AKI). OBJECTIVE This study aimed to evaluate the association between VGA prophylaxis and AKI occurrence in patients undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), while accounting for preoperative risk factors. DESIGN Retrospective single-centre study. AKI was defined according to KDIGO criteria within 7 postoperative days. PATIENTS Of the 8895 eligible patients between April 2013 and December 2021, 8198 were included. Subgroup analyses were performed according to preoperative AKI risk status (high-risk: insulin-dependent diabetes, cirrhosis, acute endocarditis, preoperative critical state, emergency surgery, or cardiac transplantation). RESULTS In our cohort, 7469 (91%) received cephalosporins and 729 (9%) received VGA. The overall AKI incidence was 16%. AKI occurred more frequently in the VGA group (29% vs. 15%, P < 0.001). After multivariable adjustment, VGA remained independently associated with AKI [odds ratio (OR) 1.29, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.03 to 1.62, P = 0.024], confirmed by propensity score analysis (OR 1.32, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.60, P = 0.005). In subgroup analyses, VGA was significantly associated with AKI in high-risk patients (OR 1.53, 95% CI 1.14 to 2.04, P = 0.004), but not in low-risk patients (OR 1.19, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.64, P = 0.285). CONCLUSION In this large retrospective cohort, VGA antibiotic prophylaxis was independently associated with increased AKI risk following cardiac surgery with CPB. This association was driven primarily by patients with preoperative risk factors for AKI. Alternative prophylactic regimens should be considered in high-risk patients when possible.

items.title: Frailty patterns in European surgical patients
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Frailty represents a multidimensional decline in physiological reserve that increases vulnerability to surgical stress. Its peri-operative dynamics and association with outcomes across diverse surgical populations remain insufficiently characterised. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to describe the prevalence of frailty before and after surgery and to evaluate its association with postoperative complications, mortality, and hospital length of stay. METHODS We conducted a prospective, multicentre European cohort study including adults undergoing elective or emergency surgery under general or regional anaesthesia across 64 participating centres in 10 countries. Each centre contributed data from one to three predefined recruitment days between April 2021 and December 2022. Frailty was assessed preoperatively and at 30 days using the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS), the FRAIL questionnaire, and the Barthel Index. The primary outcome was the association between preoperative frailty and 30-day postoperative complications (Clavien–Dindo ≥ II); secondary outcomes included 30-day mortality, postoperative cognitive impairment, and new-onset frailty. RESULTS Among 1472 patients (mean age 60.9 years; 52.9% male), preoperative frailty prevalence was 14.6% (FRAIL), 10.4% (CFS), and 10.4% (Barthel). Within 30 days, 11.9% of nonfrail patients became frail, increasing overall frailty prevalence to 21.2%. Postoperative complications occurred in 19.2% and mortality in 1.7%. Preoperative frailty was independently associated with complications: adjusted odds ratio (OR) 2.35 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.53 to 3.60], P < 0.001); 30-day mortality OR 10.9 (95% CI 1.28 to 93.0), P = 0.029). Frailty was also associated with postoperative cognitive impairment: OR 3.47 (95% CI 1.98 to 6.08), P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS Frailty is common among surgical patients, increases after surgery, and independently predicts postoperative complications and mortality. These findings highlight frailty as a dynamic and potentially modifiable marker of surgical vulnerability that should be routinely assessed and integrated into peri-operative care. TRIAL REGISTRATION ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04140370
