items.title: A tablet-based augmented reality system to reduce preoperative anxiety in pediatric patients: a quasi-experimental pilot study
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.containerTitle: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.abstract: Preoperative anxiety in pediatric patients remains a significant clinical challenge, yet existing interventions are limited by resource requirements and inconsistent effectiveness. The aim of this pilot study was to evaluate the feasibility and preliminary effects of a tablet-based augmented reality (AR) system integrated into routine perioperative patient transfer on preoperative anxiety in pediatric patients. In this single-center, quasi-experimental pilot study, 27 pediatric patients aged 3–10 years were assigned to an AR ( n = 13) or control ( n = 14) group based on surgery month. The AR system, implemented on a standard tablet device, overlaid virtual characters onto real-world surroundings to guide patients from the surgical center entrance to the operating room. The primary outcome was preoperative anxiety assessed using the modified Yale Preoperative Anxiety Scale (mYPAS) at operating room entry. Secondary outcomes included guardian-rated comfort visual analog scale scores and postoperative agitation. The AR group was younger than the control group. Median mYPAS scores at operating room entry were lower in the AR group than in the control group (28.3 [23.3–36.7] vs. 40.0 [36.7–52.9]; median difference − 11.7; 95% CI, − 18.4 to − 1.60; p = 0.01). No significant differences were observed in secondary outcomes. This pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating a tablet-based AR system into perioperative workflows. Preliminary findings also indicate that this approach may help reduce preoperative anxiety in this population. Given the pilot nature of the study, non-randomized allocation, and baseline imbalances between groups, validation in larger, well-controlled, randomized trials is required.

items.title: Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring during general anesthesia: a prospective clinical audit of adherence to international guidelines
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.containerTitle: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.abstract: Quantitative neuromuscular (qNM) monitoring is recommended whenever neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) are administered, but adherence in routine clinical practice remains inconsistent. This audit evaluated adherence to recommended qNM monitoring standards in adult patients undergoing general anesthesia at a Portuguese tertiary hospital. This prospective clinical audit evaluated adherence to recommended qNM monitoring standards in adult patients undergoing general anesthesia at a major Portuguese tertiary hospital. Over five predefined weekdays between March and May 2025, all adult patients receiving general anesthesia across six operating or procedural areas were assessed. Of 329 patients included, 308 (93.6%) received NMBAs. Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring was omitted in 13.0% despite universal device availability. Utilization was lower in ambulatory and obstetrical settings and in procedures lasting less than one hour. Increasing anesthesia duration was associated with greater monitoring use in univariable analysis, but this association was not independent of clinical location. Equipment-related limitations accounted for a small proportion of omissions. This audit demonstrates high but incomplete adherence to qNM monitoring standards. Non-adherence is clustered primarily in procedures lasting less than one hour and in ambulatory and obstetrical settings. Although equipment was universally available, factors beyond equipment availability appear to contribute to incomplete implementation. Additional research is required to better understand the reasons underlying monitoring omission. In the meantime, targeted educational strategies and reinforcement of evidence-based neuromuscular monitoring practices may further enhance perioperative patient safety.

items.title: A narrative review of methods for estimating blood pressure waveforms from photoplethysmography
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.containerTitle: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.abstract: Accurate, continuous blood pressure (BP) monitoring is important for preventing, diagnosing, and managing cardiovascular disease. Estimating the full arterial BP waveform can provide more clinical information than cuff-based measurements that report only systolic and diastolic BP. This review summarizes recent progress in predicting arterial BP waveforms from photoplethysmography (PPG) and identifies the main methodological gaps that limit clinical translation. We reviewed research published since 2021 on PPG-based BP waveform estimation. We organized the literature around core pipeline elements, including open-source datasets, preprocessing and quality control, model architectures, and validation practices. We also surveyed commercially available technologies that measure BP waveform. Data cleaning approaches can be grouped into three main categories: (1) template-based pulsation comparison, (2) feature extraction paired with classical machine learning, and (3) neural network–based quality assessment. For waveform prediction, recent work is dominated by deep learning, particularly U-Net–based architectures, autoencoder families, and attention-based models. Progress in PPG-based BP waveform prediction is rapid, but comparability and reproducibility remain major barriers. Benchmark datasets with consistent acquisition protocols, transparent preprocessing, and standardized validation criteria are needed to support fair comparison.

items.title: Impact of burst suppression duration on delirium and its diagnostic value in mechanically ventilated ICU patients
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.containerTitle: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.abstract: Intensive care unit (ICU) delirium affects up to 50% of mechanically ventilated patients. This condition is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Although bispectral index (BIS) monitoring is widely used for sedation assessment, its predictive value for delirium remains limited. Burst suppression (BS) is an electroencephalographic pattern reflecting profound cerebral dysfunction. BS has been proposed as a predictor of delirium. However, the quantitative role of burst suppression duration (BSD) in delirium risk stratification has not been established. This prospective observational study enrolled 300 mechanically ventilated adult ICU patients between April 2021 and October 2024 at Harrison International Peace Hospital. Continuous video-electroencephalogram (vEEG) monitoring was performed. BSD was quantified from the vEEG recordings. Delirium was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU). Multivariate logistic regression was used to identify independent risk factors. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of BSD. Among 300 patients, 130 (43.3%) developed delirium. The delirium group had significantly longer BSD than the control group (median 81.1 s, IQR 41.5–148.5 vs. 17.2 s, IQR 5.8–32.9; P < 0.001). Multivariate analysis identified BSD (adjusted OR = 1.018, 95% CI 1.012–1.023; P < 0.001), BIS (adjusted OR = 0.964, 95% CI 0.946–0.982; P < 0.001), age (adjusted OR = 1.024, 95% CI 1.002–1.047; P = 0.031), and hypertension (adjusted OR = 1.748, 95% CI 1.002–3.051; P = 0.049) as independent risk factors. ROC analysis demonstrated that BSD achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.871 (95% CI 0.829–0.913). The optimal cutoff of 41.5 s yielded a sensitivity of 80.8% and a specificity of 78.2%. The combination of BSD and BIS improved the AUC to 0.914 (95% CI 0.882–0.946). BSD is an independent risk factor for delirium in mechanically ventilated ICU patients. It demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy as a quantitative biomarker. The combination of BSD and BIS provides superior predictive performance. This combined approach offers a practical quantitative tool for early delirium risk stratification.

items.title: Peripheral intravenous waveform analysis – a novel tool to confirm intravascular catheter placement
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.containerTitle: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.abstract: Peripheral intravenous (IV) catheter infiltration is a common complication which can cause harmful extravasation of fluid and medications. Significant injury can occur before standard infusion pumps detect a threshold pressure. Peripheral IV waveform analysis (PIVA) uses fast Fourier transform (FFT) to measure the amplitude of the venous waveform. This study aims to evaluate if PIVA can differentiate between IV catheter positions, primarily intravenous versus subcutaneous, in a rat model. Surgical cutdown was performed on the right proximal saphenous vein. Pressure and waveforms were recorded from a 22G IV catheter open-to-air, in the vein, and in the adjacent subcutaneous (SC) tissue. Measurements were performed at baseline and after injection of 1 mL Plasmalyte and are reported as median (interquartile range). The peak amplitude corresponding to the heart rate frequency labeled as f1. Pre-flush intravascular f1, 0.0824 mmHg (IQR 0.0256, 0.1480), differed significantly from both SC, 0.0001 mmHg (0.0000, 0.0004), and open-to-air, 0.0001 mmHg (0.0000, 0.0008), conditions, ANOVA p = 0.03, pairwise p = 0.049 and 0.049, respectively. These significant differences remained after flush. Post-flush pressures between IV, 7.9 mmHg (6.6, 8.9) and SC, 20.5 mmHg (11.3, 28.8) were significantly different, p = 0.0001. There was no significant difference in pre-flush and post-flush pressure within IV, SC, and open-air groups, p = 0.687, p = 0.110 and p = 0.219, respectively. PIVA was superior to absolute pressure measurement for detecting intravascular versus extravascular placement of an IV catheter. This study demonstrates utility of PIVA as a novel method for confirming proper IV placement.

items.title: The use of a non-invasive neuromonitoring device in the emergency department: comparison with computed tomography results
items.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.containerTitle: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.abstract: Computed tomography (CT) is widely used to evaluate emergency department (ED) patients with headache, increasing costs, radiation exposure, and workload. Non-invasive intracranial pressure waveform (ICPW) monitoring has been proposed as an adjunctive triage tool. We assessed its diagnostic performance for identifying abnormal head CT findings in ED patients with red-flag headaches and explored potential resource implications. This retrospective study included 84 patients with red-flag headaches at Hospital Leforte Morumbi, Brazil (June–September 2023). All underwent non-invasive ICPW monitoring (brain4care System) and head CT during the same ED encounter. ICPW was abnormal if P2/P1 ≥ 1.2 or time-to-peak (TTP) ≥ 0.3. Sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values (PPV, NPV) were calculated against abnormal CT. CT expenditure and ED length of stay were assessed as exploratory outcomes. ICPW showed 90.0% sensitivity, 66.2% specificity, 98.0% NPV, and 26.5% PPV for abnormal CT. Median P2/P1 ratio yielded an ROC AUC of 0.778 (95% CI 0.640–0.900). Forty-nine patients (58.3%) had both normal ICPW and normal CT; their median ED stay was 3.5 h shorter than that of the overall cohort, though causality cannot be inferred. One patient had normal ICPW despite abnormal CT. Hypothetically, the normal examinations represented a projected gross CT expenditure of US$34,300. The high NPV supports further investigation of ICPW as an adjunctive risk-stratification tool, but the retrospective single-center design, small sample, and few abnormal CTs preclude definitive conclusions. ICPW should not replace clinical assessment or neuroimaging; resource implications remain exploratory hypotheses requiring prospective, multicenter validation.

items.title: Large congenital cervical teratoma in a neonate: EXIT procedure under spinal anesthesia and early surgical excision -A case report-
items.abstract: Background: Cervical teratomas are rare congenital tumors in neonates associated with high morbidity and mortality due to the potential for severe airway obstruction at birth. Here, we present a case of successful airway management using an ex utero intrapartum treatment (EXIT) procedure under spinal anesthesia for a prenatally detected cervical mass, with definitive treatment achieved by postnatal surgical excision. Case: The infant was born via emergency cesarean section after exhibiting fetal distress due to a cervical mass and underwent an EXIT procedure under spinal anesthesia. A surgical tracheostomy was performed as the newborn could not be intubated. On postnatal day 6, a 439-g cervical teratoma was successfully removed, and the patient was discharged on postnatal day 48. Conclusions: This case suggests that spinal anesthesia may represent a viable anesthetic option for EXIT procedures in neonates with cervical teratoma in selected emergency settings while maintaining uteroplacental circulation and enabling rapid airway control.

items.title: Clinical Factors Associated with Intraoperative Increase in Cardiac Troponin and Its Prognostic Value During Liver Transplantation
items.abstract: Background: Perioperative elevations of high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI) are common during liver transplantation (LT); however, the clinical significance of new-onset intraoperative elevations remains unclear. We evaluated the frequency, magnitude, associated factors, and prognostic implications of intraoperative hs-cTnI elevations, distinguishing new-onset from pre-existing elevations. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 4151 consecutive LT recipients (2008-2021). The primary endpoint was 90-day mortality. Elevated hs-cTnI was defined as > 40 pg/mL (1× upper reference limit [URL]). The relative importance of 19 variables for new-onset intraoperative hs-cTnI > 400 pg/mL (10× URL) was ranked using an exploratory shapley additive explanations (SHAP) analysis. Results: Intraoperative hs-cTnI > 1× URL occurred in 66.1% (2745/4151) of patients, including new-onset elevation in 62.5% (2304/3685) of patients with normal baselines (~90% had an increase of > 20%). In pre-existing elevation, an exploratory threshold > 22× URL was associated with mortality (adjusted HR 5.91, 95% CI 3.11-11.22; P < 0.001), whereas new-onset elevation was not (P = 0.74). Per doubling of intraoperative hs-cTnI, 90-day mortality increased overall (adjusted HR 1.21, 95% CI 1.11-1.32) and in pre-existing elevation (adjusted HR 1.29, 95% CI 1.13-1.46; both P < 0.001). Low intraoperative hematocrit, anemia, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio showed the highest SHAP importance for new-onset >10× URL. Conclusions: New-onset intraoperative hs-cTnI elevations were common during LT and linked to anemia, hypercoagulability, and inflammation. However, they did not predict 90-day mortality in patients with normal baselines; risk increased only in pre-existing elevations. Intraoperative hs-cTnI elevations should be interpreted in the context of preoperative levels.

items.title: K-MIMIC and the next stage of multimodal critical care data
Macroscopic dye distribution after classical versus extrafascial interscalene block: an exploratory comparative cadaveric pilot study
items.abstract: Background: Extrafascial injection has been proposed as a phrenic nerve-sparing alternative for interscalene brachial plexus block (ISB), but the anatomical basis for the reported reduction in phrenic nerve involvement remains incompletely characterized. We compared macroscopic dye distribution patterns between classical ISB and extrafascial injection in paired cadaveric specimens. Methods: In five formalin-fixed cadavers, bilateral ultrasound-guided injections with indigo carmine (20 ml per side) were performed. A classical ISB and extrafascial injection were applied to contralateral sides. Three blinded anatomists independently assessed staining intensity (deep, light, none) in real time during dissection. Results: Both techniques produced deep staining of C5-6 roots, upper trunk, and suprascapular nerve in 5/5 specimens. The phrenic nerve was stained in all 10 specimens (5/5 in each group); deep staining occurred in 4/5 (80%) classical ISB specimens and 0/5 extrafascial specimens, though all 5 extrafascial specimens showed only light staining. Spread to infraclavicular cords was limited with both techniques. Conclusions: Dye reached the C5-6 roots, upper trunk, suprascapular nerve, and phrenic nerve in all 5 specimens of both groups. Phrenic nerve staining intensity was lower with the extrafascial technique than with classical ISB in 4 of 5 paired cadavers, identical in 1 of 5, and never higher. The functional and clinical implications of this intensity difference cannot be determined from the present anatomical model and require prospective validation.

items.title: Commentary: from enhanced recovery toward patient-centered recovery—the role of ERAS in robotic gynecological surgery
Individualized intraoperative BIS targeting based on preoperative BIS values in the awake state: a review and strategy prospect for preventing postoperative delirium in older patients
items.abstract: Postoperative delirium (POD) is a frequent and serious complication in older surgical patients and is associated with adverse short- and long-term outcomes. Bispectral Index (BIS) monitoring is widely used to guide intraoperative depth of anesthesia. However, the conventional strategy of maintaining a uniform BIS target range may not adequately account for interindividual differences in preoperative brain function, particularly in older adults with reduced neural reserve. This narrative review integrates evidence from three complementary domains: 1) clinical studies evaluating the association between preoperative resting BIS values in the awake state and the risk of POD; 2) mechanistic and clinical evidence linking excessive anesthetic depth, particularly electroencephalographic burst suppression, to POD; 3) interventional trials assessing the effect of intraoperative BIS-guided anesthesia management on delirium outcomes. Accumulating evidence indicates that a lower preoperative resting BIS value in the awake state is potentially independently associated with an increased risk of POD in older patients. Intraoperative BIS-guided anesthesia has been shown to reduce exposure to deep anesthesia and EEG burst suppression, which are consistently linked to higher delirium incidence. These findings suggest that patients with preoperatively identified brain vulnerability may benefit from higher individualized intraoperative BIS targets, rather than a fixed universal range. Integrating preoperative resting BIS assessment into perioperative anesthesia management may enable risk stratification and support individualized regulation of anesthetic depth in older adults. When incorporated into a multimodal delirium prevention framework, this individualized approach may offer a rational pathway toward improved delirium prevention and perioperative neuroprotection in older adults, warranting validation in future prospective randomized studies.

NeuroPOCUS: what every intensivist should know
items.abstract: Ultrasound has become a paramount tool in critical care. Nowadays, it is common for intensivists to use ultrasound to evaluate cardiac function, pulmonary alterations, guide vascular access, and monitor systemic venous congestion through ultrasound-based techniques. However, the brain remains often overlooked in the point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) practice. NeuroPOCUS encompasses cerebral hemodynamic assessment, mainly at the level of the middle cerebral artery, as well as evaluation of hydrocephalus, hematoma size, midline shift and intracranial pressure. Most of these are basic or basic-plus skills. In this manuscript, we present a concise guide on what every intensivist should know about NeuroPOCUS, including basic key concepts, technique and several real illustrative figures.

items.title: From failed to failing epidural: an evolution of concepts around the management of labor epidural analgesia for a better maternal comfort and safety
items.abstract: Labor epidural analgesia has markedly improved in quality and safety over the past two decades. However, maintaining consistent analgesic efficacy throughout labor remains challenging, and inadequate blocks continue to be encountered in routine practice. In this Experts' opinion, we examine the spectrum of failed and failing epidural analgesia and identify critical periods during labor associated with an increased risk of block inadequacy. We propose pragmatic definitions for onset failure, breakthrough pain, failing epidural, and failed conversion to surgical anesthesia, based on the most recent evidence. We contend that a clear conceptual framework is essential for obstetric anesthesia teams to anticipate, recognize, and manage inadequate epidural analgesia effectively. We therefore outline practical, evidence-informed strategies for prevention and treatment. A structured and anticipatory approach to epidural management may improve maternal comfort and safety, while supporting a more patient-centered model of care.

items.title: Nutritional support in immunosuppressed critically ill patients
Histology of the parietal peritoneum: a scoping review of microanatomy and potential relevance to preperitoneal analgesia
Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome: what the intensivist needs to know
Perioperative complications at scale: a multi-center analysis of 1.2 million surgical inpatients and the ethical imperative for risk transparency
items.abstract: Abstract Background Major inpatient surgery is associated with significant postoperative morbidity, yet large-scale contemporary data characterizing complication patterns remain limited. Understanding complication epidemiology is essential for individualized risk assessment and shared decision-making. This study aimed to validate prior findings of perioperative complication rates and characterize complication patterns by type, timing, surgical service, patient demographics, and the COVID-19 pandemic period. Methods We developed a tool in early 2019 to prospectively collect perioperative outcomes for patients undergoing major inpatient surgery across 35 different medical centers. We analyzed data from 1,214,539 surgical inpatients receiving care between October 2017 and December 2023. Complications were time stamped and identified using ICD-10 codes, and categorized as pulmonary, cardiac, renal, neurologic, hemorrhagic, or septic. Complication proportions were stratified by surgical service line, postoperative day, age, sex, and American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status. Results The overall complication rate was 7.6% (range 0.52%-23.72% by service line). Cardiac surgery (23.72%), ECMO (20.31%), and neurosurgery (19.89%) had the highest complication rates. The most frequent complications within 7 days per 1000 patients were: postoperative pulmonary complications (6.41), acute kidney injury (5.36), postsurgical sepsis (4.64), acute coronary syndrome (1.00), stroke (0.69), and cardiac arrest (0.63). Complications increased with age (0.67% ages 0–10 years to 15.65% ages 91–100) and were higher in males (9.20%) than females (6.46%). Post-pandemic complication rates (7.68%) declined below pre-pandemic levels (8.32%) and were highest during the emergency surgery only phase of the pandemic (10.53%). Complication rates ranged from a facility-level low of 0.96% to a high of 15.98%, while at the procedure level (CPT codes), certain low-volume interventions had 100% complication rates. Conclusions Complications following major inpatient surgery occur in up to 1 in 4 patients in high-risk surgical populations, and vary significantly by institution and procedure. Surgical facilities should utilize similar methodologies to define their own outcomes to drive perioperative quality improvement. Furthermore, patients have a fundamental right to know these data before consenting to surgery. Institutional complication rates should be made publicly available to facilitate shared decision-making and informed consent.

items.title: Sex differences in perioperative heart rate variability and recovery in gastric cancer patients undergoing robot-assisted gastrectomy: a retrospective cohort study using wearable monitoring
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to analyze sex differences in perioperative autonomic dysfunction in gastric cancer (GC) patients using a wearable HRV monitoring device. Additionally, we explore the relationship between HRV, sex, and postoperative recovery. Methods A total of 160 GC patients were enrolled and divided into two sex-based groups, with 80 patients in each group. Perioperative HRV, inflammatory markers, and nutritional indices were monitored. Time to first flatus, postoperative length of stay (PLOS), and complications were compared between groups. Furthermore, the correlation between HRV indices and PLOS was analyzed. Results Perioperative HRV trajectories differed significantly between sexes (all sex × time interactions P < 0.001), with variable magnitude, direction and timing of across‑index sex‑related differences. Overall, females showed smaller postoperative declines and faster restoration toward preoperative HRV values. Female patients also showed lower postoperative inflammatory markers, higher cortisol (Cor) levels, shorter first flatus time. Both POD1 pNN50 and POD1 rMSSD were identified as independent predictors of prolonged PLOS. The Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve analysis revealed an apparent AUC of 0.864, and after bootstrap internal validation, the optimism-corrected AUC was 0.822, indicating good discriminative performance with expected shrinkage upon validation. Conclusion Female sex was associated with more favorable autonomic recovery (as reflected by faster HRV restoration) and lower postoperative systemic inflammatory markers, although postoperative cortisol levels were higher in females. These patterns may contribute to faster gastrointestinal recovery. POD1 pNN50 and POD1 rMSSD were identified as independent predictors of prolonged PLOS. HRV indices show promise as non-invasive biomarkers for monitoring perioperative recovery, though these exploratory findings require rigorous external validation in larger, multicenter prospective studies before any clinical application can be considered.

items.title: The impact of long-term aspirin use on patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty
items.abstract: Due to the aging population and the high incidence of osteoarticular diseases, the demand for the future development of total hip arthroplasty (THA). Aspirin use has increased substantially owing to its multiple benefits. The aim of our study was to explore the influence of Long-Aspirin Use (L-AU) on perioperative complications in patients undergoing THA. By querying the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) database, the data of patients undergoing THA from 2019 to 2022 were acquired after removing irrelevant data. Propensity score matching (PSM) was designed to reduce the impact of demographic and comorbidity characteristics on perioperative complications. T Test , Chi-Square Test, Rank Sum Test, as well as logistic regression analysis, were used for perioperative complications risk analysis and resource consumption analysis. The proportion of ICD-coded long-term aspirin use (L-AU) among patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty in the unweighted NIS analytic sample increased from 12.13% to 18.21% between 2019 and 2022. After multivariable adjustment, L‑AU was significantly associated with elevated risks of any complication, acute myocardial infarction, and acute cerebrovascular disease. Meanwhile, L‑AU was significantly associated with reduced odds of septicemia and respiratory failure, as well as lower odds of prolonged length of stay and lower total hospital costs. No statistically significant associations were observed between L‑AU and most other perioperative complications. In this retrospective analysis, long-term aspirin use was associated with selected in-hospital outcomes among patients undergoing THA, including lower odds of septicemia and respiratory failure and higher odds of acute myocardial infarction and acute cerebrovascular disease. These associations do not establish causality, and the effects of perioperative aspirin continuation, discontinuation, or resumption could not be assessed. Prospective studies with detailed medication and clinical data are needed to clarify the perioperative risks and benefits of aspirin management in this population. This shows that a total of 369,846 patients undergoing primary THA between 2019 and 2022, through exclusion of inappropriate samples among them, obtained the remaining 310,925 patients who were classified into the long-term aspirin use (L-AU) cohort (n=49,613) and matched non-L-AU cohort (n=49,613) after propensity score matching analysis.

items.title: Risky lifestyle factors among patients scheduled for ventral hernia repair: a cross-sectional study of smoking, nutrition, alcohol, and physical inactivity (SNAP)
items.abstract: Background Risky lifestyle factors, including Smoking, Nutrition (malnutrition and obesity), risky Alcohol intake, and Physical inactivity (SNAP factors), are well-established predictors of postoperative complications. While advances such as Enhanced Recovery After Surgery have improved perioperative care, evidence on preoperative risk factor optimisation remains limited, particularly in hernia surgery. The aim was to map the prevalence of SNAP factors in patients undergoing ventral hernia repair and to estimate the potential impact of targeted preoperative intervention. Methods This cross-sectional study included patients aged ≥ 18 years scheduled for primary or incisional ventral hernia repair at two Danish university hospitals (March 2024–May 2025). Data on SNAP factors were obtained through structured interviews (by telephone or at the outpatient clinic) and review of health records. The prevalence of risky lifestyle factors was analysed with 95% confidence intervals, and hypothetical scenarios were modelled to estimate the potential impact of targeted prehabilitation. Results A total of 304 participants were included. Overall, 50% [95% CI 44–56%] had at least one SNAP factor with obesity (32% [27–37%]), smoking (14% [11–19%]), and risky alcohol intake (9% [6–13%]) being the most common. A subset of patients (12% [9–16%]) exhibited two or more coexisting SNAP factors. Age ≥ 65 years was associated with a significantly higher prevalence of SNAP factors in univariate (OR 1.66 [1.02–2.73]) and multivariable (OR 1.65 [1.01–2.72]) analyses. Conclusion Patients scheduled for ventral hernia repair frequently present with risky SNAP factors, particularly obesity and smoking. These findings highlight a major potential for risk factor reduction through targeted, multimodal prehabilitation in this population. Trial registration NCT06611462.

items.title: Implementing an NT-proBNP-guided preoperative cardiac risk assessment algorithm in noncardiac surgery: a before-and-after cohort study
items.abstract: Several algorithms guide perioperative cardiovascular (CV) evaluation, and recent evidence supports more objective functional-capacity assessment and selective biomarker testing. We developed and implemented an updated evidence-based preoperative CV algorithm for patients undergoing noncardiac surgery. The goal was to identify patients at elevated risk for major adverse cardiovascular events and guide appropriate management without overutilizing cardiac testing or specialist consultation. We conducted a retrospective before-and-after cohort study at a university-affiliated hospital, comparing baseline care (March 2017-February 2020) with post-implementation period 1 (PI1; January-December 2021; NT-proBNP threshold 300 pg/mL) and post-implementation period 2 (PI2; January-August 2022; threshold 200 pg/mL). The algorithm combined clinical risk calculation, the Duke Activity Status Index, and selective NT-proBNP measurement or stress testing for asymptomatic adults with estimated perioperative CV event risk greater than 1%. Outcomes included NT-proBNP testing, cardiology referral, postoperative troponin measurement, elevated postoperative troponin/perioperative myocardial injury (PMI), 30-day myocardial infarction (MI), and mortality. Among 66,695 patients (34,990 baseline, 11,606 PI1, and 20,099 PI2), NT-proBNP testing increased from 220 (0.7%) at baseline to 174 (1.5%) in PI1 and 301 (1.6%) in PI2 ( p < 0.001 for each comparison). Among tested patients, the proportion with NT-proBNP greater than 300 pg/mL did not differ between baseline and PI1 (42.7% vs. 34.5%, p = 0.096); in PI2, 31.9% exceeded the protocol threshold of 200 pg/mL. Cardiology referrals decreased from 0.7% to 0.2% in PI1 and 0.5% in PI2 ( p < 0.001 for each; relative reductions 76.4% and 34.7%, respectively). Postoperative troponin measurement decreased from 1,343 (3.8%) to 322 (2.8%) and 550 (2.7%) ( p < 0.001 for each), whereas the proportion of monitored patients with elevated troponin/PMI increased from 13.7% to 25.5% and 19.8% ( p < 0.001 for each). Overall PMI rates were 0.5%, 0.7%, and 0.5%, respectively. Thirty-day MI and mortality did not differ. The algorithm increased selective NT-proBNP testing and reduced cardiology referrals and postoperative troponin testing without increasing stress testing or short-term adverse outcomes.

items.title: Intraoperative continuous glucose monitor accuracy compared with point of care glucose testing and assessment of preoperative medication hold parameters on glycemic control during orthopedic procedures: a observational study
items.abstract: Perioperative glycemic control includes a multitude of variables which are patient specific and may not distill to a one size fits all patient approach. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) systems present the opportunity to improve care by constantly monitoring patient glucose control perioperatively. The primary objectives of this observational study were to evaluate the performance of a CGM during the perioperative period while also assessing the glycemic control results from following preoperative medication hold times recommended by the American Diabetes Association Standards of Care (ADA SOC). CGM systems were applied prior to admission in this single center study using recommendations from the ADA SOC for medication hold times. Point of care (POC) glucose measurements were taken every 30 min intraoperatively for comparison to CGM glucose values. Phase I focused solely on CGM performance, phase II added a calibration step preoperatively to determine if performance could be further improved. Accuracy was assessed with mean absolute relative difference (MARD) between POC and CGM glucose values and error grid analysis (EGA). Glycemic control was evaluated via preoperative POC and CGM glucose values and intraoperative time below range (TBR), time in range (TIR), and time above range (TAR). Sixty patients completed the study with combined preoperative glucose values of mean (± SD) 131.1 (± 26.1) mg/dL for POC glucose and 150.7 (± 35.2) mg/dL for CGM. Intraoperative MARD in phase I was 18.1% (± 17.2) with 64.7% of CGM-POC pairs in zone A, 33.6% in zone B, and 1.7% in zone C on EGA. Phase II intraoperative MARD was 9.8% (± 6.9) with 93.6% of CGM-POC pairs in zone A, 6.4% in zone B. Combined phase I/II intraoperative TBR was 0.7%, TIR 91.5%, TAR 7.8%. One intraoperative hypoglycemic event (69 mg/dL) occurred in phase II. Postoperative (12 h) MARD for phase I was 11.4% (± 9.1), phase II 7.1 (± 5.4). CGM performance was within acceptable limits of agreement with POC glucose testing during the intraoperative period which improved following the addition of a preoperative calibration step. Glycemic control values obtained both pre and intraoperatively were within target range providing support for use of current recommended hold times.

items.title: Non-reassuring fetal status and neonatal outcome after non-elective caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia: a mediating effect of post-spinal hypotension
items.abstract: To examine both the direct and mediating effects of post-spinal hypotension in the relationship between non-reassuring fetal status (NRFS) and adverse neonatal outcomes. This secondary analysis of a previously conducted prospective observational study included term pregnant women in labor who underwent non-elective emergency caesarean sections under spinal anaesthesia. The indication for caesarean section was categorized as either NRFS or non-NRFS. The primary outcome measure for this study was adverse neonatal outcome, defined as a composite of neonatal resuscitation required immediately after delivery, a 1-minute Apgar score < 7, a 5-minute Apgar score < 7, neonatal intensive care unit admission, or in-hospital death within 7 days. Causal mediation analysis was used to investigate the relationships between NRFS, post-spinal hypotension, and adverse neonatal outcomes. Out of the 335 parturients, post-spinal hypotension occurred in 155 (46%), and adverse neonatal events were observed in 56 newborns (16%). Causal mediation analysis showed that both total and direct associations between NRFS and adverse neonatal outcomes remained significant after adjusting for confounders. However, the indirect effect through post-spinal maternal hypotension was not significant. In multivariable logistic regression analysis, NRFS and post-spinal hypotension were independently associated with adverse neonatal outcomes, with odds ratios of 10.26 (95% CI, 4.13 to 25.48; P < 0.001) and 2.03 (95% CI, 1.01 to 4.07; P = 0.044), respectively. We found no evidence that post-spinal hypotension mediated the association between NRFS and composite adverse neonatal outcomes in non-elective cesarean section, although NRFS and post-spinal hypotension were each independently associated with these outcomes.

items.title: Counting caesarean sections is not enough: a framework for measuring obstetric anaesthesia readiness in resource-constrained settings
Perioperative hemodynamic management in elderly hypertensive patients: a systematic review of monitoring-guided strategies and postoperative outcomes
items.abstract: Background Older adults receiving long-term antihypertensive therapy represent a rapidly growing surgical population in whom intraoperative blood pressure management remains contentious. Observational evidence consistently links intraoperative hypotension with adverse postoperative outcomes, but whether specific blood pressure targets or hemodynamic management strategies improve clinical outcomes remains uncertain. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov from 1 January 2013 to 15 January 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and prospective or retrospective cohort studies of haemodynamic monitoring-guided management in patients with a mean or median age of at least 65 years receiving chronic antihypertensive therapy or with documented chronic hypertension undergoing non-cardiac surgery. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data using a piloted form capturing design, setting, population, hypertension status, intervention, comparator, and raw outcome events, and assessed risk of bias (RoB 2 for RCTs; ROBINS-I for cohort studies). Quantitative pooling was prespecified only for comparisons with three or more studies sharing design, intervention class, and outcome definition; otherwise, a structured narrative synthesis with fully tabulated study-level effect data was performed. Certainty was rated with GRADE. Reporting follows PRISMA 2020. Results Nineteen studies (7 randomized controlled trials reported in 9 publications; 12 cohort studies) comprising 1,074,313 patients were included. In RCTs, higher or individualized intraoperative blood pressure targets did not reduce major vascular or organ-injury composites compared with routine targets (POISE − 3: risk ratio [RR] 0.99, 95% CI 0.89–1.11; IMPROVE-multi: RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.93–1.30), although one small trial favoured individualized systolic targets (INPRESS: RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.57–0.95); certainty was low because of inconsistency and indirectness. Observational cohorts consistently reported duration-dependent associations between intraoperative hypotension and acute kidney injury or myocardial injury (moderate certainty for the association, not for a causal effect of any specific target). Goal-directed haemodynamic therapy was neutral in the largest contemporary trial (OPTIMISE II: postoperative infection RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.88–1.18) but beneficial in smaller earlier trials (low certainty). Continuing renin–angiotensin-system inhibitors increased intraoperative hypotension (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.19–1.44) without increasing major complications (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.87–1.19; moderate certainty). A hypotension-avoidance strategy did not reduce postoperative delirium in randomized data (cogPOISE − 3: RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.79–1.38), and observational findings were inconsistent (low certainty). Conclusions Intraoperative hypotension is consistently and duration-dependently associated with organ injury in observational surgical cohorts, although much of this evidence is derived from broader non-cardiac surgical populations rather than exclusively elderly hypertensive patients. Randomized evidence specific to elderly hypertensive populations remains limited and does not demonstrate consistent benefit from higher blood pressure targets, goal-directed haemodynamic therapy, or specific antihypertensive withholding strategies.Recommendations for this population should rest on guidelines and individualized judgment rather than on claims of moderate-certainty trial evidence that the current literature does not provide. Renal denervation and other device-based therapies are outside the scope of this review and are identified as future research priorities only.

items.title: Effect of cardiac-index guided intraoperative haemodynamic therapy on postoperative outcome in non-cardiac surgery patients – a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Background Optimal perioperative haemodynamic management is essential to reduce postoperative complications. While multiple technologies allow for advanced monitoring, clear evidence on the effectiveness of Cardiac Index-guided goal-directed therapy (CI-GDT) compared to standard care in non-cardiac surgery is lacking. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to investigate the impact of CI-GDT on postoperative outcome. Methods A systematic search using PubMed and Web of Science (2010–2025) identified randomised controlled trials (RCT) comparing CI-GDT to standard care in adult non-cardiac surgery. Study selection and data extraction were conducted according to PRISMA guidelines and registered under PROSPERO (CRD420251058399). Odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) and 95% prediction intervals (PI) were calculated using a random-effects model. Risk of bias was assessed via the RoB 2 tool. Heterogeneity was quantified with I 2 , τ 2 , and Cochran’s Q. Reporting bias was evaluated by funnel plots, Egger’s test, and trim-and-fill method. Sensitivity was assessed by leave-one-out analysis. Results Twenty-one RCTs were included, of which 20 contributed data to the meta-analysis of postoperative complications. CI-GDT significantly reduced the incidence of postoperative complications (OR .59 [.45–.78]; PI .20–1.74; I 2 = 62.9%). Mortality did not differ significantly between groups (OR 0.77 [.57–1.05]; I 2 = 0%). Funnel plot and Egger’s test indicated no significant publication bias ( p =.15). Leave-one-out analysis confirmed robustness of findings. Trim-and-fill did not suggest missing studies. Certainty of evidence was graded high. Discussion/conclusion CI-GDT was associated with a lower incidence of patients experiencing at least one postoperative complication, whereas mortality did not differ significantly. However, substantial heterogeneity and a prediction interval crossing the null indicate that the benefit may not be consistent across clinical settings. These findings do not establish an independent advantage of CI targeting over other GDT strategies.

items.title: Intraoperative fluid infusion rate during major pulmonary resection within an Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) pathway: a retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Background Intraoperative fluid management remains a debated component of Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) pathways in thoracic surgery, with current guidelines recommending intraoperative infusion rates of 2–6 mL/kg/h despite limited high-quality evidence. We assessed whether the intraoperative fluid infusion rate was associated with prolonged length of stay (LOS) after major pulmonary resection. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 540 consecutive patients undergoing lobectomy, bi-lobectomy, or segmentectomy within a structured ERAS pathway, stratified by intraoperative infusion rate: G1 <4 mL/kg/h ( n= 76), G2 4–8 mL/kg/h ( n= 328, reference), and G3 >8 mL/kg/h ( n= 136). Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify risk factors for prolonged LOS (>3 nights), before we conducted a generalised (multinomial) propensity score matching on four covariates (FEV1, blood loss, operating time, open surgical approach), yielding 59 matched triplets (177 patients). Results Prolonged LOS occurred in 206 patients (38.1%) and was independently associated with high intraoperative infusion rate (OR 2.86 [1.70–4.81]; p< 0.001). Propensity score matching confirmed a statistically significant association between prolonged LOS and infusion rate with 62.7% of G3 patients experiencing prolonged LOS compared to 42.4% in G2 and 39.0% in G1 ( p= 0.020). Conclusions Within a structured ERAS programme, high intraoperative fluid infusion rates (>8 mL/kg/h) were independently associated with prolonged length of stay after major pulmonary resection, in both multivariable and propensity-matched analyses. These findings suggest that high fluid infusion rates may be associated with longer hospital stay. Future efforts should prioritise prospective evaluation of individualised fluid strategies.

items.abstract: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols reduce complications, shorten hospital stay, and lower costs without compromising safety across surgical specialties 1–3. In 2019, the ERAS Society and the European Society of Thoracic Surgeons (ESTS) published 45 evidence-based recommendations for lung resection4. Six years after publication, how widely these recommendations have been adopted in routine European practice remains largely undocumented, and survey-based implementation studies in other specialties show considerable variation between guideline-recommended and actual practice 5,6.

items.title: Effects of the sodium glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitor empagliflozin on perioperative endothelial function in patients undergoing cardiac surgery: an exploratory analysis of MERCURI-1
items.containerTitle: Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia
items.abstract: Objective To investigate whether short-term treatment with Empagliflozin (EMPA) is associated with attenuation of endothelial dysfunction and cardiac injury in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. Design An exploratory study using samples from the open-label randomized MERCURI-1 study. Setting Academic university hospital. Participants Adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass. Interventions Patients received 10 mg/day EMPA starting three days before surgery and continuing until two days postoperatively or received standard perioperative care. Measurements and Main Results Blood samples were collected at baseline (prior to EMPA therapy), on the day of surgery (before the first incision), and one day after surgery (Post-D1). Plasma biomarkers for endothelial activation (endothelin-1), vascular leakage (angiopoietin-2), glycocalyx degradation (syndecan-1), cardiac injury (Troponin I and NT-proBNP), and systemic inflammation (IL-6, IL-8 and CRP) were measured. In vitro , human cardiac microvascular endothelial cells were exposed to patient plasma, and endothelial permeability was assessed. Surgery-induced changes in biomarkers of endothelial activation and vascular leakage did not differ significantly between the EMPA and control groups. The adjusted between-group differences were 0.097 pg/mL for endothelin-1 (95% CI -0.478 to 0.672, p = 0.735), -465 pg/ml for angiopoietin-2 (95% CI -2355 to 1426, p = 0.623), and 19540 pg/ml for syndecan-1 (95% CI -10016 to 49095, p = 0.19). No significant differences were found for cardiac injury and inflammatory biomarkers. In vitro , no difference in endothelial resistance was found between the EMPA and control groups. Conclusions In this exploratory sub-study, we found no significant differences in endothelial activation, vascular leakage, cardiac injury or inflammation between the EMPA and control groups. Given the limited sample size, smaller treatment effects cannot be excluded.

items.title: Outflow Graft Kinking as a Precipitant of Right-Sided HeartMate 3 Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolization in Biventricular Support
items.containerTitle: Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia
items.abstract: We previously reported the case of a young woman with lymphocytic myocarditis and end-stage biventricular heart failure who received biventricular HeartMate 3 (HM3) assist devices (Abbott Laboratories, Abbott Park, IL) as destination therapy.1. We now present a follow up complication of right sided HM3 outflow graft thrombosis in the setting of graft kink with subsequent pulmonary embolization and massive hemoptysis necessitating venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) support for rigid bronchoscopy and intrabronchial clot extraction.

items.title: Interventions during cardiopulmonary bypass to increase tissue oxygenation as measured by mitochondrial oxygen tension
items.containerTitle: Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia
items.abstract: Objectives A low cutaneous mitochondrial oxygen tension (mitoPO 2 ) during cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) is an early indicator of insufficient tissue oxygen delivery and predicts cardiac surgery associated kidney injury (CSA-AKI). MitoPO 2 monitoring may therefore be an early trigger to improve tissue oxygenation during CPB and potentially prevent related complications such as CSA-AKI. However, currently it is unknown how mitoPO 2 can be improved during CPB. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether a range of interventions could increase low mitoPO 2 during CPB. Design An interventional before-after pilot study Setting Operating room of a tertiary academic university hospital Participants 9 adult patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery on cardiopulmonary bypass were included. Interventions The following interventions were applied during CPB, in a fixed order, each followed by a 10 min equilibrium period: increase in CPB pump flow, suppletion of albumin, a mean arterial and pressure (MAP) of 80mmHg. A linear mixed model was performed to correct for pre-intervention trends and slopes. Measurements and Main Results In this pilot study, oxygen delivery variables and mitoPO 2 were continuously recorded during CPB at 30 seconds intervals. At baseline while on CPB, conventional markers of tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery were within normal range. Increasing CPB pump flow index to achieve a flow index to 3L/min/m 2 resulted in an increased mitoPO 2 from 31 (20 – 35) mmHg to 40 (25 - 44) mmHg (p=0.016). Venous oxygen saturation concurrently increased from 77 (76 – 78)% to 81(79 – 83)% (p=0.016), indicating supraphysiological blood flow. Increasing MAP and administration of albumin did not result in a significant change in mitoPO₂. Conclusions Augmenting the CPB pump flow index significantly increased mitoPO₂. This shows that mitoPO₂ responds to changes in perfusion, supporting its potential as a physiological target to guide perfusion during cardiopulmonary bypass.

items.title: Four-Factor Prothrombin Complex Concentrate Dosing for Perioperative Bleeding in Cardiac Surgery Utilizing Cardiopulmonary Bypass
items.containerTitle: Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia
items.abstract: Objective To compare the efficacy and cost of 1000 IU versus 1500 IU four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) in adults undergoing cardiac surgery requiring cardiopulmonary bypass. Design Single-center, retrospective pre-post study. Participants Adult patients who received intraoperative 4F-PCC during cardiac surgery requiring cardiopulmonary bypass between April 2024 and October 2025. Patients receiving 4F-PCC for heart transplantation, durable ventricular assist device procedures, noncardiac surgery, or anticoagulation reversal were excluded. Interventions Patients were grouped by initial dose: 1500 IU or 1000 IU. The primary outcome was successful hemostatic response, defined as no chest re-exploration, repeat 4F-PCC, or non-red blood cell allogeneic transfusion 1 to 24 hours after 4F-PCC. Noninferiority was assessed using an adjusted absolute risk difference with a prespecified 10% margin. Secondary outcomes included total hemostatic therapy cost and chest tube output. Measurements and Main Results Of 936 screened patients, 341 met criteria: 154 in the 1000 IU group and 187 in the 1500 IU group. Successful hemostatic response occurred in 74.68% and 74.87%, respectively (P=0.97). The adjusted absolute risk difference was -0.24% (95% CI, -8.98% to 8.49%), consistent with noninferiority. The adjusted mean difference in total hemostatic therapy cost was -$885 per patient (95% CI, -$1262 to -$509), favoring 1000 IU. Chest tube output did not differ at 6 hours (343.49 vs 362.97 mL, P=0.87) or 24 hours (784.99 vs 814.62 mL, P=0.60). Conclusions In this real-world cohort of patients undergoing CPB, a reduced fixed dose of 1000 IU 4F-PCC resulted in similar hemostatic outcomes to the standard 1500 IU dose, with reductions in hemostatic agent cost. These findings support further randomized studies evaluating 4F-PCC dosing.

items.title: Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy with Left Ventricular Outflow Tract Obstruction Managed with Veno‑Venous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation and Alcohol Septal Ablation
items.containerTitle: Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia
items.abstract: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (TTC) is a reversible, stress-induced cardiomyopathy characterized by transient left ventricular systolic dysfunction, most commonly presenting with apical ballooning in the absence of obstructive coronary artery disease.1 Dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO) complicates up to 20-25% of cases and is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Older age, septal bulging, mitral regurgitation, and hemodynamic instability are risk factors for LVOTO.

items.title: Real-time hemodynamic profiling during mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair using pulse contour analysis
items.containerTitle: Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia
items.abstract: Objectives To characterize perioperative hemodynamic response patterns during transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repair (M-TEER) using pulse contour analysis (PCA), and to identify determinants of heterogeneous cardiac output responses following mitral regurgitation (MR) reduction. Design Prospective, single-center observational study. Setting Single tertiary academic medical center. Participants Sixteen consecutive patients undergoing M-TEER with the PASCAL Ace system (Edwards Lifesciences). Interventions Continuous PCA monitoring was performed from baseline until 4 h postprocedural alongside periprocedural echocardiography. The primary endpoint was the change in PCA-derived cardiac output (PCA-CO). Secondary endpoints assessed associations between hemodynamic response, procedural success, and ventricular function. Measurements and Main Results Hemodynamic responses varied according to MR reduction and ventricular function. Sustained PCA-CO improvement occurred only with successful MR reduction (≤2+; 24% ± 11%; p = 0.049). Patients with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction showed an early, transient increase in PCA-CO, reaching 108% of baseline (IQR, 86–136%) after first-device implantation (Dunn-adjusted p = 0.035), which was no longer evident at 4 h (p = 0.80). In contrast, patients with preserved ejection fraction showed a delayed, sustained increase at 4 h (14% ± 13%; p = 0.035). Patients with a left ventricular end-diastolic diameter <60 mm also showed increased PCA-CO at 4 h (12% ± 18%; p = 0.049). Changes in PCA-CO correlated inversely with systolic pulmonary artery pressure (ρ = −0.60; p = 0.026), while left atrial v-wave amplitude decreased significantly (p < 0.001). Conclusions Early hemodynamic changes after M-TEER is not universal but depends on effective MR reduction and ventricular functional reserve. Continuous PCA identified distinct response patterns despite technically successful valve repair.

items.title: Prognostic Role of Circulating Dipeptidyl Peptidase 3 in Critical Care and Perioperative Settings: A Scoping Review
items.containerTitle: Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia
items.abstract: Circulating dipeptidyl peptidase 3 (cDPP3) is an angiotensin II-degrading enzyme associated with increased mortality and hemodynamic deterioration in cardiogenic shock (CS). This scoping review aimed to systematically map the available evidence on cDPP3 as a prognostic biomarker in critical care and perioperative settings, including after cardiac surgery. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane CENTRAL from database inception through July 2026. Nineteen publications were included, comprising twelve prospective observational studies, five ancillary analyses of prospective observational cohorts or randomized controlled trials, and two post hoc analyses. Fourteen studies evaluated non-surgical conditions (worsening heart failure, acute coronary syndrome, cardiogenic shock, septic shock, cardiac arrest), four studies, enrolling 464 patients in total, evaluated perioperative populations, and one conducted in a mixed cohort of surgical and non-surgical patients. Elevated cDPP3 levels were associated with short-term outcomes including prolonged vasopressor requirements, multiorgan dysfunction, prolonged intensive care unit stay, and mortality in patients with CS, septic shock, and after cardiac surgery. Serial measurements showed that persistent cDPP3 elevation was generally associated with worse outcomes, while decreasing levels were associated with clinical improvement. Further research is needed to better understand the source and clearance of cDPP3, its prognostic role in different cardiovascular conditions, and its potential as a therapeutic target.

items.title: Hemodynamic and Anesthesia Management in Pediatric Pulmonary Artery Banding for Dilated Cardiomyopathy: A 20-Year Retrospective Cohort Study
items.containerTitle: Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia
items.abstract: Objective To describe anesthesiologic protocols and outcomes in pediatric dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) patients undergoing isolated pulmonary artery banding (PAB) Design Retrospective cohort study. Setting Single tertiary care center using PDMS for comprehensive perioperative data collection between April 2006 and February 2026. Participants 60 infants/children with DCM undergoing isolated PAB had a mean age of 10.4 months (95% CI: 7.7–13.2) and mean weight of 7.3 kg (95% CI: 6.6–8.0), and 53% were male. Preoperative LVEF was 22% (95% CI: 20–25%); RVEF was preserved at 57% (95% CI: 55–60%). 85% required inotropic support, and 17% were mechanically ventilated. Intervention PAB included perioperative management with continuous inotropic/vasoactive support to maintain systemic perfusion and hemodynamic monitoring using transesophageal echocardiography, cerebral near-infrared spectroscopy, and right ventricular pressure measurement. Measurements and Main Results Primary outcomes: hemodynamic parameters (RV systolic pressure (sRVP), sRVP/systolic arterial pressure (sAP) ratio), pharmacologic support, ventilation duration, ICU stay, and survival. Intraoperatively, sRVP was titrated to a mean of 51 mmHg (95% CI: 48–53), achieving a sRVP/sAP ratio of 0.68 (95% CI: 0.65–0.72; median 0.7). Post-PAB, 100% required inotropic/vasoactive support. Significant changes: ↑ heart rate (131→149 bpm), ↓ mean arterial pressure (58→53 mmHg), ↓ SvO₂ (76%→68%), ↓ ScerebO₂ (79%→72%) (all p <0.05). Mean ventilation duration: 95 hours (95% CI: 61–130); ICU stay: 14 days (5% trimmed mean). Estimated overall survival: 16 years (95% CI: 14–18); HTx rate: 23%; mortality: 8%. Conclusions PAB in pediatric DCM requires specialized perioperative management with universal inotropic support. The sRVP/sAP ratio of ∼0.7 confirms effective RV pressure titration. While outcomes are promising with an estimated 16-year survival, care remains resource-intensive. Limitations include the retrospective, single-center design.

items.title: Mid-Term Outcomes for Lung Transplantation in for COVID-19 Respiratory Failure: An Analysis of the United Network for Organ Sharing Database
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
items.abstract: Background Lung transplantation is a feasible therapeutic option for irreversible lung injury caused by COVID-19, but comprehensive mid-term outcome data remain limited. This study evaluated outcomes after lung transplantation for COVID-19 acute respiratory distress syndrome (CARDS) and post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis (CPF) using a national registry. Methods We performed a retrospective analysis of the United Network for Organ Sharing database from 2020 through 2024. Recipient characteristics, perioperative complications, and graft failure-free survival were analyzed in adult lung transplant recipients with a primary diagnosis of CARDS, CPF, or non-COVID restrictive lung disease (NCRLD). Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and multivariate logistic regression were performed to adjust for potential confounders. Results During the study period, 256 transplants were performed for CARDS, 338 for CPF, and 8071 for NCRLD. Post-COVID-19 recipients were younger (54 vs. 64 years, p 48 hours (67.5% vs. 43.3%, p Conclusions Lung transplantation for post-COVID-19 lung damage yields comparable short-term and mid-term survival outcomes despite higher perioperative morbidity and resource utilization. Long-term studies are needed to assess chronic lung allograft dysfunction in this population.

items.title: Prognostic Stratification of Adjuvant Immunotherapy After Neoadjuvant Chemoimmunotherapy and Quality Surgery in LA-ESCC
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: In locally advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (LA-ESCC), neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy (NCIT) plus high-quality surgery (R0 resection with systematic lymphadenectomy >19 nodes) is a promising strategy. However, the value of adjuvant immunotherapy remains unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the association between postoperative adjuvant immunotherapy and survival outcomes in a multicenter cohort. METHODS: This multicenter retrospective study enrolled LA-ESCC patients receiving NCIT from eight high-volume Chinese centers between 2019 and 2023. After screening for high-quality surgery, propensity score matching (PSM) balanced characteristics between the two groups: NCIT plus surgery (NCIT+S) and NCIT plus surgery followed by adjuvant immunotherapy (NCIT+S+ICI). The primary endpoints were overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS). A prognostic framework based on major pathological response (MPR) and postoperative pathological N stage (ypN) was constructed to refine patient selection. RESULTS: Among 724 patients with a median follow-up of 40.3 months, 3-year OS and DFS rates were 73.0% and 67.7%, respectively. After PSM, adjuvant immunotherapy significantly improved DFS (77.1% vs 65.8%, log-rank P=0.037), but not OS (83.4% vs 69.4%, log-rank P=0.058). Multivariate analysis identified ypN, MPR, and postoperative adjuvant immunotherapy as independent prognostic factors for DFS. Stratification by MPR and ypN status showed that DFS benefit from adjuvant immunotherapy was restricted to the non-MPR/ypN+ subgroup (HR=0.339; 95% CI: 0.173-0.662; log-rank P<0.001), with a significant treatment-by-subgroup interaction (P for interaction=0.025). CONCLUSIONS: Among LA-ESCC patients receiving NCIT and high-quality surgery, adjuvant immunotherapy significantly improves 3-year DFS in the non-MPR/ypN+ subgroup, with no significant benefit in other subgroups.

items.title: American Association for Thoracic Surgery Quality Gateway Procedural Outcomes Models for General Thoracic Surgery Quality Assurance
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
items.abstract: Objective To develop quality assurance models for adverse procedural events after lung resection and esophagectomy for cancer. Methods Using procedural outcomes after 16,430 lung resections and 3,068 esophagectomies for cancer at 9 hospitals in 7 hospital systems, we developed 5 individual and 2 composite outcome models from preoperative information. Random forest quantile classification for imbalanced data with model-free variable priority screening identified predictors. Out-of-bag prediction provided regularized estimates and internal validation. Hospital-holdout analysis assessed institutional benchmark stability. Results Of 71 lung resection and 63 esophagectomy preoperative variables, 35 and 29, respectively, were identified as important predictors across the 7 outcome models. These included demographics, advanced cancer, organ dysfunction, higher acuity, and planned surgical approach and resection extent. Out-of-bag calibration covered a modest range of probabilities. Out-of-bag geometric mean ranged from 0.588 to 0.713 for lung resection and 0.517 to 0.649 for esophagectomy. Continuous risk factors, particularly pulmonary function, provided high-importance information content, with complex dependency and interaction structure among predictors. Risk-factor magnitude differed among hospitals, as did their risk-adjusted outcomes according to patient risk as determined by counterfactual inference within a framework of virtual twins. For lung resection operative mortality, hospital-specific contrasts were stable when each focal hospital was excluded from the aggregate benchmark. Conclusions Using contemporary machine learning, initial models for adverse procedural events after lung resection and esophagectomy for cancer have been developed. They provide surgeons, their patients, and hospital and hospital systems tools for patient risk assessment and for informing quality improvement initiatives in general thoracic surgery.

items.title: Contemporary Results of Operations for Mitral Regurgitation Caused by Posterior Mitral Valve Prolapse: The AATS Adult Quality Gateway
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: In patients undergoing surgical repair of posterior mitral valve prolapse, we compared outcomes in high- and low-volume mitral surgery hospitals to those predicted by the AATS Adult Quality Gateway (AQG) and the Society of Thoracic Surgeons Adult Cardiac Surgery Database (STS-ACSD). METHODS: Five hospitals performed 1,517 mitral valve operations, 1,471 repairs (97%) and 46 replacements (3.0%), in the AQG training set of 55,246 adult patients. Mitral repair techniques included leaflet resection (80%), creating artificial chordae (20%), and anuloplasty (99%); surgical approach was sternotomy or partial sternotomy in 945 (64%) and anterior thoracotomy or robotic in 525 (36%). The remaining 14 hospitals performed 159 mitral valve operations, 145 repairs (91%) and 14 (8.8%) replacements. RESULTS: In high-volume hospitals, predicted mortality by AQG was 0.87% and by STS-ACSD 0.77%; however, observed mortality was 1 patient (0.070%). For major morbidity and mortality, AQG predicted 8.1% and STS-ACSD 6.5%, but observed was 4.0%. Patients undergoing valve replacement were more likely to be older and more symptomatic and had more tricuspid regurgitation and mitral anular calcification. All repair outcomes were worse (e.g., operative mortality was 3/145 [2.1%]) in low-volume hospitals. CONCLUSIONS: Requiring limited data entry and employing novel statistical methodology (e.g. virtual twins), AQG provided predictions similar to those of STS-ACSD, both confirming and augmenting understanding of the volume-outcome relationship in surgical management of posterior mitral valve prolapse.

items.title: Right Heart Failure Pheno-Endotype Drives Prognosis after Tricuspid Valve Surgery
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Tricuspid valve surgery is neither complex nor time-consuming yet is associated with high surgical mortality. Our goal was to characterize heterogeneity of right heart variables and manifestations of right heart failure in patients with severe tricuspid regurgitation and evaluate survival after tricuspid valve surgery. METHODS: From 1/2007 to 1/2014, 522 adults with severe tricuspid regurgitation underwent cardiac surgery. Median follow-up was 3.7 years. Right heart morphology and function variables were measured de novo from stored echocardiographic images. To discover possible pheno-endotypes, unsupervised cluster analysis was performed by sidClustering.rfsrc using preoperative clinical, morphologic, ventricular function, and hemodynamic variables. Variable priority classification was used to characterize resulting pheno-endotypes. Post-surgery survival was assessed by cluster. RESULTS: ), 46%; and Cluster 3 (n=224), predominantly patients with worse right ventricular dysfunction (fractional area change 30%±12%), 21% (worst prognosis). Elevated model for end-stage liver disease with sodium was the most important predictor of time-related mortality and separated Clusters 1 and 2 from Cluster 3. CONCLUSIONS: Patients presenting for cardiac surgery with severe tricuspid regurgitation cluster into 3 pheno-endotypes, illustrating clinical presentation and patient heterogeneity and predicting distinctive prognosis. Right heart function and right heart failure severity need to be recognized to guide patient selection and management.

items.title: Distal Reinterventions after Branched Stented Anastomosis Frozen Elephant Trunk Repair (B-SAFER): A Report from a Prospective Trial.
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Optimal timing for distal reintervention after frozen elephant trunk repair remains debated. We evaluated patient characteristics, clinical outcomes, and predictors of distal aortic reintervention following Branched Stented Anastomosis Frozen Elephant Trunk Repair (B-SAFER). METHODS: From May 2021 to January 2025, 405 patients underwent B-SAFER in a prospective, single-arm, nonrandomized PS-IDE cohort. Among them, 117 patients required 148 distal reinterventions. Indications for initial repair were acute type A dissection (36/189, 31%), chronic dissection (62/138, 53%), and degenerative aneurysm (19/78, 16%). Most reinterventions (n=132, 92%) were planned. Primary endpoints were operative mortality, stroke, and paralysis. Kaplan-Meier analysis assessed survival and freedom from reintervention. Median follow-up was 1.3 years, and median time to reintervention was 8.7 months. RESULTS: Mortality after first reintervention was 6.5% (n=8). Permanent stroke occurred in one patient (0.8%), with no cases of paralysis. Causes of death included sepsis (n=4), hemorrhagic shock (n=2), pulmonary embolism (n=1), and intracranial hemorrhage (n=1). Freedom from reintervention at 2 years was 64%, lowest in chronic dissections (48%), intermediate in degenerative aneurysms (71%), and highest in acute dissections (74%). Larger descending and abdominal aortic diameters were the strongest predictors of reintervention. Survival at 2.5 years was similar across groups (81% acute, 81% chronic, 77% degenerative). CONCLUSIONS: Distal reinterventions after B-SAFER are common, safe, and are associated with acceptable early outcomes. Disease chronicity and aortic diameter predict reintervention risk. Frozen elephant trunk is an effective platform for staged aortic repair, and earlier reintervention in high-risk patients warrants further study. (245).

items.title: Analyzing the Economic and Logistical Impact of Lung Procurement on Transplant Centers in the Era of Continuous Distribution
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
items.abstract: Objective The recent transition to the Composite Allocation Score (CAS) has increased travel distances for lung transplants, but an associated cost analysis has not been performed. We assessed travel costs and short-term outcomes of lung transplantation before and after transitioning to CAS. Methods The United Network for Organ Sharing database was queried for all lung transplants from 1/2020 to 12/2024. Redo and pediatric lung and multiorgan transplants were excluded. Patients were stratified between pre- and post-CAS, which began on 3/9/2023. Outcomes were distance of donor-to-recipient in nautical miles (nm), inflation-adjusted travel costs, and perioperative outcomes. Results A total of 7,835 (58.6%) pre-CAS and 5,538 (41.4%) post-CAS patients were included. Post-CAS patients were more likely female (41.7% vs. 38.5%, p 1000 nm) increased (10.7% vs. 2.0%, p Conclusions CAS has reduced waitlist duration with preserved one-year survival for lung transplant patients, but introduces greater logistical complexity and cost, which requires continued reevaluation to ensure economic viability and long-term sustainability of transplant programs.

items.title: Evolving Trends in Tracheobronchoplasty: Longitudinal Outcomes of Open and Robotic Approaches
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
items.abstract: Objective Tracheobronchoplasty (TBP) is an operation to treat excessive central airway collapse by stabilizing the posterior membranous wall of the central airways. We compare postoperative complications and longitudinal outcomes between the open and robotic TBP, with attention to evolving outcomes in robotic TBP. Methods We conducted a retrospective review of all open TBP (2018-2020) and robotic-assisted TBP (2020-2025) at a high-volume center. The primary outcomes were major complications, classified by Clavien-Dindo grade ≥3a. Secondary outcomes included quality-of-life metrics and 6-minute walk test (6MWT) at 3 and 12 months post-operatively. A subgroup analysis compared early (2020-2023) versus recent (2024-2025) robotic-assisted TBP cases. Results 132 patients were included: 69 open and 63 robotic TBP. There were no significant differences in the major complication rates on univariate or adjusted multivariable analysis (adjusted OR 0.70, p=0.47). Both groups demonstrated improvement in quality-of-life scores and 6MWT at 3 and 12 months post-operatively. Robotic TBP had longer operative times (475 vs. 397 minutes; p Conclusions Robotic TBP is safe and effective when compared to the open approach in selected patients, demonstrating comparable complication rates and durable improvements in quality-of-life measures. With shorter ICU stays and decreasing operative times, ongoing experience with robotic TBP continues to yield improvements in efficiency and postoperative recovery.
