items.title: Preoperative Predictors of Outcome for Adults Undergoing Congenital Cardiac Surgery: Multicenter Model Validation
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
items.abstract: Objective Adults with congenital heart disease (ACHD) undergoing cardiac surgery represent a growing population in whom conventional surgical risk models perform suboptimally. We externally validated a previously described ACHD-specific preoperative risk model and evaluated whether performance could be improved through recalibration/model updating. Methods We conducted a prospective, multicenter observational study of patients ≥16 years undergoing congenital cardiac surgery at four centers (March 2020-April 2023). The primary composite adverse outcome (CAO) comprised in-hospital death, prolonged ventilation >7 days, or new-onset dialysis. We evaluated discrimination and calibration of the original preoperative model (including MELD-XI, cognitive impairment, body-mass index [BMI], prior chest wall incisions, and complex anatomy) and then performed bootstrap-based model updating (200 resamples) to derive refined models with and without the Adult Congenital Heart Surgery (ACHS) procedural mortality score. Results Among 538 patients, CAO occurred in 4.3% (n=23). In external validation (n=383 complete cases), the original model preserved discrimination (AUC=0.729, 95% confidence interval: 0.602-0.855) but systematically overestimated risk, indicating need for recalibration. The refined model retained BMI, prior chest incisions, cognitive impairment, age, serum albumin level, and ventricular systolic dysfunction. Discrimination was good without procedural complexity (AUC=0.799; 0.697-0.900) and improved with inclusion of the ACHS score (AUC=0.857; 0.779-0.935). Conclusions In this prospective multicenter external validation, an ACHD-specific preoperative risk model maintained discrimination but required recalibration. Incorporating procedural complexity enhanced discrimination, supporting a hybrid patient- and procedure-based approach to guide perioperative planning.

items.title: Interstage Reinterventions in Hybrid Stage I Palliation - Impact on Survival to Comprehensive Stage II Operation
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The need for interstage reinterventions is one of the perceived limitations of Hybrid Stage 1 Palliation (HS1P). We aim to evaluate the impact of unplanned interstage reinterventions on survival to comprehensive stage II (CS2) and characterize their frequency, type, and timing. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 199 infants who underwent HS1P at a single institution from 2009 to 2025, tracking all reinterventions between HS1P and CS2. We assessed the likelihood of reaching CS2 using a series of Fine-Gray models at distinct landmarks to assess competing risks, comparing reintervention and non-reintervention groups. RESULTS: The reintervention rate in our study was 43%, with 132 unique reinterventions received in 86 patients. In the reintervention group, progression to CS2 was 78%, with 4.7% of patients dying after HS1P. Among the 33 patients (17%) who died after HS1P, 88% did not receive reinterventions and 76% died prior to HS1P discharge. Reinterventions before 90 days post-HS1P were associated with no difference in progression to CS2 (sHR 1.20, CI 0.83-1.74), but reinterventions before 150 days post-HS1P were associated with a decreased likelihood of reaching CS2 (sHR 0.61, CI 0.41-0.93). The most common reintervention target was the retrograde aortic arch (45%), with aortic atresia in 72% of these patients. CONCLUSIONS: Interstage reinterventions after HS1P are common, but, if done early, do not appear to worsen survival to comprehensive stage II. Reinterventions play an integral part of HS1P care rather than a marker of failure, especially when performed early.

items.title: Outcomes After Curative-intent Resection of Synchronous Primary Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC): Two is Worse than One
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Outcomes following curative-intent resection of synchronous primary lung cancer (SPLC) remain incompletely defined. We compared recurrence and survival in SPLC versus solitary primary tumors among patients with clinical stage I non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). METHODS: Retrospective cohort study of Veterans undergoing curative-intent resection for clinical stage I NSCLC in the Veterans Health Administration (2006-2020). SPLC was defined as two distinct clinical stage I NSCLC tumors diagnosed within six weeks, with curative-intent treatment of both tumors within one year. Propensity score matching (PSM) (1:1) was used to compare patients with SPLC to those with solitary tumors. The primary outcome was cumulative incidence of recurrence (CIR); secondary outcomes were overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS). Additional analyses examined the role of adjuvant treatment and drivers of recurrence in SPLC patients. RESULTS: Of 12,606 Veterans with resected clinical stage I NSCLC, 337 (2.7%) had SPLC. SPLC presented with larger tumors and more advanced pathologic stage. Histology was discordant between the two tumors in 44.2% of SPLC cases. In the propensity-matched cohort (281 pairs), SPLC was associated with higher CIR (HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.10-2.07), worse DFS (HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.03-1.50), and worse OS (HR 1.21, 95% CI 1.01-1.45). Within SPLC, wedge resection of both tumors was independently associated with recurrence. CONCLUSIONS: After adjustment, SPLC was associated with higher recurrence and worse survival than solitary tumors, supporting recognition of SPLC as a higher-risk phenotype within clinical stage I NSCLC.

items.title: Cardiothoracic Surgery Training Attrition (2014–2023): Predictors, Trends, and Delay-Adjusted Rates Across Traditional and Integrated Pathways.
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
items.abstract: Objectives Resident attrition disrupts training pipelines and threatens cardiothoracic (CT) surgical workforce sustainability. This study quantifies national attrition rates and identifies predictors using trainee data from the Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC), while accounting for reporting delays. Methods We analyzed de-identified records of 1,476 CT surgery residents entering ACGME-accredited programs from 2014 to 2023. Attrition was defined as departure before expected completion. Rates were stratified by year, gender, citizenship, and training pathway: integrated (TS-I) versus traditional (TS). Multivariable logistic regression, LASSO, Random Forest, and XGBoost with nested cross-validation were used to identify predictors. A parametric nowcasting model corrected for administrative reporting lag. Results The overall attrition rate was 3.9% (57/1,476), significantly higher in the TS-I than the TS pathway (7.0% vs. 2.6%, p 36 group (aOR 6.05, 95% CI 1.87-19.62) compared with those ≤30 years. Gender and citizenship were not significant after adjustment. Model performance was consistent across methods (AUC 0.67-0.72). Delay-adjusted analyses corrected an apparent decline in recent cohorts, revealing a stable underlying rate with a 3-4-year reporting lag. Conclusions Training pathways are the strongest predictor of CT resident attrition, with TS-I trainees at markedly higher risk. Correcting reporting delays is critical for accurate workforce planning. These findings support targeted retention interventions for at-risk trainees.

items.abstract: Objective We investigated the role of mitral valve repair (MVr) technique on outcomes after MVr for posterior leaflet prolapse. Methods Study patients were identified from the Society of Thoracic Surgeons Adult Cardiac Surgery Database (7/2014-12/2023). Cases included patients undergoing primary, non-emergency isolated MVr for moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation (MR) due to posterior leaflet prolapse. Three repair techniques were analyzed: triangular resection, quadrangular resection, and neochord repair, with further stratification by open versus robotic assistance. The primary endpoint was early "mitral repair failure" (MRF), defined as: ≥ moderate MR on postoperative echocardiogram, valvular reintervention during the index hospitalization or within 30 days, or 30-day readmission for valvular dysfunction/heart failure. Combined operative mortality and/or repair failure (OM/MRF) as well as need for a cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) for rhythm disturbance were secondary endpoints. Multivariable logistic regression models were derived for all outcomes. Results Of 24,383 eligible MVr cases identified, OM was low (n=168, 0.7%), and 683 (2.9%) patients required a CIED. A subset of 9,433 patients with complete postoperative echocardiography, readmission, and reintervention data comprised the primary study group. MRF occurred in 379 (4.1%) of these patients. Multivariable regression showed that open quadrangular resection was associated with increased odds of both MRF and OM/MRF (MRF OR 1.50 (1.06-2.11), p=0.02; OM/MRF OR=1.43 (1.07-1.91), p=0.02) as well as need for CIED (OR 1.31 (1.05-1.64), p=0.02). Conclusions This national-scale study of MVr associated open quadrangular resection repair with increased incidence of early MRF with or without OM as well as need for CIED.

items.title: Machine learning in risk stratification of prolonged hospital stay after congenital heart surgery
items.abstract: Objectives Extended postoperative hospital length of stay after paediatric cardiac surgery places strain on hospital resources and creates emotional and financial stress for families. However, awareness of which patients will spend relatively longer in hospital remains limited. We propose two machine learning models to predict prolonged length of stay using only electronic health record data before the surgery has taken place. Methods The first model used a fixed definition of prolonged length of stay as exceeding the 75 th percentile of the entire population (17 days). The second applied diagnosis-adjusted threshold, ranging from 8 and 49 days depending on diagnosis complexity. Both models were built using XGBoost and evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROCAUC) . An additional risk stratification was developed by applying probability thresholds on the model output to define four groups based on predicted risk. Results High ROCAUC was achieved by both the fixed-threshold model (88%) and the diagnosis-adjusted model (84%). The four-group risk stratification aligned with test-set outcomes, with prolonged length of stay cases predominantly occurring in the high-risk group and rarely in the low-risk group. Conclusions It is possible to predict prolonged length of stay, either defined using a fixed threshold or a diagnosis adjusted threshold, preoperatively, with only electronic health record data as input. It is moreover possible to stratify the patients who are at highest risk of having prolonged length of stay. Preoperative knowledge of which patients are at risk of prolonged length of stay may facilitate surgical planning and improve patient and parent communication.

items.title: R1 resection for clinical stage IIIA/B non-small cell lung cancer: should we have just given chemoradiation?
items.abstract: Objective Optimal treatment for clinical stage III (cIII) non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is debated. Recent data strongly supporting the addition of immunotherapy to neoadjuvant regimens may suggest an increasing role for surgery. The objective of this study is to compare outcomes in patients with cIIIA/B NSCLC treated with definitive chemoradiation (dCRT) versus surgery with positive microscopic margins (R1). Methods The National Cancer Database (2004-2022) was used to identify patients with cIIIA/B NSCLC (excluding N3) treated with either dCRT or surgery. Margin status was evaluated. Survival in weighted groups was analyzed by Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression. Results Of 112,197 patients, 62.7%% (n=70,324) received dCRT and 37.3% (n=41,873) underwent surgery, of which 6.2% (n=2,584) had an R1 resection. The R1 group was associated with greater comorbidity (CCI1: aOR 1.17, p=0.007; CCI2: aOR 1.22, p=0.016), middle lobe disease (aOR 1.39, p=0.002) and increasing T-stage (cT2: aOR 1.57; cT3: aOR 2.47, cT4: aOR 2.51; all p<0.001). Among R1 patients, 22.9% (n=541) received neoadjuvant therapy. Adjuvant therapy rates in the R1 group were 56.2% (n=1329) for systemic therapy and 41.7% (n=1077) for radiation. After adjustment, overall survival following R1 resection was comparable to dCRT (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.97-1.10; p=0.31). Conclusions Survival after R1 resection was not significantly different from dCRT after adjustment. These findings provide prognostic context when R1 resection occurs unexpectedly. With higher pathologic response rates identified in the era of neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy, it is anticipated that patients with cIII NSCLC will increasingly be offered surgical management.

items.title: Two Tumors, Same Size, Different Prognosis: Lung Capacity Indexing Reclassifies T Category and Identifies Higher-Risk Patients in Early-Stage NSCLC
items.abstract: Introduction Tumor size is central to non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) staging, yet it remains unclear whether absolute diameter or patient-scaled metrics better predict outcomes. We evaluated whether tumor size indexed to predicted total lung capacity (pTLC) improves prognostic discrimination in early-stage NSCLC. Methods We performed a retrospective cohort study of Veterans undergoing curative-intent resection for clinical stage I NSCLC within the Veterans Affairs (2006–2020). pTLC was estimated using European Respiratory Society reference equations, and tumor size was indexed to a reference lung capacity of 6.91 L. Tumors were categorized in 10-mm increments; "upsizing" was defined as reclassification into a higher category after indexing. Associations of absolute and pTLC-indexed size with overall survival (OS) and cumulative incidence of recurrence (CIR) were assessed using Cox and Fine–Gray regression with multivariable adjustment. Secondary analyses evaluated associations between upsizing and pathologic nodal involvement. Results Among 11,713 Veterans (mean age 68), 12.2% were upsized after indexing. Both absolute and pTLC-indexed size were associated with worse OS and CIR in a stepwise fashion. pTLC-based upsizing was associated with increased risk of death (aHR 1.08, 95% CI 1.02–1.15) and recurrence (sHR 1.13, 95% CI 1.02–1.26), even after adjustment for absolute size. Upsizing was also associated with greater odds of pathologic nodal involvement (aOR 1.23, 95% CI 1.00–1.52). Conclusion Lung capacity indexing reclassifies a subset of patients into a higher tumor size category, and these patients have worse survival, higher recurrence, and more occult nodal disease than absolute diameter alone would suggest.

items.title: A Young Surgeon’s Case for Stewardship in the Structural Heart Era
items.abstract: As transcatheter therapies mature, the surgeon's role shifts from in-room safeguard to steward of technology, complex reoperation, and lifetime valve care, anchored by operative excellence. Perspective StatementThe structural heart revolution has reshaped cardiovascular care and the surgeon's role.Drawing on a trainee's path through clinical trial research toward the operating room, this note argues that surgical involvement should track each therapy's safety curve.Operative excellence, evidencebased stewardship, and collaboration will sustain surgery's relevance to patients, trainees, and health systems. items.title: Recovery Time of Diaphragm Paralysis After Congenital Heart Surgery: A Retrospective Single-Center Cohort Study
items.abstract: Objective(s): To estimate the time to recovery from diaphragm paralysis after congenital heart surgery using interval-censored survival analysis and to characterize cumulative recovery probability over 5 years. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 111 consecutive patients < 18 years who developed diaphragm paralysis after congenital heart surgery at a tertiary center in Japan (2009-2024); 110 were analyzed after excluding 1 patient without imaging follow-up. Recovery of diaphragmatic motion was the primary outcome. Because recovery was detectable only at discrete imaging assessments, interval-censored survival methods (Turnbull estimator) were used, followed by parametric accelerated failure time modeling and a Bayesian re-analysis incorporating informative priors from a comparable published cohort. Results Recovery was confirmed in 84 patients (76.4%); 26 (23.6%) were right-censored. The median recovery time was 44 days (95% confidence interval, 41-75 days). Cumulative recovery probability was 60.5% at 60 days, 74.5% at 90 days, and 84.9% at 1 year, plateauing near 85% after 2 years with a slight increase to 87.1% at 5 years. A log-logistic distribution provided the best parametric fit. The Bayesian model yielded a posterior median recovery time of 69 days (95% credible interval, 47-102 days), and sensitivity analyses yielded consistent estimates. Conclusions Diaphragm paralysis after congenital heart surgery resolves in approximately three of four patients, with most recovering within 3 months. However, approximately 15% may not recover within a clinically meaningful timeframe, supporting the need for long-term follow-up and multicenter studies to identify risk factors for non-recovery and establish generalizable recovery time estimates.

items.title: Looking Beyond: Long-Term Post-Transplant Outcomes Stratified by STS-PEDIMACS Mechanical Circulatory Support Category
items.abstract: Background The STS-PEDIMACS classifies pediatric MCS as PP, PC, IC, and Percutaneous. While the STS-PEDIMACS provides outcomes of these devices such as bridge to cardiac transplantation, it does not provide long-term outcomes of cardiac transplantation in the transplanted patients. We used the UNOS database to study the long-term outcomes of cardiac transplantation in patients bridged with MCS as per STS-PEDIMACS classification. Methods Pediatric heart transplant recipients (2004–2025) receiving pre-transplant MCS were identified from the OPTN registry and classified according to the STS-PEDIMACS system as PP (n=1,181), PC (n=234), IC (n=660), or percutaneous support (n=57). Waitlist outcomes were additionally evaluated in 1,552 registrations with MCS recorded at listing. Kaplan-Meier, restricted mean survival time (RMST), and multivariable Cox proportional hazards analyses were performed. Results IC and percutaneous recipients were older, whereas PP and PC recipients had greater pre-transplant illness severity. Among recipients with both listing and transplant MCS data available, 95.0% had the same MCS category recorded at listing and transplantation. PC support was associated with higher post-transplant morbidity and the lowest unadjusted survival. RMST analysis demonstrated a significant 5-year survival advantage for IC compared with PP (+3.0 months; p=0.017). On multivariable Cox regression, PC remained independently associated with increased post-transplant mortality compared with PP (HR 1.97, 95% CI 1.19–3.26), whereas IC and percutaneous support demonstrated comparable adjusted risk. Conclusion Post-heart transplant outcomes are largely comparable across pediatric MCS strategies; however, PC support is associated with inferior long-term survival.

items.title: Euglycemia Does Not Prevent Neuroglycopenia After Cardiopulmonary Bypass in Neonatal Swine
items.abstract: Objective Tight glycemic control in pediatric cardiac surgery is not neuroprotective and increases the risk of hypoglycemia. Cerebral glucose uptake is mediated by glucose transporter type 1 (GluT1). Even transient cerebral glucose deprivation (neuroglycopenia) can cause irreversible neurologic injury. This investigation explores plasma and cerebral glucose relationships in the neonatal brain during and after cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). Methods Fifteen piglets underwent continuous CPB (3hrs,34°C) followed by survival for 12-24hrs post-CPB. Plasma was serially collected. Dextrose was administered to prevent hypoglycemia (<50mg/dL). Cerebral interstitial fluid (CIF) microdialysate was continuously collected. CIF and plasma glucose levels were compared to baseline using one-way analysis of variance with Dunnett's correction. Western blots evaluated GluT1 expression in cortical brain tissue harvested post-CPB and from three sham animals that underwent identical procedures without CPB. Additional metabolites were quantified using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Results Plasma glucose increased from baseline (100±18mg/dL) during CPB and remained elevated at 1-6hrs post-CPB (136±43mg/dL, p <0.001, q =0.004 ). Glucose in CIF remained similar to baseline (20.5±11.6mg/dL) during CPB, and decreased within 1-6hrs post-CPB (10.0±13.0mg/dL, p <0.001, q =0.001). CIF glucose remained reduced relative to plasma concentrations at 7-12hrs post-CPB ( p <0.001, q <0.001), but normalized within 24hrs post-CPB as GluT1 expression increased; however, adenosine triphosphate (ATP) remained depleted in cortical brain tissue ( p =0.026, q =0.061). Conclusions Cerebral glucose transport is upregulated within 24hrs post-CPB. Euglycemia and even mild hyperglycemia does not prevent neuroglycopenia and ATP depletion in the neonatal brain post-CPB. These findings provide a plausible biologic mechanism for clinical investigations demonstrating that postoperative hyperglycemia does not adversely impact neurodevelopmental outcomes, and may be beneficial.

The Society of Thoracic Surgeons (2026) Expert Consensus Document on Management of Borderline Left Heart Excluding Unbalanced Atrioventricular Septal Defect and Strategies for Biventricular Conversion
items.abstract: Background Strategies to recruit the left ventricle in borderline left heart (BLH), whether utilizing primary or staged recruitment strategy, are challenged by lack of consensus regarding optimal substrate, timing, and technique. Methods A panel of experienced congenital cardiac surgeons, cardiologists and imaging experts were convened to develop key questions related to BLH management, excluding unbalanced atrioventricular septal defect, from neonatal period through 1 year, using the PICO (Patients/Population, Intervention, Comparison/Control, Outcome) framework. Literature searches were performed for each question. Using a modified Delphi method, consensus statements were developed. Results For neonates with BLH, primary biventricular repair should be adopted cautiously, and only with favorable anatomic and physiologic criteria determined by echocardiography and/or magnetic resonance imaging. Neonates in the 'grey-zone', with smaller mitral and aortic valve sizes, endocardial fibroelastosis, indexed left ventricular diastolic volume 2 and ascending aortic flow 2 , should undergo staged recruitment to potentially facilitate growth of left-sided structures and more durable surgical rehabilitation of left ventricular inflow and outflow. Timing and type of subsequent procedures should be guided by interval cardiac catheterization and magnetic resonance imaging data. Initial palliation of grey-zone neonates can be accomplished with either surgical Norwood or hybrid stage 1 with possible atrial level restriction, and subsequent endocardial fibroelastosis resection along with aortic and mitral valve repair as components of successful complete biventricular conversion. Conclusions Biventricular approaches in BLH should be guided by integration of anatomic and physiologic criteria, with most neonates recommended for staged recruitment rather than primary repair.

items.title: Mitral Annular Calcification: Operative Decision Making and Technical Considerations
items.abstract: Background Mitral annular calcification (MAC) presents a formidable challenge in mitral valve surgery owing to risks of atrioventricular groove disruption, circumflex artery injury, and paravalvular leaks. The optimal operative strategy varies according to the severity of annular calcification, extent of ventricular extension, and the patient-specific risk profile. Methods A narrative expert review was performed synthesizing contemporary surgical series, imaging-guided approaches, and transcatheter strategies for mitral valve intervention in the setting of MAC. Technical considerations, complication avoidance strategies, and decision-making frameworks were integrated into a new severity-based operative algorithm. Results We developed a decision matrix to stratify patients into four categories to guide preoperative planning and operative decisions. MAC management lies on a spectrum between working around the MAC with no resection ("respect" the MAC) to complete MAC resection with atrioventricular groove reconstruction ("resect" the MAC). Severe or circumferential MAC demands tailored strategies, including transcatheter or hybrid approaches. In patients with mild MAC, mitral valve repair remains feasible and preferred. Moderate MAC requires individualized decision-making; repair is achievable when leaflet mobility is preserved, and decalcification permits secure annuloplasty. Replacement is favored when leaflet restriction or annular rigidity precludes durable reconstruction. The extent of decalcification should be tailored to the patient's risk profile and surgical expertise to ensure durable results. Conclusions Mitral valve intervention in the setting of MAC requires an individualized approach. We propose a practical management algorithm, stratified by patient risk and anatomic feasibility.

items.title: Regionalization and Joint Reporting: A Counterpoint Perspective
One Year Survival of High-Risk Patients Undergoing Coronary Revascularization
items.abstract: Background In high-risk patients requiring coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) we sought to evaluate the differential impact of comorbid and cardiovascular risk factors on perioperative versus one year survival with the hypothesis that different phenotypes of perioperative risk may portend different longitudinal outcomes and that not all high-risk features are equivalent. Methods The Society Thoracic Surgeons (STS) Adult Cardiac Surgery Database (ACSD) was used to assess all patients (n=75,385) ≥65 years of age undergoing isolated CABG with a predicted risk of mortality (PROM) greater than 4% (2012-2022). The database was linked with Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) claims data to evaluate one-year mortality. Change in risk-adjusted odds ratios for 30-day and 1-year mortality were assessed using landmark analysis to identify variables associated with early versus late mortality. Results A total of 67,376 (89.4%) patients survived 30-days of those 8,998 (13.4%) died between 30 days and one year. Liver disease and home oxygen were associated with increased mortality at both 30 days and 1 year. However, unresponsive state, prior CABG, percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) within 6 hours, cardiogenic shock, and temporary mechanical support were associated with early mortality but exhibited no significant effects at 1 year. Finally, cancer, Medicaid coverage, and dialysis were initially neutral for 30-day mortality but emerged as independent risk factors for 1-year mortality. Conclusions In high-risk CABG, prognostic determinants evolve over time. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating temporal risk dynamics into clinical decisions.

items.title: We Love Aortic Surgery, But It’s the Genes that Hold the Key to Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm Disease
Open TAR: Still the Benchmark
Lifetime Management of Aortic Stenosis: Expert Review of Evidence and Consensus Guidelines
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The 2025 European Society of Cardiology/European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery Guidelines introduced a Class I recommendation for transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) in selected patients aged 70 years or older with tricuspid aortic stenosis and suitable anatomy, while surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) remains recommended in younger low-risk patients. In patients with long expected survival, this framework requires careful consideration of valve durability, future reintervention, and patient preferences. This expert review, developed by the Italian Cardiac Surgery Working Group, examines contemporary evidence and consensus recommendations from a lifetime-management perspective. METHODS: We performed a narrative, evidence-based synthesis of randomized trials, trial-based meta-analyses, and propensity-matched real-world registries comparing transfemoral TAVI and SAVR, with primary emphasis on low-risk patients. Lower-intermediate-risk evidence was included only when directly relevant to lifetime management, durability, or reintervention. RESULTS: Evidence suggests that treatment effects are time-dependent: early non-inferiority of TAVI may attenuate with longer follow-up, particularly in patients with substantial life expectancy. Randomized durability data remain limited, whereas propensity-matched real-world registries have suggested possible higher late mortality after TAVI in younger, lower-risk populations. Reintervention after a transcatheter-first strategy may be associated with increasing technical complexity and procedural risk over time. CONCLUSIONS: This review supports appropriate application of current guidelines through a pragmatic framework for individualized, Heart Team-based decision-making. Transfemoral TAVI is often appropriate in patients with limited life expectancy or recognized high surgical risk when anatomically feasible. In patients with long expected survival, SAVR should retain a central role as an important reference strategy.

Locating the Gender Payment Gap Among Recent Cardiothoracic Surgery Graduates: A Bottom-up Analysis of Medicare Payments
items.abstract: Background Women comprise an increasing proportion of cardiothoracic surgery trainees, yet gender differences in Medicare payments persist. Whether these differences reflect clinical volume or payment for the same service remains unclear. Methods We analyzed 2024 Medicare fee-for-service data for cardiothoracic surgeons graduating from integrated residency or independent fellowship programs between 2013 and 2023. Cardiac and thoracic surgeons were analyzed separately; mixed-practice surgeons were excluded. Mixed-effects models assessed associations between surgeon gender, clinical activity, and standardized payments. Results Among 898 surgeons, women comprised 19% (n=107) of cardiac surgeons and 25% (n=84) of thoracic surgeons. Women received lower mean annual standardized payments than men in cardiac surgery ($79,524 vs $103,940) and thoracic surgery ($52,180 vs $66,474; both p Conclusions Women treated fewer Medicare patients, performed fewer services, billed fewer unique service codes, and received lower annual payments than men. The payment difference was largely attenuated after accounting for clinical activity, while payment for the same service did not differ by gender. These findings locate the Medicare payment difference primarily in clinical volume and breadth of practice rather than service-level reimbursement.

items.title: Aortic Valve Replacement in Patients 50-65 Years: A Target Trial Emulation
items.abstract: Background Guidelines favor surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) in patients aged 65 years or younger with aortic stenosis, yet many receive transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) without supportive data. We performed a target trial emulation of SAVR versus TAVI in this population. Methods Using the all-payer Premier Healthcare Database (2016-2024), patients aged 50 to 65 years undergoing isolated SAVR or TAVI within 90 days of an aortic stenosis diagnosis were evaluated. After trial exclusions, frailty and predicted risk were incorporated into a clone-censor-weight framework with inverse probability weighting. Reporting adhered to TARGET guidance. The primary outcome was the 5-year composite of all-cause mortality, stroke, valve reintervention, or heart failure rehospitalization. Results The clone-censor-weighted analysis included 18,549 SAVR and 18,549 TAVI patients, balanced across all covariates (standardized mean difference Conclusions For contemporary patients aged 50 to 65 years, the primary composite outcome favored SAVR over TAVI at 5 years, most markedly at centers with high young TAVI utilization. These data may guide heart team decision making and future trial design.

items.title: Statewide Trends in Morbidity and Mortality in Octogenarians Undergoing Isolated Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting
items.abstract: Background We sought to determine whether advanced age modifies the association between established preoperative risk factors and 30-day outcomes following isolated coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), compare temporal trends between octogenarians and younger patients, and characterize differences in perioperative outcomes between the two groups. Methods Using the Michigan Society of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgeons Quality Collaborative (The Society of Thoracic Surgeons Adult Cardiac Surgery Database), we identified 105,445 patients undergoing isolated CABG from 2006-2024. Outcomes and case volumes were assessed across four eras. Operative mortality was evaluated using mixed-effects logistic regression with hospital as a random effect. Secondary analyses used multiple imputation with hospital-clustered multivariable logistic regression to evaluate age-related effect modification for short-term mortality and morbidity. Results Octogenarians comprised 8.1% of cases (8,563/105,445). Operative mortality was higher in octogenarians (4.8%; n=413) than patients Conclusions In octogenarians, CABG remains associated with higher morbidity and mortality than in younger patients, with minimal changes in 30-day outcomes over the last 20 years. Most traditional risk factors demonstrated similar relative associations across age groups, with age-specific effects in select postoperative domains.

Electrosurgical Septotomy Across the Full Spectrum of Aortic Dissection
items.abstract: Objectives Transcatheter electrosurgical septotomy divides the dissection membrane to reconstitute a single aortic lumen. Reported experience is largely confined to chronic post-dissection aneurysms. We assessed the technique across the full spectrum of descending aortic dissection, including stand-alone treatment of malperfusion. Methods A retrospective intention-to-treat analysis of 21 consecutive patients scheduled for septotomy between June 2022 and May 2026. The membrane was crossed by needle re-entry and divided with an electrified through-and-through guidewire at 40-60 W under fluoroscopy, without routine intravascular ultrasound or image fusion. A perfused-lumen index (perfused lumen divided by total aortic diameter) was measured before and after the procedure. Results Septotomy was performed in 20 of 21 patients (technical success 95% on an intention-to-treat basis). Indications were landing-zone preparation (57%), malperfusion (33%), preparation for open repair, and true-lumen collapse. Malperfusion resolved in all 7 patients treated for that indication, and the perfused-lumen index rose from a median of 0.16 to 0.98 (18 patients, P < .001). There was no stroke, spinal cord ischaemia, or retrograde type A dissection. Thirty-day, in-hospital, and overall mortality were 10%, 14%, and 19%, respectively, with 1 fatal delayed aortic rupture and no intraprocedural death. Three unplanned reinterventions occurred; median follow-up was 5.1 months. Conclusions Electrosurgical septotomy was feasible across the full spectrum of aortic dissection and, in selected patients, as stand-alone treatment for malperfusion, using standard electrosurgical equipment. Given the small, heterogeneous cohort and short follow-up, these findings demonstrate feasibility rather than durability.

items.title: Corrigendum to: Building the Future: A Proposed Framework for Training Residents in Minimally Invasive Cardiac Surgery
Three Decades of Paediatric Heart Transplantation: Long-term Outcomes and the Evolving Role of Mechanical Circulatory Support
items.abstract: Heart transplantation (HTx) remains the definitive therapy for children with end-stage heart failure, while donor scarcity exposes candidates to deterioration during waiting. Mechanical circulatory support (MCS), particularly ventricular assist devices (VADs), has therefore become an increasingly important bridge to transplantation.1–5 We report the long-term experience of a single high-volume congenital heart centre over more than 3 decades, focusing on temporal changes in paediatric HTx and the evolving role of pretransplant MCS. We retrospectively reviewed 267 patients transplanted at our institution between 1988 and 2024. The cohort was defined by transplantation within the paediatric/congenital programme. Clinical, operative and follow-up data were extracted from institutional records. Overall survival was assessed by Kaplan–Meier analysis. Mechanical circulatory support before HTx was retained as a clinical variable rather than used to define the primary study groups. Mechanical circulatory support included extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) and VAD support. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Justus Liebig University Giessen (AZ 94/23; July 27, 2023).

items.title: What Are the Survival Outcomes of Patients Requiring Postcardiotomy Temporary Mechanical Circulatory Support?
items.abstract: Postcardiotomy low cardiac output syndrome (PC-LCOS) remains a poorly characterized complication of cardiac surgery, often necessitating temporary mechanical circulatory support (tMCS) with resource utilization and variable outcomes. Evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, derived from retrospective, single-centre studies. Consequently, the prognosis of patients requiring postcardiotomy tMCS remains uncertain, representing a critical concern for clinicians initiating support. In-hospital survival after postcardiotomy tMCS remains ∼40% (range 15%-55%), with varying results based on clinical severity, extent and aetiology of ventricular dysfunction, type and timing of tMCS.1,2 On-support mortality accounts for ∼60% of in-hospital deaths, predominantly occurring within the first 3 days of support and associated with greater preoperative instability, severe postoperative haemometabolic compromise, cardiac arrest, bleeding, and delayed tMCS initiation.1,3 Conversely, post-weaning mortality accounts for ∼40% of deaths and is closely related to complications including re-thoracotomy, bowel ischaemia, acute kidney injury, and septic shock.1,2 Survival according to tMCS duration follows an inverted U-shaped pattern, with the highest values (49%) among patients supported for 4-7 days. Approximately 30% of patients requiring postcardiotomy tMCS remain on support for >7 days, with in-hospital survival falling to 33% and 27% beyond 7 and 10 days, respectively.4 Survival decreases in specific populations, including patients ≥70 years of age (24%-31%), those undergoing aortic surgery (26%-33%), receiving extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (overall: 33%-35%; with favourable neurological outcome: 23%-29%),5 postoperative tMCS (36%), or central cannulation (28%-32%), although these findings should be interpreted cautiously given potential selection bias.1,4 Prophylactic, preoperatively planned tMCS initiation before cardiopulmonary bypass weaning in patients at high risk of PC-LCOS has yielded promising survival rates of up to 96%.3 Despite high early mortality, survivors to discharge have a favourable long-term prognosis, with an estimated 66% 10-year survival.1

items.title: The Standstill in Cardioplegia: Have We Reached the Peak of Myocardial Protection?
David Paul Taggart (1958-2026): In MemoriamSurgeon-scientist, patient advocate, and friend
items.abstract: The death of David Paul Taggart on August 8, 2026, at the age of 68, has deprived cardiovascular surgery of one of its most original, courageous and impactful voices. It has also deprived us both of a longstanding academic partner and friend. David was an outstanding surgeon and clinical investigator, and a relentless advocate for scientific truth who put the interests of the patient above all other considerations. David Taggart was born in Glasgow on July 1, 1958 and grew up in Scotland, with his seven siblings in a close-knit family. He studied medicine at the University of Glasgow, qualifying in 1981. His postgraduate training took him through Glasgow, Paris, Newcastle and London, including the Royal Brompton Hospital, where he trained under Sir Magdi Yacoub and Mr Christopher Lincoln; he often spoke fondly of their mentorship. He received an MD with Honours in 1989 and completed a PhD at the University of Strathclyde in 2000. In 1995 he was appointed Consultant Cardiothoracic Surgeon at Oxford’s John Radcliffe Hospital; in 2004 he became Professor of Cardiovascular Surgery at the University of Oxford. During his long and happy Oxford career, Professor Taggart—often simply called “Prof” by his many students, mentees and colleagues—conducted or participated in more than 20 original studies and clinical trials and authored more than 350 peer-reviewed publications. He served as President of the Society for Cardiothoracic Surgery in Great Britain and Ireland (SCTS) from 2010 to 2012. Although he is best known as a global expert on surgical coronary revascularization, Taggart’s early research revealed a broad intellectual curiosity in numerous areas of cardiac surgical physiology and pathophysiology. He examined hypothermia and the metabolic, endocrine and acute-phase responses to cardiopulmonary bypass and investigated postoperative respiratory dysfunction, attempting to distinguish the contributions of cardiopulmonary bypass from those of bilateral internal thoracic artery harvesting. His PhD thesis explored whether antagonism of platelet-activating factor could ameliorate the myocardial, pulmonary and cerebral consequences of cardiac surgery. Later studies led by Taggart included biochemical assessment of myocardial injury, a randomized investigation of postoperative lung injury and a randomized neuroprotection trial. Even when interventions were not consistently beneficial, Taggart published those negative findings, demonstrating his firm belief in the importance of randomized trials to provide evidence for cardiac surgical procedures. In the middle of his career, Taggart began to focus on advancing the state of the art in coronary bypass surgery. His 2001 systematic review of largely observational data found a substantial survival advantage associated with bilateral rather than single internal mammary artery grafting.1 This prompted him to build a multidisciplinary collaborative team to undertake the difficult task of testing the hypothesis prospectively. The result was the Arterial Revascularisation Trial (ART), which he conceived with the late Douglas Altman, to compare mortality rates between coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG) using standard single internal thoracic artery grafts versus bilateral internal thoracic artery grafts in a randomized controlled trial. The grant application for ART to the UK Medical Research Council and British Heart Foundation was successful, and £3.4 million (about 5 million US dollars at the time) was awarded to Taggart, the University of Oxford and the Clinical Trials and Evaluation Unit at Royal Brompton Hospital, London. Between 2004 and 2007, 3102 patients were randomized at 28 cardiac surgery sites in 7 countries to single or bilateral internal thoracic artery CABG surgery with vein grafts. Enrolment into the trial was consistently ahead of schedule which was a tribute to Taggart’s leadership and ability to convene a group of enthusiastic cardiac surgeons to participate in the trial. Clinical follow-up and data analysis have continued through 15 years, during which David partnered closely with Oxford cardiologist Marcus Flather to lead the analytic team. An interim 5-year report,2 the primary outcome report at 10 years3 and the most recent 15-year follow-up report4 were consistent and showed that for the intention-to-treat analysis there was no difference in mortality rates between the two strategies. For the secondary composite outcome of death, myocardial infarction and stroke there was a slight numerical advantage for the bilateral approach, but this was not statistically significant. Interpretation was complicated by important treatment crossovers: approximately 14% of patients assigned to bilateral grafting received only one internal thoracic artery, while approximately 22% assigned to single grafting received a radial artery as a second arterial conduit. David presented the 15-year ART results at the American Association for Thoracic Surgery meeting in May 2026. The intention-to-treat comparison remained neutral, whereas the as-treated analysis again associated actual receipt of multiple arterial grafts with significantly lower mortality. ART is an important trial because observational studies have consistently shown that bilateral internal thoracic artery grafts are associated with lower mortality compared to standard single internal thoracic artery grafts, but these studies are often confounded by unbalanced covariates like age and gender which may introduce bias in spite of statistical adjustments. Taggart was one of the pioneers of multiple arterial graft CABG and many of his operations included bilateral internal thoracic artery grafts carried out using off-pump techniques. He personally enrolled more than 400 patients in ART and his own results demonstrated about 15% proportional mortality reduction with the bilateral approach—an observation that he was proud of even if it did not change the trial’s overall conclusion. Taggart’s body of work included several studies of off-pump CABG. He was an investigator and co-author in the international CORONARY trial,5 the largest randomized comparison of on-pump and off-pump CABG. His subsequent ART sub-analyses clearly demonstrated that off-pump surgery can achieve excellent outcomes, but its success is highly dependent upon operator experience. In ART, low-volume off-pump surgeons performed fewer grafts, converted to cardiopulmonary bypass more frequently and had worse patient outcomes.6 He also investigated methods of improving the performance of saphenous-vein grafts. The VEST programme evaluated whether external stenting could reduce adverse remodelling, lumen irregularity and diffuse intimal hyperplasia. The first randomized study showed reduced intimal hyperplasia area at 1 year, and subsequent multicentre work demonstrated improved FitzGibbon patency classification and reduced intimal thickening at 2 years, although a definitive clinical benefit remained unproven.7 Taggart also brought his evidence-based approach to intraoperative assessment of graft quality, with the prospective, multicentre REQUEST registry, in which protocol-based transit-time flow measurement and high-frequency epicardial and epi-aortic ultrasonography were used in 1016 patients undergoing CABG. Intraoperative assessment prompted a change in the planned operative strategy in 25.2% of patients, including graft revision in 7.8% of patients. This project reflected Taggart’s belief that the technical quality of coronary bypass surgery should be objectively measured and verified rather than presumed at the conclusion of every CABG operation.8 The rise of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in the 1990s and early 2000s saw a corresponding decline in CABG numbers globally. Taggart was very concerned about this, not because he was worried about becoming an “extinct” cardiac surgeon but because he felt that patients were being sold short with incorrect treatment decisions in favour of PCI when treating symptomatic coronary artery disease (CAD). He expressed concerns that cardiac surgeons were being left out of the decision-making process, where the interventional cardiologist would often assess the patient and advise PCI treatment without wider consultation. His efforts, and the efforts of others, led to the concept of the “heart team” approach, whereby patients with advanced or complex CAD would be discussed in a multidisciplinary team meeting with cardiologists, cardiac surgeons and other experts to provide the best treatment strategy. Reports that pooled individual patient data from the randomized trials of PCI vs CABG for symptomatic CAD consistently showed survival advantages for CABG in patients with complex CAD, including diabetes. These results shaped the revascularisation guidelines from the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and the European Association of Cardiac and Thoracic Surgeons (EACTS) and undoubtedly allowed patients more appropriate access to CABG. Taggart was a popular speaker on this topic at international meetings, and his command of the relevant data and his fearless ability to push back against the tide of popular opinion was legendary. Taggart’s invited Ferguson Lecture at the Society of Thoracic Surgeons meeting in 2006 bore a title that broadcast his deeply held conviction: “Coronary artery bypass grafting is still the best treatment for multivessel and left main disease, but patients need to know.”9 Taggart was also well known, even notorious in some circles, for his fallout with the EXCEL study group, which conducted a large randomized controlled trial comparing PCI versus CABG in patients with left main CAD. When the 5-year results were being analysed, Taggart pointed out that mortality rates were higher in the PCI group and felt that the manuscript should emphasize the mortality outcome, but was voted down. Taggart also felt that the Universal Definition for perioperative MI should be reported in a sensitivity analysis as prespecified, and that the difference in definition of perioperative MI had effectively tilted the composite primary endpoint in favour of PCI; this was later shown to be mathematically true.10 He ultimately resigned from the EXCEL Steering Committee and took his name off the author list. This became a widely reported issue, with the New England Journal of Medicine requesting clarifications and the BBC launching an independent investigation of the data.11 This episode underscored Taggart’s trademark determination to seek the truth for patients and ensure that information is shared transparently with the scientific and clinical community. The eventual ESC/EACTS reassessment concluded that, among low-surgical-risk patients with left-main anatomy suitable for either treatment, both CABG and PCI were clinically reasonable, while proposing Class I, Level A support for CABG and Class IIa, Level A support for PCI. This controversy did nothing to diminish Taggart’s advocacy for the multidisciplinary Heart Team approach to coronary care. His commitment to ethical partnership between cardiac surgeons and cardiologists was recognized by the leadership of Transcatheter Therapeutics Asia-Pacific (TCTAP) in granting David Taggart the Master of Masters award in 2026, the first time a surgeon has ever received this prestigious award. In 2015, Taggart and Puskas co-founded the International Coronary Congress (ICC), and subsequently the International Society for Coronary Artery Surgery (https://internationalcoronarycongress.com). Now in its 12th year, ICC is the only annual international scientific meeting entirely devoted to advancing the state of the art in surgical coronary revascularization and has been attended by more than 10 000 cumulative delegates from more than 50 countries. From the inaugural meeting in 2015, Taggart delivered numerous lectures at each ICC meeting, engaged in many collegial debates and panel discussions and earned legions of admirers and friends from among his international coronary surgical colleagues. He was especially proud of having co-founded the International Coronary Congress; Taggart was an academic globalist who viewed world-class coronary surgery as something that should be available around the world. Moreover, he was convinced that coronary surgeons in all parts of the world could best advance the state of the art in coronary surgery by working and learning together. Taggart and Puskas created and personally funded the ICC Founders’ Fellowship to help defray the costs of attendance at each annual ICC meeting for young coronary surgical trainees and junior faculty; it has now been renamed the David Taggart Memorial Founders’ Fellowship. Taggart was immediately recognizable at the ICC or any other scientific meeting in his customary Oxford shirt and denim jeans, without a jacket or tie (Figure 1). David Taggart and John Puskas at the Inaugural Meeting of the International Coronary Congress, New York City, 2015. David Taggart was a tireless educator in coronary surgery globally and travelled the world delivering hundreds of invited lectures. He was a generous mentor to dozens of trainees and hundreds of colleagues worldwide. Also with Puskas, Taggart conceived and co-edited the 2021 Oxford University Press textbook entitled “State-of-the-Art Surgical Coronary Revascularization,” the first and only major textbook devoted solely to every nuance of surgical coronary revascularization.12 Taggart had many interests outside of cardiac surgery. He had an encyclopaedic knowledge of contemporary art. He loved sailing in the Mediterranean, snowboarding in the Alps, appreciated a good pub anywhere and possessed a mischievous sense of humour. In June 2026, only weeks before his death, he married Kathleen Hargreaves, his life partner, in an elegant ceremony in the Cotswolds, England. After a Mediterranean honeymoon, Taggart lectured in Asia in July 2026. Typical of David’s self-determination, he continued to live and to work as he saw fit, without breaking stride, despite his terminal illness. David Taggart’s greatest professional legacy is not an operation, conduit, clinical trial or controversy. It is an attitude towards our profession: surgeons must generate evidence rather than merely invoke experience; difficult improvements should not be dismissed because they require advanced training; important negative results deserve publication; and allegiance to institutions, specialties and even professional colleagues must remain subordinate to allegiance to our patients. He was a genuinely honest and honourable professional colleague. He was a tremendously productive academic partner for more than 20 years for each of us and a close friend to us both. We will miss him dearly. Godspeed, David Taggart. None declared. None declared. AI was used to confirm the accuracy of references and dates.

items.title: Coronary Dominance and Variations in Right Ventricular Failure After Left Ventricular Assist Device Implantation
Antithrombin III use in pediatric and neonatal ECMO: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Background Antithrombin (AT) supplementation has been increasingly incorporated into pediatric extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) anticoagulation protocols to address heparin resistance and optimize anticoagulation. However, considerable variability exists in monitoring practices, replacement strategies, and reported clinical outcomes. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate contemporary evidence regarding AT supplementation in pediatric ECMO. Methods A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science identified studies evaluating AT monitoring or supplementation during neonatal or pediatric ECMO through September 2025. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data on monitoring strategies, replacement protocols, anticoagulation parameters, thrombosis, bleeding, and mortality. Comparative studies reporting extractable dichotomous outcomes were included in random-effects meta-analyses. Results Twenty-five studies met inclusion criteria, consisting predominantly of retrospective single-center cohorts. Marked heterogeneity was observed in indications for supplementation, replacement thresholds (50-100%), therapeutic targets (60-120%), formulations, dosing strategies, and anticoagulation monitoring. AT supplementation consistently increased AT activity, improved anti-factor Xa measurements, and in several studies, reduced unfractionated heparin requirement. However, higher anti-Xa levels and increased AT activity did not consistently translate into improved clinical outcomes. Meta-analysis demonstrated no significant association between AT supplementation and thrombosis (OR 1.10, 95% 0.54-2.24), bleeding (OR 1.15, 95% CI 0.85-1.54), or mortality (OR 1.24, 95% CI 0.63-2.43). Pharmacokinetic investigations suggested standard dosing frequently underestimates replacement requirements in pediatric ECMO. Conclusion Current evidence supports the role of AT supplementation in improving laboratory markers of anticoagulation, but does not demonstrate consistent reductions in bleeding, thrombosis, or mortality. Wide variation in monitoring, dosing, and outcome definitions limits comparisons across studies. Future multicenter investigations should prioritize standardized definitions, age-specific therapeutic targets, and prospective evaluation of replacement strategies to better define the role of AT supplementation in pediatric ECMO.

items.title: Optimal timing of surgical intervention for post-myocardial infarction ventricular septal rupture: A comprehensive evidence review
items.abstract: Background Ventricular septal rupture (VSR) is a rare but devastating complication of acute myocardial infarction, historically associated with extremely high mortality rates. The optimal timing of surgical repair-balancing the risks of operating on friable, acute necrosis against the dangers of progressive cardiogenic shock during a waiting period-remains a central clinical dilemma. Methods A systematic narrative review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases were searched from 2000 to 2024 for studies comparing early (≤7 days) versus delayed (>7 days) surgical repair of post-MI VSR. Data were extracted on patient characteristics, mechanical circulatory support (MCS) use, surgical techniques, and clinical outcomes, including operative mortality, reoperation rates, and long-term survival. Results Evidence from contemporary observational studies confirms that delayed surgical repair is associated with significantly lower operative mortality compared to early repair, primarily due to superior tissue integrity and lower rates of residual shunt. However, this mortality gap has substantially narrowed in the contemporary era with routine use of advanced MCS, particularly veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) and Impella devices. These technologies enable hemodynamic stabilization, transforming early repair from a salvage procedure to a more controlled intervention. Modern management has evolved from a rigid temporal dichotomy to a patient-tailored strategy emphasizing immediate stabilization, risk stratification, and selective MCS bridging to the optimal surgical window. Conclusion While delayed repair remains preferred for hemodynamically stable patients, early repair supported by advanced MCS represents a viable and often necessary strategy for patients with refractory shock. The decision paradigm has shifted toward “stabilize, support, then repair,” requiring multidisciplinary heart team collaboration. Future directions include standardized MCS protocols, validated risk scores, and exploration of hybrid percutaneous-surgical approaches to further improve outcomes for this high-risk population.

items.title: Effects of patient demographic and clinical data on the assessment of cerebral oxygen monitoring values during coronary artery bypass grafting
items.abstract: Objectives To determine the effects of patient demographic and clinical data on regional cerebral oxygen saturation (rSO2) values. Design Prospective observational study. Setting Training and research hospital. Participants Eighty patients who were scheduled for elective on-pump coronary artery bypass grafting. Interventions Near-infrared spectroscopy was used to monitor bilateral brain oxygen saturation at twelve time points (T1–T12). Measurements and main results The right and left rSO2 values showed a ≥20% decrease pattern from T3 to T12. Patients with a ≥20% decline in the right rSO2 were older and had a higher baseline mean arterial pressure (MAP) and longer cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) times. Patients with a ≥20% decline in the left rSO2 had a higher baseline MAP. Age, baseline MAP, female sex and CPB time for the right rSO2 and baseline MAP values and female sex for the left rSO2 values were positively associated with a ≥20% decline in univariate logistic regression analyses. Baseline MAP and CPB time for the right rSO2 values and baseline MAP for the left rSO2 values retained their statistical significance in multivariate logistic regression analyses. Activated clotting time (ACT) showed a statistically significant and inverse relationship with the left rSO2 values. Conclusions Higher baseline MAP values for right and left rSO2 values and longer CPB times for right rSO2 values were independently associated with a ≥20% decline. ACT was inversely associated with a ≥20% decline in the left rSO2 values. Univariate analysis revealed that older age and female sex were associated with a ≥20% decline in rSO2values. Clinical trial number The study was registered at Clinicaltrials.gov (NCT07228546).

items.title: Standardizing cardiopulmonary bypass management for left ventricular assist device implantation: A clinical framework and checklist
items.abstract: Background Patients undergoing left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation often present with end-stage heart failure, severe pulmonary hypertension, and systemic inflammation. During this procedure, cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) acts as a double-edged sword: it provides essential life support but can exacerbate right ventricular (RV) dysfunction and trigger severe vasoplegia. Despite the critical nature of the transition from CPB to mechanical support, there is a lack of standardized, phase-specific CPB management protocols. Methods Based on current guidelines, frontline perfusion experience, and an interdisciplinary approach integrating mechanical engineering principles with surgical practice, a comprehensive clinical framework for CPB management was developed. The protocol deconstructs the procedure into four distinct phases: pre-bypass assessment, on-bypass management, weaning, and post-bypass care. Results A four-stage standardized checklist and an intraoperative emergency quick reference card were created to facilitate clinical translation. Key interventions include identifying anatomical “minefields,” maintaining a golden balance of hemodilution, executing a dynamic flow-speed handover to prevent suction events, and managing hemodynamics cautiously during protamine administration to mitigate RV dysfunction. Conclusions Standardizing CPB management during LVAD implantation provides a practical tool to optimize hemodynamic stability and improve perioperative safety.

items.title: Lunar phases, meteorological conditions, astrological signs, and postoperative outcomes of acute type A aortic dissection: Results of a retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Background Acute type A aortic dissection (ATAAD) is a surgical emergency associated with high mortality. While patient-related risk factors are well-established, beliefs persist regarding the influence of lunar phases, meteorological conditions, and astrological signs on disease occurrence and outcomes. Methods We retrospectively analysed all patients who underwent emergency surgery for ATAAD at Bordeaux University Hospital between 1996 and 2020. The primary objective was to assess the association between environmental factors (lunar phases, atmospheric pressure, temperature, and astrological signs) and ATAAD incidence. Secondary objectives included assessing their association with 30-day mortality and postoperative morbidity (intensive care unit length of stay, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation use, and mesenteric infarction). Meteorological data were available for 603 patients from 2010 onward. Results Among 920 patients (70% male; mean age 63 ± 13 years), the 30-day mortality rate was 9.7%. Lunar phases were not associated with ATAAD incidence (first quarter 26%, last quarter 25%, new moon 25%, full moon 24%; p = 0.91), mortality, or complications. Atmospheric pressure showed no association with ATAAD occurrence or outcomes. Temperature showed a weak correlation with ATAAD incidence (r = 0.11, p = 0.01), but not with mortality. Astrological signs were not associated with ATAAD incidence, mortality, or morbidity. Longer cardiopulmonary bypass duration (odds ratio [OR] = 0.994 per minute; p = 0.01) and diabetes (OR = 4.63; p = 0.01) were associated with 30-day mortality. Conclusions Environmental factors were not associated with ATAAD incidence or outcomes. Established clinical factors remain the primary determinants of mortality.

items.title: Impact of hypothermia level on neurological and renal outcomes in emergency aortic surgery: a single-centre experience
items.abstract: Background Temperature management during emergency surgery for acute aortic syndrome is critical for neurological, renal, and systemic protection. Recent European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (EACTS) guidelines recommend moderate hypothermia with antegrade cerebral perfusion for hemiarch procedures. Nevertheless, deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA) remains common. This study evaluates neurological and other postoperative outcomes across different intraoperative temperature ranges. Methods A single-centre retrospective study of consecutive patients undergoing surgery for acute aortic syndrome between 2018–2023. Demographic, intraoperative, and postoperative data on mortality, hospitalization, neurological, renal outcomes, and blood product usage were collected. Patients were stratified by intraoperative temperature: deep (≤20°C), low-moderate (20.1–24°C), high-moderate (24.1–28°C), and mild (>28°C) hypothermia. Logistic regression identified predictors of binary adverse outcomes. A sensitivity analysis was conducted using 24.0°C as the threshold in hemiarch surgery patients. Results A total of 175 patients (median age 64 years; 37% female) were included; of whom 89% underwent hemiarch replacement. Cardiopulmonary bypass duration decreased progressively with warmer intraoperative temperatures, ranging from 270.5 minutes in deep hypothermia to 164 minutes in mild hypothermia. The 30-day mortality was 18.9% ( n = 33/175), and the overall stroke rate was 19.4% ( n = 34/175). Among patients undergoing hemiarch repair, warmer temperatures were associated with lower stroke incidence (mild hypothermia 11%) compared with high-moderate (8.8%), low-moderate (26%), and deep hypothermia (27%) ( p = 0.049), and with shorter intensive care admission ( p = 0.036). However, multivariate regression showed that the four-category comparison did not reach significance for the assessed outcomes once adjusted for confounding variables. A sensitivity analysis at 24.0°C showed an independent association with reduced stroke risk (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.08-0.64, p = 0.005). Discussion Our findings support current EACTS recommendations favouring moderate-to-mild hypothermia for hemiarch replacement, with potential protective effects. Further studies should determine the optimal temperature strategy for patients undergoing total arch replacement.

items.title: Interpreting persistent vasopressor dependence during VA ECMO weaning
Comparing hemolysis among extracorporeal pumps: A large-scale retrospective study
items.abstract: Background Hemolysis is a frequent and clinically relevant complication during extracorporeal life support (ECLS, or ECMO), associated with acute kidney injury, systemic inflammation, and increased mortality. Direct comparisons between pumps regarding hemolysis are limited. This study evaluated and compared hemolysis profiles among several devices in clinical practice. Methods We conducted a retrospective, single-center cohort study adult patients who received veno-arterial (V-A) or veno-venous (V-V) ECMO between January 2020 and December 2023 ( N = 230). Patients were categorized by one of four ECMO pump types, and hemolysis was assessed using lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and plasma-free hemoglobin (pfHb) as primary markers. Multivariable linear mixed-effects models were used to analyze associations between pump type and hemolysis, adjusting for several covariates including revolutions per minute (RPM), hematologic indices, ECMO mode, and severity scores. Results Partial thromboplastin time ( p < 0.005), hemoglobin ( p < 0.001), and use of continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT, p < 0.001) were positively correlated with both LDH and pfHb concentrations and hemolysis, while fibrinogen ( p < 0.03) was inversely correlated. Without RPM adjustment, NovaLung exhibited the highest LDH (680.3 U/L) and pfHb (29.4 mg/dL), followed by the Cardiohelp, Rotaflow, and CentriMag. In the RPM-adjusted analysis, LDH was highest in Cardiohelp (737.4 U/L), followed by the Rotaflow, CentriMag, and NovaLung; whereas pfHb was highest in Cardiohelp (25.8 mg/dL), followed by the Rotaflow, NovaLung, and CentriMag. Conclusions This study provides a clinical associations of the safety and performance of four centrifugal pumps in real-world ECMO practice in adults. We demonstrate that pump-specific RPM may be potentially correlated with hemolysis during ECMO in clinical practice, illustrating that the diagonal pump, which operated at the highest RPMs, was associated with the highest hemolysis in models without the RPM adjustment. Future studies are warranted to further clarify the impact of hemolysis on outcomes.

items.title: ICare-FASTER (Improving Care by Faster Risk Stratification Through Use of High-Sensitivity Point-of-Care Troponin in Patients Presenting With Possible Acute Coronary Syndrome in the Emergency Department): A Stepped-Wedge Cluster-Randomized Trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Point-of-care high-sensitivity cTn (cardiac troponin; hs-cTn) testing has the potential to expedite decision-making and reduce emergency department (ED) length of stay for patients presenting with possible myocardial infarction by ensuring that results are consistently available when sought by clinicians. We assessed the real-life effectiveness and safety of implementing point-of-care hs-cTn testing in the ED. METHODS: We conducted a pragmatic, stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trial. The control arm was usual care with an accelerated diagnostic pathway using a single-sample rule-out step with a central laboratory hs-cTn assay. The intervention arm used the same pathway with a point-of-care hs-cTnI assay. The primary effectiveness outcome was ED length of stay assessed using a generalized linear mixed model. The safety outcome was myocardial infarction or cardiac death within 30 days. RESULTS: Six sites participated, with 59 980 ED presentations (44 747 individuals; mean 61±19 years of age; 49.5% female) from February 2023 through January 2025; 31 392 presentations were during the intervention arm. After adjustment for covariates associated with length of stay, the intervention reduced length of stay by 13% (95% CI, 9%–16%; P <0.001), corresponding to a reduction of 47 minutes (95% CI, 33–61 minutes) from a mean length of stay in the control arm of 376 minutes. The 30-day myocardial infarction or cardiac death rate was similar in the control and intervention arms (0.39% and 0.39%, respectively; P =0.54). CONCLUSIONS: Implementation of whole-blood hs-cTnI testing at the point of care into an accelerated diagnostic pathway was safe and reduced length of stay in the ED compared with laboratory testing. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.anzctr.org.au ; Unique identifier: ACTRN12619001189112.

items.title: Opportunistic Screening for Chagas Disease Using an Artificial Intelligence–Enabled ECG: Prospective Evaluation of Feasibility and Diagnostic Accuracy
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chagas disease (ChD), a neglected cardiovascular condition, affects 7.5 to 10.5 million people worldwide. Opportunistic screening during routine electrocardiography may allow earlier detection of unrecognized infections, enabling timely antiparasitic therapy or optimized cardiac care. This study prospectively evaluated the feasibility and diagnostic accuracy of an artificial intelligence (AI)–enabled ECG model enriched with 3 epidemiological questions (AI-ECG-EPI model) as an opportunistic screening for ChD in endemic regions of Brazil. METHODS: We conducted a prospective study embedded in the Telehealth Network of Minas Gerais, Brazil, across 107 municipalities in hyperendemic and endemic regions. From October 2023 to September 2024, adults undergoing routine tele-ECGs were eligible. The primary exposure was the output of the AI-ECG-EPI model: all positive individuals and a 3:1 sample of negative individuals were invited for serology (index test–dependent sampling), the reference standard. Weighted analyses (inverse probability) accounted for this sampling design. Diagnostic metrics included sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios, area under the receiver operating characteristics curve, and area under the precision recall curve. The AI-ECG-EPI model was compared with both an epidemiological questions model and an AI ECG–only model. RESULTS: Among 75 779 eligible ECGs, the AI-ECG-EPI model was available for 59 154 individuals; 6812 (11.5%) screened positive. A total of 7804 selected were invited for serology, and 3509 completed testing (2517 positive; 992 negative). ChD was confirmed in 36.8% of positive and 9.3% of negative individuals. The weighted prevalence of ChD was 12.2%. Sensitivity was 34.3%, specificity 91.6%, harmonic mean of precision and recall score 0.52, and diagnostic odds ratio 5.69. The AI-ECG-EPI model showed higher discrimination than both the epidemiological questions model and AI ECG–only model (area under the receiver operating characteristics curve, 77.6% versus 70.0% and 64.5%, respectively; P <0.001). Precision recall curves showed higher precision across most recall levels. Exploratory analysis suggested improved risk reclassification (net reclassification improvement, 0.503). Performance was higher in women and in individuals with Chagas cardiomyopathy. CONCLUSIONS: In this community-based study, an AI-ECG-EPI model integrated into a public telecardiology network enabled feasible opportunistic screening for ChD in primary care. It showed acceptable diagnostic accuracy, with higher discrimination than epidemiological questions and AI ECG–only models, and identified many previously undiagnosed patients in endemic regions, supporting its potential role in scalable screening strategies. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT02646943.

items.title: Correction to: Abstract 4365705: Cardiology Medications and Medicare Spending: Opportunities for Savings Using Mark Cuban Cost Plus Drug Company and Costco Member Prescription Program Pricing
Radiation Vasculopathy of the Coronary Arteries: State-of-the Art Review
items.abstract: Radiation-associated coronary artery disease (RACAD) is a distinct form of coronary artery disease with several specific biological and clinical aspects as well as key knowledge gaps. RACAD is prevalent in patients with cardiac exposure to radiotherapy. As radiotherapy is integral to the effective treatment of many thoracic malignancies, improved long-term survivorship is coupled with increased risk for RACAD. Ionizing radiation induces free radical generation and activation of proinflammatory cascades, leading to endothelial dysfunction and accelerated atherosclerosis. Risks for RACAD are determined both by radiotherapy, including the radiation dose and the proximity of coronary arteries to the radiotherapy field, and by patient-specific factors, such as younger age, higher baseline cardiovascular risk, and concurrent cardiotoxic systemic therapies. Importantly, radiotherapy delivery is highly individualized on the basis of tumor location and treatment strategy, resulting in heterogeneous coronary exposure to radiation and patient-to-patient variability. Clinical presentation may occur early, within 1 to 2 years, especially in patients with higher cardiac radiation doses (eg, lung or esophageal cancer), or after a latency period of 5 to 20 years with lower cardiac dose radiation exposure (eg, left-sided breast cancer). Patients generally present with symptoms similar to conventional coronary artery disease. However, RACAD symptoms may be underrecognized in cancer survivors due to overlapping treatment-related fatigue, pulmonary disease, or competing oncologic symptoms. Diagnosis and management generally follow standard coronary artery disease guidelines while incorporating cancer-specific considerations, such as planned oncologic surgeries, bleeding risk, postradiotherapy complications such as atretic internal mammary arteries, and cardiotoxic effects of systemic cancer therapies. Primary prevention of RACAD is critical, emphasizing advances in precision radiotherapy, including delivery techniques with improved coronary dosimetry, and cardiac shielding. Key knowledge gaps include understanding long-term outcomes with contemporary 3-dimensional conformal radiotherapy techniques, validated cancer-specific risk prediction models on the basis of coronary dosimetry, optimal surveillance protocols, targeted molecular pharmacotherapies, and risk analysis of percutaneous versus surgical management of RACAD. Prospective studies are needed to develop cancer- and dosimetry-specific risk calculators, validating cardioprotective interventions, and improving multidisciplinary cardio-oncology collaboration to optimize early detection of RACAD and timely intervention in the growing population of cancer survivors.
