Key studies in acute cardiovascular care
Beyond the lifestyle paradigm: environmental triggers and susceptible cardiovascular phenotypes
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Air pollution before and during the COVID-19 pandemic: changes in risk of acute myocardial infarction’, by M. Ishii et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag102 and the discussion piece ‘Beyond clinical phenotypes: endotype-specific environmental cardiovascular susceptibility’, by M. Ishii et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag814. We read with interest the nationwide study by Ishii et al.1 on short-term fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure and acute myocardial infarction (AMI) before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. The most striking finding, in our view, was not the pollution–AMI association itself but how it behaved across phenotypes: PM2.5-associated risk of myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) fell during the pandemic, while no comparable change was seen for infarction with obstructive coronary disease.1 This selective attenuation raises a question that extends well beyond this dataset: can a single environmental exposure preferentially trigger different cardiovascular phenotypes, depending on the susceptibility of the individual exposed? MINOCA is not one disease but several—coronary vasospasm, microvascular dysfunction, thromboembolism, spontaneous coronary dissection, and other mechanisms.2 Each pathway could plausibly respond differently to the inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, autonomic imbalance, and prothrombotic tendency that air pollution is known to provoke.3 Read this way, the data from Ishii et al.1 support a susceptibility–trigger–phenotype model: pollution supplies the trigger, an individual's vascular or coronary substrate determines the susceptibility, and the clinical event is the resulting phenotype—a different starting point from treating PM2.5 as a generic risk factor that simply raises AMI incidence across the board.

items.title: Beyond clinical phenotypes: endotype-specific environmental cardiovascular susceptibility
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Air pollution before and during the COVID-19 pandemic: changes in risk of acute myocardial infarction’, by M. Ishii et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag102 and the discussion piece ‘Beyond the lifestyle paradigm: environmental triggers and susceptible cardiovascular phenotypes’, by S. Saeed et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag813. We thank Saeed et al.1 for their thoughtful commentary on our study and for proposing a susceptibility–trigger–phenotype framework for environmental cardio vascular risk. We agree that this perspective may help move the field beyond viewing fine particulate matter (PM2.5) as a uniform cardiovascular risk factor. Our study showed that the association between short-term PM2.5 exposure and acute myocardial infarction varied according to clinical phenotype. Attenuation of the PM2.5-associated risk for myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) during the COVID-19 pandemic was observed, whereas no significant change was observed in myocardial infarction with obstructive coronary artery disease.2 However, these observational data do not indicate that changes in PM2.5 exposure cause the temporal difference, nor can they identify the mechanisms underlying MINOCA. This distinction is important because MINOCA is an umbrella syndrome encompassing heterogeneous coronary mechanisms, including epicardial spasm, microvascular spasm, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, coronary thromboembolism, and other mechanisms.3

items.title: From individual markers to reformulable processing signatures in hypertension prevention
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Markers of ultra-processed food and incident arterial hypertension in the UK Biobank’, by K. M. Krost et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag614 and the discussion piece ‘Characterizing co-occurrence patterns of potentially disease-relevant markers of ultra-processed food’, by K. M. Krost et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag843. Krost et al.1 should be commended for moving the ultra-processed food debate from a binary label towards ingredient-level markers. In 101 560 UK Biobank participants, they identified four marker-of-ultra-processing (MUP) categories associated with incident arterial hypertension and, importantly, showed that several other categories were not.1 Their key translational opportunity may lie one level above individual MUPs: constructing processing-marker signatures that can be linked to food reformulation. The Marker Likelihood Index (MLI) converts each reported food item into marker-bearing food mass according to the marker’s frequency across matched commercial products.1 Consequently, flavour, colouring agent, sweetener, and varieties of sugar may encode a recurring product phenotype rather than four separable exposures. Supplementary Figure 2 makes this co-occurrence empirically visible.1 The resulting percentage of total food intake represents marker-bearing food exposure rather than the ingested dose of the marker itself: a 50-g portion with an MLI of 0.6 contributes 30 g of marker-bearing food, not 30 g of additive.1 We view these features not as weaknesses, but as an opportunity to ask a more policy-relevant question: which combinations of markers characterize foods whose replacement is associated with lower hypertension risk?

items.title: Characterizing co-occurrence patterns of potentially disease-relevant markers of ultra-processed food
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Markers of ultra-processed food and incident arterial hypertension in the UK Biobank’, by K. M. Krost et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag614, and the Discussion Forum contribution ‘From individual markers to reformulable processing signatures in hypertension prevention’, by Y. Z. Huang, https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag842. We thank Dr. Huang for his interest in our study on markers of ultra-processed food (MUPs) and incident arterial hypertension in the UK Biobank and his thoughtful comments. We agree that an important translational opportunity lies in moving beyond individual MUP analyses towards MUP patterns that can inform food reformulation. As MUPs co-occur within the same foods, associations observed for individual markers may partly reflect shared underlying product characteristics. We therefore consider the proposed investigation of MUP co-occurrence patterns an important direction for future research. An important step towards characterizing these MUP co-occurrences is to define potentially disease-relevant MUPs and distinguish them from MUPs without evidence of adverse health associations. Thus, identifying MUPs that are consistently associated with adverse health outcomes using Cox proportional hazards regression models can provide an important starting point for investigating the biological mechanisms that may underlie these associations. Together with our findings on incident arterial hypertension,1 evidence from two further UK Biobank studies on mortality2 and depression risk3 suggests that added flavour, colouring agent, and sweetener may represent potentially disease-relevant MUPs. Future studies should investigate whether these MUPs are also associated with further adverse health outcomes, including other cardiometabolic diseases and various types of cancer. The next step should include mechanistic studies investigating the pathways by which these disease-relevant MUPs might affect human physiology and health. Randomized controlled crossover trials, building on previous studies investigating the effects of ultra-processed foods (UPF),4 could further characterize these MUPs by comparing otherwise closely matched foods or diets with and without these MUPs and assessing relevant clinical outcomes.

items.title: Familial hypercholesterolaemia and thymic ageing in a Chinese cohort
items.abstract: Background and Aims Lifelong exposure to elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol in familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) patients not only increases the risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, but also affects other organs beyond the cardiovascular system. In a large FH cohort, this study investigated the effects of hypercholesterolaemia on the thymic output and explored whether lipid-lowering therapy can reverse these effects. Methods According to the Dutch Lipid Clinic Network criteria, 562 heterozygous FH patients (236 treatment-naïve, 326 on lipid-lowering therapy) and 295 age-matched healthy controls (HCs) were enrolled. Thymic output was measured by circulating CD4+ recent thymic emigrants (RTEs) with flow cytometry, and T-cell receptor excision circles in sorted naïve CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Repertoire diversity and clonal expansion were evaluated by T-cell receptor beta sequencing. Results Compared with HCs, treatment-naïve FH patients displayed a significantly reduced percentage of CD4+ RTE among naïve CD4+ T cells, particularly in those aged 18–30 years or carrying highly pathogenic LDLR variants. T-cell receptor excision circle analysis supported reduced thymic output in both CD4+ and CD8+ naïve T cells. Quantified thymic ageing further showed that FH patients reached the median CD4+ RTE percentage of HCs ∼6 years earlier (males: 19.12 vs 25.51 years; females: 19.18 vs 25.58 years). Consistent with reduced thymic output, FH patients showed skewing towards high-frequency T-cell receptor beta clones. Statin-treated FH patients, particularly females, showed higher circulating CD4+ RTE levels than statin-naïve FH patients. Conclusions Hypercholesterolaemia was associated with reduced thymic output, while statin-treated patients showed partially preserved circulating CD4+ RTE levels, supporting integrated metabolic and immunologic strategies for FH management.

items.title: Correction: Fifth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2026): On behalf of the Joint European Society of Cardiology (ESC)/American College of Cardiology (ACC)/American Heart Association (AHA)/World Heart Federation (WHF) Task Force for the Universal Definition of Myocardial InfarctionEndorsed by the European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (EACTS) and the Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS)Affirmation of Value by the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI)
Acute heart failure in emergency settings
items.abstract: Acute heart failure (AHF) represents a major cause of emergency medical care worldwide and continues to carry a substantial burden of morbidity and mortality despite advances in chronic heart failure management. Most patients with AHF present to emergency departments (EDs), where the first hours of care are critical to determine prognosis. Of these, some have been previously evaluated and treated by prehospital emergency medical services before ED arrival. This consensus document summarizes the current evidence and provides practical advice to emergency physicians for the diagnosis, treatment, and disposition of patients with AHF in these emergency settings (emergency medical services and ED). It emphasizes the importance of a rapid phenotypic classification into acute decompensated heart failure, acute pulmonary oedema, isolated right ventricular failure, or cardiogenic shock, as a key tool to guide early management and triage decisions. It reviews evidence on prehospital and ED management, including the use of biomarkers, imaging, ventilatory support, diuretic and vasodilator strategies, and early initiation or continuation of guideline-directed medical therapy. It also discusses risk stratification and disposition decisions supported by validated tools. Finally, it identifies major knowledge gaps and future research priorities, including pragmatic trials to assess prehospital interventions, biomarker-guided therapy, and early initiation of disease-modifying treatments. Ultimately, this consensus document is aimed to contribute to the improvement of outcomes in AHF.

items.title: Correction to: 2026 ESC Guidelines on cardiac rehabilitation: Developed by the task force on cardiac rehabilitation of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC)Endorsed by the European Society of Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine (ESPRM) and World Organization of Family Doctors (WONCA)
Guidelines on rehabilitation and a focus on lifestyle-related cardiovascular prevention
items.abstract: For the podcast associated with this article, please visit https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/pages/Podcasts. This Issue starts with an ESC Guidelines article entitled ‘2026 ESC Guidelines on cardiac rehabilitation’, by Maria Bäck from the University of Gothenburg, Sweden, and colleagues.1 These updated practical guidelines establish a comprehensive, patient-centred framework for cardiac rehabilitation, an important form of treatment frequently underutilized in daily clinical practice.2–4 The Issue continues with a focus on Epidemiology, prevention, and healthcare policies. Pregnancy represents a critical period during which the maternal cardiovascular (CV) system adapts to profound haemodynamic and metabolic demands. When these adaptive mechanisms are impaired, adverse pregnancy outcomes (APOs)—including hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, gestational diabetes, pre-term birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and pregnancy loss—occur.5–8 In a State of the Art Review article entitled ‘Adverse pregnancy outcomes and long-term cardiovascular risk: lifelong connections’, Veronica Giorgione Nunes from St George's University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust in London, UK, and colleagues summarize current evidence with four aims: (i) to quantify the magnitude of CV risk after specific APOs; (ii) to outline shared pathophysiology linking APOs and CV disease (CVD); (iii) to chart the temporal course of the CV legacy from early post-partum CV findings to later organ damage; and (iv) to translate these insights into pragmatic strategies for prevention, covering optimal fourth-trimester care and the system gaps that impede its delivery.9 Extensive epidemiological evidence demonstrates that APOs are not isolated obstetric events but early clinical markers of cardiometabolic dysfunction that identify women at increased risk of coronary artery disease (CAD), heart failure, stroke, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and premature CV mortality. Shared mechanisms include endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and insulin resistance, establishing a continuum between obstetric complications and later CVD. Early post-partum studies reveal persistent hypertension, adverse cardiac remodelling, and metabolic abnormalities that mediate much of the long-term excess CV risk. These findings redefine the ‘fourth trimester’ as a preventive window in which timely blood pressure surveillance, metabolic screening, and lifestyle optimization can yield durable CV benefit. Integrated cardio-obstetric care models, digital follow-up, and systematic transition to primary care are crucial for maintaining long-term prevention. Addressing persistent gaps in limited provider awareness, fragmented follow-up, and disparities across socially disadvantaged populations remains critical. Recognizing pregnancy complications as indicators of underlying CV vulnerability offers an opportunity to shift prevention upstream and promote lifelong CV health for women. A construct is only as actionable as the diagnostic pathway that supports it. Recent patient-led advocacy and policy initiatives—including the designation of March as Endometriosis Awareness Month—have strengthened public and professional recognition of this debilitating disease and promoted earlier clinical evaluation. In a Viewpoint article entitled ‘Endometriosis as a cardiovascular risk enhancer’, Benjamin Marchandot and Oliver Morel from the University Hospital of Strasbourg, France, aim to highlight endometriosis as a potential CV risk factor in women and propose a practical approach for incorporating it into atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD) risk assessment and prevention.10 Endometriosis is a chronic, systemic neuroinflammatory disorder affecting an estimated ∼190 million people worldwide (∼1 in 10 women of reproductive age). Convergent epidemiological and mechanistic evidence links endometriosis to increased risk of ASCVD, yet contemporary risk frameworks rarely capture this contribution, and prevention pathways remain inconsistent. In parallel, the diagnostic landscape is shifting; alongside imaging and specialist centres, non-invasive molecular signature-based assays may compress the diagnostic interval from years to days, opening a practical window for earlier CV risk profiling. This viewpoint reframes endometriosis as a sex-specific, non-communicable CV risk enhancer and sets out a pragmatic, testable two-step prevention pathway. Step 1 prioritizes systematic identification and consistent documentation of endometriosis in symptomatic individuals, with explicit risk tagging to trigger CV assessment. Step 2 activates a guideline-aligned prevention strategy: structured baseline assessment; use of existing risk estimation tools with endometriosis documented as a risk enhancer; guideline-based management of traditional and lifestyle-related risk factors; and timed reassessment with escalation where warranted. A coordinated research agenda, spanning phenotypic stratification, risk prediction modelling, pragmatic intervention trials, and health-economic evaluations is outlined to test clinical benefit and scalability before guideline-level adoption. Ambient PM2.5 exposure is a known potent CV risk factor.11–13 Myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA) represents a subtype of acute MI (AMI) distinct from myocardial infarction with obstructive coronary disease (MI-CAD). In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Air pollution before and during the COVID-19 pandemic: changes in risk of acute myocardial infarction’, Masanobu Ishii from Kumamoto University, Japan, and colleagues investigate changes in the association between short-term exposure to PM2.5 and AMI subtypes following the COVID-19 pandemic.14 Public health measures during the COVID-19 pandemic may have altered exposure patterns, offering a natural experiment. Using data from the nationwide JROAD-DPC database, this study analysed ∼270 000 first-admission AMI patients, including ∼23 000 with MINOCA, between April 2012 and March 2022. A time-stratified case-crossover design with conditional logistic regression estimated the odds ratio (OR) for each 10 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5 exposure at a 2-day lag. The study period was divided into pre-pandemic and post-pandemic phases using 7 April 2020 as the threshold. Sensitivity analyses used alternative pandemic onset dates. Each 10 μg/m3 increase in lag-2 PM2.5 was significantly associated with an increased risk of AMI. Although the ORs for overall AMI and MI-CAD remained largely unchanged between periods, a significant attenuation of the PM2.5-related risk for MINOCA was observed (pre-pandemic OR 1.303; post-pandemic OR 1.230; P for interaction = .017). Sensitivity analyses confirmed these findings. The authors conclude that short-term exposure to PM2.5 is associated with increased risk of AMI. The observed reduction in MINOCA risk following the COVID-19 pandemic suggests that public health interventions aimed at reducing air pollution exposure may reduce CV risk, particularly in specific AMI subtypes. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Gianluigi Guida, Giandomenico Disabato, and Massimo Piepoli from IRCCS Policlinico San Donato in Milan, Italy.15 These authors note that Ishii et al. must be congratulated for their study which once again has highlighted the significant impact of environmental factors, such as air pollution, on CV health, providing some insights into the implicated pathophysiological mechanisms, and demonstrating the effects of changes in exposure and behaviour. The pandemic provided a unique opportunity to observe these effects, emphasizing the potential for targeted interventions to reduce pollution-related heart disease. The observational nature of the study inherently limits causal interpretation, and residual confounding from unmeasured factors cannot be entirely ruled out. Future research should clarify which behavioural and environmental changes most impact MINOCA risk, explore subtype-specific susceptibilities, assess global applicability, and evaluate the role of co-exposures. Tailored interventions could offer significant benefits, especially for populations most sensitive to environmental triggers. Physical exercise is an important protective factor.16–18 While vigorous physical activity (VPA) is known to provide greater health benefits per unit time than moderate activity, the spectrum of these benefits across different chronic diseases and the relative importance of physical activity (PA) intensity vs volume remain unclear. In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Volume vs intensity of physical activity and risk of cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular chronic diseases’, Jiehua Wei from Central South University in Changsha, China, and colleagues examine associations between the proportion of VPA (%VPA) relative to the total volume of PA and the incidence of multiple chronic disease outcomes.19 This prospective population-based cohort study included ∼96 400 participants (mean age 62 years, women: 56%) with device-measured data (wrist-worn accelerometers) and ∼375 700 participants (mean age 56 years, women: 52%) with self-reported PA data (IPAQ) from the UK Biobank. Main outcomes included incidence of eight chronic diseases: major adverse CV events (MACE), atrial fibrillation (AFib), type 2 diabetes (T2D), immune-mediated inflammatory diseases, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), chronic respiratory diseases (CRD), CKD, and dementia, as well as all-cause mortality. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals. In the device-measured data, non-linear inverse dose–response relationships were observed between %VPA and all outcomes (all P < .001), and these patterns remained consistent across strata of total PA volume. In multivariable models adjusted for total PA volume, participants with >4% VPA had 29%–61% lower risks of these outcomes compared with those with 0% VPA. Joint analyses and population attributable fraction revealed distinct disease-specific patterns: immune-mediated inflammatory diseases showed very strong intensity dependence with minimal contribution from PA volume (20% for intensity vs 1% for volume), while MACE (17.8% vs 6%), AFib (16.2% vs 5%), CRD (21% vs 5.6%), and dementia (32% vs 8.1%) demonstrated intensity predominance with modest contribution from PA volume, and T2D (27% vs 17.7%), MASLD (22% vs 16.6%), CKD (23% vs 15.3%), and all-cause mortality (31% vs 14%) showed more balanced contributions from both intensity and volume (Figure 1). Structured Graphical Abstract19 The authors conclude that a higher %VPA, independent of the volume of total activity, is inversely associated with eight major chronic diseases and all-cause mortality. Intensity consistently demonstrates a higher preventive potential than total PA volume. These findings support, whenever possible, prioritizing higher intensity activities in clinical and public health interventions aimed at preventing non-communicable diseases. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Fabian Schwendinger, Arno Schmidt-Trucksäss, and Henner Hanssen from the University of Basel, Switzerland.20 The authors underscore that across studies, a consistent finding emerges: higher intensity PA is associated with meaningful reductions in multiple health outcomes. Yet translation into routine clinical practice remains challenging. While intensity has become an increasingly refined construct in research, its implementation in primary and secondary prevention remains limited. While accumulating evidence supports PA intensity as a central component of prescription, most clinical recommendations continue to prioritize total PA rather than explicitly prescribing vigorous intensity as a primary therapeutic variable. Ultimately, PA and exercise prescription rely on shared decision-making. Primarily, recommendations to engage in PA need to match the fitness, health status, and biological age of the individual. For older frail individuals, for example, repeated sit-to-stand exercises may represent high relative intensity, whereas brisk or fast walking, or their combination as interval-type exercise, may be the most efficient trigger for cardiometabolic adaptations and improved individual health outcomes. This is because, even if the absolute intensity does not exceed the vigorous threshold (i.e. 6 METs), the intensity expressed relative to a person's exercise capacity may still be vigorous. In principle, the rule of thumb ‘the more the merrier’ for PA volume applies as a classic dose–response relationship, and potential side effects of higher doses of regular daily PA may be negligible. To simplify matters, any prescription of PA volume according to the general recommendation is an important cornerstone of a multi-modal treatment strategy to reduce the burden of CVD as well as overall chronic non-communicable disease. However, according to Wei et al., prioritizing higher intensity PA over volume, especially in the prevention of immune-mediated inflammatory disease, CRD, CVD, and dementia, may be key to achieve optimal health outcomes. This, however, must be shown in large, population-based randomized controlled trials. An optimal diet is important in CV prevention.21–23 Preservative food additives are substances added to prolong the shelf life of packaged products, protecting them against deterioration caused by microorganisms and/or growth of pathogens, and alterations caused by oxidation, such as fat rancidity and colour changes. items.title: Sex differences in cardiovascular disease burden, risk factors, and disease spectrum in Europe: a global burden of disease 2023 analysis within the ESC Atlas framework
items.abstract: Despite growing recognition of sex disparities in cardiovascular disease (CVD), contemporary, harmonized analyses of sex-specific burden in the European region that could inform targeted prevention strategies, remain limited. Sex-specific patterns in CVD burden and risk factor exposure across 55 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) member countries were examined using data from the 2023 Global Burden of Disease study. Risk factor exposure was quantified using age–sex-standardized summary exposure values for 10 established cardiovascular risk factors. Disease incidence and mortality for major CVD categories, including maternal hypertensive disorders, were estimated by calculating age–sex-standardized rates per 100 000 person-years using the 2013 European Standard Population. Analyses were performed by sex at country, regional, and ESC-wide levels and over time (1990–2023). In 2023, in the ESC region, the overall CVD burden was broadly similar in men and women, with women accounting for 55% (6.0 million) of cases and 50% of deaths (1.5 million). This apparent parity, however, concealed marked sex differences in disease composition, risk exposure, and geographic disparities. Compared with men, women had a lower proportion of CVD due to ischaemic heart disease (21% vs 38%) and a higher contribution from peripheral arterial disease (23% vs 19%). Major differences were also apparent in risk profiles, particularly for behavioural risk factors—with summary exposure values of tobacco and alcohol being 10%–20% points higher in men than women; contrasting with cardiometabolic factors, such as high body mass index and low physical activity, that were often 5%–15% points higher in women than men, and more modest differences in environmental and biological risks, including air pollution, fasting glucose, or cholesterol. Cardiovascular disease burden further varied widely across countries and disparities affected women more strongly than men, with an approximately three-fold difference between the lowest- and highest-incidence countries in women, compared with a two-fold difference in men, and even larger disparities in mortality and premature mortality (up to 25-fold in women). Maternal hypertensive disorders substantially shaped both the scale and composition of CVD burden in women, accounting for 25% of incident CVD in women and exhibiting substantial geographic variation, with up to 18-fold differences in incidence across countries. These findings challenge conventional approaches that treat CVD as a homogeneous condition. In particular, the substantial contribution of non-ischaemic conditions and maternal hypertensive disorders to the burden in women, alongside distinct patterns of risk exposure and wider geographic disparities, underscore the importance of adopting a life-course and sex- and gender-informed approach to cardiovascular prevention and policy.

items.title: A decade-long device–valve interaction: severe aortic regurgitation after residual ventricular septal defect closure
items.abstract: A NTI1008"49-year-old woman underwent tetralogy of Fallot repair at age 16, including closure of a 25 mm intracristal ventricular septal defect (VSD) and right ventricular outflow tract reconstruction. Sixteen years later, a postoperative residual VSD was closed transcatheterly. Eleven years after device implantation, echocardiography showed mild-to-moderate aortic regurgitation (AR), which progressed to severe over 2 years, while the ascending aortic diameter increased from 38 to 45 mm despite 6-month surveillance. At the current admission, three-dimensional transoesophageal echocardiography showed the occluder impinging on the non-coronary and right coronary cusps at the commissure, restricting cusp motion and producing severe AR on colour Doppler (Panel A). Computed tomography confirmed protrusion into the aortic valve complex (Panel B). At surgery, both cusps were markedly thickened and firmly adherent to the occluder at the commissure (Panel C). The protruding portion of the device and adherent cusp tissue were excised (Panel D), followed by mechanical aortic valve replacement (Panel E). Recovery was uneventful, with normal prosthetic function at 1 month.

items.title: When platelets are under pressure: an angiotensin II-TGF-β axis in hypertensive patients leads to receptor PAR4 overexpression
items.abstract: Angiotensin II-TGF-β1-Smad2 signalling promotes PAR4 overexpression and platelet priming in hypertension. The schematic depicts the proposed mechanism by which an angiotensin II-high hypertensive phenotype drives megakaryocyte reprogramming and platelet hyperreactivity. In normosensitive individuals and in hypertensive patients without increased angiotensin II signalling, TGF-β1, Smad2 activation, and platelet PAR4 expression remain unchanged, resulting in quiescent platelets. In contrast, increased angiotensin II signalling promotes TGF-β1/Smad2 activation in megakaryocytes, leading to increased PAR4 expression in newly generated platelets. PAR4-high platelets display increased platelet activation markers and are associated with enhanced thrombotic risk. Valsartan, through angiotensin II type 1 receptor blockade, attenuates this pathway and may reduce PAR4-dependent platelet activation in this specific hypertensive phenotype.

items.title: Fifth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction and an update on lipoprotein(a) and inflammation
items.abstract: For the podcast associated with this article, please visit https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/pages/Podcasts. This Issue starts with an ESC Guidelines article entitled ‘Fifth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2026): On behalf of the Joint European Society of Cardiology (ESC)/American College of Cardiology (ACC)/American Heart Association (AHA)/World Heart Federation (WHF) Task Force for the Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction Endorsed by the European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (EACTS), and the Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) Affirmation of Value by the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI)’, by Nicholas Mills from the University of Edinburgh, UK, and colleagues. The authors of this very much-awaited Fifth Universal Definition provide an updated, pathophysiology-based classification of Myocardial Infarction that standardizes the diagnosis, improves clinical care, promotes research, and defines disease coding.1 The Issue continues with a focus on dyslipidaemias. In a State of the Art Review article entitled ‘Lipoprotein apheresis in the era of new lipid-lowering therapies’, Francesco Sbrana from Fondazione Toscana Gabriele Monasterio in Pisa, Italy, and colleagues aim to review the current role of lipoprotein apheresis (LA) in managing severe lipid disorders, particularly homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (HoFH), and to highlight its benefits, current challenges, and potential future clinical applications.2 HoFH is a rare and severe genetic disorder characterized by extremely elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels from birth, resulting in a very high risk of premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and aortic outflow obstruction from both the aortic valve and supravalvular aortic stenosis. During the 1960s, in a pioneering way, LA was used to treat children with HoFH. Over the years, LA has evolved into increasingly selective methods, which have been used in paediatric HoFH since the 1990s. Today, LA is able to selectively remove atherogenic apoB100-containing lipoproteins from the blood: the main component of LDL-C, very LDL-cholesterol, and lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)]. LA has demonstrated protective effects in the endothelium and microcirculation, prevention of the development of new aortic and coronary lesions in HoFH, reducing the incidence of major cardiovascular events, and proving helpful in subjects who fail to reach the LDL-cholesterol target or who have elevated Lp(a) levels in secondary prevention. Although advances in pharmacological therapies (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin Type 9 inhibitors, antisense oligonucleotides, and siRNA-based treatments) have expanded the options for lipid management, LA remains a safe therapeutic approach for patients with severe lipid disorders, including HoFH, to reduce their cardiovascular risks. Currently, to put LA into perspective, some obstacles need to be overcome, including: (i) the underdiagnosis of HoFH and high Lp(a) levels; (ii) therapeutic inertia resulting from the use of new lipid-lowering drugs with partial achievement of lipid targets; and (iii) availability of qualified LA centres and practitioners. Further prospective studies may prove useful to identify other therapeutic scenarios for LA, such as renal disease, diabetic foot ulcer, peripheral arterial disease, pre-eclampsia, macular degeneration, or sudden sensorineural hearing loss. In these clinical settings, prospective, randomized clinical trials are therefore warranted. In a State of the Art Review article entitled ‘Homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia: insights from the Global HICC Registry’, Willemijn Schonck from the University of Amsterdam in The Netherlands, and colleagues outline the rationale, structure, and objectives of the HoFH International Clinical Collaborators (HICC) and highlights the key contributions of this global initiative to date in advancing the full clinical spectrum from diagnosis to outcomes in patients living with HoFH.3 To address the global paucity of observational data, the HICC registry was established. To date, over 950 HoFH individuals from 45 countries have been included. The median age at diagnosis was 12 years, and untreated LDL-C levels were markedly elevated (median 14.7 mmol/l). At diagnosis, 9% had ASCVD or (supra)aortic valve disease, and despite the widespread use of lipid-lowering therapy (LLT), only 4% achieved guideline-recommended LDL-C goals. Early initiation of LA was associated with greater LDL-C reductions and delayed ASCVD onset. Cardiovascular burden remains substantial, with a median age at death of 37 years. No sex differences were observed in age or clinical characteristics at diagnosis, treatment patterns, or timing of ASCVD, although the usual sex gap in cardiovascular disease onset was absent. Profound global disparities persist, including limited genetic screening, restricted access to LLT, and earlier onset of major adverse cardiovascular events in non-high-income countries. Reproductive care for women remains highly variable and understudied. The HICC aims to guide global stakeholders in improving clinical outcomes for individuals with HoFH through earlier diagnosis, equitable access to advanced therapies, and broader inclusion of underserved regions. By generating evidence from routine clinical care and patient-reported data, identifying gaps in care, and fostering international collaboration, HICC seeks to advance a more equitable and effective global approach to HoFH management. There is growing interest in Lp(a).4–13 Current guidance recommends better LDL-C control in patients with elevated Lp(a), as Lp(a)-lowering therapies are unavailable. Whether risks attributable to Lp(a) are mitigated in patients with CAD who achieved LDL-C < 55 mg/dl remains unknown. In a Fast Track Congress article entitled ‘Lipoprotein(a) and residual cardiovascular risks in Japanese patients with coronary artery disease who achieve guideline-recommended low-density lipoprotein cholesterol goals’, Yu Kataoka from the National Cerebral and Cardiovascular Center in Suita, Japan, and colleagues investigate whether elevated Lp(a) levels contribute to cardiovascular outcomes in Japanese patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) and to what extent lowering LDL-C < 55 mg/dl mitigates this risk.14 A multicentre retrospective observational study analysed 1581 Japanese patients with CAD. Risk of major cardiovascular events (MACE) was compared according to Lp(a) levels (<30, ≥30 and <50 mg/dl, and ≥50 mg/dl) and amongst LDL-C strata (<55 mg/dl vs ≥55 mg/dl) 8 weeks after PCI. During the 5.1-year observation amongst patients with LDL-C ≥ 55 mg/dl (n = 1069), MACE occurred in 21% with risk of MACE increasing with Lp(a) levels (3.9, 7.9, and 11.0 events per 100 person-years for <30, ≥30 and <50 mg/dl, and ≥50 mg/dl, log-rank P < .001). Amongst those with LDL-C < 55 mg/dl (n = 512), the proportion with MACE was lower overall (4.3%, P < .001). However, elevated Lp(a) levels still identified those at higher risk of MACE (1.4, 4.7, and 7.5 events per 100 person-years in Lp(a) < 30, ≥30 and <50 mg/dl, and ≥50 mg/dl, P < .001). The standardized 5-year MACE rate was over two and five times higher in patients with Lp(a) ≥ 30 and <50 mg/dl and ≥50 mg/dl compared with Lp(a) < 30 mg/dl. The ROC analyses identified Lp(a) ≥ 28 mg/dl as the threshold for MACE (AUC = .68, P < .001). The authors conclude that whilst lower achieved LDL-C attenuates in part the risk from Lp(a), elevated Lp(a) levels still associate with worse cardiovascular outcomes. The Lp(a) threshold amongst Japanese patients with CAD at risk of recurrent events appears lower than in Caucasian populations which merits further evaluation. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Florian Kronenberg from the Medical University of Innsbruck, Austria.15 The author notes that from a clinical practice perspective, the data strongly support routine measurement of Lp(a) at least once in all adults, as recommended by recent ESC/EAS and US recommendations, and particularly in Japanese and other East-Asian patients in whom risk thresholds appear lower. In those with elevated Lp(a), clinicians should pursue long-term intensified LDL-C lowering and systematically address all modifiable risk factors, recognizing that such measures attenuate but do not abolish Lp(a)-mediated risk, as also demonstrated in the Japanese study. These recommendations are strongly supported and extended to Japanese practice by Kataoka et al.: achieving LDL-C < 55 mg/dl was associated with lower standardized 5-year MACE rates across all Lp(a) categories compared with remaining above this threshold. Even in patients with high Lp(a), lowering LDL-C into the guideline-recommended range attenuated, although it did not eliminate, risk. These observations are consistent with the concept that LDL-C and Lp(a) confer largely independent risks, and that lowering LDL-C is necessary but insufficient when Lp(a) is markedly elevated. We are now just a short time away from the results of the first outcome trial of a potent, specific Lp(a)-lowering therapy. Until now, we have only been able to speculate on the potential clinical consequences of these therapies. The first outcome studies will hopefully clarify what Lp(a) levels are required for study inclusion and whether there are heterogeneities in the results across different subgroups. This will help us design future Lp(a)-lowering programmes that are globally inclusive rather than anchored to thresholds derived from White populations alone. Inflammation plays a key role in atherothrombosis and markers of inflammation predict cardiovascular events.10,16–19 An elevated level of either interleukin-6 (IL-6) or high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) is associated with poor cardiovascular outcomes after acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Whether the prognostic information provided by hsCRP and IL-6 is independent and complementary after ACS is unclear. In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein prognostic value following acute coronary syndrome’, Johan Wouter Jukema from Leiden University Medical Center in The Netherlands, and colleagues aim to determine whether baseline levels and changes in IL-6 and hsCRP, individually or together, independently predict MACE and death after acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in statin-treated patients.20 The ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial compared alirocumab with placebo in post-ACS patients on optimized statin therapy. In post-hoc analyses, the relation between log-transformed hsCRP and IL-6 levels and risk of MACE and all-cause death was assessed in proportional hazards models. A total of about 11 800 patients had baseline hsCRP and IL-6 data; 1306 had a MACE primary endpoint and 458 died. Median hsCRP, IL-6, and LDL-C were 1.54 mg/l, 5 pg/ml, and 86 mg/dl, respectively. hsCRP and IL-6 had moderate correlation (r = 0.52). In models for one biomarker adjusted for the other biomarker, treatment assignment, age, sex, diabetes, LDL-C, and time since index ACS, hsCRP was a significant independent predictor of MACE (P < .0001) and IL-6 was not (P = .21); both independently predicted death (P < .0001 for hsCRP and P = .0003 for IL-6). Relationships did not depend on treatment (all Pinteraction > .25). When dichotomized at 2 mg/l (hsCRP) and 5 pg/ml (IL-6), risks of MACE and death were significantly elevated when both, but not when one marker was elevated (Figure 1). Inflammasomes are key signalling platforms that detect noxious stimuli and activate the highly pro-inflammatory cytokine, IL-1β, which stimulates elaboration of IL-6 by inflammatory cells and CRP by the liver. When dichotomized at conventional thresholds (5 pg/ml for IL-6; 2 mg/l for hsCRP), MACE and death following ACS were significantly higher only when both biomarkers were elevated. ACS, acute coronary syndrome; CI, confidence interval; CRP, C-reactive protein; hsCRP, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein; IL, interleukin; MACE, major adverse cardiovascular events; NLRP3, nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat-containing pyrine receptor 3.20 The authors conclude that in patients with recent ACS, hsCRP independently predicts MACE, while both hsCRP and IL-6 predict death. Together, the two markers provide complementary prognostic information. hsCRP conveys independent information on inflammatory risk beyond that provided by IL-6. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Erik Stroes and Maxim Annink from the University of Amsterdam in The Netherlands.21 The authors highlight that the study by Jukema et al. makes a strong case for rethinking how we assess inflammatory risk after ACS. The observation that combined rather than individual biomarker elevation drives MACE risk is itself an argument against relying on any single inflammatory marker. This is supported by recent work by Nurmohamed et al. showing that targeted proteomics can identify inflammatory proteins predictive of MACE even in patients with low CRP levels, pinpointing pathways that CRP misses altogether. Just as lipid risk assessment has evolved from LDL-C alone towards integrated evaluation including Lp(a) and triglyceride-rich remnants, inflammatory risk stratification should move towards multi-marker panels that capture the diversity of proatherogenic inflammatory pathways. Such panels could help select patients for emerging and probably costly anti-inflammatory therapies, aligning treatment intensity with individual pathobiology. The goal is not a single number that summarizes inflammation, but a profile that guides precision, and perhaps intensity, of the intervention. As anti-inflammatory cardiovascular therapies progress from proof-of-concept to clinical implementation, translating the optimal inflammatory signature into scalable, actionable tools will be an important next step. In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Cholesterol-lowering therapy from childhood/adolescence and long-term outcomes in familial hypercholesterolaemia: the SAFEHEART study’, Antonio Vallejo-Vaz from the University of Seville, Spain, and colleagues assess the long-term impact of contemporary management of FH on LDL-C and cardiovascular events.22 Evidence supporting initiation of cholesterol-lowering medication (CLM) in childhood to lower this cumulative cholesterol burden and cardiovascular sequelae is sparse. SAFEHEART is an observational prospective cohort study including children/adolescents (age <18 years) with genetically confirmed heterozygous FH (FH-Ch), their non-affected children and adolescents’ relatives (non-FH-Ch), and FH parents (FH-P). Impact of CLM, LDL-C burden, and cardiovascular events were assessed. Overall, 348 FH-Ch, 165 non-FH-Ch, and 288 FH-P were included (50% female; median untreated LDL-C: 5.46, 2.63, and 7.19 mmol/l, respectively). Median follow-up was 12.4 years. At follow-up, 84% FH-Ch, 4.2% non-FH-Ch, and 95% FH-P were receiving CLM. FH-Ch started therapy at a median age of 14.5 vs 36 years in their FH-P. Latest on-treatment LDL-C was 3 mmol/l in FH-Ch and 2.44 mmol/l in FH-P; LDL-C among non-FH-Ch (not on CLM) was 2.72 mmol/l. By age 30–40 years, median LDL-C burden over life was 5909 and 10 207 mg/dl*years among FH-Ch and FH-P, respectively. By age 39 years, the rate of cardiovascular events was 0.0%, 0.3%, and 5.2% among non-FH-Ch, FH-Ch, and FH-P, respectively. The authors conclude that treatment of FH from childhood/adolescence reduces the cumulative LDL-C burden compared with later onset treatment from adulthood in affected parents and permits attainment of LDL-C levels close to non-FH individuals; this finding is associated with the observation of a reduction in the cardiovascular risk of young FH patients. These findings support FH as a paediatric condition requiring early-life detection and treatment. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Archna Bajaj and Marina Cuchel from the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA.23 The authors highlight that in the SAFEHEART registry there were differences reported in the treatment of young female patients compared with males. Intense lipid-lowering treatment, defined as treatment that would be expected to decrease LDL-C by at least 50%, was present in 61% of males from the HeFH children/adolescents group, but only in 50% of females, highlighting a gap that needs to be addressed, particularly as females are often undertreated over their lifetime due to required interruption of lipid-lowering treatment for periods of pregnancy and lactation. In summary, while great strides have been made in the diagnosis and treatment of HeFH patients, aided by the development of novel LDL-C-lowering therapies in recent years, there still remains a considerable gap in improving the management of such patients across real-world settings. items.title: Correction: Peri-aortic fat to assess cardiovascular aging using an AI-driven radiomic biomarker
Giant aortic aneurysm in a child with a lethal arteriopathy due to a novel mutation in the FBLN4 gene
items.abstract: A lethal inherited arteriopathy syndrome associated with a novel, homozygous mutation (D203A) of the EFEMP2 (FBLN4) gene was discovered in an ethnically unique cohort of 22 infants from Kerala, India.1 EFEMP2 encodes fibulin-4 that has been identified as a critical determinant of elastogenesis. This connective tissue disease is characterized by a severe vascular phenotype with gross dilatation, elongation, tortuosity and narrowing of elastic arteries, in addition to cutis laxa, joint hyperlaxity and typical facial features.2 Although classified under Autosomal Recessive Cutis Laxa 1B in OMIM, this particular syndrome has a far more lethal outcome than other inherited arteriopathy syndromes including Arterial Tortuosity Syndrome, Loeys-Dietz Syndrome and Marfan Syndrome. In an expanded cohort of 63 patients, the median age at death is 15 months. Our current patient, an isolated survivor, a 14-year-old girl presented with symptoms of dyspnoea on exertion. She was diagnosed with the above-mentioned mutation 5 years ago and was on follow-up for the ascending aortic aneurysm. Her current CT aortogram and 3D reconstruction revealed a dilated ascending aorta of maximum diameter of 12 cm and occupying almost the entire left hemithorax. Due to the mass effect, there was complete left bronchus compression at its origin with a fully collapsed left lung (Figure A–D). The abdominal aorta, arch vessels and intracranial arteries showed a tortuous course consistent with the disease. She underwent ascending aorta and arch replacement using a dacron graft and had an uneventful recovery and is doing well at 2 years follow-up (Figure E and F).

items.title: Clonal haematopoiesis and the cardiovascular–kidney–metabolic continuum
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Clonal haematopoiesis and cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome: a cohort study’, by A. Chang et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag655 and the discussion piece ‘Defining CKM progression by a cardiovascular endpoint: a built-in circularity’, by A. Kazory and A. Koratala, https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag857. We thank Drs Kazory and Koratala for their thoughtful response to our recent report on clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) and cardiovascular–kidney–metabolic (CKM) syndrome.1 The authors note that development of clinical cardiovascular disease (CVD) was used to determine progression to Stage 4 CKM. However, Stage 4 was not an outcome definition created for our study; clinical CVD defines Stage 4 within the established CKM staging framework. Now codified in multi-society guidelines,2 the CKM syndrome framework conceptualizes CKM as a continuum culminating in clinical CVD at Stage 4. Accordingly, evaluating whether an exposure is associated with transition from Stages 0–3 to Stage 4 is consistent with the framework itself. We respectfully wish to clarify that this does not create ‘built-in circularity.’ Clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential does not contribute to the definition of CKM stage or the Stage 4 outcome; rather, our analysis asked whether baseline CHIP was cross-sectionally associated with CKM stage and prospectively associated with transition to a prespecified CKM stage. That CHIP has previously been associated with CVD informs the interpretation of this finding, but does not make the analysis circular.

items.title: Defining cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic progression by a cardiovascular endpoint: a built-in circularity
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Clonal haematopoiesis and cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome: a cohort study’, by A. Chang et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag655 and the discussion piece ‘Clonal haematopoiesis and the cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic continuum’, by A. Chang and M. C. Honigberg, https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag858. We read with interest the study by Chang et al. examining the association of clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) with cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome.1 The authors provide an important analysis linking CHIP, inflammatory proteomic signatures, and adverse cardiovascular outcomes. However, we question whether these longitudinal findings truly demonstrate CKM progression or largely reflect the already established association between CHIP and cardiovascular disease (CVD). The primary longitudinal outcome was progression from CKM stages 0–3 to stage 4. Yet, stage 4 is defined by the development of clinical CVD, such as coronary artery disease or heart failure. Thus, among participants without CVD at baseline, ‘progression to CKM stage 4’ essentially meant developing CVD. This is important because CHIP is already known to be tightly associated with several cardiovascular outcomes.2 Therefore, showing that CHIP predicts a composite of cardiovascular events does not necessarily mean that it predicts progression of the broader, multi-component CKM syndrome. The magnitude of the reported associations further reinforces this concern. The strongest associations were observed for specific cardiovascular outcomes: spliceosome and JAK2 CHIP were associated with heart failure with hazard ratios (HRs) of 2.62 (95% CI 2.01–3.41) and 2.79 (95% CI 1.58–4.91), respectively, and JAK2 CHIP was associated with peripheral artery disease with an HR of as high as 3.80 (95% CI 1.81–7.98). Interestingly, the signal became substantially weaker when examined within the broader CKM construct: non-DNMT3A CHIP was associated with progression to stage 4 with an HR of 1.24 (95% CI 1.17–1.31), while any CHIP had an HR of only 1.13 (95% CI 1.09–1.17); its cross-sectional association with greater CKM severity was only minimal (OR 1.04; 95% CI 1.01–1.08). This striking dilution suggests that the apparent CKM-level signal is largely inherited from its cardiovascular component rather than reflecting an independent multi-component CKM phenomenon.

items.title: Weekly Journal Scan: PREMIUM evidence that aspirin omission in STEMI patients undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention is unjustified and unsafe
items.abstract: Comment on ‘Aspirin Omission at the Time of Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in STEMI’ which was published in The New England Journal of Medicine, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2606997. DAPT with low-dose aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor remains the default treatment strategy for 12 months after an acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in patients without high bleeding risk.2 Its rationale extends beyond the prevention of stent thrombosis, as the simultaneous inhibition of thromboxane A2- and adenosine diphosphate (ADP)-dependent platelet activation reduces also recurrent atherothrombotic events arising from non-target lesions in the coronary circulation and other vascular territories.3 However, evidence from randomized trials and meta-analyses has challenged the need for a uniform DAPT strategy, suggesting that shorter DAPT regimens, particularly in appropriately selected patients at low ischaemic risk, may reduce bleeding without compromising protection against ischaemic events.4–7 The STOPDAPT-3 trial found that immediate aspirin omission with prasugrel monotherapy at the time of PCI in 6002 Japanese patients with ACS or HBR did not reduce major bleedings and was associated with an excess of early coronary events, including stent thrombosis.4 Of note, in the control group, DAPT was maintained for the first month after PCI, followed by aspirin monotherapy, thus testing aspirin withdrawal specifically during the period of highest thrombotic risk rather than a long-term aspirin-free strategy. The NEO-MINDSET trial, in which aspirin was stopped as early as 2 days after PCI for ACS, failed to demonstrate non-inferiority and showed numerically more death, MI, stroke, and a three-fold higher incidence of stent thrombosis.5

items.title: Micro- and nanoplastics in acute coronary thrombosis: exposure, enrichment, or a dual mechanism?
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Micro- and nano-plastics in the coronary circulation and air pollution exposure in ischaemic heart disease presentation’, by P. Paolisso et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag447 and the discussion piece ‘Coronary micro- and nanoplastics in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction: antecedent exposure or post-thrombotic enrichment’, by J. Qin et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag800. We thank Qin et al.1 for their thoughtful commentary on our study of micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) in the coronary circulation across the spectrum of coronary artery disease. The authors raise two principal points: whether the proximal-to-peripheral gradient observed in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) reflects antecedent exposure or post-thrombotic enrichment and whether smoking confounds the association between MNPs and acute coronary thrombosis. We welcome the opportunity to clarify these issues. We agree that our cross-sectional, single-timepoint sampling design cannot definitively separate focal accumulation preceding plaque rupture from secondary enrichment occurring after thrombotic occlusion. We emphasize that this local mechanism cannot alone account for our findings. Indeed, our most robust finding was not the concentration gradient itself but the markedly different rate of patients with detectable MNPs across the three groups, highest in STEMI, intermediate in chronic coronary syndromes, and lowest in controls, a binary difference in presence vs absence that local stasis or thrombus-related sequestration at a single occlusion site does not readily explain. Moreover, we deliberately used peripheral arterial blood, sampled at the vascular sheath and remote from the culprit lesion, as the reference compartment for this comparison to avoid confounding from local thrombus formation and flow disruption at the site of coronary occlusion. Peripheral arterial MNP concentrations were also significantly higher in STEMI than in chronic coronary syndromes or controls, a systemic difference that stasis or thrombus-related sequestration at the occlusion site cannot explain.2 We therefore view antecedent exposure and post-thrombotic local enrichment not as competing explanations but as plausibly coexisting phenomena: a higher systemic MNP burden predisposing to atherothrombotic events, superimposed on focal concentration once coronary flow is disrupted. The design proposed by the authors—comparing polymer burden and composition across peripheral blood, upstream and downstream coronary blood, aspirated thrombus, and plaque tissue from the same patient—is precisely the direction we are now pursuing, building on prior work demonstrating MNPs within coronary and peripheral thrombi and within atherosclerotic plaque itself.3–6

items.title: Coronary micro- and nanoplastics in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction: antecedent exposure or post-thrombotic enrichment?
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Micro- and nano-plastics in the coronary circulation and air pollution exposure in ischaemic heart disease presentation’, by P. Paolisso et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag447 and the discussion piece ‘Micro- and nanoplastics in acute coronary thrombosis: exposure, enrichment, or a dual mechanism?’, by R. Marfella et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag803. We read with interest the study by Paolisso et al., who quantified micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) in paired peripheral and coronary blood samples from patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), chronic coronary syndromes, and angiographically normal coronary arteries. The paired sampling design, rigorous contamination controls, and complementary analytical methods are important strengths. However, the spatial gradient observed in STEMI permits an alternative interpretation.1 In STEMI, MNP concentrations were highest in coronary blood sampled upstream from the culprit occlusion before lesion crossing (Tube B), followed by downstream coronary blood after lesion crossing (Tube C) and peripheral arterial blood (Tube A). This pattern may reflect focal accumulation before plaque rupture, but all samples were obtained after a TIMI 0/1 thrombotic occlusion had formed. Markedly reduced flow and stasis near the occlusion, prolonged residence of circulating particles, or incorporation into thrombotic material could also produce secondary enrichment. Plastic polymers have been detected in coronary thrombi from patients with myocardial infarction and in thrombi retrieved from coronary, cerebral, and deep venous sites. These observations establish that thrombi can contain plastic particles, but not whether the particles promoted thrombosis or became incorporated during clot formation. The proximal-to-peripheral gradient should therefore be regarded as lesion-associated enrichment rather than evidence that focal deposition necessarily preceded the acute event.1–3

items.title: Cortisol in cardio-kidney-metabolic disease
items.abstract: Despite guideline-directed therapy, many patients with cardio-kidney-metabolic (CKM) disease remain uncontrolled due to therapeutic inertia, adherence barriers, and underrecognized secondary causes. Hypercortisolism, ranging from mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) to overt Cushing syndrome, is an increasingly recognized contributor. MACS is associated with a 2.5-fold higher risk of cardiovascular death and increased prevalence of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and kidney impairment. Cortisol excess promotes muscle insulin resistance, hepatic gluconeogenesis, β-cell dysfunction, sodium retention, and vascular remodelling, worsening glycaemia and blood pressure, leading to poor CKM outcomes. Recent prospective studies suggest that hypercortisolism is more prevalent than previously suspected in selected CKM phenotypes, including 24% in patients with difficult-to-control T2DM in CATALYST and 27% in patients with resistant hypertension in MOMENTUM. The overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test remains the diagnostic test of choice. Therapeutic strategies include adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitors, glucocorticoid receptor antagonists, and pituitary-directed therapies in selected cases, while surgery remains the first-line treatment for surgically remediable disease. This review summarizes the epidemiology and mechanisms linking cortisol excess to CKM dysfunction, and also highlights the need for clinical trials, standardized diagnostic thresholds, and assays to enable integration of cortisol-targeted therapies into management pathways to mitigate residual CKM risk. This review will serve as a practical guide for cardiologists to manage a potentially reversible contributor to poor CKM control.

items.title: Extensive type B aortic dissection with Michels type IX hepatic arterial anatomy causing acalculous gangrenous cholecystitis
items.abstract: A 36-year-old man with hypertension presented with a 3-day history of abrupt-onset back and chest pain, followed by abdominal pain. Computed tomography angiography demonstrated an acute Stanford type B aortic dissection (Panel A, arrowheads) extending from the proximal descending thoracic aorta to both common iliac arteries, with multiple re-entry tears and severe ostial compromise of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) (Panel A, red arrow). Three-dimensional reconstruction showed a replaced common hepatic artery arising from the SMA (Michels type IX anatomy1; Panel B, blue arrows), rendering the entire hepatobiliary arterial inflow SMA-dependent. The gallbladder was markedly distended without visible calculi (Panel C, asterisk). Angiography confirmed non-opacification of the SMA origin and poor distal perfusion. Endovascular aortic repair involved three overlapping stent grafts and supra-aortic branch reconstruction. Subsequent SMA stenting restored visceral flow (see Supplementary data online, Figure S1). Persistent abdominal pain and gastrointestinal bleeding prompted immediate laparoscopy. Moderate bile-stained ascites was present. The small bowel and colon were viable, but the gallbladder was gangrenous, measuring 10 × 8 × 6 cm, with focal bile leakage (Panel D). Laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed. The opened specimen showed haemorrhagic mucosal necrosis without gallstones (Panel E), and haematoxylin and eosin staining confirmed haemorrhagic necrosis with acute inflammation (Panel F). Michels type IX anatomy is rare, occurring in 2.96% of 5002 patients.2 Here, the variant rendered cystic arterial perfusion SMA-dependent; SMA malperfusion from the type B dissection therefore caused acalculous gangrenous cholecystitis despite viable bowel. Clinicians should consider gallbladder ischaemia in this setting.

items.title: Acquired ventricular septal defect in the setting of a catecholaminergic storm
items.abstract: A 58-year-old man was admitted to the cardiac intensive care unit following an episode of chest pain and severe hypertension (277/110 mmHg) during haemodialysis. Electrocardiography showed intermittent left bundle branch block, and high-sensitivity troponin I peaked at 27 582 ng/L. A loud holosystolic murmur was noted the following day. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 15 mm ventricular septal defect (VSD; Figure A, Supplementary data online, Video S1), while cardiac catheterization confirmed a significant left-to-right shunt (Qp:Qs 2.2) with normal coronary arteries (see Supplementary data online, Video S2). Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed no late gadolinium enhancement (Figure B). Given marked blood pressure lability and recurrent hypertensive crises, secondary causes were investigated. Plasma metanephrines were elevated, and 18F-DOPA positron emission tomography identified a right adrenal lesion consistent with pheochromocytoma (white arrow; Figure C), which was surgically resected, resulting in blood pressure control. At follow-up, signs of left ventricular volume overload and rising pulmonary pressures prompted consideration of VSD closure. Owing to comorbidities, the Heart Team favoured a percutaneous approach with surgical backup. Patient-specific three-dimensional printing enabled detailed characterization of the tortuous VSD trajectory and its relationship with adjacent structures, particularly its proximity to the right ventricular free wall, informing device type, size, and delivery strategy (Figure D, Supplementary data online, Video S3). Percutaneous closure was successfully performed using a dedicated VSD occluder under fluoroscopic and transoesophageal echocardiographic guidance (Figure E–1F, Supplementary data online, Video S4). The post-procedural course was uneventful. At 2-month follow-up, there was significant clinical and haemodynamic improvement (Qp:Qs 1.2). To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of an acquired VSD associated with pheochromocytoma.

items.title: Weekly Journal Scan: rethinking factor XIa inhibition after acute coronary syndromes
items.abstract: This comment refers to ‘Milvexian with Antiplatelet Therapy after Acute Coronary Syndrome Event’, published in the New England Journal of Medicine; https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2608717. FⅪa inhibitors were developed around a very attractive -though not novel- therapeutic proposition: pathological thrombosis might be reduced while largely preserving physiological haemostasis, potentially dissociating efficacy from safety.2,3 LIBREXIA ACS tested this hypothesis in a contemporary ACS setting and prompts consideration of what this strategy of anticoagulation may offer to patients receiving intensive antiplatelet therapy. Moreover, most patients had undergone revascularization during the index hospitalization and were receiving guideline-directed medical therapy. The rationale for adding an oral anticoagulant in this intensively treated population rests on the persistence of high levels of thrombin generation and FⅪ despite effective platelet inhibition. This concept had found clinical support in the results of the ATLAS ACS 2–TIMI 51 trial, in which low-dose rivaroxaban added to antiplatelet therapy reduced cardiovascular death, MI, or stroke, at the cost of increased major and intracranial bleeding.4 FⅪa inhibition with milvexian offered the theoretical possibility of preserving this antithrombotic benefit with less interference with physiological haemostasis.

items.title: AI algorithms and external validation: promises, pitfalls, and a practical blueprint
items.abstract: External validation involving the testing of a frozen AI model on independent data from other sites, populations, time periods, or devices provides the clearest estimate of intended-use setting performance when those external data are deployment-representative of the expected population, measurement processes, and clinical workflow. It yields realistic estimates of discrimination and calibration, exposes shortcut learning and distribution shift, quantifies clinical utility through decision-analytic measures, and reveals subgroup disparities requiring mitigation. Yet common pitfalls undermine credibility: quasi-external splits with hidden relatedness; spectrum and prevalence mismatch; site, workflow, and hardware effects; label noise and reference-standard drift; analytic flexibility and selective reporting; small, underpowered samples; reliance only on the area under the curve; unreported threshold tuning; and leakage. A practical blueprint emphasizes pre-registration; representative, multi-site cohorts spanning geography, time, and acquisition; prevention of patient and temporal overlap; comprehensive evaluation of discrimination, calibration (including calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, and calibration plots), and net benefit with confidence intervals; pre-specified subgroup and fairness audits; transparent labelling procedures and uncertainty analyses; principled sample-size calculations; and minimal, well-documented model updating (recalibration before revision). Finally, external validation should connect to post-deployment governance via drift detection, performance triggers, and change-control plans, complemented by site-specific local evaluation to ensure safety and reliability across diverse clinical environments. When executed to these standards, external validation transforms promising prototypes into dependable clinical tools, clarifying where a model performs, where it fails, and what adaptations are necessary for safe, equitable, and sustainable use. This framework links statistical evaluation to clinical use, model updating, and post-deployment monitoring.

items.title: A rare cause of syncope
items.abstract: A 52-year-old woman presented with syncope 6 months earlier. Ambulatory electrocardiography revealed sinus arrest, leading to a diagnosis of sinus node dysfunction and implantation of a right atrial leadless pacemaker. Subsequently, she developed palpitations and transient visual disturbances. A right ventricular Aveir leadless pacemaker was implanted (Panel A; Supplementary S1), but symptoms persisted, predominantly after physical activity. Ambulatory electrocardiography showed a pacing burden of 0.23%, 3123 premature atrial contractions, and 40 premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) with two morphologies. Device interrogation revealed no malfunction. Echocardiography showed no significant structural disease or systolic dysfunction. Exercise electrocardiography documented non-sustained ventricular tachycardia coinciding with syncope (Panel B). At rest (heart rate, 72 beats/min; LVEF 60%), exercise stress echocardiography showed limited mobility of the atrial leadless pacemaker without definite tricuspid-valve interaction (Supplementary S2). With increasing workload and heart rate above 90 beats/min, excursion of the free end progressively increased. At peak exercise (heart rate, 131 beats/min; LVEF 72%), the free end intermittently contacted the septal tricuspid leaflet, coinciding with increased PVC frequency (Panels C and D; Supplementary S3).
