items.title: Prevalence-dependent thresholding and the safety of ruling out left main disease
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Standard clinical and stress ECG variables to exclude left main and left main-equivalent disease: the MASTER study’, by M. De Carlo et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag464 and the discussion piece ‘Prevalence-dependent thresholding and the safety of ruling out left main disease’, by M. De Carlo et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag860. De Carlo et al. report a clinical and exercise electrocardiographic model intended to defer coronary angiography or coronary computed tomography angiography in patients with suspected chronic coronary syndromes. At an assumed 5% prevalence of left main coronary artery disease (LMCAD) and a 1:100 misclassification cost ratio, the negative predictive value was 98.2%.1 Their Discussion further states that a lower LMCAD prevalence would increase both sensitivity and negative predictive value, making adoption more advantageous. That interpretation is not supported by the supplementary analyses: after prevalence-dependent threshold selection, the higher negative predictive value at 0.9% prevalence was accompanied by lower sensitivity. At 5% prevalence, optimism-adjusted sensitivity and negative predictive value were 85.3% and 98.2% at the 1:100 ratio and 74.4% and 97.7% at 1:50.1 At 0.9% prevalence, Supplementary Table 7 reported sensitivities of 64.5% and 63.0%, with a negative predictive value of 99.5% under both ratios.1 The Mayo Clinic validation showed the same pattern: sensitivity fell from 87.2% to 79.5% at 1:100 and from 84.6% to 69.2% at 1:50, despite higher negative predictive values.1 These estimates imply that the proportion of affected patients missed increased from 14.7% to 35.5% at 1:100 and from 25.6% to 37.0% at 1:50. A lower prevalence reduces the absolute number of false negatives per 1000 patients, but it does not reduce the probability of missing LMCAD among patients who have the disease.

items.title: An uncontainable ‘ball’ in the heart: a giant right sinus of Valsalva aneurysm
items.abstract: An ‘uncontainable ball’ was found swinging relentlessly within the heart of a 38-year-old previously healthy woman presenting with a three-day history of chest tightness. Auscultation identified a 3/6 blowing murmur over the aortic area. Laboratory tests revealed elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (43.4 pg/mL), NT-proBNP (4198.0 pg/mL), D-dimer (16 311 ng/mL), INR 1.7, and marked leukocytosis (WBC 20.82 × 109/L, neutrophil 84%). Hepatic and renal functions were severely impaired (ALT 1263 U/L, AST 1005 U/L, urea 10.20 mmol/L), with mildly elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (7.45 mg/L). Transthoracic echocardiography unveiled the culprit—a giant (5 × 3 cm), thin-walled, ball-like aneurysm of the right sinus of Valsalva (Panels A and B; Supplementary data online, Videos S1 and S2). With every heartbeat, this ‘ball’ tumbled unrestrictedly between the right atrium and right ventricle, hammering the tricuspid valve and generating severe tricuspid regurgitation. Aortic CTA confirmed a contrast-filled saccular structure adjacent to the right coronary sinus with an ill-defined superior margin (Panels C and D), alongside multiple pulmonary emboli in the left lower lobe pulmonary artery and its branches, bilateral pleural effusions, and massive ascites. Given the critical condition, emergent surgery was performed after informed consent. Preoperative transoesophageal echocardiography re-identified the same uncontainable ‘ball’ with a 0.8 cm neck, continuous blood filling, and a 0.9 cm rupture on the right atrial side (Panels E and F; Supplementary data online, Videos S3–S5). 3D transoesophageal echocardiography clearly shows the aneurysm and the rupture site at the right atrial side (Panel G). Intraoperative findings confirmed a thin-walled aneurysm communicating between the aortic sinus and the right atrium (Panels H and I; Supplementary data online, Video S6). The procedure was completed uneventfully.

items.title: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation vs surgical replacement in low-risk aortic stenosis: time-dependent late mortality in a pooled analysis of trials
items.abstract: The expansion of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) to low-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis (AS) has been driven by randomized trials reporting favourable early outcomes and non-inferiority to surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR), through early and intermediate follow-up.1 However, longer-term assessment is essential for patients with a longer life expectancy, in whom durability, reintervention risk, and survival are central to treatment selection.2 Recently released extended follow-up data from pivotal lower-risk trials have raised concerns that the early advantages of TAVI may attenuate over time, with emerging signals related to late mortality, valve durability, and reintervention.3–5 However, these trials were underpowered to evaluate all-cause mortality as an individual endpoint. Moreover, conventional time-to-event analyses may obscure clinically important time-dependent differences between two treatment strategies exhibiting non-parallel patterns of early and late risk. We therefore conducted a pooled reconstructed time-to-event analysis of randomized low-risk trials with extended follow-up of up to 7 years.

items.title: Obesity, frail obesity, and outcomes after durable left ventricular assist device implantation: a pooled analysis of the MOMENTUM 3 trials
items.abstract: Background and Aims Obesity in patients supported by left ventricular assist devices (LVADs) is linked to excess mortality and haemocompatibility-related events. Whether this association persists with the fully magnetically levitated HeartMate 3 (HM3) pump is unknown. This analysis tested outcomes with obesity and the additive influence of co-existing frailty (‘frail obesity’) in the contemporary era. Methods The study pooled 2200 HM3 recipients from the MOMENTUM 3 pivotal randomized trial (n = 515) and Continued Access Protocol (n = 1685). Obesity was defined as body mass index (BMI) ≥30 kg/m2 and frailty by a 40-item Rockwood cumulative-deficit frailty index (FI), with clinically relevant frailty defined as FI ≥0.325 (moderate–severe frailty); BMI was excluded from the FI to avoid mathematical coupling. The primary endpoint was survival to transplant, recovery, or 24 months of support free of disabling stroke (modified Rankin score >3) or pump replacement reoperation. Results Obese patients (n = 887, 40.3%) were younger, less often with ischaemic aetiology, and more frequently women, but more often had diabetes and hypertension, than non-obese patients. Unadjusted 2-year outcomes were similar between groups (freedom from the primary endpoint: 75.1% vs 77.1%, log-rank P = .34; survival: 79.9% vs 81.2%, P = .57). After covariate adjustment, obesity was independently associated with a higher risk of the primary endpoint (hazard ratio [HR] 1.30, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.07–1.58) and all-cause mortality (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.10–1.67), as well as heart failure hospitalization, infection, and arrhythmia, but not stroke, bleeding, or early right heart failure. Frailty affected 67.3% of obese recipients (571/849) and was associated with a higher adjusted risk of the primary endpoint (HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.09–2.10), overall mortality and non-haemocompatibilty-related morbidity endpoints. The obesity-by-frailty interaction was not significant for either the primary endpoint (P = .436) or mortality (P = .215), indicating additive rather than synergistic risk; frail–obese patients nonetheless carried the highest absolute risk of any subgroup. Frailty improved by at least one severity class by 6 months in 75.9% of frail–obese patients, and improvement was associated with better survival (adjusted HR 0.14, 95% CI 0.07–0.26). Conclusions In the HM3 era, obese and non-obese recipients had similar unadjusted 2-year outcomes; however, after adjustment for baseline case-mix, obesity was independently associated with a higher risk of both the primary endpoint and all-cause mortality, together with heart failure hospitalization, infection, and arrhythmia. Frailty was independently associated with adverse outcomes across nearly all endpoints and was highly prevalent among obese recipients; the combination of obesity and frailty was additive but not synergistic, with frail–obese patients carrying the highest absolute risk. Frailty, however, proved substantially reversible after LVAD support, and its improvement was associated with markedly better survival. Obesity and frailty should therefore be assessed together, rather than through BMI thresholds alone, with recognition that frailty status is dynamic after implantation and that improvement in frailty is associated with markedly better survival.

items.title: Heart failure therapy in congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries: effect on right ventricular function and survival
items.abstract: Background and Aims The aim of the study was to assess the effect of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) on cardiac function, neurohormonal activation, and mortality in adults with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries (cc-TGA) presenting with systemic right ventricular (RV) systolic dysfunction. The study hypothesis was that GDMT use (assessed using the GDMT score) was associated with improved cardiac function (higher RV free wall strain [RVFWS]), less neurohormonal activation (lower N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide [NT-proBNP] levels), and lower mortality. Methods GDMT score, RVFWS, and NT-proBNP levels were assessed at baseline and 1-year follow-up. GDMT uptitration was assessed using ΔGDMT (GDMT at 1-year minus GDMT at baseline). Improvements in RV systolic function and neurohormonal activation were defined as a relative increase in RVFWS of >20% and a relative decrease in NT-proBNP levels of >20%, respectively. Results Of 213 patients (age 43 ± 15 years; 54% male), baseline GDMT score was 1.97 ± 1.27, and ΔGDMT score was 0.74 ± 0.39. Baseline RVFWS was −18 ± 5%; 25% had improved RV systolic function. Baseline NT-proBNP was 369 (142, 1004) pg/mL; 56% had improved neurohormonal activation. Higher baseline GDMT score and ΔGDMT score were associated with improvement in RV systolic function and neurohormonal activation. Overall, 34 (16%) patients died, and higher baseline GDMT score and ΔGDMT score were associated with a lower risk of mortality and of the composite adverse event endpoint (heart failure hospitalization, death, and heart transplantation). Clinical benefits of GDMT use were observed only in patients with moderate/severe RV systolic dysfunction, and not in patients with mild RV systolic dysfunction. Conclusions GDMT use was associated with improved outcomes in patients with moderate/severe RV systolic dysfunction.

items.title: Atherosclerotic plaque healing: mechanisms and clinical relevance
items.abstract: Atherosclerotic plaque healing is a dynamic biological mechanism that occurrs after plaque disruption and represents an endogenous reparative response within the atherosclerotic lesion. This process unfolds through three partially overlapping phases: endogenous thrombus lysis, granulation tissue formation, and re-endothelialization. Through the coordinated interaction of circulating cells, vascular wall components, and soluble mediators, plaque healing promotes fibrous repair and structural stabilization of the disrupted plaque. For many years, plaque healing remained primarily a histopathological observation described in post-mortem studies. The advent of high-resolution intracoronary imaging, particularly optical coherence tomography, has enabled in vivo visualization of the characteristic layered morphology of healed plaques, providing direct clinical confirmation of these early pathological findings. These observations have significantly improved our understanding of the clinical significance of plaque healing. Healed plaques are more frequently observed in patients with chronic coronary syndromes, supporting the concept that healing contributes to plaque stabilization. At the same time, recurrent cycles of plaque disruption followed by repair may lead to progressive luminal narrowing, thereby contributing to the long-term progression of coronary atherosclerosis. This review provided an updated overview of the clinical significance and implications of healed plaques in coronary artery disease, the mechanisms underlying plaque healing, and examines emerging intracoronary and non-invasive imaging modalities that allow their in vivo identification.

items.title: Unintended shifts in high-priority adult heart transplant listings after the OPTN’s September 2025 policy change
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: The Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network amended Status 2 heart allocation criteria in September 2025, requiring documented failure of high-dose inotropes before candidates could qualify via intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) or percutaneous endovascular ventricular assist device (PEVAD) support. Using OPTN data, we compared seasonally matched pre-policy (September 2024-June 2025, n=4,206) and post-policy (September 2025-June 2026, n=4,231) adult candidates. While standard Status 3 high-dose inotrope listings increased 2.0% to 4.1% and standard Status 2 IABP/PEVAD listings decreased 18.2% to 11.0%, Status 1 listings and Status 2 exceptions increased 7.7% to 10.6% and 17.5% to 21.5%, respectively (all p<0.001). Consequently, combined initial Status 1/2 listings were unchanged (44.5% vs 44.0%, p=0.71). Furthermore, overall transplant volume remained similar, but status at transplant shifted from standard Status 2 toward Status 2 exceptions and Status 1. Tightening standard Status 2 eligibility was associated with redistribution across high-priority pathways rather than reduced high-priority listings.

items.title: Menstrual Health in Children, Adolescents, and Young Adults with Cardiac Disease: An Underrecognized Component of Heart Failure, Mechanical Circulatory Support, and Transplant Care
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Background Menstrual abnormalities, including heavy menstrual bleeding, amenorrhea, and dysmenorrhea, are frequently encountered among children, adolescents, and young adults with congenital and acquired heart disease, yet remain underrecognized in routine cardiovascular care. Anticoagulation, thrombosis risk, heart failure physiology, and limited high-quality evidence complicate management and contribute to substantial variation in practice. Methods The Advanced Cardiac Therapies Improving Outcomes Network convened a multidisciplinary working group of cardiologists, hematologists, gynecologists, adolescent medicine specialists, and allied health providers. Following a literature search, the group met monthly via virtual meetings to synthesize current evidence and clinical experience and develop consensus guidance. Results The consensus emphasizes routine, developmentally appropriate menstrual screening and recognition that traditional definitions of heavy menstrual bleeding may underestimate its clinical impact in patients with heart disease. Management requires individualized assessment of bleeding risk, thrombotic risk, cardiac physiology, and patient preferences. Menstrual abnormalities may warrant broader evaluation for changes in overall health, cardiac status, or energy availability. Conclusions Menstrual health is integral to comprehensive cardiovascular care. Integrating screening and individualized management into cardiology practice may reduce morbidity, improve quality of life, and support equitable, sex-informed care. Further research and culturally responsive, multidisciplinary implementation are needed to strengthen the evidence base and improve care consistency.

items.title: Heart transplantation in adult Fontan patients: New insights from Fontan-associated liver disease beyond traditional predictors
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Structured Abstract Background Fontan patients are considered high risk for heart transplantation (HT) owing to their complex anatomy, multiple prior chest entries, and universal Fontan-associated liver disease (FALD). The impact of FALD and other preoperative factors remains, however, uncertain. Objectives We sought to identify factors associated with 90-day mortality after isolated HT in adults with Fontan circulation, with particular focus on the relationship between liver-related parameters and post-transplant outcomes. Methods A retrospective cohort study of all adult Fontan patients undergoing isolated HT was conducted. Factors associated with 90-day mortality were assessed using appropriate univariate analyses and penalized multivariable logistic regression. ROC analysis was used to derive liver size cut-offs and compare the discriminative performance of selected variables. A descriptive analysis of adult Fontan patients undergoing combined heart-liver transplantation (CHLT) was also performed for contextual comparison. Results Thirty-seven patients (mean age 30 years) underwent isolated HT; 19% (n=8) died within 90 days. Factors associated with increased 90-day mortality were >4 previous chest entries, major perioperative bleeding, and small liver size [total liver volume (TLV) ≤1366 mL, total liver volume indexed to body surface area (TLVi) <786 mL/m 2 and liver transverse dimension (LTD) <21 cm]. Multiple chest veno-venous collaterals, >4 previous chest entries, and small liver were strongly associated with bleeding and subsequent fatal complications including sepsis, graft dysfunction, and bowel ischaemia. Within the study period, five other patients had undergone CHLT. All had biopsy confirmed advanced liver disease with features of clinically significant portal hypertension or hepatocellular carcinoma. One patient died within 90 days following prolonged cardiopulmonary bypass, major bleeding, graft dysfunction and sepsis, culminating in multiorgan failure. Conclusions In Fontan patients undergoing isolated HT, >4 previous chest entries, major bleeding, and small liver volume were associated with increased 90-day mortality. Objective liver metrics (TLV ≤1366 mL, TLVi <786 mL/m 2 , TLD <21 cm) may provide adjunctive risk stratification for Fontan patients considered for isolated HT; however, these measures and proposed thresholds remain exploratory and require external validation. CHLT is a viable option, although non-liver related transplant risk factors may similarly influence outcomes. Detailed liver assessment and management at experienced, high-volume congenital transplant centres are important to optimizing outcomes in this complex population.

items.title: Reanimationless Rapid Recovery Versus Thoraco-Abdominal Normothermic Regional Perfusion for Donation After Circulatory Death Heart Transplantation Following Prolonged Asystolic Warm Ischemia
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Background Donation after circulatory death (DCD) heart transplantation has expanded the donor pool, yet contemporary recovery strategies remain constrained. Rapid Recovery with Extended Ultra-Oxygenated Preservation (REUP) is a non-reanimation DCD recovery strategy that eliminates the need for donor heart reperfusion prior to transplantation. As prolonged asystolic warm ischemic time (AWIT) during circulatory arrest has raised ongoing concerns, whether REUP achieves outcomes comparable to TA-NRP in DCD donors with prolonged AWIT remains unknown. Methods We performed a retrospective single-center study of DCD heart transplant recipients whose donor hearts were recovered using either TA-NRP or REUP and preserved with 10°C static cold storage. Donors with AWIT Results Eighty-two DCD heart transplant recipients met inclusion criteria, including 55 TA-NRP and 27 REUP recipients. Compared with TA-NRP donors, REUP donors were older (42.0 vs 33.7 years) and experienced longer total ischemic times (285 vs 219 minutes). Severe PGD occurred in 4 TA-NRP recipients (7.3%) and no REUP recipients (0.0%). Ninety-day mortality was 12.7% versus 7.4%, respectively. In weighted bootstrap analyses, REUP was associated with a directional signal toward lower severe PGD (OR 0.22, 95% CI 0.09-1.02; directional consistency 97.4%) and lower 90-day mortality (OR 0.56, 95% CI 0.09-2.57; directional consistency 76.3%), although confidence intervals were wide. Conclusions Among DCD heart transplant recipients with AWIT ≥10 minutes, REUP demonstrated early graft function and short-term survival comparable to TA-NRP despite a more challenging donor profile. These findings support further prospective multicenter evaluation of REUP as a broadly deployable non-reanimation DCD heart recovery strategy.

items.title: Impact of donor care unit opening and use on lung donation from deceased organ donors after brain death
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Deceased donors after brain death (DBD) transferred to donor care units (DCUs) have higher rates of lung donation than donors remaining in hospitals, but contributions of regional DCU availability and donor transfer to lung donation remain unknown. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Cohort study using Organ Procurement & Transplantation Network (OPTN) deceased donor registry files, including adult DBDs managed in donation regions with operating DCUs, 2017-2024. Multivariable logistic regression and G-computation were used to test the hypothesis that individual donor transfer to DCU, rather than regional DCU availability, is associated with a higher likelihood of lung donation (primary outcome). RESULTS: Among 27,795 DBDs managed by 28 OPOs, lung donation rate was 28.6% (7,958 donations). After adjustment for donor characteristics, predicted lung donation rates were similar before (29.1%, 95% CI 27.9-30.2) and after (28.9%, 95% CI 28.3-29.6) regional DCU adoption. Despite wide variation in regional transfer rates (5.2-96.7%), greater regional transfer was not associated with lung donation. After adjustment for donor factors, organ recovery year, and organ procurement organization, donor transfer to DCUs (vs. hospitals) remained associated with higher odds of lung donation overall (aOR 1.32, 95% CI 1.20-1.46) and for each DCU type (independent (aOR 1.41, 95% CI 1.21-1.65) and hospital-based (aOR 1.27, 95% CI 1.12-1.44)). CONCLUSIONS: Superior lung donation rates were seen only for donors transferred from regional hospitals to DCUs. There was no observable association between the proportion of donors transferred and lung donation, suggesting that superior donation outcomes may reflect the selection of donors for transfer rather than system-wide effects of DCU availability.

items.title: En bloc heart-lung transplantation in the modern donor era: Dual-organ recovery and preservation challenges
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Combined heart-lung transplantation remains a rare but essential therapy for selected patients with end-stage cardiopulmonary disease that cannot be addressed by isolated heart or lung transplantation. Modern donor allocation, increasing recipient acuity, donation after circulatory death, and longer transport distances have made graft preservation a critical determinant of whether scarce en bloc grafts can be used safely. Unlike isolated organs, the intact heart-lung bloc presents competing preservation requirements: the heart and lungs differ in ischemic tolerance, optimal storage temperature, perfusate chemistry, airway management, and tolerance of pressure and volume during recovery. Across conventional static cold storage, controlled hypothermic transport, regulated airway-pressure devices, 10°C storage, and emerging donation after circulatory death recovery pathways, this review integrates contemporary approaches for donation after brain death and donation after circulatory death while distinguishing direct en bloc evidence from single-organ extrapolation. The evidence base remains observational and constrained by procedural rarity. Future progress will require multicenter preservation-specific data collection and graft-specific systems that treat the heart-lung bloc as an integrated physiologic unit rather than as 2 isolated organs transported together.

items.title: Resource Utilization and Forecasting in Heart Failure Patients with Durable Left Ventricular Assist Devices
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Heart failure patients treated with durable left ventricular assist devices (LVADs) require significant resource utilization. Patient volume and contact points based on implant volume remain poorly quantified. We retrospectively reviewed 268 patients implanted with a durable LVAD at a single, experienced center from 2011 through 2022 and recorded survival, telephone encounters, office visits, and all-cause hospitalizations. Telephone encounters peaked at 10.4 per patient-month and declined to approximately 5 after 24 months; 66% were anticoagulation-related. Office visits peaked at 3.0 per patient-month and declined to approximately 0.7 after 18 months. Hospitalizations decreased from 2.7 per patient-year in year 1 to approximately 1 by year 5. Five-year survival with HeartMate 3 (HM3) was 61.4%. Applying HM3 survival to constant annual implant volumes yielded estimated 5-year censuses of 39, 96, and 193 surviving patients for 10, 25, and 50 annual implants, respectively. These findings may inform LVAD program capacity and staffing.

items.title: Association Between Elevated Donor-Derived Cell-Free DNA and Donor-Specific Antibodies in Heart Transplantation: Antibody-Mediated Rejection and Long-Term Outcomes
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Background Donor-derived cell-free DNA (dd-cfDNA) and donor-specific antibodies (DSA) are both used for non-invasive surveillance after heart transplantation (HT). Whether DSA provides incremental value beyond dd-cfDNA for detecting antibody-mediated rejection (AMR) and predicting outcomes is uncertain. Methods In this single-center retrospective study of adult HT recipients with paired dd-cfDNA and DSA results (September 2019 to December 2024), biopsies within 30 days of sampling were paired for analysis. Significant rejection was defined as acute cellular rejection (ACR) grade ≥2R and/or AMR (pAMR ≥1). Associations were modeled among biopsy-paired samples using patient-clustered generalized estimating equations, and mortality using time-dependent Cox and Bayesian joint models. Results We analyzed 2,856 dd-cfDNA/DSA pairs from 287 recipients, of which 763 were biopsy-paired. Elevated dd-cfDNA was more frequent in DSA-positive samples (19.3% vs 10.5%; p=0.006). Among biopsied samples, AMR was associated with DSA (OR 5.93, 95% CI 1.82-19.26) and elevated dd-cfDNA (OR 6.21, 95% CI 2.07-18.60). Relative to negative concordance, the risk of significant rejection was similar with isolated DSA-positivity (OR 3.83) and isolated dd-cfDNA-positivity (OR 3.80) and was highest with double-positivity (OR 15.70, 95% CI 4.71-52.30). Adding DSA with MFI ≥4000 to dd-cfDNA increased the AUC for AMR from 0.73 to 0.84 (p=0.03). Among 15 deaths, dd-cfDNA, but not DSA, was associated with mortality (HR 2.12, 95% CrI 1.24-3.39). Conclusions dd-cfDNA and DSA carried similar, additive information for rejection, with double-positivity identifying the highest-risk phenotype. In exploratory analyses, DSA at MFI ≥4000 added to dd-cfDNA for AMR, and dd-cfDNA was the only marker associated with mortality.

items.title: Donor-Recipient Sex Mismatch is Associated with Severe Primary Graft Dysfunction after Heart Transplantation
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The association between sex and primary graft dysfunction after heart transplantation (HT) remains unclear. We evaluated whether recipient sex and donor-recipient sex matching are associated with severe primary graft dysfunction (PGD) in a contemporary, multicenter cohort. METHODS: We analyzed data from the International PGD Consortium comprised of adult HTs from 2010 to 2024 across 14 centers. Associations between sex-related variables and severe PGD were assessed using multivariable logistic regression, and adjusted for ischemic time, pre-transplant durable left ventricular assist device (LVAD), dialysis, congenital heart disease, and predicted heart mass (PHM) ratio. RESULTS: Among 3,994 recipients, 1,030 (25.8%) were female. Female recipients were younger (54 vs. 57 years) with fewer comorbidities, and less frequently bridged on a durable LVAD (19.8% vs. 29.1%). Although female recipients had a lower incidence of PGD than male recipients (7.1% vs. 9.4%), recipient sex was not independently associated with PGD after multivariable adjustment. Female donor to male recipient sex mismatching had the highest PGD incidence of 11.5% and was associated with a 43% increase in the odds of severe PGD (p=0.030). While sex-mismatch was associated with an increased incidence of PGD, size mismatch by PHM ratio was not an independent predictor. CONCLUSION: In this large international registry, donor-recipient sex mismatch, specifically among male recipients of female donor hearts, was independently associated with severe PGD, even when appropriately size matched. These findings inform risk stratification for development of severe PGD after HT.

items.title: Waitlist Outcomes of Multiorgan Heart Transplant Candidates
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: In recent years, the number of patients undergoing simultaneous multiorgan heart transplant (MOT) has increased significantly. However, there is no unified policy for MOT allocation, allowing Organ Procurement Organizations to individually determine priority for match runs across all organ types. We evaluated if heart transplant (HT) candidates listed simultaneously for a kidney or liver are at a disadvantage on the waitlist. METHODS: Adult HT candidates registered with the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients between 2019-2023 were included. Candidates were waitlisted statuses 1-6 within the heart allocation system in order of medical urgency. The primary outcomes were transplantation and removal from the waitlist for death or clinical deterioration, estimated with cumulative incidence functions for the first-year after listing, stratified by both waitlist status and type of organ listing. Rates of transplantation and removal from the waitlist at 1 year were reported. Using cox proportional hazards models, cause-specific hazards of transplantation and removal, holding waitlist status constant were estimated. RESULTS: Of 20,588 HT candidates, 9.3% were heart kidney (HK) and 1.4% were heart liver (HL) candidates. Irrespective of status, heart-alone candidates had higher cumulative incidence of transplant (70.6% vs. 67.9% HK, p < 0.01; vs. 63.6% HL, p < 0.01), and lower cumulative incidence of removal from the waitlist for death or deterioration (5.3% vs. 10.3%, p < 0.01); vs. 10.4%, p < 0.01). In adjusted analysis and stratified by candidate listing center, MOT listing was significantly associated with lower likelihood of transplant (HK: HR 0.71, 0.68-0.75; HL: HR 1.13, 1.09-1.17), and a significantly higher risk of delisting due to death or deterioration (HK: HR 2.08, 1.81, 2.39; HL: HR 2.45, 1.75, 3.42). Hemodialysis-dependent HK candidates experienced the highest cumulative incidence of death or deterioration at 1 year (13%) compared to non-hemodialysis dependent (8.7%, p < 0.01) and heart-alone (5.3%, p < 0.01) candidates, but similar to HL candidates (10.4%, p = 0.32). CONCLUSION: MOT candidates, especially HK, had worse waitlist outcomes with lower rates of transplantation and higher incidence of removal from the waitlist compared to heart-alone candidates. These outcomes demonstrate a need for MOT allocation based on criteria more reflective of medical urgency.

items.title: Cell and Gene Therapy in Lung Transplantation: From Experimental Promise towards Clinical Translation
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Lung transplantation (LTx) remains the only definitive therapy for selected patients with end-stage lung disease, yet outcomes are limited by early ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) and primary graft dysfunction (PGD), and by chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD) as the leading cause of late graft failure. These entities share overlapping injury and repair pathways, including alveolocapillary barrier disruption, microvascular dysfunction, innate immune activation, and maladaptive remodeling, which remain incompletely controlled by current perioperative management and systemic immunosuppression. This review summarizes cell and gene therapy approaches in LTx and frames these strategies around the IRI/PGD-to-CLAD continuum. Stromal cell therapies, regulatory immune cell approaches, and cell-free or cell-derived products such as extracellular vesicles and mitochondrial transfer are discussed, with emphasis on route, dose, persistence, and the graft microenvironment as determinants of biological activity. Gene modulation strategies and delivery platforms relevant to the lung, including viral vectors, lipid nanoparticles, and virus-like particles, are outlined, together with preclinical gene therapy strategies targeting IRI and allograft rejection. Ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP) is highlighted as a practical window for organ-confined delivery and early mechanistic assessment prior to implantation. Key translational considerations are outlined, including product characterization and potency, clinically interpretable dosing, and the need for harmonized endpoints and pharmacodynamic readouts to improve comparability across studies.

items.title: Structural determinants of regional lung transplant listing rates in metropolitan France: A national ecological panel study
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Regional lung transplant listing rates in metropolitan France range from 2.4 to 11.4 new listings per million inhabitants per year across individual region-years, and from 4.7 to 8.3 when averaged over 2016-2023. We examined how geographic access, chronic respiratory disease burden, pulmonologist workforce composition, and socioeconomic deprivation relate to new waitlist inscriptions. METHODS: Ecological panel study of 12 metropolitan French regions (2016-2023; 96 region-years). The outcome was annual new lung transplant listings per million inhabitants. Predictors were population-weighted distance to the nearest authorised transplant centre (and binary centre presence), office-based and hospital-salaried pulmonologist density, chronic respiratory disease prevalence, and the European Deprivation Index (EDI). We used pooled ordinary least squares with year fixed effects, Driscoll-Kraay (DK) and small-sample cluster-robust standard errors. RESULTS: In the primary model, listing rates were higher with transplant programme presence (β = +0.86 listings/million/year; 95% DK CI 0.53-1.20), hospital-salaried pulmonologist density (β = +0.066; 95% DK CI 0.02-0.11), and lower socioeconomic deprivation (EDI β = -0.085; 95% DK CI -0.15 to -0.02). Office-based pulmonologist density was associated with listing rates unadjusted but attenuated after adjustment for centre presence, consistent with geographic co-location. With cluster-robust standard errors accounting for correlation within regions, the estimates were unchanged but all confidence intervals included zero. CONCLUSIONS: Inequalities in access to lung transplant listing in France may be in part driven by transplant programme distance, limited hospital-embedded pulmonology, and socioeconomic deprivation. These structural barriers are likely shared by other centralised, single-payer transplant systems. Additional studies using patient-level data to confirm these findings are needed to support interventions targeting these mechanisms.

items.title: Introducing an ELSA-IE Approach to Accelerate the Translation of Innovative Technologies in Lung Preservation - The LifeLUNG Project
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Despite significant advances in ex vivo machine perfusion and innovation in graft modulation, successful translation of preclinical research into clinical practice is limited by the lack of multi-disciplinary exchange early in the research pipeline. LifeLUNG is a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Doctoral Network funded by the European Union that aims to improve long-term outcomes in lung transplantation by leveraging ex vivo lung perfusion platforms to genetically modify donor lungs to modulate immune responses, reduce injury, and prevent graft rejection. LifeLUNG introduces an ELSA-IE approach, integrating Ethical, Legal, and Social Aspects research, Implementation science, and health Economics with preclinical research to navigate translational uncertainties and reduce the risk of late-stage innovation failure. By fostering the continuous exchange of insights and challenges among researchers, patients, and health systems, LifeLUNG aims to accelerate the responsible and clinically viable translation of lung transplantation innovations.

items.title: Not All PVR Reductions Are Created Equal: Lessons From the CADENCE Trial
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: The CADENCE trial evaluated sotatercept in combined post- and pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension associated with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (CpcPH-HFpEF). We analyzed the pathophysiological implications of the observed pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) reduction.A hemodynamic comparison was conducted contrasting the mechanistic effects of sotaercept with conventional pulmonary vasodilators.In CADENCE, PVR and pressure reductions occurred without marked cardiac output augmentation, contrasting with flow-mediated recruitment typical of traditional vasodilators. Sotatercept-induced PVR reduction may reflect true vascular reverse remodeling rather than vasodilation, underscoring the need to discriminate resistance reduction mechanisms in CpcPHHFpEF.

items.title: Utility of Donor-Recipient HLA Matching in Heart Transplantation in the Era of Extended Donor Organ Preservation: A Multi-Institutional Analysis
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Closer human leukocyte antigen (HLA) match between the donor and the recipient leads to better outcomes after kidney transplantation. Since extended donor preservation is now possible in heart transplantation (HT), we examined the possible impact of prioritization of HLA matching in HT. METHODS: We included single organ HT recipients reported to the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) transplanted in 2010-2019. Outcomes included survival, treated rejection and development of cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) across 5 and 10 year follow-up after transplant. We examined associations between matches at A, B, DR, DPB, DQA, DQB and DPA loci and the outcomes in univariable and multivariable analyses. RESULTS: There were 5176 patients in the 5Y cohort with a median of 9 (IQR 8; 11) HLA mismatches and 9118 patients in the 10Y cohort with a median of 6 (IQR 5; 7) HLA mismatches. In adjusted analyses, there was no significant association between donor-recipient HLA match and mortality, treated rejection or CAV in the 5Y cohort. In the 10Y cohort, HLA mismatch was a risk factor for mortality (HR 1.06, CI 1; 1.12, p=0.047) and treated rejection (HR 1.13, CI 1.07;1.2, p<0.001) in adults. Among pediatric patients, HLA mismatch conferred a nominally higher risk of mortality (HR 1.14, CI 0.97; 1.34, p=0.121) and treated rejection (HR 1.08, CI 0.96;1.21, p=0.226). CONCLUSIONS: We show that the current impact of donor-recipient HLA match on post-HT outcomes is relatively small. While novel organ preservation techniques may make HLA matching feasible, our data do not support its adoption into future iterations of the HT allocation system.
