items.title: Left Ventricular Assist Device Implantation in Dextrocardia: Lessons From a Complex Redo Case
items.abstract: Dextrocardia with situs solitus poses significant surgical challenges for left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation, particularly in patients with prior sternotomy and complex valvular disease. We report on a 60 year old man with dextrocardia, advanced heart failure, prior mechanical mitral valve replacement, and bicuspid aortic valve disease who underwent successful Corheart 6 LVAD implantation during redo sternotomy with concomitant bioprosthetic aortic and mitral valve replacement. Intraoperative findings included extensive pannus/thrombus on the mechanical mitral prosthesis (causing relative stenosis) and an unsuspected 10 g left atrial thrombus, both of which were removed. Total cardiopulmonary bypass time was 330 minutes, and aortic cross‑clamp time was 233 minutes. Postoperative acute kidney injury requiring dialysis resolved, and the patient was discharged after 137 days. At 1 year follow-up, the left ventricular end-diastolic diameter decreased from 69 to 66 mm, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) remained stable (28–25%), New York Heart Association (NYHA) class improved from IIIb‑IV to II, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) recovered from 32 ml/min at 9 months to 51 ml/min at 1 year.

items.title: When Human Tissue Meets the Driveline: Implications of Tissue Integration to Combat Driveline Infections
items.abstract: Driveline infection remains a common complication of ventricular assist device (VAD) therapy. These infections often progress from the exit site through the subcutaneous tract to the deeper tunnel and, in severe cases, the pocket, underscoring the vulnerability of the driveline–tissue interface. In this review, we examine the biological and mechanical factors governing tissue-driveline interactions and their implications for tissue integration of the implanted driveline. Dysregulated inflammation, impaired vascular maturation, abnormal extracellular matrix remodeling, repetitive micromotion and traction, and biomaterial–tissue mismatch may all compromise optimal tissue ingrowth of the driveline. Insufficient tissue integration can lead to the formation of microgaps within the driveline tunnel, providing a potential niche for microbial colonization and biofilm formation, thereby contributing to persistent driveline infections. Recognizing the potential association between inadequate tissue integration and the occurrence of driveline infection shifts the focus from microbial eradication alone toward optimizing driveline–tissue interactions across different segments of the driveline. Such an approach may help reduce the incidence of driveline infections in patients requiring long-term VAD support. Finally, strategies to promote tissue integration and long-term driveline stability, including driveline surface engineering, modulation of physicochemical properties, and optimization of surgical techniques, are discussed.

items.title: Predictors of Survival in Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Supported Immunocompromised Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Patients
items.abstract: Immunocompromised patients frequently develop acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) requiring venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO), yet evidence on prognostic factors in this population remains limited. This single-center retrospective study evaluated 90 day outcomes and identified predictors of mortality in immunocompromised ARDS patients supported with VV-ECMO. Between September 2009 and December 2021, 112 ARDS patients (49 immunocompromised and 63 immunocompetent) who received VV-ECMO were included. Baseline characteristics and outcomes were compared between groups; multivariate Cox regression analyzed 90 day mortality predictors, with subgroup analyses by immune status. Ninety day mortality was comparable between nonimmunosuppressed and immunosuppressed patients. Pre-ECMO platelet count <75 × 10 9 /L was the sole independent predictor of 90 day mortality, and this association was observed exclusively in immunocompromised patients. Immunocompromised patients with a platelet count ≥75 × 10 9 /L achieved survival comparable to immunocompetent patients, whereas those with a platelet count <75 × 10 9 /L had fewer ventilator-free and ECMO-free days. Immunocompromised status per se was not independently associated with 90 day mortality in VV-ECMO–supported ARDS patients. Pre-ECMO platelet count emerged as a critical risk stratification tool: immunocompromised patients with a platelet count ≥75 × 10 9 /L demonstrated favorable outcomes, whereas those with lower counts were at substantially increased risk.

items.title: Clinically Motivated Redesign of the Pennsylvania State University Child Ventricular Assist Device
items.abstract: Building on validated in vitro and chronic in vivo testing of the Penn State University (PSU) Child Ventricular Assist Device (CVAD), the four-bladed prototype rotor (Rev 0.0) was redesigned using established analytical and computational methods to improve hydraulic efficiency while preserving hemodynamic performance and biocompatibility. Applying turbomachinery principles at the nominal operating condition (3 liters/minute [LPM], 8,000 revolutions/minute [RPM]), a five-bladed design (Rev 1.0) was created with an ideal inflow angle ( β 1 = 41.0°) and outflow angle ( β 2 = 27.4°). In silico simulations of Rev 1.0 across the prototype’s operating range (7,000–9,000 RPM, 1–5 LPM) demonstrated an approximately 40% improvement in hydraulic performance. The Rev 1.0 rotor was then evaluated on a benchtop mock circulatory loop using fresh ovine blood, confirming the in silico gains. The normalized index of hemolysis (NIH), measured at two clinically relevant conditions (1.5 LPM and 3.3 LPM, both at ~80 mm Hg), was 0.052 ± 0.054 and 0.047 ± 0.033 mg/dL, respectively, and high-molecular-weight multimers of von Willebrand factor were preserved within normal to borderline ranges. By achieving target flows and pressures at approximately 1,000 RPM lower speeds, the redesign reduces power requirements and enables longer untethered operation, advancing a fully implantable PSU CVAD toward a critical unmet need in pediatric advanced heart failure.

items.title: Sensitivity of Damage Markers for Mechanical Trauma to Erythrocytes in Mechanical Circulatory Support Devices: A Multispecies Study
items.abstract: Mechanical circulatory support (MCS) advancement relies on fully understanding remaining hemocompatibility issues, including identifying and monitoring a variety of damage markers, as hemolysis alone is insufficient to understand the full scope of total blood damage. It is also important to understand how these alternative markers vary between species, as animal surrogates are often used in device development. This work focuses on evaluating erythrocyte-derived extracellular vesicles (ErEVs) released during MCS perfusion as an alternative marker for monitoring erythrocyte damage. Porcine, bovine, and human washed red blood cells (RBCs) were perfused through a blood circulatory loop using the CentriMag pump. Both hemolysis and ErEV production were monitored over time to compare the sensitivity of both to mechanically induced trauma and to observe species-dependent differences. All species produced significant increases in ErEV concentrations, while only human and bovine erythrocytes produced significant increases in free hemoglobin. There were no differences in the normalized index of hemolysis between species, but bovine RBCs produced significantly more ErEVs than human or porcine, which were similar. Regarding damage marker sensitivity, ErEV generation appears to be a promising complementary marker to hemolysis and potentially more sensitive for porcine and bovine models, while more testing is needed for human.

items.title: Ex Vivo Heart Perfusion Versus Cold Storage in Prolonged Preservation Period: A Juvenile Porcine Experimental Model
items.abstract: Cross-clamp times greater than or equal to 4 hours are critical for donor heart viability. We compared cold storage (CS) and normothermic ex vivo heart perfusion (EVHP) during prolonged preservation using a juvenile porcine model. Twenty-two piglet hearts (~10 kg) were assigned to CS or EVHP for 6 or 8 hours, followed by 2 hours of working-mode (WM) perfusion. Metabolism, cardiac function, and cell damage were compared using two-sample t-tests or Fisher’s exact tests, and temporal changes during perfusion were assessed using linear mixed-effects models and generalized estimating equations. During EVHP, the minimal rate of pressure change decreased, and arterial lactate levels increased after 5–6 hours. Compared to CS, EVHP hearts showed higher left atrial pressure (6 vs. 0 mm Hg, p = 0.011), arterial lactate levels during WM ( p < 0.001), and NFκB-p65 levels ( p = 0.002) at 6 hours, and lower cardiac output (90 vs. 120% of normal, p = 0.026), higher left atrial pressure (7 vs. 3 mm Hg, p = 0.009), higher arterial lactate levels during WM ( p < 0.001), and increased neutrophil infiltration ( p = 0.033) at 8 hours. Ex vivo heart perfusion hearts deteriorated beyond 5–6 hours and showed greater hemodynamic, metabolic, and inflammatory changes at both 6 and 8 hours. Ex vivo heart perfusion enhancements reducing immune response and inflammation are crucial for expanding the donor pool.

items.title: UNOS Registry Analysis: How Does Heart Transplant Recipient Weight Affect Waitlist Days?
items.abstract: Body weight of heart transplant (HTx) recipients affects waitlist days. However, no prior report exists to articulate this in detail. The aim of this study is to analyze the effect of recipients’ weight to HTx. The United Network of Organ Sharing (UNOS) registry was analyzed under the current allocation from 2018 to 2023. The cohort was divided into three even weight groups: low (<77.1 kg), middle (77.1–92.1 kg), and high (>92.1 kg). Candidate/donor demographics, weight distributions, waitlist days in UNOS Status, cumulative incidence of HTx and delisting, post-HTx survival, and cutoff weight for earlier HTx were analyzed. A total of 16,664 HTx recipients were included (5,535: low, 5,537: middle, and 5,592: high). Donors and recipients had a weight distribution mismatch ( p = 0.003). For waitlist days, status 1 was comparable; however, the high group with status ≥2 had approximately twice longer waitlist days than the low group. The high group had a lower incidence of HTx ( p < 0.001) and higher delisting ( p = 0.02) than the low group. One year survival was comparable ( p = 0.28). The weight cutoff for earlier HTx was 80 kg with a 21.6% increased rate of HTx (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.216; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.171–1.263, p < 0.001). Recipients weighing <80 kg had earlier HTx and a higher incidence of HTx. The effect of pre-HTx weight management requires further study.

items.title: Heparin Retention and Dispersion Following Injection of Locking Fluid in an Acute Hemodialysis Catheter: A Simulation Study
items.abstract: Heparin locking is used to maintain patency of acute hemodialysis catheters; however, unintended leakage of locking solution into the systemic circulation may increase bleeding risk. Ideally, locking solution would remain confined to the catheter lumen, maintaining patency while minimizing systemic anticoagulation, yet the mechanisms governing heparin retention and dispersion remain inadequately understood. Patient-specific computational fluid dynamics simulations incorporating non-Newtonian blood flow and species transport were performed using a microcomputed tomography-derived model of an acute dual-lumen hemodialysis catheter to evaluate the effects of injection rate, venous blood flow, and lock volume. Injection of the manufacturer-recommended 1.4 ml lock volume over durations of 0.5–5 seconds resulted in 13–16% (900–1100 U) of injected heparin entering the systemic circulation, yielding transient therapeutic systemic heparin concentrations. Rapid injections increased distal penetration of the locking solution and improved heparin retention (from 84% to 87%). Heparin clearance following injection occurred in two phases consisting of rapid early convective washout followed by prolonged slow diffusive clearance. Reducing lock volume substantially decreased systemic heparin exposure while preserving therapeutic intraluminal heparin concentrations. These findings provide mechanistic insight into catheter locking behavior and suggest that optimization of lock volume may reduce unintended systemic anticoagulation while maintaining catheter patency.

items.title: Meet the Authors
From the Editor’s Desk: The Future Has Arrived!
Percutaneous Echo-Guided Cervical Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Cannulation by Intensivists in Neonates and Children
items.abstract: Cervical cannulation is the standard approach for venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) in neonates and small children but is traditionally performed surgically. We report our initial experience with bedside percutaneous ultrasound- and echocardiography-guided cervical VA-ECMO cannulation performed by intensivists. Three pediatric patients underwent percutaneous right common carotid artery and internal jugular vein cannulation. Vascular access, guidewire advancement, tract dilation, and cannula positioning were guided by ultrasound and transthoracic echocardiography. Median age was 5 months (range, 20 days–6 years) and median weight 7 kg (range, 3–15 kg). Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation was initiated for extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation in two patients and refractory cardiogenic shock in one. Cannulation was successful in all patients without surgical conversion, with a median skin-puncture-to-flow time of 32 minutes (range, 28–35). Target flow (>100 ml/kg/min) was achieved in two patients. No major cannulation-related vascular or cardiac complications occurred. Two patients died on ECMO, while one survived without signs of stroke on follow-up magnetic resonance imaging. Vascular integrity was documented by postmortem examination or Doppler follow-up. Bedside percutaneous echo-guided cervical VA-ECMO cannulation by experienced intensivists appears technically feasible in pediatric patients. Further studies are needed to establish safety, reproducibility, effectiveness, and potential advantages over conventional surgical cannulation.

items.title: Direct Computed Tomographic Visualization of the Mixing Point During Peripheral Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation
Dynamic Early Postreperfusion Physiology Is Associated With Organ Recovery After Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
items.abstract: Prognostication after extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) predominantly relies on characteristics available before or at initiation of extracorporeal support. We investigated whether the early metabolic response to extracorporeal reperfusion provides complementary information on subsequent recovery. We retrospectively analyzed 91 patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated with ECPR. Lactate was assessed before and 12 h after extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) initiation. Outcomes included in-hospital mortality, successful ECMO weaning, cerebral edema/hypoxic brain injury, and favorable neurological survival. Associations were adjusted for low-flow duration. Twelve hour lactate was lower in survivors than nonsurvivors (5.45 vs . 9.04 mmol/L; p = 0.002), whereas prereperfusion lactate did not differ. In paired measurements (n = 38), mortality discrimination increased from an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.47 before reperfusion to 0.80 at 12 h. Each 5 mmol/L higher 12 h lactate was associated with mortality (odds ratio [OR] = 2.73), lower odds of ECMO weaning (OR = 0.44), and cerebral edema/hypoxic injury (OR = 2.07) after low-flow adjustment. Early metabolic response after extracorporeal reperfusion was associated with survival and both circulatory and cerebral recovery. Dynamic post-reperfusion physiology may provide complementary information beyond static pre-reperfusion assessment.

items.title: Iliohypogastric and Ilioinguinal Nerve Block for Awake ECPella Cannulation in Pediatric Patients With Nonpostcardiotomy Cardiogenic Shock
items.abstract: In pediatric cardiogenic shock, endotracheal intubation may carry a high risk of cardiac arrest during anesthesia induction. This single-center retrospective case series (2020–2025) evaluated the feasibility, safety, and outcomes of ultrasound (US)-guided ilioinguinal–iliohypogastric (IhIG) nerve blocks (0.05–0.1 ml/kg of 0.25% ropivacaine) under light sedation to facilitate awake venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and Impella (ECPella) surgical cannulation. Five adolescents (median age: 13 years, range: 7–17; median weight: 45 kg, range: 21–58) with nonpostcardiotomy cardiogenic shock underwent successful IhIG block placement in the pediatric intensive care unit by anesthesia-trained intensivists, followed by surgical cannulation in the catheterization laboratory. Intubation and mechanical ventilation were avoided during initial cannulation and throughout ECPella duration. Three patients required a modified chimney Y-graft for cannula placement, and two experienced local surgical bleeding. All five patients survived to hospital discharge, with three achieving direct biventricular recovery. Based on these preliminary data, US-guided IhIG nerve block seems a feasible and safe strategy for awake ECPella cannulation in selected pediatric patients, successfully avoiding high-risk invasive ventilation and general anesthesia.

items.title: Impact of Showering Methods on Driveline Exit Site Microbiology and Driveline Infection in Patients With Left Ventricular Assist Devices
items.abstract: Driveline infection (DLI) remains a major complication in patients with a left ventricular assist device (LVAD). This study evaluated the impact of different showering methods on bacterial colonization at the driveline exit site (DLES) and the incidence of DLI. Patients who underwent LVAD implantation at our institute from 2008 to 2021 were included and classified into two groups: the open group, in which the DLES was exposed and washed with running water, and the covered group, in which the DLES was sealed with a waterproof dressing during showering. The primary outcome was the incidence of DLI within 3 years following hospital discharge. A total of 103 patients were included (the open group, n = 47; the covered group, n = 56). The DLI-free rate was significantly higher in the covered group than the open group (77% vs. 49%; p = 0.003). Pseudomonas aeruginosa was detected less frequently at the DLES, and DLI caused by P. aeruginosa was significantly reduced in the covered group. Multivariate analysis suggested that the open showering method was an independent risk factor for DLI (hazard ratio, 2.816; 95% confidence interval, 1.325–5.984; p = 0.007). The covered showering method was associated with a significantly lower incidence of DLI, particularly infections caused by P. aeruginosa .

items.title: Outcomes and Complications of Axillary Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump Support: A Single-Center Experience
items.abstract: Axillary intra-aortic balloon pump (axi-IABP) support has emerged as an alternative to femoral access for patients with advanced heart failure, offering improved mobility and potential benefits in pretransplant conditioning; however, data on associated complications remain limited. We conducted a retrospective study of 55 patients who underwent axi-IABP placement between January 2019 and July 2025 at our institution. The cohort had a median age of 59 (interquartile range [IQR], 52–65) years and presented with cardiogenic shock requiring mechanical circulatory support (MCS). Axi-IABP successfully bridged 87.3% of patients to advanced therapies. A total of 83 complications were identified in 60.0% of patients, most commonly malposition in 23.6% of patients, gas leak alarms in 16.4% of patients, and kinking in 16.4% of patients. Serious vascular complications were infrequent. The median time to first complication was 10.5 (IQR, 2.75–25.5) days. Female sex was associated with a higher hazard of first complication when controlled for height (adjusted hazard ratio [HR] = 2.75, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.04–7.27; p = 0.041). In conclusion, axi-IABP is an effective bridging strategy that enhances patient mobility but is associated with a high rate of device-related complications, predominantly mechanical in nature, underscoring the importance of careful patient selection and monitoring.

items.title: Levosimendan and Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Weaning: Still an Open Question?
Beyond VA-ECMO Cannulation: Socioeconomic Disparities and Pathways to Definitive Therapy
Response to the Letter to the Editor: Beyond VA-ECMO Cannulation: Socioeconomic Disparities and Pathways to Definitive Therapy
Renal Decline Before Heart Transplantation in Left Ventricular Assist Device-Supported Recipients: United Network for Organ Sharing Analysis
items.abstract: Although baseline renal impairment and post-heart transplantation (HT) dialysis are established clinical predictors, the prognostic impact of pre-HT renal decline in patients bridged with left ventricular assist devices (LVADs) remains unclear. We retrospectively analyzed patients from the United Network for Organ Sharing registry who underwent HT following LVAD support between 2009 and 2024. Renal decline was defined as a greater than or equal to 40% reduction in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) from listing to HT. Among 10,454 patients, 624 (6.0%) experienced pre-HT renal decline. Patients with renal decline had longer waitlist durations (median 297 vs. 197 days; p < 0.001), lower eGFR at HT (42.0 vs. 70.6 ml/min/1.73 m 2 ; p < 0.001), and higher rates of post-HT dialysis (23.7 vs. 12.8%; p < 0.001). Independent predictors of renal decline included longer waitlist time and perioperative blood transfusions, whereas HeartMate 3 LVAD use was protective. Renal decline was independently associated with an increased risk of post-HT dialysis (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]: 2.64) and all-cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR]: 1.16), with post-HT dialysis strongly predicting mortality (aHR: 3.48). Renal deterioration is a significant predictor of post-HT dialysis and mortality in LVAD-bridged patients. Incorporating renal trajectory into risk stratification may enhance candidate selection and promote perioperative renal protection strategies.

items.title: Cardiac Output From Right Ventricular Pressure: Not the Solution for Venovenous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation
items.abstract: Cardiac output (CO) monitoring is challenging during venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV ECMO), as thermodilution techniques are unreliable. Cardiac output from right ventricular pressure (RVP) waveforms has recently been considered. We evaluated whether RVP-derived CO (CO RV ) accurately reflects cardiac output measured by echocardiography (CO US ) during VV ECMO. Ten anesthetized pigs underwent femoro-jugular VV ECMO implantation. A Swan-Ganz IQ catheter provided continuous CO RV monitoring throughout the experiment. Cardiac output was modulated using either dobutamine (5–20 µg/kg/min) or landiolol (10–40 µg/kg/min) infusions. Agreement between CO RV and CO US was assessed using Pearson correlation and Bland–Altman analysis. Overall, 596 paired CO measurements were performed in seven animals. Cardiac output ranged from 1.05 to 9.46 L/min. Correlation between CO RV and CO US was poor ( R = 0.24; R 2 = 0.057; p < 0.05). Bland–Altman analysis showed a mean bias of +1.94 L/min with wide limits of agreement (−1.44 to +5.32 L/min). Correlations between individual right ventricular pressure waveform components and CO US were heterogeneous and weak to moderate (diastolic RVP, R = 0.36; right ventricle +d P /d t [delta pressure/delta time] R = 0.40; systolic RVP R = 0.60). CO RV is not reliable during VV ECMO in our experiment. Further studies are needed to assess CO RV performances.

items.title: Current Global Trends and Challenges of Pediatric Ventricular Assist Device Programs: An ACTION Collaborative Survey
items.abstract: Ventricular assist devices (VADs) have become an established therapy for children with end-stage heart failure, yet multinational data describing pediatric VAD programs remain limited. We conducted a 12 question survey through the Advanced Cardiac Therapies Improving Outcomes Network (ACTION) involving 74 international healthcare professionals from pediatric VAD programs outside North America. The survey assessed device and resource availability, multidisciplinary team composition, program challenges, and future priorities. Fifteen responses representing 15 centers from 14 countries were received, including 13 centers with established pediatric VAD programs. Most centers (91%, 10/11) managed 1–5 pediatric VAD patients annually. Berlin Heart EXCOR and HeartMate 3 were available in 85% (11/13) of centers, while only 46.7% (7/15) had a dedicated VAD coordinator. Major barriers included inadequate education for intensive care unit (ICU) and nursing staff and patients (69%, 9/13), financial constraints (54%, 7/13), limited device availability (46%, 6/13), and lack of outpatient VAD experience, with 31% (4/13) of centers reporting no experience discharging patients on VAD support. Substantial variation in device availability, multidisciplinary resources, and program experience exists across regions. These findings highlight important gaps in pediatric VAD care and support international collaboration to improve education, infrastructure, and access to advanced heart failure therapies.

items.title: Acute Right Heart Failure Following Left Coronary Myocardial Infarction in Left Ventricular Assist Device–Supported Patients: A Case Series and Mechanistic Insight
items.abstract: Right heart failure (RHF) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients supported with durable left ventricular assist devices (LVADs). While right coronary artery infarction is a recognized cause of acute RHF, the ventricular consequences of left coronary system infarction in LVAD-supported patients are not well characterized. We describe two patients supported with HeartMate III LVADs who developed acute RHF within 24–48 hours after successful revascularization of acute left coronary system occlusions (mid-left anterior descending artery and left main coronary artery). Both had previously stable LVAD function and no evidence of advanced RHF. After revascularization, each developed hypotension, rising central venous pressure, reduced LVAD flows, and echocardiographic evidence of severe right ventricular (RV) dilation and dysfunction with septal shift toward the left ventricle. Hemodynamic deterioration reversed with inotropic support, diuresis, and LVAD speed adjustment, without mechanical RV support. These cases suggest left coronary acute myocardial infarction (AMI) may precipitate acute RHF in LVAD-supported patients through septal ischemia with impaired ventricular interdependence, acute increases in RV afterload, and relative RV ischemia despite patent right coronary arteries. Heightened surveillance and early echocardiographic assessment after left-sided AMI in LVAD recipients may enable prompt recognition and timely intervention.

items.title: From Marker of Risk to Marker of Response: Using Biomarkers to Guide Heart Failure Rehabilitation
Correction to: Circulating Biomarkers as Predictors of Improvement in Physical Function in Hospitalized Older Adults With Geriatric Syndromes: Findings From the REHAB-HF Trial
Genotype, Phenotypic Severity, and Survival in Pediatric Dilated Cardiomyopathy: A Report From the Pediatric Cardiomyopathy Registry
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) frequently presents with heart failure in children. Whether a genetic cause of DCM is associated with disease severity or eventual outcome in pediatric DCM is unclear. METHODS: A multiinstitutional prospective pediatric cohort study (0–18 years) with nonsyndromic DCM was undertaken from 2013 to 2016. A panel of 37 cardiomyopathy-associated genes was interrogated by exome sequencing with analysis for pathogenic or likely pathogenic (LP) variants. Clinical severity and outcomes of death, cardiac transplant, and continuing left ventricular dysfunction versus echocardiographic normalization were assessed. RESULTS: A total of 279 DCM probands (47% male) with a median (interquartile range) age at diagnosis of 1.6 (0.4–10.4) years were enrolled. Median follow-up was 1.1 (0.2–4.0) years. Gene variants designated as pathogenic/LP were identified in 18 of the 37 genes evaluated, and of all positive variants, TTN (17%), TNNT2 (15%), MYH7 (15%), RBM20 (9%), and LMNA (8%) were most frequently implicated. Only 19% of the overall cohort yielded an identifiable genetic cause, without any difference between ancestries. Children >12 years old had the highest genetic yield at 34% ( P <0.05). Symptoms of heart failure occurred in 62% of patients who carried a pathogenic/LP gene variant, at or within 12 months of presentation, but neither heart failure symptoms, nor echocardiographic severity was associated with having a pathogenic/LP variant. The rate of death or cardiac transplant did not differ with the presence or absence of a pathogenic/LP variant and exceeded 60% by 10 years after diagnosis. On competing risks analysis, a trend ( P =0.09) toward greater echo normalization, was noted in those without a pathogenic/LP variant by 10 years after diagnosis. CONCLUSIONS: A genetic cause was detected in a minority of children and was not associated with the phenotypic severity of DCM at diagnosis. Echocardiographic normalization of left ventricular function over time was noted more frequently in patients who did not have an identified pathogenic/LP variant.

items.title: Influenza Vaccine Effectiveness Across Nutritional Status Categories in Patients Hospitalized With Acute Heart Failure: A Secondary Analysis of the PANDA II Trial
Diastolic Dysfunction in Congenital Heart Disease: A Pressure-Volume Loop Analysis of Borderline Left Heart
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Diastolic dysfunction is a major driver of morbidity in congenital heart disease, but its mechanisms are poorly understood. It remains unknown whether left ventricular (LV) diastolic dysfunction in borderline left heart patients is caused by a defect in active relaxation or in passive stiffness. We applied gold-standard pressure-volume (PV) loop analysis to define the mechanism of diastolic dysfunction in patients with borderline LV. METHODS: We analyzed invasive PV loops from children with bLV (n=13) and a pragmatic comparison group of patients with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries (ccTGA, n=14). PV loops were generated during transient preload alteration. Active relaxation was assessed by the isovolumetric relaxation time constant (τ) and maximal rate of pressure decline (dP/dt min ) indexed to peak systolic pressure. Passive stiffness was quantified by the stiffness constant (β), derived from the multibeat end-diastolic PV relationship. To account for size differences, β was calculated using indexed ventricular volumes (iβ), and also converted to a dimensionless stiffness constant (β w =β×ventricular wall volume). RESULTS: Active relaxation measures were similar between groups (τ bLV, 28 [23.5–29.5] versus ccTGA, 24 [21–28] msec, P =0.11; dP/dt min /peak systolic pressure bLV: −10.6 [−11.0 to −9.4] versus ccTGA: −9.9 [−10.5 to −8.7] s − 1 , P =0.17). In contrast, patients with bLV had markedly abnormal passive stiffness. The end-diastolic PV relationship was shifted upward and to the left, and the stiffness constants were higher in the bLV group (iβ bLV, 0.10 [0.04–0.35] versus ccTGA, 0.03 [0.02–0.04] m 2 /mL, P =0.003; β w bLV, 4.08 [1.6–7.52] versus ccTGA, 1.21 [0.95–1.77]; P =0.002). CONCLUSIONS: The primary mechanism of diastolic dysfunction in bLV is increased passive ventricular stiffness, while no differences were detected in active relaxation. These findings suggest a limited role for lusitropic medications and therapeutic strategies that focus on mitigating ventricular stiffness (such as surgical endocardial fibroelastosis resection) may be more valuable.

items.title: Exercise Right Atrial Stiffness From Pressure-Volume Loops and Prognosis in Pulmonary Hypertension
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: In pulmonary hypertension (PH), risk assessment focuses on right ventricular function and may overlook exercise-related right atrial (RA) functional limitation. We investigated whether RA stiffness during exercise reflects impaired right-heart filling reserve and is associated with prognosis beyond conventional measures. METHODS: We prospectively enrolled 68 participants in this observational study, including 42 with precapillary PH. Participants who had PH ruled out and patients with postcapillary PH formed reference groups. Participants underwent 3-dimensional echocardiography, right heart catheterization, and invasive RA pressure-volume loop analysis at rest and during standardized semisupine exercise. RA filling stiffness was derived from the reservoir phase. Patients with precapillary PH were stratified by median exercise RA filling stiffness. RESULTS: At rest, high- and low-stiffness groups had comparable right ventricular function, afterload, and cardiac index, but the high-stiffness group exhibited impaired phasic RA strain and venous congestion (median [interquartile range] liver stiffness, 7.1 [6.0–8.8] versus 5.2 [4.8–5.8] kPa; P =0.021). During exercise, mean RA pressure increased similarly, but the high-stiffness group had impaired peak cardiac index (3.3±1.0 versus 4.1±0.9 L/min per m 2 ; P =0.015) and RA strain. Unlike resting RA stiffness, high exercise RA stiffness was independently associated with mortality (adjusted hazard ratio, 4.37 [95% CI, 1.20–15.96]). A model including RA conduit strain and right ventricular functional reserve discriminated high RA stiffness (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, 0.90). CONCLUSIONS: RA stiffness during exercise integrates resting congestion with limited cardiac reserve and unmasks mortality risk missed by resting metrics. RA conduit strain and right ventricular functional reserve noninvasively identify the high-stiffness subgroup.

items.title: Antecedent Kidney Function and Cardiovascular Mortality in Over 300 000 Patients With Incident Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic kidney disease is a frequent comorbidity in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) and has been proposed as a contributor to its development. However, the spectrum of antecedent kidney function before incident HFpEF and its association with subsequent cardiovascular outcomes remains unclear. METHODS: We conducted a multicenter cohort study across 170 US Veterans Affairs hospitals, including patients with incident HFpEF diagnosed between January 1, 2000, and June 30, 2025. HFpEF was ascertained using natural language processing-derived left ventricular ejection fraction ≥50% closest to the incident HF date and a validated HFpEF algorithm incorporating loop diuretic use, elevated natriuretic peptide levels, and an HFpEF–age, body mass index, and atrial fibrillation score >0.5. Antecedent kidney function was classified using 2 estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) measurements obtained ≥90 days apart before incident HFpEF and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio. We characterized antecedent kidney function, including albuminuria (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio ≥30 mg/g), and examined its associations with 5-year cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization. Competing-risk analysis was performed accounting for noncardiovascular death as a competing event for cardiovascular death. RESULTS: Of 304 712 patients meeting HFpEF ascertainment criteria, 236 910 comprised the final cohort; 51% had antecedent eGFR ≥60 mL/min per 1.73m 2 . Overall, 15% had an eGFR ≥90 mL/min per 1.73m 2 . Patients with eGFR <60 mL/min per 1.73m 2 were older and had more diabetes and hypertension. 51% of the patients with eGFR <60 mL/min per 1.73m 2 had body mass index <30 kg/m 2 , including 20% with body mass index <25 kg/m 2 . Progressively lower antecedent kidney function was associated with graded increases in cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalization. Among decedents, the proportion of deaths attributed to cardiovascular causes increased from 25% in the preserved eGFR (≥90 mL/min per 1.73m 2 ) without documented albuminuria to 32% with albuminuria and 38% with advanced kidney dysfunction ( P <0.001). CONCLUSIONS: In this nationwide study of patients with incident HFpEF, antecedent kidney dysfunction was common but not uniformly present before HFpEF onset. Furthermore, among patients who developed HFpEF, antecedent kidney dysfunction identified a higher-risk phenotype, with progressively greater cardiovascular mortality and heart failure hospitalization with declining kidney function.

items.title: Heart Failure Presenting With Concurrent Chylothorax and Chylous Ascites Resolved by Revascularization in Ischemic Cardiomyopathy: A Case Report and Review
Multiomics Integration Reveals a Skeletal Muscle Metabolic Myopathy in Cardiometabolic HFpEF
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Skeletal muscle dysfunction is a major peripheral determinant of exercise intolerance and physical disability in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Metabolic and mitochondrial dysfunction are considered to be key components of skeletal muscle dysfunction, but comprehensive profiling of metabolic pathways has not been conducted. Elucidation of dysregulated metabolic pathways is essential to determine viable targets for the treatment of exercise intolerance in HFpEF. METHODS: Male ZSF1 Obese rats (HFpEF, n=8) and Wistar Kyoto lean normotensive controls (Control, n=8) were studied at 26 weeks of age. The gastrocnemius was analyzed using bulk RNA sequencing, proteomics, metabolomics, and lipidomics. Differential expression across all omics layers was determined using standard statistical modeling with thresholds of absolute fold‑change >1.5 and FDR <0.05, unless otherwise specified. Additional targeted plasma and skeletal muscle metabolomics and lipidomics were performed in HFpEF and control rats, including analyses of the soleus and the extensor digitorum longus, to validate features associated with predominantly oxidative and glycolytic muscle, respectively. RESULTS: Pathway-level analysis for RNA sequencing and proteomics revealed significant downregulation of oxidative phosphorylation (natural enrichment score (NES), −2.1; P <0.005), electron transport chain (NES, −2.0; P <0.005), and tricarboxylic acid cycle cycle (−1.8; P <0.05). The most upregulated pathways were PPAR signaling (NES, 2.2; P <0.0001), tryptophan metabolism (NES, 1.8; P <0.005), and amino acid oxidation (NES, 1.8; P <0.005) pathways. Metabolomics revealed an accumulation of tricarboxylic acid cycle cycle intermediate, isocitrate, and phosphate reduction. Branched-chain amino acids were significantly increased, whereas amino acids related to tryptophan metabolism were reduced and shifted towards increased serotonin accumulation. Phospholipid species were differentially regulated with increased palmitoylated phosphatidylcholines but reduced arachidonoyl-phosphatidylcholine species. Phosphatidylethanolamines species (16:0/16:1–18:0/18:2) were increased. CONCLUSIONS: HFpEF skeletal muscle shows signatures of profound mitochondrial and peroxisomal dysfunction with lipid overload, impaired branched chain amino acid and tryptophan metabolism, and a shift in membrane phospholipid composition, supporting an acquired metabolic myopathy in cardiometabolic HFpEF.

items.title: A REBIRTH of Disease-Specific Therapy
Bromocriptine for Myocardial Recovery in Peripartum Cardiomyopathy
items.abstract: Background There is evidence suggesting that bromocriptine potentially improves outcomes among women with peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM); however, there is currently no randomized controlled trial comparing bromocriptine vs placebo on top of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) in a diverse, multiethnic cohort in North America. Objectives The REBIRTH trial will enroll 200 women with PPCM to evaluate whether the addition of oral bromocriptine to GDMT is superior to placebo for improving myocardial function and event-free survival. In addition to the randomized trial, REBIRTH will enroll 50 women with PPCM excluded from randomization because of breastfeeding into an observational cohort. Methods The principal inclusion criteria are ≥18 years of age, within 5-months postpartum, and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≤40%. The primary endpoint is LVEF at 6 months postrandomization. Secondary endpoints include LVEF at 12 months, survival free from major events (ie, death, heart transplantation, or implantation of a durable left ventricular assist device), and survival free from heart failure hospitalization for up to 3 years. Results The study is currently enrolling women in both the randomized trial and observational breastfeeding cohort. Primary results are expected to be reported in 2027. Conclusions REBIRTH will determine whether the addition of bromocriptine to GDMT for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction improves postpartum myocardial recovery and clinical outcomes in a diverse cohort of women with PPCM. (Randomized Evaluation of Bromocriptine in Myocardial Recovery Therapy for PPCM [REBIRTH]; NCT05180773).

items.title: Assessment and Reversibility of Hepatic Abnormalities in Heart Failure
items.abstract: Hepatic abnormalities in non-Fontan heart failure result from congestive hepatopathy and hypoperfusion-related ischemic injury, compounded by neurohormonal activation and systemic inflammation. Assessment of liver disease severity is challenging because standard liver biochemistries, serum fibrosis markers, severity score models, elastography, and imaging modalities have limited diagnostic accuracy in congestive hepatopathy, and hepatic fibrosis is often heterogeneous on histology in this population. Management focuses on optimization of cardiac function through medical therapy or mechanical circulatory support. Although liver biochemical abnormalities frequently improve with restoration of cardiac function, histologic reversibility is variable and not consistently observed. In patients with advanced heart failure needing heart transplantation, histologic cirrhosis and/or fibrosis accompanied by portal hypertension may merit consideration of combined heart-liver transplantation, but correlation between fibrosis and clinical outcomes varies. There remains an unmet need for tests that can reliably assess liver disease severity and predict liver outcomes in non-Fontan congestive hepatopathy.

items.title: Cardiac Structure and Function in Women After Preeclampsia
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Preeclampsia increases the risk of long-term heart failure (HF) by 4-fold. Unfortunately, however, universal guidelines for postpartum HF surveillance are lacking. Stage B/subclinical HF has been shown to predict risk of major adverse cardiac outcomes. Some suggest that initiating cardioprotective therapy at this early stage can reduce progression to symptomatic HF. OBJECTIVES: The aim of this review was to explore cardiac structure and function in women with a history of preeclampsia and to identify when subclinical HF develops in this group. METHODS: A systematic search of MEDLINE, EMBASE and CINAHL was conducted according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines to identify all studies assessing left ventricular function on transthoracic echocardiography in women with a history of preeclampsia. RESULTS: A total of 45 case-control studies comprising 8,991 women, including 2,288 women with a history of preeclampsia, were included in the final analysis. During pregnancy, women with preeclampsia had a higher left ventricular mass index (LVMI) (standard mean difference: 10.85 [95% CI: 6.30-15.39]), relative wall thickness (0.05 [95% CI: 0.03-0.08]), E/e' (1.58 [95% CI: 1.02-2.13]), isovolumetric relaxation time (8.74 [95% CI: 3.14-14.34]), lower E/A ratio (-0.27 [95% CI: -0.51 to -0.04]) and reduced absolute global longitudinal strain (GLS) values (2.27 [95% CI: 0.43-4.11]), indicating reduced myocardial function compared with normotensive controls. Postpartum, GLS remained reduced, and LVMI remained elevated in women with a history of preeclampsia. This difference persisted out to 10 years postpartum. There was no significant difference in all other variables >6 months postpartum. Evidence for persistent LVMI elevation >6 months postpartum was not robust in sensitivity analyses excluding overlapping cohorts. Left ventricular ejection fraction and right ventricular function remained similar in the preeclampsia and control groups throughout. CONCLUSIONS: Preeclampsia is associated with subclinical myocardial dysfunction, characterized by impaired GLS and increased LVMI. Persistent impairment in GLS was observed up to 10 years postpartum, whereas the association with elevated LVMI beyond 6 months postpartum should be interpreted with caution. Further studies are required to assess when subclinical myocardial dysfunction progresses to symptomatic clinical HF.

items.title: Bayesian Survival Analysis for Heart Failure Clinical Trials in the Presence of Competing Risks
Transcriptomics Identifies a Small Set of Circulating Biomarkers and Signaling Pathways Dysregulated in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
items.abstract: Background It is sometimes challenging to distinguish hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) from other cardiomyopathies with left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH). At present, no circulating biomarkers to distinguish HCM have been established. Objectives The authors aimed to identify plasma microRNA (miRNA) biomarkers unique to HCM. Methods In this multicenter case-control study, the authors performed comprehensive plasma transcriptomics profiling in cases with HCM and controls with hypertensive LVH, transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), and aortic stenosis (AS). For each disease group, they chronologically split the patients into training and test sets. The authors identified miRNAs that were significantly (Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted P Results The authors analyzed 2,656 miRNAs in patients with HCM (n = 294), hypertensive LVH (n = 321), ATTR-CM (n = 167), and AS (n = 38). They identified 3 miRNAs (miR-454-3p, miR-98-5p, and miR-5581-3p). The logistic regression model using the 3 miRNAs had an area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve of 0.95 (95% CI: 0.93-0.97) with a sensitivity of 0.95 and a specificity of 0.90 in the test set. Conclusions Comprehensive plasma transcriptomics profiling identified a small set of circulating miRNAs to distinguish HCM from other cardiomyopathies with LVH.

items.title: A Decade of DCD Heart Transplantation
Family Screening and Disease Predictors in Gene-Elusive Dilated Cardiomyopathy
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Family screening is recommended in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), but risk stratification of relatives of probands without pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants (gene-elusive) remains uncertain. OBJECTIVES: This study sought to define the incidence, prognosis, and predictors of disease development in first-degree relatives of gene-elusive DCM probands. METHODS: First-degree relatives of gene-elusive DCM probands from 4 international referral centers who underwent baseline electrocardiography and echocardiography were included. The primary outcome was the development of the disease, defined as DCM or isolated left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction (LV ejection fraction: <50%). Major adverse cardiac events were exploratory secondary outcomes. Age-adjusted Cox models with family-clustered robust standard errors were used to identify disease predictors. RESULTS: Among 292 relatives (median age: 36 years, 48% male), 14 (5%) were affected at baseline. During a median follow-up of 52 months, 21 additional relatives developed disease, corresponding to an incidence rate of 17 per 1,000 person-years. Familial DCM (HR: 4.24; 95% CI: 1.38-13.1; P = 0.012), QRS duration >120 ms (HR: 7.24; 95% CI: 2.25-23.3; P < 0.001), lower LV ejection fraction (HR: 3.73; 95% CI: 2.46-5.65; P < 0.001), and LV dilatation (HR: 6.19; 95% CI: 2.27-16.9; P < 0.001) were predictors of disease development. Age at diagnosis in probands significantly correlated with age at onset in relatives (r = 0.80; 95% CI: 0.55-0.92; P < 0.001). Major adverse cardiac events occurred in 9 patients (4%). CONCLUSIONS: First-degree relatives of gene-elusive DCM probands have a relatively low but non-negligible risk of disease development. Familial clustering, electrocardiographic or echocardiographic abnormalities, and age of disease expression in the proband may help tailor surveillance intensity.

items.title: NT-proBNP and Clinical Outcomes in Patients With HFrEF According to Atrial Fibrillation
items.abstract: Background The Chinese traditional medicine qiliqiangxin (QLQX) improves outcomes in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) when added to guideline-directed medical therapy. Objectives This post hoc analysis of the QUEST (Qiliqiangxin in Heart Failure: Assessment of Reduction in Mortality) trial assessed the efficacy and safety of QLQX according to baseline N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels, and examined whether the prognostic value of baseline NT-proBNP varied by atrial fibrillation (AF) status. Methods QUEST enrolled 3,110 patients with HFrEF and NT-proBNP ≥450 pg/mL, and followed them for a median of 18 months. The primary outcome was cardiovascular (CV) death or heart failure (HF) hospitalization. NT-proBNP was analyzed by quartiles and as a continuous variable. Results Median baseline NT-proBNP was 1,731 pg/mL. Higher baseline NT-proBNP independently predicted greater risk of the primary outcome (adjusted HR for Q4 vs Q1: 4.03 [95% CI: 3.12-5.20]). The prognostic value of baseline NT-proBNP for all outcomes was consistent irrespective of AF status. At 3 months, QLQX reduced NT-proBNP by 10% compared with placebo. The HRs for the primary composite with QLQX vs placebo were 1.13 (95% CI: 0.73-1.76), 0.76 (95% CI: 0.54-1.06), 0.73 (95% CI: 0.55-0.95), and 0.75 (95% CI: 0.59-0.95) from the lowest to the highest NT-proBNP quartiles, respectively (P interaction = 0.48). Results were consistent for CV death, HF hospitalization, and total HF hospitalizations, and when NT-proBNP was modeled continuously (all P interaction ≥ 0.30). Conclusions The treatment effect of QLQX on CV events was consistent across the spectrum of baseline NT-proBNP in HFrEF. Baseline NT-proBNP strongly predicted the risk of CV outcomes and mortality, irrespective of AF status. (Qiliqiangxin in Heart Failure: Assessment of Reduction in Mortality [QUEST]; ChiCTR1900021929).

items.title: Does Race Still Matter in Heart Failure?
Redefining Noninvasive Post-Transplant Surveillance
A New Frontier in Heart Failure
Pulmonary Hypertension and Its Association With Cardiac Transplant Outcomes
Evaluation of an Echocardiography-Based Artificial Intelligence Algorithm for Early HFpEF Detection
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Early heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is difficult to identify because of nonspecific symptoms and subtle echocardiographic abnormalities. EchoGo HF, an FDA-cleared artificial intelligence (AI) model, estimates HFpEF probability from a single apical 4-chamber echocardiographic clip, but has been validated only in patients with clinically adjudicated HFpEF. OBJECTIVES: This study aims to evaluate whether AI-HFpEF can detect early HFpEF in community-dwelling adults without a clinical heart failure (HF) diagnosis and predict incident clinical HFpEF in patients within a health system. METHODS: The authors included 2 community cohorts (the MESA [Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis] Early HF study and the DHMS [Dallas Hearts and Minds Study]). Early HFpEF was defined by impaired exercise capacity or health-related quality of life with objective evidence of elevated cardiac filling pressures in patients without clinically diagnosed HF. The AI-HFpEF model was applied to resting echocardiograms, and the diagnostic performance was assessed. Multivariable models examined associations between AI-HFpEF output and early HFpEF phenotype. Separately, we included adults in the UTSW (University of Texas Southwestern) Health System with structurally normal echocardiograms and no prior HF (2018-2024) and assessed the association of AI-HFpEF output with incident HFpEF (adjudicated using a validated registry) using Cox regression. RESULTS: FPEF (AUROC: 0.83 vs 0.77), and diagnostic positivity was associated with early HFpEF (OR: 6.76; P < 0.001), shorter exercise duration, and lower peak oxygen uptake. In the UTSW cohort (N = 6,876; median follow-up = 33 months; incident HFpEF = 3.4%), an AI-HFpEF diagnostic positive result was associated with >2-fold higher incident HFpEF risk (aHR: 2.08; P < 0.001). This association persisted across all conventional diastolic dysfunction grades. CONCLUSIONS: AI-HFpEF identified the early HFpEF phenotype in community-dwelling adults and independently predicted incident clinical HFpEF among patients in a health system.

items.title: Echocardiography After Preeclampsia
Sex Differences in Health Status in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction
Identifying High-Risk Patients

Editorial Board
From Proband to Relative
Leadless Cardiac Resynchronization Results in Left Ventricular Reverse Remodeling
Implications of SGLT2 Inhibitors, GLP-1RAs, and Nonsteroidal MRAs on the Anticipated Burden of Heart Failure
items.abstract: Background Several treatments that reduce the risk of heart failure (HF) have been introduced recently. Their impact on the future burden of HF in the U.S. has not been well characterized. Objectives This study aims to estimate the potential impact of recently approved cardiometabolic medications on the future burden of HF in the United States. Methods Using a nationally representative sample of persons in the United States 30-79 years of age without cardiovascular disease at baseline, we used the PREVENT (Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease Events) equation to estimate the 10- and 30-year burden of HF and the projected impact of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists on these estimates. The authors estimated the total number of HF cases that could be averted with risk-based treatment and calculated the number needed to treat to prevent HF. Results An estimated 5.5 million (95% CI: 5.1-5.8 million) U.S. adults 30-79 years of age without established cardiovascular disease will develop HF over 10 years. It is estimated to decrease to 5.1 million (95% CI: 4.7-5.4 million) with indicated treatment with a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor, 5.2 million (95% CI: 4.8-5.6 million) with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, 5.4 million (95% CI: 5.0-5.7 million) with nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and 4.8 million (95% CI: 4.4-5.2 million) with the use of combination therapy. The use of combination therapy in eligible persons with an estimated 10-year HF risk of ≥10% would result in 6.8 million (95% CI: 6.1-7.5 million) eligible participants, and 498,000 (95% CI: -663,000 to -319,000) fewer cases of HF, with a number needed to treat of 14 (95% CI: 10-22) to prevent 1 incident case. Conclusions The projected burden of HF in the U.S. is substantial. A risk-based approach to preventive treatment may help reduce this considerably. The feasibility of such an approach deserves further investigation.

items.title: Reinitiation of Optimal Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy After Coronary Bypass Grafting in Heart Failure With Reduced Ejection Fraction

Management of Heart transplant recipients for the non Heart Transplant health care provider. A Clinical Consensus Statement of the Heart Failure Association (HFA) and the Association of Cardiovascular Nursing & Allied Professions (ACNAP) of the ESC
items.abstract: Heart transplantation (HTx) remains the gold standard treatment for selected patients with advanced heart failure and survival after transplantation has substantially improved over recent decades. As a consequence, the number of long-term HTx recipients continues to increase, and these patients are now frequently encountered in routine practice outside specialized transplant centers. Their management remains complex due to the use of chronic immunosuppression, transplant-specific complications, and a growing burden of comorbidities in the perspective of increasing longevity. Non-transplant cardiologists, general practitioners, and other healthcare professionals are therefore increasingly involved in their care but often have limited experience of post-transplant management. This clinical consensus statement from the Heart Failure Association (HFA) and the Association of Cardiovascular Nursing & Allied Professions (ACNAP) of the ESC provides practical support and a structured framework for healthcare providers involved in the care of HTx recipients outside dedicated transplant centers. The document reviews key aspects of post-transplant management, including outlining principles of care according to time from transplantation, essential knowledge around immunosuppressive therapy and drug monitoring, recognition and initial management of rejection, infection prophylaxis and treatment, and surveillance of long-term complications such as cardiac allograft vasculopathy, malignancy, chronic kidney disease, and metabolic disorders. In addition, specific clinical situations frequently encountered in practice—including fertility and pregnancy, non-cardiac surgery, rehabilitation, and palliative care—are discussed. Particular emphasis is placed on the organization of shared-care models between transplant centers and community providers and on identifying clinical scenarios requiring early referral. Through providing practical recommendations and a structured framework for follow-up, this document aims to support non-specialist clinicians in the safe management of HTx recipients and to facilitate timely collaboration with transplant centers.

items.title: Short-term safety, feasibility, and performance of a novel soft robotic biventricular mechanical circulatory support device avoiding blood contact – The MISSION reBEAT trial
items.abstract: Aims Mechanical Circulatory Support (MCS) remains limited in advanced heart failure due to blood-contact complications and the absence of biventricular support. We report the first prospective clinical trial of a novel soft-robotic, biventricular, pulsatile technology placed externally around the heart without blood contact, designed to deliver individualized cardiac assistance (reBEAT®, AdjuCor GmbH, Munich, Germany). Methods and Results The system was temporarily applied in 10 end-stage heart failure patients immediately before elective LVAD implantation. Devices were custom-manufactured using preoperative CT scans to match individual cardiac anatomy. Safety, feasibility, and effects on haemodynamics were evaluated. Implantation was rapid (3±2 min), demonstrating procedural feasibility. We observed two procedure-related adverse events while no device- or procedure-related severe adverse events occurred. Absence of new ECG abnormalities, and no tissue injury confirmed safety. An iterative assessment on haemodynamics provided key insights into individualized cardio-circulatory support. While device presence reduced preload dependent haemodynamics in some patients, low average support pressures of 65–66 mmHg produced variable improvements towards baseline, predominantly on the pressure signal: mean arterial pressure (MAP; 67.5 ± 10.6 vs. 76.2 ± 11.7 mmHg, p<0.01), stroke work (SW; 347.8 ± 118.2 vs. 434.1 ± 131.0 mJ, p<0.01), and cardiac power output (CPO; 407.9 ± 108.2 vs. 503.7 ± 116.2 mW, p<0.01). Additionally, effects were observed on atrioventricular valve function and interventricular balance, which were not significant. Conclusion This soft-robotic biventricular MCS platform provides short term evidence of a safe and feasible approach to pulsatile biventricular support without blood contact. Significant increases in MAP, CPO, and SW towards baseline indicate functional effects. Continuous device-driven workflow improvement is mandatory and further data are required to refine individualized optimization strategies. This technology may offer a novel biventricular assist modality. Its reduced complexity may enable broader adaption for both temporary and durable support. Avoiding blood contact and enabling balanced biventricular assistance will be central drivers of its continued clinical development.

items.title: Dipeptidyl peptidase 3-positive circulatory shock: from targetable intensive care unit endotype to Horizon Europe precision-therapy trial
items.abstract: Circulatory shock remains one of the defining emergencies of intensive care medicine. Whether triggered by severe infection, major burns, trauma, major surgery or acute cardiovascular disease, its common denominator is failure of the circulation to deliver adequate tissue perfusion. Despite major progress in source control, antimicrobial treatment, burn and trauma care, haemodynamic monitoring and organ support, the immediate therapeutic armamentarium is still dominated by fluids, vasopressors, inotropes and mechanical support. These measures are often life-saving, but they are largely supportive. They do not directly address molecular drivers that may convert tissue injury into refractory vasoplegia, myocardial dysfunction, renal hypoperfusion and multiorgan failure.1 A major conceptual advance in critical care is the movement from syndromic classification towards biologically defined, treatable endotypes. Shock is traditionally divided into septic, cardiogenic, hypovolaemic, obstructive or distributive forms. Yet patients in these categories may share downstream mechanisms of circulatory collapse. One emerging example is the endotype defined by elevated circulating dipeptidyl peptidase 3 (cDPP3).2 DPP3 is an intracellular zinc-dependent peptidase and is estimated to be causal in up to 50% of all shock entities (Figure 1).2 After acute cellular injury and after excessive inflammatory response, however, it can be released into the circulation, where it degrades angiotensin II and related vasoactive peptides. In a critically ill patient who depends on endogenous vasoconstrictor reserve to maintain perfusion pressure, excessive extracellular DPP3 activity may disturb the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, reduce vascular tone, aggravate myocardial depression, impair renal perfusion and increase catecholamine requirements.2 DPP3-positive circulatory shock: from cell injury to organ dysfunction and therapeutic neutralization. Acute cellular injury and inflammatory response caused by sepsis, burns, trauma or major surgery can release intracellular DPP3 into the circulation. Rapid cDPP3 point-of-care testing may identify a biomarker-positive shock endotype suitable for targeted treatment evaluation. Extracellular DPP3 degrades angiotensin II and related vasoactive peptides, disturbing RAAS signalling and contributing to vasoplegia, myocardial dysfunction, renal hypoperfusion, escalating vasopressor demand and multiorgan dysfunction. Anti-DPP3 antibody therapy with Invobenitug, formerly Procizumab, is designed to neutralize circulating DPP3, preserve angiotensin signalling and restore haemodynamic control. cDPP3, circulating dipeptidyl peptidase 3; RAAS, renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system This mechanism is clinically plausible because it links tissue injury and inflammation to haemodynamic collapse across apparently distinct shock entities. Sepsis causes widespread cellular and endothelial injury; burns combine tissue destruction, inflammation and capillary leak; trauma and major surgery can produce cell death, haemorrhage, inflammation and reperfusion injury. In each setting, DPP3 release could represent not merely a biomarker of injury severity but a mediator of circulatory decompensation. Observational studies have associated high cDPP3 concentrations with circulatory failure, acute kidney injury, organ-support requirements and mortality in critically ill patients across multiple studies and cohorts.3,4 Within the prospective heterogeneous shock study FROG-ICU, elevated cDPP3 has similarly been linked to adverse outcome, supporting the broader relevance of this biology beyond a single aetiology.5 For bedside clinicians, the key question is whether cDPP3 can move from risk marker to actionable test.2 A clinically useful endotype should be measurable rapidly, identify patients with a shared biological mechanism, enrich for treatment response and be relevant to outcomes that matter in the intensive care unit (ICU). DPP3 fulfils several of these requirements.2 It is measurable in blood, point-of-care testing has been developed for rapid stratification, and proposed thresholds can define biomarker-positive populations for trial enrolment.2 This is particularly important in shock, where therapeutic windows are short and treatment decisions must be made before complete mechanistic certainty is available. The therapeutic implication is direct: if extracellular DPP3 contributes to loss of angiotensin signalling and haemodynamic control, neutralising circulating DPP3 may preserve vasoactive peptide activity and restore cardiovascular stability. Importantly, this concept differs from simply substituting catecholamine support. In patients with severe vasoplegia, high-dose norepinephrine may restore macrocirculatory perfusion pressure while regional and microcirculatory perfusion remain impaired. By neutralising cDPP3 and thereby preserving endogenous angiotensin signalling, anti-cDPP3 therapy may address an upstream trigger of vasoplegia, potentially reducing catecholamine exposure while also mitigating regional hypoperfusion. Invobenitug, formerly known as Procizumab or AK1967, is a humanised monoclonal antibody designed to neutralise extracellular DPP3 activity.6 Preclinical studies in models of shock have shown rapid haemodynamic improvement, reduced catecholamine exposure and protection of cardiovascular, pulmonary and renal function.7,8 First clinical experience in refractory shock and early-phase development have supported tolerability and biological activity, although definitive efficacy remains to be proven in randomized trials.9 In a first-in-human named-patient-use case series of three extremely critically ill patients with refractory septic shock and septic cardiomyopathy, anti-DPP3 antibody Invobenitug administration was well tolerated and was followed by shock reversal in all three patients within 48 hours, accompanied by a marked reduction in norepinephrine requirements, normalization of lactate concentrations, improved oxygenation and renal function, and a pronounced decrease in inflammatory markers including interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein.9 Regarding potential interactions with commonly used ICU drugs, Invobenitug, as a monoclonal antibody targeting extracellular DPP3, is not expected to interact through classical cytochrome P450 metabolism or transporter-mediated pathways, and no specific pharmacokinetic interactions with antibiotics, anticoagulants, sedatives, vasopressors or inotropes are currently anticipated. Nevertheless, patients with shock are exposed to complex and rapidly changing polypharmacy. Therefore, concomitant medication, organ function, coagulation parameters, infection treatment, vasopressor exposure and safety laboratory values will require systematic monitoring in clinical trials. Translating this molecular rationale into a clinically testable treatment strategy requires biomarker-selected randomized evaluation in the relevant shock populations. CURE-SHOCK is an 8 Million Euro Horizon Europe-supported, investigator-initiated Phase 2a programme evaluating Invobenitug in DPP3-positive circulatory shock due to sepsis, burns or trauma/major surgery. The trial is designed as a prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, international study enrolling biomarker-positive adults selected by rapid DPP3 testing. Participants will receive Invobenitug plus standard care or placebo plus standard care, with clinically meaningful endpoints including shock reversal, cardiovascular organ-support requirements, safety, short-term mortality, biomarker trajectories, renal replacement therapy, mechanical ventilation, discharge outcomes and health-economic endpoints. The consortium links intensive care, biomarker science, burn medicine, trauma expertise and biotechnology across Germany, Poland and Ukraine. This European structure is not merely administrative. It is scientifically important because it allows evaluation of a shared molecular mechanism across heterogeneous but mechanistically connected shock populations. Understanding DPP3-positive circulatory shock also clarifies what this approach is not. It is not a replacement for source control, haemorrhage control, antibiotics, burn surgery, fluid resuscitation or vasopressors. Nor should cDPP3 be interpreted as a universal explanation for all shock states. Rather, it represents a potentially treatable layer of biology superimposed on the primary insult. The clinical challenge will be to determine when DPP3 activity is high enough, early enough and mechanistically relevant enough to justify targeted intervention. Beyond CURE-SHOCK, the broader development pathway illustrates how a mechanism-based shock therapy may be translated into ICU practice. A first-in-human Phase 1 study successfully evaluated safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics of escalating single intravenous doses of Invobenitug in healthy male volunteers.10 A subsequent multicentre, randomized, double-blind Phase 1b/2a study is currently evaluating Invobenitug in patients with cardiogenic shock and elevated cDPP3 concentrations, with the aim of defining safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and an optimal dose for further development [ClinicalTrials.gov: Invobenitug also known as Procizumab in patients with cardiogenic shock and elevated cDPP3. NCT06832722]. While this pivotal efficacy programme focuses on cardiogenic shock, CURE-SHOCK extends the same biological concept to DPP3-positive non-cardiogenic circulatory shock due to sepsis, burns, trauma or major surgery. If ongoing trials confirm safety and favourable efficacy signals, DPP3-positive shock could become a prototype for precision medicine in the ICU: rapid biomarker identification, mechanism-based enrichment, targeted biological neutralization and endpoints tied to organ-support needs. For intensivists, the broader lesson may be even more important. Shock may no longer be understood only as a haemodynamic syndrome to be supported, but as a set of molecularly defined endotypes that can be diagnosed and treated at the bedside. items.title: Efficacy of empagliflozin in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction according to the presence of echocardiographic features of diastolic dysfunction in the EMPEROR-Preserved trial
items.abstract: Aims To define the impact of diastolic dysfunction (DD) on the response to empagliflozin treatment in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. Methods and Results Diastolic dysfunction was defined by left atrial volume index ≥34 ml/m2, the ratio of early diastolic mitral inflow velocity to early diastolic mitral annular tissue velocity (E/e) ≥ 13 or left ventricular mass index >115 (males) or >95 (females). We created three categories of increasing DD (0, 1, or ≥2 DD criteria at baseline) to describe the effect of DD on response to empagliflozin therapy and adverse effects. Of 5988 patients in the EMPEROR-Preserved trial, 3766 (63%) had no documented baseline DD, 1619 (27%) had one, and 603 (10%) had two or more measures. Baseline DD was associated with sex, race, ethnicity, and region and was more common with lower heart rate, DBP, body weight, and eGFR. Despite baseline DD not being significantly associated with the primary endpoint of hospitalization for heart failure or cardiovascular death within the placebo group, a progressive treatment effect across the three DD categories was seen (trend test P-value .0014), with estimated hazard ratios of empagliflozin vs placebo of 0.91 (none present), 0.64 (1 present), and 0.49 (≥2). A significant treatment-by-subgroup trend test was also observed for the total number of hospitalizations for heart failure. Both Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Clinical Summary Score improvement at week 52 and safety profile were consistent across DD categories. Conclusion Baseline detection of echocardiographic DD predicted improved clinical response to empagliflozin in a graded fashion, but the reasons cannot be reliably determined from this analysis.
