items.title: SARS-CoV-2 mRNA Vaccination in Pregnancy and Child Neurodevelopment at 18 to 30 Months
items.abstract: Importance Little is known about neurodevelopmental outcomes of children exposed to SARS-CoV-2 messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccine during pregnancy. Evidence on long-term offspring outcomes after in utero exposure to SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccination is needed to inform vaccine recommendations in pregnancy. Objective To evaluate whether there is an association between SARS-CoV-2 vaccination during or shortly before pregnancy and offspring neurodevelopmental measures. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter, prospective, cohort study of 18- to 30-month-old children was conducted at 14 centers of the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development Maternal-Fetal Medicine Units Network from 2024 through 2025. Women who received a SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine during or within 30 days prior to pregnancy (exposed) were matched with women who did not (unexposed) by delivery site, delivery date, insurance status, and race and ethnicity. These data were analyzed from June 2025 to May 2026. Exposures Maternal receipt of at least 1 dose of an mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccine during, or within 30 days prior to, the index pregnancy vs no SARS-CoV-2 vaccination during pregnancy or within 30 days prior. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was Ages and Stages Questionnaire version 3 (ASQ-3) total score, which was deemed to be equivalent between the exposed and unexposed groups if the 90% CI of the median difference was between −10 and 10. Secondary outcomes included domain-specific ASQ-3 scores, the Child Behavior Checklist, Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers, and Early Childhood Behavior Questionnaire scores. Results Of 3956 screened, 271 exposed and 240 unexposed children were enrolled. Matching on all characteristics was possible in 217 pairs. Of the 434 children enrolled, 258 (59.4%) were Non-Hispanic White, 96 (22.1%) Non-Hispanic Black, 52 (12.0%) Hispanic, and 28 (6.5%) were not represented by any of the above racial or ethnic groups. Median age at assessment was 25.8 [24.6 to 28.3] months, 221 were female (50.9%), and 213 were male (49.1%). Exposed mothers were more likely to be nulliparous; their children were slightly younger at assessment and more likely to have been vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2. The primary outcome of ASQ-3 score was equivalent between the exposed and unexposed groups (255 vs 260, adjusted median difference, −3.4; 90% CI, −9.8 to 3.0). There were no significant differences in secondary outcomes. Conclusions and Relevance In this multicenter cohort study, ASQ-3 scores were equivalent between 18- to 30-month-old children whose mothers did or did not receive mRNA SARS-CoV-2 vaccination during or immediately prior to pregnancy. These findings support continued recommendations for SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccination during pregnancy.

items.title: Vitamin K Deficiency and Associated Bleeding in Infants
items.abstract: This cross-sectional study examines changes in intramuscular vitamin K receipt and incidence of vitamin K deficiency and vitamin K–deficient bleeding among US infants between 2017 and 2025.

items.title: Problematic Social Media Use and Depression Symptoms in Younger Teens: It’s a 2-Way Street
Problematic Social Media Use and Depressive and Anxiety Symptoms in Adolescents
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE Given limited longitudinal data on social media use and mental health, this study examined within-person lagged associations between problematic social media use and depressive and anxiety symptoms across 5 annual assessments among adolescents. METHODS This prospective cohort study used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study, years 2 to 6. The analytic sample included 11 279 participants (aged 12.01 ± 0.66 at year 2; 47.6% female) with at least 1 measure of problematic social media use and depressive or anxiety symptoms across years 2 to 6. RESULTS Across 5 years, random-intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs) indicated positive bidirectional lagged associations between problematic social media use and depressive symptoms from year 3 to year 4 and from year 4 to year 5. No significant cross-lagged associations were observed from year 2 to year 3 or from year 5 to year 6. For anxiety symptoms, no significant cross-lagged associations were observed across years. In multigroup RI-CLPMs, sex differences were observed in both models, but stronger cross-lagged associations among female than male participants were specific to depressive symptoms. CONCLUSIONS Problematic social media use and depressive symptoms showed year-specific bidirectional lagged associations, whereas within-person prospective associations between problematic social media use and anxiety symptoms were not observed. Sex differences were more apparent for depressive symptoms, for which lagged associations were stronger and more consistently bidirectional among female participants. Clinical and policy efforts should prioritize problematic features of social media use and consider developmental timing and sex-specific risk profiles in screening and intervention.
items.limitations: However, several limitations warrant consideration. First, although the cross-informant design, which paired adolescent-reported PSMU with caregiver-reported symptoms, reduced same-source inflation, caregivers may underrecognize internalizing symptoms that are less observable. Second, the annual timing of assessments limited our ability to capture shorter-term processes through which PSMU and emotional distress may unfold. Third, the cross-lagged effects were modest in absolute size. Fourth, PSMU was assessed only among adolescents who reported having at least 1 social media account, which limits the population to which these findings apply.

items.title: Oral Health for Adolescents: Technical Report
items.abstract: Excellent oral health is a fundamental need for all adolescents as they gain health independence and autonomy. Pediatricians already perform an essential and vital function by incorporating an oral health history, physical examination, and anticipatory guidance into adolescent well visits. This technical report provides support for this work, as highlighted in the clinical report, with an overview on adolescent oral health including growth and development, medical issues, and treatments for adolescents with complex medical needs.

items.title: Oral Health for Adolescents: Clinical Report
items.abstract: This clinical report marks a significant milestone in the United States, addressing oral health in the adolescent from the pediatrician’s perspective. Poor oral health can affect adolescents in many ways, including pain, missed school, overall health, and decreased social engagement. Oral health issues particularly pertinent to adolescents include oral sports injury prevention, orthodontic issues, and certain behaviors contributing to poor oral health outcomes. This statement will provide pediatricians: Evidence-based information on practice-based skills for the prevention and management of oral health issues in adolescent patients. Recommendations to incorporate these skills in the health supervision visit.

items.title: Driving Legislative Change for Access to Medications
items.abstract: An insurance company denied coverage for an inflammatory bowel disease medication, stating that the lack of a pediatric Food and Drug Administration indication made that treatment experimental. This was legally permissible. The patient’s pediatric gastroenterologist partnered with others to create a new state law that mandated insurance coverage for medications in children when the treatment was covered for adult patients and there were data to support pediatric efficacy and safety. Coalition building included support from a hospital system, community petitions, and interactions with legislators. Family and physician testimony supported passage of the law, in effect since 2023. The patient was able to obtain the necessary treatment, and the law has been used to help other children gain access to prescribed treatments. This process can serve as a model for similar advocacy in other states.

items.title: Prehospital Pediatric Ventilation Quality Following Use of a Feedback Device: A Randomized Study
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE Manual ventilation is a lifesaving intervention for children in respiratory arrest, yet the quality of pediatric ventilation delivered by emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians across geographically distinct sites is poorly characterized. We evaluated baseline EMS ventilation performance and whether a ventilation feedback device (VFD) improves adherence to national and international ventilation guidelines for ventilation rate, tidal volume, and mask seal. METHODS We conducted a single-anonymized, randomized, crossover study of EMS clinicians from 5 EMS agencies across 3 metropolitan sites in the United States. Using a simulated 3-year-old toddler manikin, participants completed 2 sequential 2-minute respiratory arrest scenarios separated by a 10-minute washout period. Participants performed ventilation with and without real-time VFD feedback in randomized order. The EOLifeX VFD recorded ventilation rate, tidal volume, and mask leak with each breath. Adherence to age-based guidelines was analyzed using generalized linear mixed-effects models with participants nested within sites. RESULTS We enrolled 123 participants across 5 agencies. With VFD feedback, guideline-recommended tidal volumes were achieved in 87% of breaths compared with 16.2% without feedback. Ventilation rate adherence improved from 65% to 88.6%. Mask leak of less than 30% occurred in 88.4% of ventilations with feedback vs 80% without feedback. CONCLUSION In our simulation study, EMS clinicians rarely met manual ventilation guidelines for pediatric patients in respiratory arrest. The use of a VFD substantially improved guideline adherence, suggesting broad potential to improve ventilation performance.

items.title: Paraneoplastic Autoimmune Multiorgan Syndrome: Diagnostic Lessons for Pediatricians
items.abstract: We report the challenging diagnosis of an 11-year-old boy, presenting with subacute erythroblastopenia, followed by a multisystemic immune-mediated syndrome characterized by polymorphic mucocutaneous manifestations, associated with severe myositis related to a dermatomyositis-like phenotype and mild hepatitis. A progressive lymphadenopathy led to a delayed diagnosis of T-lymphoblastic lymphoma associated with paraneoplastic autoimmune multiorgan syndrome. To achieve remission of this paraneoplastic syndrome, Janus kinase inhibitor was required in addition to antitumor therapy. This case highlights several key points: (1) Pediatricians should consider a paraneoplastic origin when facing juvenile dermatomyositis with atypical features, such as hematologic and mucosal abnormalities; (2) in uncertain cases, early collaboration with oncologists is needed to optimize diagnostic and therapeutic strategies; (3) the choice of immunomodulatory therapy is critical in addition to antitumor therapy.

items.title: Experiences of Ableism in Pediatric Healthcare
items.abstract: BACKGROUND There is growing evidence of ableism in pediatric health care, but our limited understanding of the experiences of ableism inhibits further evaluation and intervention. The study objective was to describe community perspectives of the experiences of ableism in pediatric health care for children with disabilities. METHODS Participants completed a group concept mapping study using web-based software to input experiences of ableism in health care. Following a formal statement reduction, participants sorted unique experiences into conceptual clusters. Data were mapped to generate a similarity matrix. A multidimensional scaling algorithm generated a point map, and a hierarchical cluster analysis grouped statements into clusters. Focus groups validated and labeled clusters. RESULTS Participants (n = 132) generated 658 statements about ableism experiences. After reduction, 145 experiences were categorized in 11 conceptually distinct clusters: 1) substandard care including withholding care, 2) dehumanizing language and behaviors, 3) negative assumptions, 4) inflexible organizational policies and practices, 5) inaccessible built environment and lack of accommodations, 6) lack of access to resources, 7) unfair standards and normalized inequity in health systems, 8) dismissal of the lived experience and caregiver expertise, 9) intersectional identities and judgements of worthiness to receive care, 10) restrictions driven by insurance coverage and policy, and 11) complexity in community and health services navigation. CONCLUSIONS Wide-ranging experiences of ableism occur in pediatric health care interactions. The lived experiences of ableism identified in this study provide insight for future research in pediatric health care.

items.title: Ableism Is a Crisis in American Pediatric Health Care
A Neonate With Excessive Weight Loss and Electrolyte Abnormalities
items.abstract: A 7-day-old girl was brought to the hospital for excessive weight loss. Initial evaluation revealed electrolyte abnormalities, including hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Stepwise assessment was undertaken to evaluate potential endocrine, renal, and metabolic causes, with supportive interventions initiated. Over the course of hospitalization, her electrolytes and weight gradually improved. Further workup, including imaging and genetic testing, was performed to clarify the underlying etiology. Our panel of experts first discuss the approach to weight loss in neonates and then review the assessment and management of neonatal electrolyte disturbances, highlighting endocrine, renal, and genetic considerations that may guide clinical care.

items.title: The Community Pediatrics & Advocacy Curriculum: Standardizing Advocacy Education in Pediatric GME
items.abstract: Pediatricians are essential advocates for their patients in many contexts. The evolving role of the pediatrician as an advocate has led to a distinct need for the development and standardization of advocacy curricula in pediatric graduate medical education. With an increased emphasis placed by the Accreditation Council on Graduate Medical Education and the American Board of Pediatrics on advocacy as an essential skill for general and subspecialty pediatricians, the authors provide a framework for pediatric advocacy education based on a new socioecological model of pediatrician advocacy. The authors highlight the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)’s history of advocacy curriculum development and how it has shaped the approach to advocacy training in the field of pediatrics over the last 2 decades. A curricular framework, including goals, learning objectives, and exemplar activities, was developed from this previous work and compiled through expert consensus and further peer review by experts identified through the AAP’s Community Pediatrics Training Initiative. The current paper outlines the process of curating these tools, thereby creating an accessible and feasible baseline for programs.

items.title: Coverage Trends by Citizenship Status Among Medicaid Income-Eligible Children: 2012–2024
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES To evaluate coverage correlates and trends by citizenship status among a nationally representative sample of Medicaid income-eligible children. We also examined the associations of coverage policies, including the Affordable Care Act’s (ACA’s) Medicaid expansion and state-level expansions to children regardless of immigration status, with children’s coverage outcomes. METHODS This repeated cross-sectional study used multivariable logistic regression analysis and 2012 to 2024 American Community Survey data. The main sample included children aged 1 to 17 years in all US states with household incomes under the Medicaid income eligibility limit. Binary outcomes included uninsured, Medicaid, and private coverage. RESULTS From 2012 to 2024, uninsurance declined from 37.9% to 31.0% among noncitizen children and from 8.2% to 6.1% among citizen children; the coverage gap by citizenship consistently exceeded 20 percentage points. Factors associated with lower uninsured rates among noncitizen children included high parental English proficiency, higher socioeconomic status, living in a metropolitan area, and non-Hispanic Asian ethnicity. The ACA’s Medicaid expansion was associated with lower uninsured rates among citizen children, but associations were not statistically significant overall or among noncitizen children. State coverage expansions to children regardless of immigration status were associated with an 8.2 percentage-point reduction in the uninsured rate (95% CI −12.5 to −4.0) before and after their implementation among noncitizen children. CONCLUSIONS Significant and persistent coverage gaps by citizenship remain among Medicaid income-eligible children. Gaps were substantially ameliorated, although not completely eliminated, in states that expanded their Medicaid programs to cover children regardless of immigration status.

items.title: Vaccine-Induced Antibody and T Cell Immunity to Measles and Varicella in Children With ALL
items.abstract: Abstract Children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) are treated with multiagent chemotherapy that causes profound changes to the immune system. There are limited data on how disease and therapy impact antigen-specific immune memory, leading to inconsistent guidelines on best practices for revaccination of this population. Here, to inform vaccine guidance, we investigated whether immunity derived from routine childhood measles and varicella zoster virus (VZV) vaccines is maintained during and after therapy for childhood ALL. We report that antibodies against measles and VZV were significantly reduced in children with ALL (n=45) compared to healthy controls (n=13), particularly in older children in whom a longer time had passed since their most recent vaccine dose. However, the avidity of the measles and VZV-specific antibodies was indistinguishable between groups. Despite changes to the composition of the T cell compartment, both overall and antigen-specific T cell function were preserved in children with ALL. These data provide compelling evidence for revaccination of children following ALL treatment. Intact T cell responses suggest that post-treatment revaccination would be effective.

items.title: Hydrocephalus: Treatment, Current Research, and Challenges
items.abstract: Hydrocephalus is a complex neurological condition characterized by derangements in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dynamics including disrupted CSF flow/absorption and/or excess CSF production that leads to ventricular enlargement and presents both diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Its origins span from congenital anomalies to acquired cases following hemorrhage, infection, or tumors. Hydrocephalus is suspected in the setting of appropriate clinical signs/symptoms, and the diagnosis is confirmed with brain imaging and, in rare cases, invasive intracranial pressure monitoring. Surgical intervention is the mainstay of modern hydrocephalus management, with CSF diversion via an implanted shunt being the most common management strategy. However, for a subset of patients, endoscopic third ventriculostomy can also effectively manage hydrocephalus without the need for an implanted device. This article highlights both genetic and acquired forms of hydrocephalus, reviews the surgical interventions for managing hydrocephalus and commercially available shunt technologies, discusses the shortcomings of current management strategies, and explores the ongoing development of next-generation shunt technology including smart shunts and antifouling catheter coatings that aim to reduce shunt malfunction rates. Additionally, we review current bench research investigating the cellular/molecular mechanisms involved in hydrocephalus induction including studies on ventricular lining disruption and the role of aquaporins in hydrocephalus.

items.title: Frontline Staff Vaccine Communication During Pediatric Well-Child Encounters: A Mixed-Methods Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES Evidence-based vaccine communication from clinicians is associated with improved parental vaccine acceptance. However, vaccine communication practices of frontline staff, including medical assistants (MAs) and receptionists, remain largely unknown. We aimed to characterize these practices during well-child encounters in pediatric primary care. METHODS We conducted a mixed-methods study with direct observations of frontline staff in 2 pediatric practices in Denver, CO, during well-child encounters in the summer (no influenza vaccine available) and fall (influenza vaccine available) of 2024, recording the frequency and format of vaccine communication. Following the observations, we conducted semi-structured interviews with MAs to explore their vaccine communication practices, perceived roles, comfort, and training. RESULTS We observed 174 encounters (127 MA–parent, 47 receptionist–parent interactions). Vaccine communication occurred in at least 51% (95% CI, 43%–60%) of MA interactions vs 6% of receptionist interactions (P < .001). When vaccines were recommended, MAs used a presumptive format in 46% (95% CI, 34%–59%) of encounters overall, but far less during influenza season (21% vs 76%; P < .001). Interviews revealed that MA communication styles evolved through on-the-job experience and peer-to-peer learning rather than formal training, with influenza vaccines treated as optional rather than routinely recommended. CONCLUSIONS MAs frequently communicate with parents about vaccines during well-child encounters but underutilize evidence-based presumptive communication, particularly for influenza vaccines. Communication practices are learned informally through peer-to-peer learning, highlighting a significant opportunity for targeted training to support team-based vaccine communication in pediatric primary care.

items.title: Immunogenicity and Safety of PHH-1V COVID-19 Vaccine as a Heterologous Booster in Adolescents
items.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES PHH-1V, a protein-based, non-mRNA, bivalent, adjuvanted COVID-19 vaccine, has demonstrated strong immunogenicity and favorable safety as a booster in adults. This study evaluated PHH-1V as a heterologous booster in adolescents. METHODS HIPRA-HH-3 was a phase IIb, open-label, multicenter, noninferiority trial assessing the immunogenicity and safety of PHH-1V in 240 healthy adolescents (≥ 12 to < 18 years) primed with BNT162b2. Immunogenicity (N = 90) was assessed by measuring neutralizing antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 variants and total binding antibodies in adolescent participants vs young adults (≥ 18 to ≤ 25 years) (N = 81) from a previous trial, who had also been boosted with PHH-1V. T-cell responses at day 14 post booster were also evaluated. Antibody durability and adverse events (AEs) were assessed through day 336. RESULTS Neutralizing titers—against Omicron BA.1 (primary endpoint), WH1, Beta, and Delta variants—and total binding antibodies were significantly higher in adolescents than in young adults (P < .001), demonstrating noninferiority (margin < 1.5). T-cell responses against BA.1 and Beta also increased significantly (P < .001). Cross-variant antibody titers remained above baseline (day 0) through day 336. AEs were mostly mild/moderate, primarily injection-site pain and headache within 28 days. No related serious AEs were reported. CONCLUSIONS As a heterologous booster in adolescents, PHH-1V is safe and elicits cellular and sustained humoral responses with cross-variant immune recognition, which support the use of PHH-1V in adolescent vaccination strategies. Data in younger and specific risk groups are still needed.

items.title: Reasons for Nicotine Pouch Use Among US Youth: 2025
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE To document prevalence of reasons for nicotine pouch (NP) use and associations with use patterns among US youth. METHODS Data were from US youth reporting ever NP use in the nationally representative 2025 Monitoring the Future survey. We estimated (1) prevalence of 10 reasons for NP use (yes/no) and (2) association of each reason with past 30-day NP use (yes/no) and frequency (1–30 days). For comparison, we contrasted reasons for NP and e-cigarette use among youth reporting NP use (n = 57) or e-cigarette use (n = 397) on at least 10 of the past 30 days. RESULTS Among 484 respondents reporting ever NP use (6.1% of youth surveyed on NP use and reasons), the most common reasons were experimentation (32.3%), nicotine buzz (30.5%), relaxation (22.7%), appealing flavors (17.4%), convenience (16.5%), socializing (16.0%), boredom (11.7%), and ability to conceal use (11.0%). To quit smoking (6.2%) and feeling addicted (2.1%) were less common. Flavors, convenience, and feeling addicted were positively associated with both past 30-day NP use (prevalence ratios [PRs] range = 1.50–2.35) and frequency (incidence rate ratios [IRRs] range = 1.60–2.55). Nicotine buzz, relaxation, socializing, concealment, and to quit smoking were only associated with past 30-day use (PRs range = 1.57–1.85). Experimentation was inversely associated with frequency (IRR = 0.42). The prevalence of reasons overlapped between NPs and e-cigarettes, with relaxation, convenience, nicotine buzz, and flavors most prevalent among youth regularly using each product. CONCLUSIONS Prevention and regulatory strategies addressing NP use reasons, particularly flavors and convenience, are warranted. Existing effective strategies targeting youth nicotine vaping may be applicable to NP use.
items.limitations: Findings are subject to limitations inherent to self-report and potential sampling error. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. Participants selected reasons from a predefined list, which may not capture the full range or relative importance of reasons. It is also unclear how well adolescents differentiated reasons. For example, convenience could be interpreted as ease of use, ease of access, or concealability.

items.title: Children and Families Affected by Parental Substance Use: Clinical Report
items.abstract: Children and adolescents whose parents have an alcohol or substance use disorder are at increased risk of short- and long-term sequelae, ranging from medical conditions to psychosocial, safety, and behavioral challenges. In the course of providing health care services to children, pediatricians and other pediatric clinicians are likely to encounter families affected by parental substance use and are in a unique position to support the well-being of both the child and family. The purpose of this clinical report is to briefly discuss the epidemiology of substance use during pregnancy and while parenting in the United States; highlight the influence of bias, racism, and other structural inequities on families affected by substance use; describe the known risks associated with prenatal and postnatal parental substance use; discuss use and interpretation of toxicology testing as part of a substance exposure evaluation; review approaches to screening for prenatal and parental substance use; propose key topics for anticipatory guidance in the pediatric clinic; identify and address concerning parental and child presentations related to parental substance use leading to concern for child abuse or neglect; and provide recommendations for pediatric clinicians involved in the care of children from families affected by substance use.

items.title: Pediatric Hospital at Home: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: CONTEXT Hospital at Home (HaH) is an acute care model that delivers hospital-level services to the patient’s home as a substitute for conventional inpatient admission. Although pediatric HaH programs are well established internationally, the evidence base remains limited. OBJECTIVE To map the operational characteristics, outcomes, and evidence gaps of pediatric HaH programs. DATA SOURCES A comprehensive literature search was conducted for studies published between January 1, 2000, and July 25, 2025. STUDY SELECTION Eligible studies included programs with patients aged 18 years or younger and aligned with the World Hospital at Home Congress definition. DATA EXTRACTION Data were extracted on study characteristics; implementation, infrastructure, and program design; clinical safety and effectiveness; cost-effectiveness and economic impact; and patient, caregiver, and/or clinician perspectives and experiences. RESULTS Thirty-four studies met eligibility criteria. Most were observational, with few randomized or nonrandomized controlled studies. Programs varied substantially in admission pathways, staffing, eligibility criteria, monitoring, and clinical populations. Studies demonstrated low escalation and readmission rates, infrequent serious adverse events, high caregiver satisfaction, and generally comparable or lower health care costs relative to conventional inpatient care. Few studies directly evaluated clinical effectiveness, included rigorous economic analysis, or incorporated child and clinician perspectives. LIMITATIONS The literature was limited by heterogeneous study populations, program designs, outcome reporting, and variable definitions and descriptions of HaH models, introducing potential for misclassification. CONCLUSIONS Pediatric HaH shows promise as a safe and family-centered alternative to conventional hospitalization, though the existing evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, highlighting the need for more rigorous evaluation.

items.title: Developmental Trajectories of Executive Function From 2 to 13 Years in Children Born Very Preterm
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE Children born very preterm (VP; <32 weeks’ gestation) are at risk of executive function (EF) difficulties, yet limited longitudinal research has examined how these evolve from early childhood to adolescence for this population. This study described developmental trajectories of parent-reported EF from ages 2 to 13 years in children born VP and full term (FT). METHODS Participants were from the Victorian Infant Brain Study (VIBeS) longitudinal cohort comprising 224 children born VP (<30 weeks’ gestation) and 77 born FT (≥37 weeks’ gestation). EF difficulties were measured at 2, 5, 7, and 13 years using the parent-rated Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF) and its preschool version. Trajectories were estimated using multilevel mixed effects models. RESULTS EF difficulties were 0.3 to 0.7 SD higher in the VP than FT group across all BRIEF scales at each follow-up, and this difference tended to be greater in boys and those with higher socioeconomic risk. For both VP and FT groups, Global Executive Composite (GEC) and Shift T-scores increased from 2 to 13 years, Inhibit and Working Memory T-scores remained largely stable, and Emotional Control and Plan/Organize T-scores increased between 2 and 7 before stabilizing between 7 and 13 years. CONCLUSION Children born VP showed persistent EF difficulties from early childhood into adolescence, with little evidence of developmental catch-up to FT peers. These findings highlight the need for early and ongoing monitoring and intervention throughout development. Further research is needed to understand the role of sex and socioeconomic risk in the developmental course of behavioral EF difficulties.

items.title: Zika-Related Microcephaly in the First 5 Years After Birth
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE To characterize clinical manifestations and complications of children with Zika-related microcephaly in the first 5 years after birth. METHODS A cohort of children with Zika-related microcephaly were observed up to age 60 months as part of the Microcephaly Epidemic Research Group Pediatric Cohort. RESULTS Among the 181 children, 43.1% were male and 77.2% were born at term. The median birth weight was 2700 g, with 64.8% classified as small for gestational age. Notably, 22.3% were diagnosed with microcephaly after birth, and 48.8% had severe microcephaly. Most common phenotypic characteristics were craniofacial disproportion (54.1%), arthrogryposis (35.9%), and exacerbated occipital protuberance (35.5%). Approximately one-third (33.1%) presented with dysphagia (n = 151 evaluated at median age of 28.2 months), and 13.3% of children had gastrostomies (median age of 24 months). Hearing anomalies were detected in 9.7% (n = 93 evaluated at median age of 30 months). In ophthalmological evaluation, 30.4% showed changes in the retina and 28.5% in the optic nerve; strabismus was observed in 53.4%. During neurological assessment (median age at first assessment of 15.9 months), 73.8% presented with abnormalities. Imaging examinations showed ventriculomegaly and cortical atrophy in 75.3% and 64.4% of the children, respectively. Electroencephalography was performed based on clinical indication in 84 children, of whom 92.9% had pattern alterations. Over the 5 years, 62.4% were hospitalized, mainly for respiratory problems and seizures. CONCLUSIONS The study highlights the severity of Zika-related microcephaly. Future research should prioritize continued systematic monitoring of these children to understand the frequency and timing of late-onset manifestations and complications, including death.

items.title: Dual Remission of Atopic Dermatitis and Frequently Relapsing Nephrotic Syndrome With Dupilumab
items.abstract: Nephrotic syndrome in children and atopic dermatitis (AD) share a common type 2 inflammatory substrate driven by interleukin (IL)-4 and IL-13 dysregulation. We report the case of a 9-year-old girl with AD and frequently relapsing steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome. Given the broad atopic phenotype and increasing relapse frequency despite dual immunosuppressive therapy, dupilumab 300 mg every 2 weeks was introduced. The patient achieved rapid and complete clearance of cutaneous lesions alongside sustained complete remission of nephrotic syndrome, maintained over nearly 2 years. Both corticosteroids and tacrolimus were fully discontinued within 2 months of dupilumab initiation, with no subsequent relapse of either condition. This case supports the hypothesis that dupilumab may represent an effective steroid-sparing therapeutic option in children with nephrotic syndrome arising in an atopic context.

Literacy Promotion and Child Health: The Role of Reach Out and Read
items.abstract: This Special Article draws on a State of the Art Plenary, Literacy Promotion and Child Health: Reach Out and Read at 37, presented at the 2026 Pediatric Academic Societies meeting, which reviewed the evolution of Reach Out and Read (ROR) as a clinical intervention, a subject of research, and an increasingly incorporated component of pediatric primary care. The ROR model, supported by a national organization, now reaches 4.8 million children and families throughout the United States. Much of this growth has been driven by clinicians seeking to support family relationships, child development, and educational trajectories through primary care, especially for families at social risk. This article is based on 6 brief talks, each identified by theme and speaker, focusing on the original concept and rationale for early literacy promotion in pediatric primary care; ROR as an instrument for social justice in the context of brain development, toxic stress, and resilience; efforts to define critical elements of the intervention and strengthen them through training and engagement of both practicing clinicians and residents; a multistage collaborative research effort centering parent leaders across the ROR network in the design of the CONNECT Survey, a measure of the parent/caregiver-clinician relationship; and the crucial contribution of parent voice. Research on ROR has shown positive effects on parent reading and child vocabulary; more recent research, highlighting parent/caregiver voices, emphasizes the importance of modeling by clinicians and of the relationships between primary care clinicians and families.

items.title: Shared Clinical Decision-Making for Vaccines: Looking Backward and Ahead
Dupilumab in Pediatric Eosinophilic Esophagitis
items.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES Dupilumab is an approved biologic therapy for eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE); however, real-world pediatric data remain limited. The aim of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of dupilumab in children with EoE enrolled in the international European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (ESPGHAN)-funded pEEr registry, with a focus on combined remission, treatment deescalation, and predictors of sustained response. METHODS DU-PED is a multicenter, retrospective cohort study including children with confirmed EoE treated with dupilumab in routine clinical practice. The primary outcome was combined remission at 6 and 12 months, defined as simultaneous clinical (≥75% Pediatric Eosinophilic Esophagitis Symptom Score [PEESS] v2.0 reduction or symptom resolution), endoscopic (EoE Endoscopic Reference Score [EREFS] ≤2), and histologic remission (<15 eos/high-power field [HPF]). Secondary outcomes included longitudinal changes in disease domains, treatment deescalation, predictors of remission, and safety. Multivariable logistic regression and ROC analysis were performed. RESULTS A total of 109 patients from 22 centers were included (median age 16 years; 75% male). Combined remission was achieved in 53% at 6 months and 86% at 12 months. PEESS v2.0, EREFS, and peak eosinophil counts significantly improved over time (P < 0.001). At 12 months, 81% of patients were receiving dupilumab monotherapy, and 94% reduced concomitant EoE-directed therapy. Higher baseline proximal eosinophil density was independently associated with a lower likelihood of sustained combined remission at 12 months (odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.96–0.99). Dupilumab was well tolerated, with no treatment discontinuations. CONCLUSIONS In a large international registry-based pediatric cohort, dupilumab achieved high and durable rates of combined remission and enabled substantial treatment simplification, supporting its role as an effective long-term treatment strategy for pediatric EoE.

items.title: Racial and Ethnic Differences in Pediatric Perioperative Cardiac Arrest Survival
items.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE Perioperative cardiac arrest (POCA) is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Disparities in perioperative outcomes have been reported, but whether similar differences exist following pediatric POCA remains unclear. We evaluated racial and ethnic differences in 30-day mortality after pediatric POCA. METHOD Within the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program for Pediatrics (NSQIP-P) registry, we identified 2646 children under 18 who underwent inpatient, noncardiac surgery (2012─2024) and experienced POCA. Race and ethnicity were categorized as Hispanic, non-Hispanic Asian, non-Hispanic Black or African American, non-Hispanic white, or other. Crude and adjusted risk ratios for 30-day mortality following POCA were estimated. RESULTS Among 2646 children with POCA, 47.9% (n = 1268) were non-Hispanic white, 28.2% (n = 745) non-Hispanic Black, 4.0% (n = 106) non-Hispanic Asian, 16.2% (n = 430) Hispanic and 3.7% (n = 97) Other race. Overall, 30-day mortality was 32.9% (871/2646). Mortality was similar across racial or ethnic groups (P = .72). In adjusted analyses, mortality risk did not differ significantly for non-Hispanic Black (adjusted relative risks [aRR] 1.02, P = .80), Hispanic children (aRR 1.06, P = .43), or children of other race (aRR 1.02, P = .88) compared with non-Hispanic white children. Emergent surgery (aRR 1.62, P < .001) and preoperative inotrope use (aRR 1.41, P < .001) were independently associated with increased mortality. CONCLUSION We found no significant racial or ethnic differences in mortality risk following POCA among children undergoing inpatient surgery. Mortality was associated with clinical and perioperative factors, including emergent surgery and preoperative inotrope use. This suggests that efforts to identify drivers of disparities in pediatric postsurgical mortality must look beyond POCA outcomes alone.

items.title: Complications in Pediatric Cancer Patients With Staphylococcus aureus Bloodstream Infection
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infections (BSIs) can cause significant morbidity in children with cancer. Current guidelines recommend central venous catheter (CVC) removal, though the necessity remains uncertain. We assessed risk factors for complications among affected patients, focusing on impact of CVC removal vs salvage. METHODS This multicenter retrospective study includes pediatric oncology patients with S aureus BSIs from 2005 to 2022. The complication outcome period (72 hours to 6 months after initial positive culture) was divided into short-term (72 hours to 8 days) and late periods (8 days to 6 months). The composite primary outcome included occurrence of at least 1 major complication: recurrent BSIs, deep abscess/myositis, S aureus–related death, exit site infection, meningitis, endocarditis, or osteomyelitis. Multivariable logistic regression with propensity score weighting for CVC removal was performed. RESULTS Among 322 BSI episodes, 90.7% (n = 292/322) had a CVC at presentation; salvage was attempted in 55.5% (n = 162/292). The primary outcome was met in 21.2% (n = 62/292) of episodes with a CVC, more frequently in the CVC salvage (25.3%, n = 41/161) vs removal (16.2%, n = 21/130) group. CVC salvage was independently associated with the primary outcome (OR, 3.37; 95% CI, 2.08–5.61; P < .01) in short-term (OR, 21.8; 95% CI, 7.09–95.4) and late (OR, 1.83; 95% CI, 1.06–3.18) periods. Methicillin resistance, male sex, invasive infection at presentation, implanted ports, sepsis, and persistent blood culture positivity were also independently associated with the primary outcome. CONCLUSIONS CVC removal was associated with fewer short-term and late complications in pediatric cancer patients with S aureus BSIs, supporting recommendations for catheter removal in this population.

items.title: Middle Lobe Displacement Post Lobectomy in a Child With Congenital Pulmonary Airway Malformation
items.abstract: Congenital pulmonary airway malformations (CPAMs) are an important cause of structural lung disease in children and may remain undetected until later childhood. Although surgical resection is well established for symptomatic lesions, the long-term anatomical effects of lobectomy in pediatric patients remain incompletely understood. Postoperative changes in lung mechanics and lobar positioning can result in uncommon airway complications that are often under-recognized and diagnostically challenging. Obstruction of the right middle lobe (RML) bronchus due to postoperative lobar displacement is particularly rare, with reported cases originating from the adult surgical literature. We report a 9-year-old girl with mild persistent asthma who presented with an infected cystic lesion in the right upper lobe consistent with CPAM. She completed antimicrobial therapy and underwent right upper lobectomy, with pathology confirming type 1 CPAM. One month later, she developed a persistent cough refractory to optimized asthma treatment. Chest computed tomography (CT) demonstrated hyperinflation and poor visualization of the right upper and middle lobe bronchial orifices. Bronchoscopy identified RML bronchial obstruction, and fluoroscopy-guided bronchoscopy confirmed superior displacement of the RML with resultant bronchial kinking, likely related to postoperative lobar migration. Endobronchial stenting was unsuccessful, and further surgical intervention was not advised because of the anticipated risks of a second operation. Conservative management was pursued, resulting in modest symptomatic improvement, with the patient remaining clinically stable for 2 years. This case highlights a rare postoperative complication of CPAM resection in a child and emphasizes the need for heightened awareness, multidisciplinary evaluation, and pediatric-focused studies to guide management.

items.title: Penicillin Allergy Delabeling in Children
items.abstract: Nearly 10% of the global population has been labeled as having a penicillin allergy. Of those labeled, about 95% are not truly allergic, yet most do not receive any allergy evaluations. Patients with penicillin allergy labels are more likely to have worse clinical outcomes and incur higher health care costs, largely because they do not receive penicillin and other first-line β-lactam antibiotics for the treatment of infectious diseases. Consequently, the process of evaluating and removing inaccurate penicillin allergy labels—a process known as “delabeling”—has become increasingly supported by a growing body of evidence. Recently, penicillin allergy has garnered substantial public interest with the proposal of federal legislation to include evaluation of penicillin allergy during routine medical visits for Medicare patients. Although this moves delabeling into the generalist purview, most of the emphasis on penicillin allergies and delabeling has been on adult patients. Yet, penicillin allergy is a pressing issue for pediatrics, as most penicillin allergy labels are placed in childhood. Pediatric literature similarly demonstrates negative clinical and public health consequences of inaccurate penicillin allergy labels. Recent guidelines have strongly recommended a proactive effort to identify and delabel inaccurate penicillin allergies in children. To facilitate this process, simple delabeling procedures, such as direct oral challenge with amoxicillin, have been recommended for patients with low-risk allergy status, based on historical reaction verification, because of their safety and accuracy. These advancements are relevant to practicing pediatricians across specialties and practice locations.

items.title: Islamic Fatwa Guiding the Use of Pasteurized Donor Human Milk
items.abstract: Neonatologists noted hesitancy in Minnesota’s Muslim community to use pasteurized donor human milk, even when medically advised for premature and ill babies, due in part to religious concerns about milk kinship. To address these concerns and promote equitable health outcomes, we forged a coalition of partners including the Minnesota Islamic Council, Children’s Minnesota, M Health Fairview/University of Minnesota, Minnesota Milk Bank for Babies, Brighter Health Minnesota, and the Minnesota Breastfeeding Coalition. On Nov 16th, 2023, the Minnesota Islamic Council issued a fatwa, or a religious clarification, encouraging the use of pasteurized donor human milk for babies when a mother’s own milk is not available. The fatwa provides information on the health benefits of human milk for newborns, clarifies Islamic teachings, and encourages the use of donor human milk when indicated. This is believed to be the first fatwa regarding donor milk use in the United States, although there are precedents in other countries. We believe that this landmark decision, along with collaboratively developed patient and family education materials, will help clinicians across the country navigate conversations with Muslim families about pasteurized donor human milk in an empathetic and culturally sensitive manner, while simultaneously improving outcomes for babies and decreasing disparities. This effort also serves as an example to pediatricians interested in addressing specific religious or cultural concerns about an aspect of pediatric care in a community-centered manner.

items.title: Low-Level Pyuria and Antibiotic Prescribing for Suspected Urinary Tract Infection in Children
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE Our objective was to understand the impact of urinalysis results on clinician antibiotic prescribing for pediatric patients evaluated at ambulatory visits. We hypothesized that responses to low pyuria levels contribute disproportionately to overtreatment. METHODS This cross-sectional study combined electronic health record and abstracted symptom data from emergency department and urgent care visits to 4 Northern California settings. We sampled ambulatory visits by patients aged between 2 months and 17 years who underwent urinalysis between January 1, 2022, and December 31, 2023. We used multivariable logistic regression to assess relationships between urinalysis results, clinical covariates including age, and empiric antibiotic initiation. We estimated attributable impact of these relationships on overtreatment for patients in whom urinary tract infection (UTI) was excluded by culture criteria. We similarly estimated impact on treatment for those with culture-confirmed UTI. RESULTS Among 1150 patients with median age 6.3 years, 191 (16.6%) received antibiotics. Low pyuria levels (trace leukocyte esterase, 10-69 white blood cells [WBC]/mm,3 5-10 WBC/high-power field) were associated with antibiotic initiation with adjusted odds ratio 6.62 (95% CI 3.72–11.79) compared with no pyuria. The adjusted attributable fraction (aAF) for overtreatment at this level was 17.0% (95% CI 10.3%-23.2%), with aAF 1.8% (95% CI 1.1%-2.4%) for UTI treatment. Differential impacts on overtreatment and UTI treatment were consistent in age-stratified analyses. CONCLUSIONS To promote selective UTI treatment, clinicians should consider degree of pyuria in context with age, risk factors, symptoms, and other urinalysis results. Health system interventions should be designed to mitigate excess influence of low pyuria levels and promote integrated diagnostic assessments.

items.title: Facial Dysmorphism in Infants Following Combined Prenatal Exposure to Alcohol and Tobacco
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES Alcohol and smoking have well-established teratogenic effects; however, despite their frequent co-use during pregnancy, the combined impact on fetal development remains less understood. Facial dysmorphism is a sensitive marker of embryonic disruption. This study investigated whether concomitant prenatal exposure to alcohol and tobacco exerts synergistic effects on infant facial dysmorphism, facial size, and growth trajectories. METHODS This longitudinal study included 634 infants from a high-risk population in South Africa. Prenatal alcohol and smoking behaviors were assessed using a modified timeline follow-back interview at each visit, capturing frequency and quantity. Three-dimensional facial images were obtained at 1 month and 1 year postnatally. Infants were categorized into 5 exposure groups: control, continuous alcohol only, continuous smoking only, continuous coexposure, and continuous smoking with any alcohol. Group differences were evaluated using anthropometric measurements and dense surface modeling to assess facial dysmorphism, size, and growth trajectories. RESULTS Continuous prenatal coexposure to smoking and alcohol was associated with the greatest facial dysmorphism and reduced facial size compared to controls and single-exposure groups. Effects were largely sex specific, with stronger alterations in girls. Coexposure was also associated with ocular changes, including reduced palpebral fissure length and increased canthal index. Single exposures showed more limited effects, and facial growth trajectories were not significantly influenced by exposure. CONCLUSIONS Combined prenatal exposure to alcohol and tobacco is associated with greater facial dysmorphism than single exposures. These findings highlight the importance of interventions targeting alcohol and smoking cessation during pregnancy to reduce teratogenic risk.

items.title: Increasing Chlamydia/Gonorrhea Screening in Adolescents Across a Multisite Primary Care Network
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE To increase chlamydia and gonorrhea (CT/GC) screening among sexually active female adolescents in a large pediatric primary care network using a multifaceted quality improvement (QI) intervention, with secondary aims to increase male screening and case detection. METHODS From 2021 to 2025, we implemented a sequential QI intervention including Adolescent Health Questionnaire implementation, financial incentives, electronic health record (EHR) best practice advisories, and universal screening protocols across 33 practices. The primary outcome was CT/GC screening rates for sexually active female patients aged at least 15 years at well visits. Secondary outcomes included male screening rates and case detection rates. We evaluated outcomes using statistical process control and run charts. RESULTS During the study period, 136 241 adolescents aged 15–19 years received care across the network, with monthly well care visits increasing over time (average 1472-1681 visits/month). CT/GC screening rates for sexually active female patients increased from approximately 25% to 75%, with the most substantial improvements following universal opt-out protocols. Male testing rates similarly increased from approximately 20% to 75%. Monthly chlamydia case counts for female patients increased from approximately 8 cases/month to a peak of approximately 25 cases/month during the highest-volume testing period. For male patients, cases increased from approximately 4 to 16 monthly. Improvements occurred across demographic groups regardless of insurance type, race, or ethnicity. CONCLUSIONS A systematic, EHR-enabled QI intervention significantly improved adolescent CT/GC screening rates while increasing case detection. Universal opt-out screening protocols proved most effective in achieving comprehensive screening and identifying previously undiagnosed infections, demonstrating the clinical value of systematic CT/GC screening in pediatric primary care.

Hemodynamic Patterns Relative to Vasopressin Initiation and Subsequent Septic Shock Progression in Children: A Retrospective Cohort, 2020–2023
items.abstract: Objectives: To describe the hemodynamic patterns associated with starting vasopressin in children with septic shock and to compare the early patterns based on subsequent progression of shock. Design: Retrospective cohort (2020–2023) study. Setting: Single-center, tertiary PICU in Australia. Patients: Children younger than 18 years with septic shock. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Hemodynamic variables collected at 1-minute intervals during a 1-hour observation period after starting vasopressin infusion were reviewed and collated according to whether shock subsequently progressed in the following 5 hours. In a cohort of 30 children (median age, 9 yr [interquartile range, 2–14 yr]), eight had shock progression, which was defined by echocardiography, lactate, and use of extracorporeal support. Cases with subsequent shock progression, as opposedto not, had an associated higher Phoenix score (7 [7–8] vs. 6 [5–6]; p = 0.01). The vasopressin starting dose in the shock vs. nonshock progression groups was 0.03 U/kg/hr (0.02–0.06 U/kg/hr) vs. 0.02 U/kg/hr (0.02–0.04 U/kg/hr; p = 0.72). We failed to find an association between ventricular dysfunction at baseline and the shock progression group vs. no shock progression (4/6 vs. 7/18; mean difference, 28%; 95% CI, –16% to 71%; p = 0.36). In the shock progression group, earlier pulse pressure continued on a decreasing trajectory following vasopressin initiation, despite increasing systolic and diastolic blood pressures. In those without shock progression, pulse pressure increased marginally. The difference between groups in the median pulse pressures during the observation period was 7.5 mm Hg. Conclusions: In this hypothesis-generating, retrospective study of children with septic shock treated with vasopressin, subsequent shock progression was associated with early decreasing pulse pressure. Further studies are needed to test whether early changes in pulse pressure after starting vasopressin can be used as a potential marker of subsequent shock progression.

items.title: Efficacy of an Ultrasound Guided Intravenous Access Training Program in a Pediatric Cardiac Intensive Care Unit

Timing of the Adrenaline Administration in Witnessed Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Retrospective, National Cohort Study in Japan, Using a 2014–2020 Dataset
items.abstract: Objectives: We evaluated the association between the timing of initial adrenaline administration and outcomes in witnessed pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Design: A multicenter, retrospective cohort study addressing resuscitation time bias by performing a risk-set matching analysis using time-dependent propensity scores. Setting: Analysis of data from the Japanese Association for Acute Medicine OHCA (JAAM-OHCA) registry, which is a nationwide, multicenter, prospective collection of prehospital and in-hospital data involving Japanese patients with OHCA. Patients: Pediatric patients (< 18 yr) with witnessed OHCA who received adrenaline, during the period June 2014 to December 2020. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: We compared patients who received adrenaline in specific time intervals (1–10, 11–15, 16–20, 21–25, or 26–30 min) after first contact with emergency medical services with those who still had not received adrenaline during the same time. The primary and secondary outcomes were survival and favorable neurologic outcome at one month, defined as a Pediatric Cerebral Performance Category score of 1–3. We identified a total of 259 OHCA patients who had received adrenaline at 1–10, 11–15, 16–20, 21–25, 26–30, and 31 minutes or later; at each respective time point, there were 15, 39, 62, 55, 37, and 51 patients. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs for 1-month survival at each time group compared with patients at risk were: 1–10 minutes, RR, 2.94 (95% CI, 0.38–22.81); 11–15 minutes, RR, 0.97 (95% CI, 0.30–3.12); 16–20 minutes, RR, 1.00 (95% CI, 0.29–3.48); 21–25 minutes, RR, 1.35 (95% CI, 0.54–3.40); and 26–30 minutes, RR, 1.71 (95% CI, 0.27–10.78). We failed to identify an association between time interval and greater or lesser probability of survival or neurologic outcome. Conclusions: In the JAAM-OHCA registry, with pediatric data from 2014 to 2020, we failed to identify an association between earlier adrenaline administration and greater probability of 1-month survival or favorable neurologic outcomes.

items.title: Extubation Failure and Duration of Respiratory Support Postextubation in Children: Australian and New Zealand Multicenter, ICU Registry Data, 2014–2021
items.abstract: Objectives: To compare postextubation failure and duration of noninvasive respiratory support postextubation in children receiving continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC). Design: Retrospective cohort using the Australian and New Zealand Pediatric Intensive Care (ANZPIC) registry. Setting: Ten PICUs and 24 mixed adult/pediatric units. Patients: All children extubated between 2014 and 2021 who required noninvasive respiratory support. Interventions: None. Measurements: Postextubation failure rate requiring reintubation and duration of noninvasive respiratory support. Secondary outcomes were length of stay (LOS) in the PICU, time from extubation to discharge from the PICU, hospital LOS, and prevalence of death during hospital admission. Results: Of 31,910 extubation episodes in 23,930 children, 7,156 children received noninvasive respiratory support. Propensity matching yielded 1418 pairs for CPAP and HFNC. We failed to identify an association between postextubation failure and the use of CPAP vs. HFNC (107/1418 [7.6%] vs. 115/1418 [8.1%]; rate ratio, 0.93 [95% CI, 0.72–1.25]). There was an associated difference in median (interquartile range [IQR]) duration of postextubation respiratory support when CPAP was compared with HFNC, 72.0 hours (IQR, 30.5–72.0 hr) vs. 30.5 hours (IQR, 17.2–72.0 hr); median difference, 41.5 hours (95% CI, 37.7–45.2 hr). Median PICU LOS on CPAP vs. HFNC was 10.2 days (IQR, 5.1–20.9 d) vs. 7.1 days (IQR, 3.9–14.3 d); median difference, 2.2 days (95% CI, 1.6–2.8 d). Use of HFNC as opposed to CPAP was associated with shorter PICU LOS postextubation and hospital LOS. Last, we failed to identify an association between postextubation support and in-hospital mortality. Conclusions: In the ANZPIC registry, 2014–2021 dataset, we failed to identify an association between type of postextubation form of respiratory support and postextubation failure rate. However, being supported with CPAP as opposed to HFNC was associated with longer duration of postextubation respiratory support in the PICU.

items.title: Prevalence and Outcomes of Refeeding Syndrome in Critically Ill Children: A Retrospective Study in a Tertiary Care Setting
items.abstract: Objectives: To determine the prevalence and outcome of refeeding syndrome in critically ill children admitted to the PICU. Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting: Single PICU in a tertiary care university-affiliated hospital. Patients: Children of age 1 month to 18 years hospitalized in the PICU between January 2018 and December 2022 were included in this study. Intervention: None. Measurement and Main Results: We identified children with refeeding syndrome based on the 2020 guidelines established by the American Society for Parenteral and Enteral Nutrition. The outcomes measured included length of hospitalization, complications, and mortality rates. During the study period, a total of 404 children were admitted to the PICU, with 94 children (23.3%) classified as undernourished. Refeeding syndrome was diagnosed in 53 children (13.1%). Comorbidity with chronic neurologic conditions was prominently associated with greater adjusted odds of refeeding syndrome. An increase in BMI was associated with lower odds of developing refeeding syndrome. The median duration of hospital stay was significantly longer for children with refeeding syndrome compared with those without it. Conclusions: This study suggests that children at greater risk of developing refeeding syndrome were those with comorbid chronic neurologic conditions. Close monitoring of metabolic disturbances is crucial in the care of these patients.

items.title: Peripheral IV Catheter Longevity With Ultrasound Guidance in the PICU: Single-Center Retrospective Cohort, 2016–2018
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare associated outcomes between ultrasound-guided peripheral IV catheter (USGPIV) insertion and device longevity in critically ill children. DESIGN: Retrospective observational cohort study. SETTING: Tertiary medical-surgical pediatric PICU with cardiac patients. PATIENTS: Patients admitted to the PICU requiring peripheral vascular access between January 1, 2016, and October 1, 2018. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We identified patients who underwent USGPIV and landmark-guided peripheral IV catheters (LMGPIV) placed within 2 weeks of a USGPIV, and made comparisons between the procedures. There were 507 USGPIV and 292 LMGPIV placements. Of these, 334 USGPIV and 278 LMGPIV had longevity data. Log-rank analysis with median (interquartile range, IQR) data showed an associated greater catheter longevity in USGPIVs vs. LMGPIVs, respectively: 5 days (IQR, 2–9 d) vs. 3 days (IQR, 1–4 d), p value of less than 0.001. When restricted to either patients admitted with cardiac disease or those with known difficult vascular access, the association between USGPIVs and LMGPIVs and greater longevity remained, respectively: cardiac cases, 5 days (IQR, 2–9 d) vs. 3 days (IQR, 2–6 d); p = 0.038 and difficult access, 5 days (IQR, 2–9 d) vs. 2 days (IQR, 1–4 d), p value of less than 0.001. CONCLUSIONS: In this single-center experience of using USGPIV placement over 28 months (2016–2018), USGPIV placement was associated with greater catheter longevity. These findings suggest that USGPIV placement is potentially a means for improving PIV insertion and maintenance.

items.title: Lung Morphology Assessed by Ultrasound and Positive End-Expiratory Pressure During Mechanical Ventilation for Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure: Secondary Analysis of a Multicenter PICU Cohort From Spain and Portugal, 2020–2021
items.abstract: Objectives: In pediatric patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF), we aimed to determine whether positive end-expiratory pressure alignment with lung ultrasound (LUS) morphology was associated with shortened duration of mechanical ventilation. Design: Exploratory, secondary analysis of a prospective, multicenter cohort study carried out in 2020–2021. Setting: Twenty-five PICUs in Spain and Portugal. Patients: Children from 1 month to 18 years with AHRF undergoing invasive mechanical ventilation. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Data from lung morphology using a 12-zone LUS score between 12 and 48–72 hours after PICU admission were classified as focal or nonfocal. PEEP was considered “aligned with morphology” when greater than or equal to 10 cmH 2 O in cases with nonfocal lung morphology, and less than 10 cmH 2 O in cases with focal morphology. The primary outcome was ventilator-free days (VFDs) at 28 days, analyzed using competing-risk regression and reported as the subdistribution hazard ratio (SHR) with 95% CI. Among 160 children, 101 children (63.1%) had nonfocal morphology. PEEP was aligned with morphology in 84 of 160 children (52.5%). Aligned vs. nonaligned PEEP was associated with lower median (interquartile range [IQR]) driving pressure (13 cmH 2 O [IQR, 12–15 cmH 2 O] vs. 16 cmH 2 O [IQR, 15–18 cmH 2 O]; p < 0.001) and higher median VFDs (22 [IQR, 19–24] vs. 17 [IQR, 12–19]; p < 0.001). In adjusted competing-risk models, PEEP alignment with lung morphology was associated with greater cumulative probability of extubation at 28 days (SHR, 1.87 [95% CI, 1.30–2.69]). Stratified analyses confirmed the associated greater probability for both focal (SHR, 1.96 [95% CI, 1.20–3.21]) and nonfocal morphology cases (SHR, 2.23 [95% CI, 1.30–3.82]). Conclusions: In pediatric cases of AHRF, lung ultrasound-defined morphology identifies clinical and physiologic heterogeneity. PEEP aligned with LUS morphology was associated with greater cumulative probability of extubation at 28 days. These multicenter data from Spain and Portugal (2020–2021) suggest that LUS may be a potentially useful bedside tool for personalized mechanical ventilation in children.

items.title: Flow-to-Compliance Ratio as a Bedside Marker of Strain Rate in Pediatric Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: Analysis of Observational Cohort Data From 2022
items.abstract: Objectives: To determine the relationship between the ratio of peak inspiratory flow and respiratory system compliance (Flow/C RS ) and strain rate in cases of pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (PARDS). Design: Secondary analysis of observational cohort data collected in 2022. Setting: Single-center tertiary PICU in Chile. Patients: Thirty-one mechanically ventilated patients with early PARDS, 15 years or younger. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: All patients were supported with volume-controlled ventilation during measurement of pulmonary mechanics, including tidal volume (V t ), inspiratory time (Ti), inspiratory flow, and respiratory system compliance (C RS ). End-expiratory lung volume (EELV) was assessed using the nitrogen multiple-breath wash-in/washout method. Lung strain (V t /EELV), strain rate (lung strain/Ti, s –1 ), and the Flow/C RS ratio ([L·min –1 ]/[mL·cm H 2 O –1 ]) were calculated. The median (interquartile range [IQR]) strain rate was 0.56 s –1 (IQR, 0.40–0.73 s –1 ) and the median Flow/C RS ratio was 0.94 (IQR, 0.77–1.20). In the complete dataset, Flow/C RS ratio demonstrated a moderate positive correlation with measured strain rate (Spearman, ρ = 0.42; 95% CI, 0.08–0.67; p = 0.009). Linear regression confirmed a proportional relationship ( R 2 = 0.17; p = 0.022), but the Bland-Altman analysis showed systematic bias (mean difference, −0.43 ± 0.29 s −1 ) with 95% limits of agreement from −0.99 to 0.14 s −1 . Sensitivity analysis excluding three outliers (leaving data from 28 patients) demonstrated a stronger association (ρ = 0.63; p = 0.0018) and improved model fit ( R 2 = 0.41; p < 0.001), with the following equation: strain rate = 0.61·(Flow/C RS ) + 0.01. Conclusions: In PARDS, the Flow/C RS ratio is associated with measured strain rate but exhibits systematic bias, precluding direct interchangeability. Flow/C RS may serve as a pragmatic bedside marker reflecting deformation-velocity behavior. Prospective validation in larger and more heterogeneous cohorts is required.

items.title: Platelet Transfusion Practices in the PICUs: Multicenter, Observational Study, in Türkiye and Northern Cyprus, 2024
items.abstract: Objectives: We aimed to describe the use of platelet transfusions among critically ill children managed in Türkiye in late 2024. Secondarily, we sought to determine these practices in relation to the 2022 Transfusion and Anemia Expertise Initiative-Control/Avoidance of Bleeding (TAXI-CAB) recommendations for critically ill pediatric patients. Design: Prospective study (October–December 2024). Setting: 22 PICUs in Türkiye and Northern Cyprus. Patients: Patients of 1 month to 18 years who received at least one platelet transfusion in the PICU. Interventions: None Measurement and Main Results: Out of 2693 PICU admissions, 200 patients (7.4%) received 577 platelet transfusions. Of the transfusions, 383 of 577 transfusions (66.4%) were for prophylaxis, most frequently for isolated thrombocytopenia (194/383, 50.7%). Regarding the transfusion threshold for prophylaxis, in the 194 cases of isolated thrombocytopenia, the median (interquartile range [IQR]) pretransfusion platelet count was 24 (IQR, 16–38) × 10 9 /L, which differed from the TAXI-CAB consensus statement guidance of less than 10 × 10 9 /L. Platelet transfusion, as opposed to not, was associated with 20-fold greater odds of 28-day mortality ( p < 0.001), and among the 200 patients receiving platelets, multivariable analysis showed that lower pretransfusion platelet count, support with invasive mechanical ventilation, and hospital-acquired infections collectively accounted for 34% of the variance in model performance for classifying 28-day mortality. Conclusions: Our 2024 national, multicenter PICU study across Türkiye and Northern Cyprus shows that around two-thirds of transfusion episodes were for prophylaxis, and multivariable logistic regression modeling identified patient factors associated with greater odds of 28-day mortality. The median pretransfusion threshold for isolated thrombocytopenia was around 20 × 10 9 /L, which is double the less than 10 × 10 9 /L in the 2022 TAXI-CAB consensus statement. Given the heterogeneity of critically ill patients and practice environments, understanding the reasons behind these practices may help inform future research and consensus recommendations.

items.title: Online Abstract Translations
Pediatric Resident ICU Exposure Before and After the 2025 Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education Requirement Revision
Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Pediatric Lung Transplantation: An Extracorporeal Life Support Organization Registry Study, 2000–2022
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: We aimed to identify factors associated with greater odds of survival, as well as odds of successful lung transplantation (LTx) in pediatric patients undergoing extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) as a bridge-to-LTx (BTT) or supported with ECMO after LTx. DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study using the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) registry. SETTING: International ECMO centers submitting data to the ELSO registry. PATIENTS: Pediatric patients younger than 19 years old who were supported with ECMO before or after LTx between 2000 and 2022. INTERVENTIONS: None. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: We identified 194 pediatric patients who used ECMO as a bridge to LTx, and 63% survived to hospital discharge. We failed to identify an association between ECMO modality (i.e., venovenous vs. venoarterial) and odds of survival. Central venoarterial ECMO cannulation was associated with greater odds of receiving a LTx compared with not receiving a LTx (30/85 [35%] vs. 15/109 [14%]; odds ratio [OR], 3.42; 95% CI, 1.69–6.91). In the 109 patients who did not receive a LTx, ECMO cannulation delayed after hospital day 7 was associated with lower odds of survival (OR, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.15–0.75). ECMO post-LTx occurred in 95 patients, 62% received venoarterial or veno-venoarterial ECMO, and 48 of 95 (51%) survived to hospital discharge. In patients requiring ECMO post-LTx, cystic fibrosis was associated with lower odds of survival (OR, 0.31; 95% CI, 0.12–0.79) and pulmonary hypertension was associated with greater odds of survival (OR, 5.04; 95% CI, 1.68–15.1). CONCLUSIONS: Our data show that ECMO was used to support children as a BTT and for stabilization of postoperative LTx recipients. Early initiation of ECMO was associated with greater odds of survival in patients undergoing BTT who did not receive LTx. Further studies, including additional patients and focused LTx-related data, are needed to better characterize and delineate treatment options in this population.
