Efficacy and Safety of Ulinastatin in the Treatment of Patients with Sepsis: The ADJUST Trial
External validation of the SNAPP score for hepatocellular carcinoma recurrence after living donor liver transplantation
items.abstract: Binary morphologic criteria cannot capture biologic heterogeneity among living donor liver transplantation (LDLT) recipients. SNAPP score (tumor size, number, AFP, PIVKA-II, PET/CT) yields a graded recurrence-risk estimate but lacks independent validation. We externally validated SNAPP for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) recurrence after LDLT. SNAPP was applied without refitting in 230 LDLT recipients with HCC at 2 Korean centers and benchmarked against Milan, French-AFP, Metroticket 2.0, MoRAL, RETREAT, and 3 LDLT-derived selection systems (Kyoto, Medanta LDLT, and National Cancer Center Korea). Discrimination, calibration, Brier score, and reclassification were assessed using IPCW-weighted methods with bootstrap 95% CIs. Among 230 patients (median follow-up, 91.5 mo), 49 (21.3%) recurred. SNAPP achieved discrimination comparable to the best pretransplant tool, MoRAL (Harrell C-index, 0.756; 95% CI, 0.690–0.821), and exceeded Milan (0.503; Holm-adjusted p =0.01). Discrimination was numerically higher than Metroticket 2.0 (0.605) and 3 LDLT-derived systems (C-index difference, 0.10–0.15), but none of these differences survived correction for multiplicity (Holm-adjusted p =0.24). RETREAT, a posttransplant benchmark, reached 0.807. Calibration-in-the-large was −0.068; slope, 0.59 (95% CI, 0.43–0.77). Within Milan-eligible patients (n=217), SNAPP resolved a monotonic, ~5.9-fold gradient in 5-year cumulative recurrence (11.9%, 48.8%, 70.0%). Reclassification favored SNAPP over Milan, French-AFP, and Metroticket 2.0; the center-adjusted hazard ratio per point was 1.79 (95% CI, 1.51–2.14). SNAPP showed discrimination comparable to MoRAL and exceeded Milan, with numerically higher but not definitively superior discrimination compared with Metroticket 2.0, French-AFP, and 3 LDLT-specific selection systems, while resolving biologic heterogeneity within Milan-eligible candidates using only pretransplant variables. With near-zero calibration-in-the-large but a slope below unity, SNAPP supports risk stratification at listing, though individualized probability estimates require recalibration.

items.title: A tale of two cholangiopathies: Divergence, parity, and paradox

Differences in donation after circulatory determination of death (DCD) liver donor management—An international survey initiated by the International Liver Transplantation Society (ILTS), Society for the Advancement of Transplant Anesthesia (SATA), and Liver Intensive Care Group of Europe (LICAGE)
items.abstract: We conducted a survey to evaluate variability in determination of death and management of donation after circulatory determination of death (DCD) liver donors across different countries. In all, 153 centers from 17 countries were included (48.4% US, 51.6% non-US). Most reported using onset of hemodynamic instability, rather than withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy (WLST), as the beginning of the waiting time for decision-making related to organ acceptance (76.1% US vs. 47.1% non-US). Actual and maximum acceptable waiting times were comparable between groups (43.7 vs. 50.2 and 50.8 vs. 60.3 min, respectively), frequently exceeding limits defined by national policies. Onset of hemodynamic instability was most commonly defined using systolic blood pressure (SBP) alone (51.4% US vs. 31.6% non-US) or a combination of SBP and oxygen saturation (SpO 2 ) (41.6% US vs. 56.6% non-US). Less commonly, centers used SpO 2 (4.2% vs. 3.9%) or arrythymia alone (1.4% US vs. 0.0% non-US). Thresholds for SBP and SpO2 were similar between US and non-US centers (SBP 80 mm Hg; and 80% for both). Sedation and analgesia for donor comfort were used less frequently in US centers compared with non-US centers (27.8% vs. 48.1%, p =0.02). Decision-making regarding waiting time was more commonly performed by a multidisciplinary team outside the US (26.1% vs. 52.0%). Over half of US and non-US centers reported using machine perfusion in over 50% of DCD grafts (64.9% vs. 51.9%). When used, normothermic regional perfusion cannulation was more commonly initiated after declaration of death (71.6% US vs. 62.0% non-US). These findings demonstrate substantial variability in DCD donor management. Standardization of definitions and practices, particularly with regard to exclusion of hemodynamic stability period from warm ischemic time (WIT), may improve consistency in decision-making related to organ acceptance.

items.title: Benefits and risks of induction immunosuppression in pediatric autoimmune liver disease from SPLIT Registry
items.abstract: The optimal induction regimen for pediatric liver transplantation (LT) in patients with Autoimmune Liver Disease (AILD) is not well-defined. This study compared outcomes between corticosteroids only, anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG), and IL-2 receptor antagonists (IL2RA; Basiliximab/Daclizumab). A retrospective review of 445 pediatric LT recipients with AILD (Autoimmune hepatitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, or autoimmune sclerosing cholangitis) was conducted using the SPLIT database. Re-transplants were excluded. Primary outcomes included biopsy-confirmed rejection, culture-proven infection, graft loss, and mortality. Baseline demographics were comparable across groups. At 30 days post-LT, the IL2RA group demonstrated a significantly lower rate of biopsy-confirmed rejection (11.2%) compared to corticosteroids only (20.9%) and ATG (28%; p =0.05). Conversely, the ATG group experienced a significantly higher incidence of culture-proven infections between days 30–90 (42.9%) compared to corticosteroids only (10.2%) and IL2RA (17.9%; p =0.03). In multivariable-adjusted models, ATG induction was associated with a 10-fold higher risk of sub-acute culture-proven infection at 30–90 days (aOR=10.0, 95%CI: 1.4–71.8, p =0.02) compared to corticosteroids alone. However, neither ATG (aOR=0.47) nor IL-2RA (aOR=0.63) significantly altered the odds of early acute rejection at 0–30 days ( p >0.30). No significant differences were observed in graft loss, mortality, disease recurrence, or post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder up to five years post-transplant. In pediatric AILD, induction with IL2RA significantly reduces early acute rejection without increasing infection risks or compromising long-term graft and patient survival.

items.title: Letter to the Editor: A more urgent case for building the hybrid living and deceased donor liver transplant pathway
Serum ammonia improves early risk stratification beyond West Haven criteria in acute liver failure
items.abstract: The prognosis of patients with acute liver failure (ALF) presenting with low-grade hepatic encephalopathy (HE) defined by the West Haven criteria (WHC) is difficult to establish. We studied the association between HE severity, assessed by WHC and serum ammonia, and outcomes across different age groups. Retrospective analysis of the prospective multicentre United States ALF Study Group registry (2000–2016). Exposures were WHC and serum ammonia on day 1 after inclusion. Endpoints were transplant-free survival (TFS) and mortality due to cerebral events on day 21. Findings were validated in a different and more recent (2010–2023) European cohort. Among 1092 patients, the median age was 39 years and 526 (48.2%) had acetaminophen toxicity. On day 1, 968 (88.6%) patients were in the intensive care unit, and 669 (61.3%) were receiving any specific organ support (ventilation, vasopressors, or renal replacement therapy). TFS and cerebral mortality on day 21 were 45.2% and 6.3%, respectively. Patients with hyperammonemia (≥50 µmol/L) on day 1 had lower TFS on day 21 than others, both for WHC grades 1–2 (53.0% vs. 65.2%) and 3–4 (31.8% vs. 60.9%). Higher ammonia on day 1 was independently associated with lower TFS on day 21, irrespective of WHC grade (odds ratio of 0.958 per each 10 µmol/L increment). Ammonia on day 1 of ≥100 µmol/L showed a significant threshold effect for TFS or cerebral mortality on day 21. Patients <40 years had the highest probability of cerebral mortality on day 21. In ALF, serum ammonia may help to define HE and assess prognosis earlier, irrespective of WHC grade. Patients with early serum ammonia of ≥100 µmol/L require optimized monitoring and treatment.

items.title: The pre-transplant cystatin C-to-serum creatinine ratio is associated with key clinical outcomes following liver transplantation
Development and internal validation of the Laboratory-based Liver Frailty Index (Lab-LFI)—A prediction model for frailty in patients with cirrhosis
items.abstract: Frailty, as measured by the Liver Frailty Index (LFI), is a well-established predictor of outcomes in cirrhosis, but testing requires in-person encounters. We sought to develop a blood-based biomarker index that correlates with frailty. Seven serum/plasma analytes [myostatin, IL-6, growth differentiation factor-15 (GDF-15), testosterone, leucine-rich alpha-2 glycoprotein (LRG1), fetuin-A, and IGF-1] were measured by ELISA in 527 ambulatory cirrhosis patients. “Frail” was defined as LFI≥4.4. The cohort was split in half; the “Lab-LFI” was developed using LASSO regression in the training set and validated in the test set. Other machine learning methods [generalized additive model (GAM), Random Forest, and XGBoost] were considered to compare discrimination. Of 527 patients (median age 59, MELD 14), 114 (21.6%) were frail. All 7 biomarkers were associated with frailty. In the test set, Lab-LFI’s c -statistic was 0.80 (95% CI 0.74–0.87) for frailty. The GAM, random forest, and XGBoost approaches produced similar discrimination ( c -statistics 0.79–0.82); as such, the LASSO model was chosen for maximum interpretability. The addition of clinical variables to the LASSO model, including MELD labs and sex, did not improve discrimination ( c -statistic 0.79, 95% CI 0.72–0.85). Patients were stratified by Lab-LFI using a cutpoint maximizing the Youden index; after adjusting for MELD and liver disease etiology, the high-risk group had higher pre-transplant death/waitlist dropout (HR 1.77, 95% CI 1.17–2.68, p =0.007). We developed and internally validated the Lab-LFI, a frailty prediction model consisting of 7 laboratory-based biomarkers. Lab-LFI enables blood-based assessment of physical function, as MELD does with liver function.

items.title: Work-life chaos: Enhancing mental health during times of strife
items.abstract: The practice of medicine can be both be professionally fulfilling and inherently demanding. Physicians are often perceived as invincible, yet recurrent exposure to patient suffering, high-stakes decision-making, and institutional pressure can profoundly impact mental health. These challenges may be particularly pronounced in organ transplantation, where transplant teams navigate life-and-death decisions, complex longitudinal care, and the responsibility of stewarding scarce organs. Using narrative reflection, this article highlights the dialectic that is inherent in the culture of medicine but seldom discussed: the expectation that physicians not only “do well” by delivering high-quality care and also “be well” themselves. Personal experience with complicated grief, functional impairment, and subsequent recovery is discussed within broader literature indicating increased rates of depression, anxiety, and burnout among physicians compared to the general population. Barriers to seeking support, including stigma, unclear institutional pathways, and concerns over professional repercussions are outlined. Evidence-based interventions, including values exercises, physician-coaching, confidential support programs, and structured return to work policies are discussed as strategies to facilitate early identification of distress and foster sustainable recovery.

items.title: A randomized controlled trial of normothermic versus dual-hypothermic oxygenated ex-situ perfusion in DCD liver transplantation
items.abstract: DCD liver transplantation has expanded worldwide but remains associated with an increased risk of complications. Sequential use of normothermic regional perfusion (NRP) followed by ex-situ machine perfusion (MP) is increasingly adopted but the choice of MP technique remains controversial. This randomized controlled trial compares outcomes of dual-hypothermic oxygenated perfusion (D-HOPE) versus normothermic machine perfusion (NMP) following NRP in DCD liver transplantation. After NRP, 50 grafts (44 controlled and 6 uncontrolled DCD) were randomized 1:1 to D-HOPE or NMP using concealed allocation with sequentially numbered sealed envelopes. Ex-situ perfusion was not performed for additional assessment. The primary endpoint was 1-year incidence of serious adverse events (SAE), including graft or patient loss and biliary or vascular complications. Secondary endpoint included other perioperative outcomes. We have also performed an exploratory analysis to identify predictive factors of graft loss and SAE. No case of primary non-function or vascular complication occurred. One-year graft and patient survival were both 88% in the D-HOPE group and 100% in the NMP group ( p =0.07). One-year SAE rate was similar (16%vs.20%, p =0.31). Biliary leakage and postoperative dialysis rate were comparable between the two groups (16%vs.0%, p =0.12). Blood pH variation, lactate and IL-6 levels during NRP, perfusate lactate trend, portal flow, IL-6, IL-10 and TNF levels during D-HOPE and perfusate pH variations and IL-10 levels during NMP were related to graft loss. Conclusions: When applied after NRP, D-HOPE and NMP provide comparable mid-term clinical outcomes in DCD liver transplantation. Differences in specific complications may require individualized selection of ex-situ MP. The limited sample size and number of events preclude definitive conclusions regarding differences in individual complications or the relative efficacy of either ex-situ perfusion strategy. The observed differences in specific complications and exploratory associations with perfusion parameters warrant evaluation in larger prospective studies.

items.title: Reply: Day-7 thresholds in a moving target—separating small-for-size physiology from early allograft dysfunction in LDLT
Letter to the Editor: Day-7 thresholds in a moving target—separating small-for-size physiology from early allograft dysfunction in LDLT
AUD care is transplant care: Lessons from the LIFT clinic
Pre-transplant vulnerability and clinically consequential osteonecrosis after liver transplantation
items.abstract: Osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH) after liver transplantation (LT) frequently progresses to joint collapse and surgical intervention. Although corticosteroids have traditionally been implicated in its pathogenesis, their independent contribution under contemporary immunosuppressive protocols remains uncertain. We aimed to identify factors associated with clinically consequential ONFH, with particular attention to pre-transplant disease burden and systemic vulnerability. This retrospective cohort study included 1,836 adults who underwent first-time LT between 2000 and 2023. To minimize time-dependent bias, corticosteroid exposure was assessed as cumulative dose over a fixed 3-month post-transplant period and examined using risk-set percentile analysis and an adjusted Cox model. Additional candidate factors were screened using covariate-balancing approaches and evaluated in a full-cohort multivariable Cox model. ONFH developed in 64 patients (3.5%) at a mean of 5.86±4.58 years after LT, and 71.9% of affected patients subsequently underwent surgical intervention. Corticosteroid exposure was not significantly associated with ONFH after adjustment for baseline covariates ( p =0.47), and findings were consistent across analyses accounting for time-dependent bias. In contrast, other diagnoses including primary biliary cholangitis or Wilson disease (HR 4.21; 95% CI, 1.19–14.91; p =0.03) and preoperative enteral nutrition requirement (HR 2.98; 95% CI 1.03–8.64; p =0.04) were associated with increased risk. Cumulative smoking exposure ( p =0.08) and time-weighted average MELD score ( p =0.07) demonstrated suggestive associations with ONFH risk. Clinically consequential ONFH after LT may be influenced more by pre-transplant vulnerability and nutritional frailty than by corticosteroid exposure alone. These findings support a vulnerability-based framework for post-transplant ONFH and may help identify recipients who could benefit from heightened clinical awareness and timely diagnostic evaluation when compatible symptoms develop.

items.title: Letter To The Editor: Who should receive a graft for unresectable colorectal liver metastases? Lessons from real-world TransMet validation for living-donor programs
Reply: Who should receive a graft for unresectable colorectal liver metastases? Lessons from real-world TransMet validation for living-donor programs
Can robotic living donor hepatectomy be safely offered to all donors? evidence, experience, and program development
items.abstract: Robotic living donor hepatectomy (R-LDH) aims to improve the safety and experience of healthy donors by combining three-dimensional visualization, wristed instrumentation, precision, and stable ergonomics with the benefits of minimal access. This review article summarizes current evidence and offers a pragmatic approach for centers to transition from open to routine robotic donation. Available evidence from retrospective feasibility series, matched cohorts, multicenter analyses, and registry data suggests that R-LDH may reduce donor morbidity compared to open and some evidence of fewer recipient biliary complications, although current evidence remains heterogeneous and largely non-randomized. Available comparative data, including single-center and international registry analyses, suggest lower morbidity with the robotic approach than with laparoscopy, although these comparisons remain limited and would benefit from confirmation in prospective multicenter studies. Learning-curve studies and prospective series suggest that with standardized technique, simulation, and early proctorship, proficiency appears achievable within a limited number of cases, with reduced complications over time. A center-readiness structure focused on “People” (trained team), “Process” (protocolized pathways with explicit conversion criteria), “Platform” (reliable robot access, ICG, ERAS), and “Proof” (prospective audit and external validation) supports phased adoption from standard to complex anatomy. Persistent barriers include limited robotic platform access, scheduling constraints, heterogeneity in reporting, and incomplete cost data, though shorter hospital stay, less pain, and faster return to normal daily activities may partially or potentially offset procedural costs in high-volume programs. In appropriately prepared centers, routine consideration of R-LDH for eligible donors may represent a reasonable donor-centered strategy. Concrete steps are outlined that surgeons and hospital leaders can undertake to implement R-LDH safely, monitor outcomes, and improve equitable access.

items.title: Are we over-immunosuppressing liver transplant recipients?
AASLD AGA clinical Practice Guideline on management of primary biliary cholangitis
items.abstract: Background & Aims: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease associated with progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, liver transplantation, and premature mortality. Despite effective therapies, important challenges remain in the diagnosis and management of PBC, including identification of antimitochondrial antibody–negative disease, assessment of response to ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), risk stratification, treatment of patients with inadequate response, management of cholestatic pruritus, and prevention of recurrent disease after liver transplantation. The aim of this guideline was to develop evidence-based recommendations addressing these key areas of clinical care. Methods: The American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) and the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) convened a multidisciplinary panel to develop clinical practice recommendations for adults with PBC. Systematic reviews were performed for 6 prioritized clinical questions. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation framework was used to prioritize clinical outcomes and assess evidence, and its Evidence to Decision Framework was used to develop recommendations. Results: The guideline panel agreed on 6 recommendations. These recommendations address the use of PBC-specific antinuclear antibodies in antimitochondrial antibody–negative suspected PBC, UDCA as first-line therapy, liver stiffness measurement for prognostication, peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor agonists for patients with inadequate response or intolerance to UDCA, linerixibat for moderate to severe pruritus, and UDCA prophylaxis post-transplantation to reduce disease recurrence. The certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to very low. Conclusions: The guideline emphasizes early diagnosis, optimization of first-line therapy, risk-based treatment escalation, symptom management, and prevention of post-transplantation disease recurrence to improve patient outcomes and quality of life.

items.title: Two diseases, one trial: Designing integrated treatments for alcohol-associated hepatitis and alcohol use disorder
Apolipoproteins in HBV infection: ApoC1 links HBV entry, morphogenesis, and cholesterol homeostasis
Baveno VI criteria validation and development of a new non-invasive strategy for varices rule-out in patients with HCC (SAPHE-R: Stiffness, ALBI, Platelets, HEpatocellular carcinoma Rule)
items.abstract: Background and Aims: The accuracy of Baveno criteria for avoiding endoscopy in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is uncertain, and systematic upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (UGE) may not be necessary. We evaluated Baveno VI criteria performance in this population and developed an alternative non-invasive rule to exclude esophagogastric varices of any grade, rather than high-risk varices (HRV). Methods: Patients with BCLC 0-C HCC and compensated advanced chronic liver disease (cACLD) from the Italian Liver Cancer (ITA.LI.CA) database, with available liver stiffness measurement (LSM), UGE, and blood tests within 6 months of diagnosis, were included. Independent predictors of varices identified by logistic regression were combined through grid search to derive a rule-out strategy (SAPHE-R), validated by bootstrap resampling and in an independent cohort (Vienna). Results: The derivation cohort comprised 598 patients (age, 69 years; male sex, 75.3%; viral etiology, 69.3%; BCLC 0/A, 77.9%; ALBI 1, 54.2%; varices, 33.4%; HRV, 11.2%). Baveno VI criteria missed 8.5% of varices and 6.0% of HRV, sparing 31.1% of UGE. Independent predictors of varices were incorporated into SAPHE-R (LSM≤16 kPa, platelet count ≥160×10 9 /L, ALBI grade 1), which missed 4.0% of varices (HRV 3.0%, spared UGE 17.6%). In the validation cohort (n=149), SAPHE-R missed 4.8% of varices (HRV 3.1%, spared UGE 14.8%). Results remained consistent in sensitivity analyses. In an exploratory analysis, no HVPG-defined CSPH was observed among SAPHE-R rule-out patients (0/22). Conclusions: Baveno VI criteria showed suboptimal performance in patients with HCC and cACLD, whereas SAPHE-R provided a reliable non-invasive strategy to rule out varices, facilitating variceal risk assessment in patients with HCC.

items.title: Single-cell landscape of alcohol-related hepatitis reveals serum amyloid a hepatocytes as key drivers of disease pathogenesis
items.abstract: Background & Aims: Alcohol-related hepatitis (AH) is a severe form of alcohol-related liver disease (ALD). The cellular subpopulations that contribute to AH and dynamics remain poorly understood. This study aimed to identify key cellular subpopulations and their interactions in AH and explore key mechanisms contributing to disease pathogenesis. Approach & Results: Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed starting from liver biopsies from patients with AH, early-stage ALD, and healthy individuals. Immunofluorescence was used to validate protein expression of selected markers. Liver biopsy-derived organoids were generated and exposed to a conditioned medium recapitulating AH (AH-medium) to assess serum amyloid A (SAA) secretion by ELISA. Circulating SAA levels were measured in plasma samples obtained from patients at different stages of ALD. Our analysis revealed an atlas of several cell subpopulations of AH, including hepatocytes expressing SAA, scar-associated (SA) endothelial cells, Fibulin-3 + mesenchymal cells, SA-macrophages expressing MMP19, activated CD4+ and stressed/effector CD8+ T cell subsets, and hyperactivated neutrophils expressing FPR2. Cell-communication analysis predicted a strong SAA-FPR2 interaction between hepatocyte and neutrophil subpopulations in AH. We confirmed that AH-hepatocytes secreted SAA in organoid cultures after stimulation with AH-medium. We also found out that circulating SAA levels were elevated in AH and were associated with reduced survival. Conclusions: The SAA-FPR2 pathway emerges as a potential mediator of inflammation in AH, offering potential therapeutic targets for this severe disease. This study provides new insights into the cellular heterogeneity and dynamics in ALD progression, dissecting AH at a single-cell level.

items.title: Trends in the etiologies and outcomes of idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury in the united states: The DILIN prospective registry, 2004 to 2024
items.abstract: Background & Aims: Idiosyncratic drug-induced liver injury (DILI) is an infrequent cause of liver disease. The aim of this study is to report on temporal changes in the etiology and outcomes of idiosyncratic DILI in the United States DILIN Prospective study. Methods: The presenting clinical features and outcomes of consecutive high causality DILI cases followed for 6 months at multiple DILIN sites from 2004 to 2024 were compared over time and by suspect drug class, age, sex, and prior chronic liver disease (CLD) status. Results: Amongst the 1983 high causality cases, median age was 52 years, 59% were female, 54% had hepatocellular injury and antibiotics (41%) were the leading drug class. The median peak total bilirubin, INR and severity scores decreased significantly over time, as did the proportion of cases attributed to antimicrobials, including isoniazid and nitrofurantoin, and to central nervous system agents. In contrast, the proportion of herbal and dietary supplement (HDS) and antineoplastic drug cases (including checkpoint inhibitors), increased significantly. Patients with CLD had higher mortality compared to non-CLD patients. Pediatric patients presented more frequently with hepatocellular injury but had a lower overall and liver related mortality compared to adults. Oncology DILI patients had a 6-month mortality rate of 30% with most deaths attributed to non-liver related causes. Conclusions: Over the past 20 years, a decreasing proportion of DILI cases are attributed to antibiotics while an increasing proportion are attributed to HDS products and antineoplastics. Oncology patients and those > 65 years old have significantly higher overall and liver-related mortality.

items.title: A phase 2b/3 trial of saroglitazar in primary biliary cholangitis
items.abstract: Background: Saroglitazar, a dual PPAR alpha/gamma agonist, improved serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels in patients with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) in a phase 2a clinical trial. Methods: EPICS-III is a phase 2b/3 adaptive, double-blind, randomized controlled trial in patients with PBC who had an inadequate response to or were intolerant of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA). In phase 2b, 37 participants received placebo or saroglitazar magnesium 1 or 2 mg for 16 weeks. Saroglitazar magnesium 1 mg (0.97 mg of saroglitazar) was selected for phase 3, which randomized 148 patients to saroglitazar (n=97) or placebo (n=51) for 52 weeks. The primary endpoint was biochemical response at week 52, defined as ALP <1.67 x ULN with ≥15% reduction from baseline and total bilirubin below ULN; the key secondary endpoint was ALP normalization. Results: Baseline characteristics in the phase 3 efficacy population were comparable except for higher baseline ALP and other liver biochemistries in the saroglitazar group. Biochemical response was achieved in 56.7% versus 9.8% with placebo (difference, 48.0%; 95% CI, 35.3 to 60.8; p <0.001). Among participants with baseline ALP ≤3xULN, biochemical response rates were 79.0% versus 14.3%, and 83.1% versus 14.7% in the per-protocol analysis. ALP normalization occurred in 8.2% with saroglitazar versus 0% with placebo (difference, 8.5%; 95% CI, 2.9 to 14; p =0.016). Among participants with baseline 5-D Itch score ≥12, the week-24 treatment difference was −3.2 points (95% CI, −5.66 to −0.82) but was not maintained at week 52. Adverse events occurred in 81.1% with saroglitazar versus 90.5% with placebo, and serious adverse events occurred in 6.3% and 11.1%, respectively. Conclusion: Saroglitazar 0.97 mg significantly improved biochemical response and ALP normalization and was well tolerated over 52 weeks.

items.title: Phase 1b study of miricorilant in patients with presumed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH)
items.abstract: Background and Aims: Miricorilant, an oral nonsteroidal selective glucocorticoid receptor modulator, is being investigated as a therapy that modulates hepatic cortisol activity in patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). This phase 1b study evaluated miricorilant’s efficacy and safety. Approach and Results: Seventy patients with presumed MASH received oral miricorilant daily (30–150 mg) or intermittent (100–200 mg once, twice, or thrice weekly) dosing regimens for 12 or 24 weeks. Across dosing regimens, reductions in relative liver fat content (LFC) ranged from 10.1% to 76.6%. Improvements in MASH liver function markers and the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) score were observed across regimens. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAE) leading to drug interruption/discontinuation occurred in 12.9% of patients (n=9) each; most were due to aminotransferase elevations during an excessively rapid drop in LFC (up to 70.2% at week 6) and in patients receiving daily dosing. Intermittent dosing enabled more patients to complete 12 weeks of treatment without discontinuation due to TEAEs. Intermittent dosing with miricorilant 100 mg twice weekly had the best benefit-risk profile; this cohort demonstrated a mean LFC reduction of 28.2% at week 12, with a corresponding decline in liver enzymes (ALT, −3.8 U/L; AST, −6.0 U/L). Patients in this cohort also had numerical improvement in lipid profiles, glycemic markers, and fibrosis biomarkers. Conclusions: Intermittent miricorilant dosing of 100 mg twice weekly achieved meaningful reductions in LFC and improved liver health markers with a favorable safety profile. This regimen is being evaluated in the phase 2b MONARCH study (NCT06108219).

items.title: Government digital maturity and liver-related mortality: A multinational ecological study
A pivotal Phase 2 study of derazantinib for previously-treated, locally advanced or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma with FGFR2 aberrations: FIDES-01
items.abstract: Background & Aims: To evaluate safety and efficacy of FGFR1–3 kinase inhibitor derazantinib, in advanced intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) harboring FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements ( FGFR2 F ), mutations ( FGFR2 M ), or amplifications ( FGFR2 A ), previously treated with chemotherapy. Approach & Results: Open-label, non-controlled Phase 2 trial. Patients with advanced iCCA, ≥1 prior chemotherapy, and FGFR2 F (Substudy 1) or FGFR2 M /FGFR A (Substudy 2), received once-daily oral derazantinib 300 mg until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, consent withdrawal or investigator decision to stop. Efficacy was assessed by central radiology review using RECIST v1.1. Primary endpoints were objective response rate (ORR; Substudy 1) and 3-month progression-free survival (PFS3; Substudy 2). Other endpoints were PFS, ORR (Substudy 2), disease control rate (DCR), duration of response (DOR), and overall survival (OS). In Substudy 1, ORR and DCR were 22.3% (23/103 partial responses) and 75.7%, respectively; median (95% CI) PFS was 8.1 (5.5,8.3) months, DOR was 6.5 (4.6,9.2) months, and OS was 17.2 (12.5,22.4) months. In Substudy 2, PFS3 was 63% (27/43), ORR was 9.3% (3 partial, 1 complete response), DCR was 69.8%, and OS was 11.9 (8.4,15.9) months. There were no Grade 4 or 5 drug-related events. FGFR inhibitor class-specific toxicities included drug-related hyperphosphataemia (38%, Grade 3: 3%) and dry eye (36%). Nail disorders (10%, any grade or causality), stomatitis (5%), retinal events (5%), and palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia (1%) were infrequent. Conclusions: In previously chemotherapy treated, FGFR-inhibitor-naïve patients with iCCA harboring FGFR2 fusions, mutations, or amplifications, derazantinib showed clinically meaningful efficacy with durable objective responses, and a manageable safety profile.

items.title: Acute-on-chronic liver failure: A global multisociety consensus on definitions
items.firstAuthor: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)
items.abstract: The acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) multisociety harmonisation initiative represents a global collaborative effort to establish a unified, evidence-based framework for the definition, diagnosis, grading, and management of ACLF. Building on the strengths of existing regional definitions and integrating diverse international perspectives, this consensus provides a pragmatic, globally applicable foundation for clinical practice, research, and education. It also establishes a common framework for patient stratification, organ dysfunction and failure assessment, critical care management, liver transplantation, and the design of future phase II/III trials. Standardised, regulatory-aligned endpoints are expected to improve cross-study comparability, strengthen collaboration, and accelerate development of effective ACLF therapies.

items.title: MRI-based biomarkers for risk stratification and assessment of treatment response in Metabolic dysfunction-associated Steatotic liver disease
items.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects up to 38% of the population globally. Liver biopsy, the historical reference standard, is invasive, subject to sampling error and not scalable. MRI-based biomarkers provide non-invasive, quantitative whole liver assessment. MRI proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) is the most accurate noninvasive measure of steatosis (thresholds of 6.4%, 17.4% and 22.1% for grades ≥1, ≥2 and 3), and a ≥30% relative reduction is associated with histologic response. Liver stiffness by magnetic resonance elastography (MRE-LS) is the most accurate imaging biomarker for fibrosis: MRE-LS of 3.1-4.4 kPa corresponds to F2-F3 and ≥5 kPa to cirrhosis, and each 1-kPa increase is associated with a 43% higher risk of hepatic decompensation. Iron-corrected T1 is a sensitive but nonspecific marker of disease activity whose prognostic value requires further study. Composite scores, MAST, MEFIB, and MASH Resolution Index, combine imaging and blood tests for advanced fibrosis diagnosis and response assessment. MRE is cost-effective compared with vibration-controlled transient elastography for detecting advanced fibrosis. Artificial intelligence may broaden access by automating analysis and enabling PDFF from routine MRI. We review the evidence supporting these biomarkers for diagnosis, prognosis and regulatory use, and their role in clinical trials and in treatment decisions for approved MASH therapies.

items.title: Introducing Michael Ronan Lucey, MD, the 78th President of AASLD
Elafibranor for primary biliary cholangitis at ALP below 1.67 × ULN: Progress toward a goal, no evidence yet of arrival
2026 Late Breaking Abstracts

Treatment with elafibranor to normalize alkaline phosphatase in patients with primary biliary cholangitis and incomplete response to ursodeoxycholic acid: Results from the phase III randomized controlled ELSPIRE trial
items.abstract: Background & Aims: Definitions of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) treatment response commonly include alkaline phosphatase (ALP) <1.67× upper limit of normal (ULN). However, ALP >ULN is associated with active disease and reduced transplant-free survival, whereas ALP normalization is associated with better complication-free survival. Elafibranor, a peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR)-α/δ agonist, has been shown to be effective and well-tolerated as a second-line treatment in patients with PBC and ALP ≥1.67x ULN. We report phase III ELSPIRE trial results, evaluating the effect of one year of elafibranor treatment on ALP normalization (ALP ≤ULN; ≤120 U/L) in patients with PBC and ALP >1–<1.67× ULN after incomplete response/intolerance to ursodeoxycholic acid. Approach & Results: In ELSPIRE, 92 patients were randomized, double-blind, 2:1 to elafibranor 80 mg (n=62) or placebo (n=30) for 52 weeks, stratified by ALP at randomization (>1–≤1.33× ULN vs. >1.33–<1.67× ULN). At Week 52, 85.3% of patients receiving elafibranor achieved the primary endpoint of ALP normalization, versus 23.3% receiving placebo (treatment difference: 62.0%; 95% CI: 44.3, 79.7; p <0.0001). Least squares mean percentage change from baseline in ALP at Week 52 was –36.5% with elafibranor versus –4.2% with placebo ( p <0.0001). A greater proportion of patients receiving elafibranor versus placebo achieved ALP normalization with ≥15% reduction from baseline and complete biochemical response (normal ALP, total bilirubin, transaminases, albumin, and INR). Elafibranor was well tolerated; no new safety signals were observed. Conclusions: These results support elafibranor as second-line treatment with UDCA for patients with PBC and ALP >1–<1.67× ULN, with ALP normalization as an achievable treatment goal.

items.title: AASLD EXPO: Diagnosis and management of hepatitis delta virus (HDV) infection
items.abstract: Background: HDV infection represents a rare co-infection or super-infection among persons with HBV infection and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality due to an increased risk of liver events such as hepatic decompensation and HCC. Methods: The Expert Practice Opinion (EXPO) document was developed by subject matter experts and commissioned by the AASLD Practice Guidelines Committee to provide timely guidance on the screening, diagnosis, and management of HDV infection. Writing group members performed a targeted literature review and generated EXPO statements which were agreed upon by group consensus. Results: All individuals who are HBsAg positive should be tested at least once for HDV infection with HDV antibody. HDV antibody positive individuals should undergo HDV RNA testing to confirm active infection. All individuals with chronic HDV should undergo further evaluation including non-invasive fibrosis testing, preferably with elastography. Lab monitoring and HCC surveillance imaging is suggested every 6 months. All adults with chronic HDV viremia and compensated liver disease should be considered candidates for HDV therapy with bulevirtide for chronic virologic suppression, or alternatively bulevirtide plus peg-IFN alfa-2a for individuals without contraindications to peg-IFN and who desire a finite duration regimen. Considerations for patient selection, treatment regimen, monitoring, assessment of response, and care of patients in special populations are summarized in the document. Conclusions: All HBsAg positive individuals should be screened for HDV. All adults with chronic HDV and compensated liver disease are candidates for HDV therapy. Recent advances in HDV treatment offer hope for meaningful improvement in clinical outcomes.

items.title: ATTEST 2027: A Framework for AI Transparency Tiered by Evidentiary Stakes
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is now being used across scientific research workflows, from data extraction and code generation to literature synthesis and manuscript drafting. Scientific journals and professional organizations agree that authors should disclose AI assistance. But disclosure that treats all AI use equally with a single generic declaration reveals little about the nature of AI’s influence on evidence generation. Polishing grammar carries a different risk than extracting outcomes from clinical notes, classifying pathology, or making causal inference. We propose ATTEST ( A I T ransparency T iered by E videntiary St akes), a framework that evaluates AI assistance by its consequences. ATTEST classifies AI use into eight broad categories of functions, each scored at one of four risk tiers (Low, Medium, High, Very High). The framework is operationalized by a declaration checklist that authors complete at submission. Within this tiered system, we propose minimum reporting standards by function, cross-cutting requirements, and obligations for reviewers and editors. The goal is to make AI’s role in evidence generation transparent to readers, reviewers, and editors so they can evaluate the integrity of scientific findings.

items.title: What’s new in point-of-care lung ultrasound: reading the new recommendations
Promoting equity, diversity and inclusion in intensive Care: a position paper of the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine
items.firstAuthor: The ESICM Diversity and Inclusion Group

items.title: Perceived inappropriateness of care among ICU clinicians is associated with burnout and intention to leave the job
Principles of drug dosing for obese patients in the intensive care unit
items.abstract: Purpose The increasing prevalence of severe obesity in intensive care unit (ICU) patients has led to several challenges with medication dosing. Doses listed in product labels or tertiary references typically do not account for the pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic variability encountered with obesity, leading to the potential for treatment failure or an adverse effect. The purpose of this review is to provide guidance for ICU clinicians when crafting pharmacotherapy regimens in critically ill patients with extreme obesity. Methods A literature search was performed to identify relevant articles pertaining to the pharmacokinetics or pharmacodynamics of medications in obese patients. Articles describing both general treatment principles and medication specific assessments were retrieved. Bibliographies were searched for additional publications. Results Evidence guiding medication use in critically ill obese patients is limited by the small number of patients with more extreme forms of obesity, the lack of clinical outcome measurements, and the few studies that are specific to the ICU. Obesity-related alterations in pharmacokinetic parameters, such as apparent volume of distribution and drug clearance, may hinder attainment of pharmacodynamic targets. Individualized dosing strategies are essential to optimize therapeutic outcomes. This review provides dosing recommendations for selected ICU medications and proposes a practical framework to guide medication dosing decisions in this patient population. Conclusion Drug dosing in critically ill obese patients should be individualized by assessing pharmacokinetic variability and whether pharmacodynamic goals can be achieved. Selecting the correct weight for weight-based calculations or dose for fixed regimens is paramount for achieving these goals. Consultation with a clinical pharmacist may be beneficial.

Phenotyping ARDS: A pragmatic path forward with the POLARIS international cohort
Restoring patients’ voice in intensive care: augmentative and alternative communication for human-centred care
Beyond avoiding failure: the proactive and beneficial role of appropriate antimicrobial therapy in the ICU
Physiology-guided ventilation as an equity intervention: from kilograms to compliance
European Society of Intensive Care Medicine consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the intensive care unit
items.abstract: A human-centred partnership in the intensive care unit (ICU) aims to integrate person-centred care, communication, emotional support, equity, and collaboration into ICU environments. The European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) developed a consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the ICU following a systematic, multi-phase, evidence-informed methodology incorporating the views of ICU professionals, academics, and patient and family representatives. This international multidisciplinary panel of 46 members conducted rapid reviews addressing 20 Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcomes (PICO) questions across six domains: person-centred care; communication and transparency; emotional well-being; equity, diversity, and inclusion; ICU environment; technology and innovation. Based on the evidence synthesis, 53 draft statements were developed and evaluated through a two-round eDelphi study. The final set of statements was discussed and ratified at an expert consensus meeting with the initial panel of experts and with patients and family representatives. A total of 201 international stakeholders participated in round 1 and 149 in round 2. Members of the expert consensus meeting ultimately endorsed 43 consensus statements. Key recommendations supported flexible family visitation, structured interdisciplinary communication, empathy-based staff training, psychological support for patients and ICU professionals, culturally responsive care, environmental interventions to improve sleep and reduce delirium, and the integration of digital supported technologies. The consensus statement on human-centred partnership in the ICU provides a comprehensive framework for clinicians with evidence-informed directions to deliver high-quality practice across diverse ICU settings. By prioritising person-centred care, communication, inclusivity, and well-being alongside responsible technological innovation, the experiences and outcomes of patients, families, and ICU professionals may improve.

items.title: Heat stroke presenting with choreiform dyskinesias: an unusual MRI pattern
ARDS at 60: beyond lung protection to lung repair
Optimizing post-extubation respiratory support in high-risk patients
What do the findings of compartmentalised sub-phenotypes in lungs of patients with pneumonia mean for critical care?
Ventilator-associated pneumonia after traumatic brain injury: a timing-sensitive ecological framework of neuroimmune–pulmonary vulnerability
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is frequent after traumatic brain injury (TBI), but its biological meaning and outcome impact remain incompletely defined. Traditional models emphasise mechanical ventilation, aspiration, colonisation, endotracheal tube biofilm, and hospital pathogens. These mechanisms remain essential, but they do not fully explain the early clustering, heterogeneous susceptibility, changing bacteriology, and variable mortality effect observed after TBI. MAIN TEXT: Severe brain injury creates an early vulnerable host state through impaired consciousness and airway protection, neuroimmune dysregulation, autonomic and endocrine activation, altered pulmonary immune surveillance, and, in many patients, extracranial trauma, shock, transfusion, or thoracic injury. These processes interact with ventilation, antibiotic pressure, and rapid respiratory microbiome disruption. Early VAP may reflect abrupt loss of control after injury and intubation, whereas late VAP may reflect persistent or secondary failure driven by biofilm maturation, antibiotic selection, multidrug-resistant pathogens, and intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired immune dysfunction. Clinically, VAP consistently prolongs ventilation, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and resource use, while its independent effect on mortality is phenotype- and context-dependent. CONCLUSIONS: This model proposes a timing-sensitive ecological framework in which established mechanisms may converge early and with particular clinical intensity after severe TBI, creating a vulnerable host-microbe state that may lower the threshold for clinically apparent infection. Future studies should distinguish isolated TBI from polytrauma, compare TBI with other acute brain injuries and non-neurological ventilated populations, and incorporate dynamic immune, microbial, and trajectory-based outcomes. HIGHLIGHTS: VAP after TBI should be viewed as a timing-sensitive interaction between ventilator exposure and early host vulnerability, not as a distinct disease entity or as a pneumonia pathway unique to traumatic brain injury. The TBI-focused contribution lies in the early convergence of otherwise non-unique mechanisms: impaired airway control, aspiration risk, neuroimmune-endocrine activation, treatment exposure, dysbiosis, and extracranial injury burden, rather than in any single TBI-specific mechanism. Isolated TBI and TBI with polytrauma are biologically different phenotypes and should be separated in future studies. Early and late VAP may represent different phases of loss of pulmonary host-microbe containment; this distinction is probabilistic rather than TBI-specific in itself and requires validation in TBI-stratified cohorts. Mortality remains clinically relevant but context-dependent; VAP more consistently modifies recovery trajectory, ventilator dependence, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and possibly neurological recovery.

items.title: Family suffering after critical illness: understanding buffers and stressors
Diagnosis: the forgotten ICU procedure
Immunological signatures of sepsis in abdominal solid organ transplant recipients: A multilayer and multicentric prospective cohort study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction resulting from a dysregulated host response to infection. Patients with prior abdominal solid organ transplantation (SOT) are highly susceptible to infection due to chronic immunosuppression, yet exhibit improved survival once sepsis occurs. The underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. METHODS: We conducted a post hoc analysis within a prospective multicenter cohort of septic patients (SepsisDataNet.NRW; n = 538). Clinical outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression. Immune profiling included serum cytokines, flow cytometric immunophenotyping, plasma proteomics, and intracellular signaling using proximity ligation assays (PLA) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). To reduce clinical confounding, complementary exploratory analyses were performed in a non-septic kidney transplant cohort (e:KID). RESULTS: SOT patients demonstrated improved 30-day survival compared with non-SOT patients (84% vs. 66%; adjusted HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.26-0.95). Cytokine analysis revealed lower IL-6 and TNF-α levels alongside higher IL-18 concentrations, indicating an altered inflammatory profile. Flow cytometry showed reductions in adaptive immune cells but relatively preserved innate immune function, reflected by higher monocytic HLA-DR expression. Proteomics identified enrichment of innate immune, complement, and lipid metabolic response networks. PLA-based cellular analyses revealed increased GLUT1 expression and enhanced TFAM/TFB2M interaction in SOT patients, indicating a distinct immunometabolic marker profile. In e:KID patients paired serum metabolomics demonstrated higher glucose and lower lactate concentrations 12 months after transplantation, accompanied by broader alterations in lipid and branched-chain amino acid profiles. CONCLUSION: In patients with sepsis, abdominal SOT is associated with significant better survival than in non-SOT patients. Septic abdominal SOT patients display a distinct immune phenotype characterized by attenuated systemic inflammation, relative preservation of selected innate immune readouts, and alterations in immunometabolic markers.

items.title: Sodium bicarbonate therapy for metabolic acidosis in critically ill patients: a Bayesian systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
items.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate the effects of sodium bicarbonate therapy on mortality and renal outcomes in critically ill adults with metabolic acidosis. METHODS: We performed a systematic review and Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing intravenous sodium bicarbonate with placebo or usual care in adult intensive care unit patients with metabolic acidosis. MEDLINE, Embase and CENTRAL were searched from inception to December 2025, with an updated search on 2 April 2026. The primary outcome was short-term all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included renal replacement therapy (RRT) initiation, 90-day mortality, RRT-free days, vasopressor-free days, intensive care unit and hospital length of stay and adverse events. RESULTS: Four RCTs including 1544 patients were analysed. Sodium bicarbonate did not show a clear short-term mortality benefit (RR 0.94, 95% CrI 0.73-1.22), with a posterior probability of benefit of 72.1%. For RRT initiation, sodium bicarbonate was associated with a lower risk (RR 0.74, 95% CrI 0.59-0.98), with a posterior probability of benefit of 97.2%. Effects on other outcomes were small or imprecise, and no consistent safety signal was identified. CONCLUSION: Current randomised evidence does not demonstrate a clear survival benefit from sodium bicarbonate therapy in critically ill adults with metabolic acidosis, but suggests a high probability of reducing RRT initiation. Further trials should define the patients most likely to benefit. PROSPERO registration: CRD420251246519.

items.title: Establishing curriculum priorities for intensive care recovery education: an international Delphi study
items.abstract: PURPOSE: To effectively support recovery, intensive care unit (ICU) clinicians require training to identify patients at risk of post-intensive care syndrome and implement interventions during and after ICU admission. This study aimed to identify and prioritise curriculum topics for educating interprofessional ICU clinicians on evidence-based ICU recovery care across the continuum of critical illness. METHODS: A two-round e-Delphi study followed by a structured consensus meeting endorsed by the European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM) was conducted. A steering committee generated an initial list of curriculum topics. In round 1, participants rated topic importance (9-point Likert scale) and suggested additional topics. In round 2, they rated newly identified topics and ranked priorities. Topics reaching consensus (≥70% rating as critical [7-9]; ≤15% rating as not important [1-3]) were discussed during the final consensus meeting. RESULTS: Participants' mean age was 43.5 (±10.5) years and they were predominantly female (n = 90, 66.7%). Priority topics included early mobilisation during ICU admission, post-intensive care syndrome, delirium prevention and management, implementation of the ABCDEF bundle, and cognitive support and rehabilitation. The final set of learning modules for a future curriculum was established. CONCLUSION: Priority topics and learning modules for an expert-developed curriculum framework for ICU recovery were established with interprofessional ICU clinicians through a structured international consensus process with moderate levels of participant retention between the two Delphi rounds and full consensus agreement among experts. This framework may support in delivering recovery-focused care across the continuum of critical illness.

Is a norepinephrine dose threshold already too late for adjunctive vasopressin initiation?

Individualized treatment effects of high flow nasal oxygen in immunocompromised patients
items.abstract: Rationale High flow nasal oxygen (HFNO) has become a common first-line practice for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (ARF). In immunocompromised patients, ARF is the leading cause of ICU admission, yet a randomized trial found no overall benefit of HFNO in this population. Objectives To assess whether baseline characteristics influence HFNO's effectiveness in preventing invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) in immunocompromised patients with ARF. Methods A causal forest machine-learning algorithm was derived in the HIGH trial (776 patients randomized to HFNO or conventional oxygen) to predict the HFNO effects on day-28 IMV incidence. Patients with a "do-not-intubate" order (n = 72) were excluded. Model performance was validated through 500 bootstrap iterations and patients were categorized into terciles based on predicted HFNO benefit. Transportability of the model was assessed in an independent observational cohort (818 patients). Main results Among the 704 participants, HFNO's average effect on day-28 IMV was not significant. However, substantial heterogeneity in treatment responses was identified (predicted benefit: from 20.2% [IQR 15.5%-23.9%] absolute IMV risk reduction with HFNO to 7.4% risk reduction [2.9%-11.2%] with conventional oxygen). Patients with the highest predicted benefit were older, more frequently solid organ transplant recipients, less neutropenic, more severely hypoxemic/tachycardic, but with lower non-respiratory sequential organ failure assessment (SOFA) scores. In this subgroup, HFNO was associated with a significant lower incidence of IMV. In the observational cohort, the benefit-ranking performance was preserved, although absolute effect estimates were less calibrated. Conclusions These results suggest HFNO might benefit specific immunocompromised patients with ARF. Further prospective studies are needed to validate these findings.
